ipso habitantis, prophete, apostoli, angeli, Dei, cum antea terra et cinis esset. Quod propter operationis excellentiam multa nomina habet haec agendi ratio.
99. Propterea multis et variis et gloriosis nominibus eam celebraverunt divini Patres. Viam doctam appellaverunt, laude dignam actionem et ingeniosam contemplationem, orationem omni latitudini praestantem, mentis vigilantiam, spirituale opus, futuri saeculi opus; angelicam vitam, cœlestem agendi rationem, divinam conversationem, regionem viventium, mysticam intuitionem, spiritualem mensam, divinum paradisum, cœlum, cœlestem regiam, Dei regnum, tenebras supra lumen, vitam in Christo absconditam, Dei supernaturalem visionem, et his similia nomina; quos divinos Patres, nos qui luto ac terra formati, cum malis et impuris cogitationibus verbisque et operibus vivimus, sequentes, tuas preces, dilectissime, adimplere ardenter statuimus; sane quidem, ut postulasti, et supra nostram inmensuram dicere non dubitavimus, propter tui dilectionem, et propter Patrum mandatum. Hujus angelicae vitae dux, ipsa est Verbi ac Filii Dei nova et ineffabilis providentia et incarnatio, ingeniti Patris beneplacitum, et cooperatio sancti Spiritus.
ETHICON.
Quod cum Dei auxilio et gratia oportet nos pro viribus festinare et pugnare, ut digni habeamur jam nunc, tanquam ex pignore his supernaturalibus et maximis donis, neque pro, ter parram malen tiam hac, eheu! amittamus; quod utinam non accidat.
100. Quoniam igitur, dilectissimi, tot ac tanta nobis bona proponuntur, non modo in spe et promissionibus futuro tempore adimplendis, sed re ac veritate, festinemus, resistamus, dum tempus habemus, curramus, pugnemus, ut his et nos, parva et opportuna cura ac brevi labore, maximam autem partem Dei gratia, digni efficiatur. « Non enim sunt condignae passiones hujus temporis ad futuram gloriam quae revelabitur in nobis »*, ut ait divinus ille praeco Paulus, quem audire debemus. Imo vero jam inde festinantes inviemus, ex hoc tempore, tanquam primitias ac pignus. Si enim qui in regias cognationes et in regium consortium ex humili fortuna adoptantur nihil non faciunt et opere et voce et cogitatione, et postquam id fastigium assecuti sunt, vitam ipsam saepius contemnunt pro istiusmodi gloria et honore, tam caduco ac temporaneo, ad perniciem interdum omnino, non ad utilitatem vergente, quanto magis oportet nos eniti et festinare, qui ad communionem ac nuptias et conjunctionem Dei invitamur, omnium regum regis et Creatoris, et solius incorruptibilis ac in aeternum permanentis, suisque gloriam et bo-


[811] {#pg.147.811}
norem præbentis inustrem ac stabilem; neque id solummodo, sed potestatem accepimus filios Dei fieri. « Quotquot eum receperunt, inquit, dedit eis potestatem filios Dei fieri, iis qui credunt in nomine ejus * ». Dat potestatem, non tyrannice trahit aut contra nostrum propositum cogit; semper enim tyrannis eum qui opprimitur contra oppressorem armat, ut malum malo curetur. Hoc modo honorat præcipuam nostræ libertatis dignitatem, ita ut bonum fiat omnino Dei operantis benevolentia et gratia; nostræ tamen voluntatis et curæ actus sit. Et ille quidem quanquam Deus et Dominus, quidquid ipsi faciendum erat, fecit; omnes enim similiter condidit, et pro omnibus mortuus est, ut æqualiter omnes salvaret. Nobis autem relicta est libertas accedendi, credendi, amicitiam jungendi, cum timore et ardore et charitate Domino illi misericordi serviendi qui nos vere ac sollicite dilexit; ita ut pro nobis libenter mortem voluerit subire, mortem vero probrosam, ut nos a diaboli, antiqui hostis, tyrannide liberaret, et cum Patre et Deo uniret; et hæredes quidem Dei, cohæredes autem sui efficeret; quod mirabilius et beatius est. Negitur parva ac brevi indolentia, et incuria, et falsa lætitia nos indignos efficiamus tantis bonis ac mercedibus et gaudiis; sed nihil non faciamus, nihil non operemur; neque ipsi vitæ nostræ pro illo pareamus, quoniam et ipse propter nos, id cum esset Deus, facere non dubitavit, ut sic his prorsus et omnibus donis coronisque digni efficiamur. Quæ utinam nos omnes accipiamus, benevolentia et gratia optimi illius ac misericordis Domini ac Dei et Salvatoris nostri Jesu Christi, qui adeo semetipsum propter nos humiliavit, ac qui se humiliantibus supernaturalem et vivificam suam gratiam ex tunc efficaciter abundanterque concedit; quoniam illi debetur omnis gloria et honor et adoratio cum ingenito et purissimo ipsius Patre, et coæterno et sanctissimo et optimo et vivifico ipsius Spiritu, nunc et semper et in sæcula sæculorum. Amen. quæ et nunc ὐπὲρ ἡμῶν ἐνεργῶς πλουσίως ἐπιδαψιλεύοντος· ὅτι αὐτῷ πρέπει πᾶσα ἡ δόξα, καὶ ἡ τιμή, καὶ ἡ προσκύνησις, ἅμα τῷ ἀνάρχῳ καὶ ἀχράντῳ αὐτοῦ Πατρί· καὶ τῷ συναΐδίῳ, καὶ παναγίῳ, καὶ ἀγαθῷ, καὶ ζωοποιῷ αὐτοῦ Πνεύματι· νῦν καὶ ἀεί, καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Ἀμήν.

καὶ Δημιουργοῦ, καὶ μένου ἀφθάρτου καὶ εἰσαεὶ διαμένοντος, καὶ δόξαν καὶ τιμὴν παρέχοντος· τοῖς οἰκείοις, εὐκλεᾶ καὶ μόνιμον· καὶ οὐ μόνον τοῦτο δὲ, ἀλλὰ γε καὶ ἐξουσίαν εἰληφότας τέκνα Θεοῦ γενέσθαι. « Ὅσοι γὰρ, φησὶν, ἔλαβον αὐτὸν, ἔδωκεν αὐτοῖς ἐξουσίαν, τέκνα Θεοῦ γενέσθαι, ταῖς πιστεύουσιν εἰς τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ. » Δίδωσιν ἐξουσίαν, οὐ τυραννικῶς ἕλκει καὶ παρὰ πρόθεσιν ἡμετέραν βιάζεται· ἀεὶ γὰρ ἡ τυραννὶς, κατὰ τοῦ τυραννοῦντος τὴν τυραννούμενον ὁπλίζει, ἵνα κακῷ τὸ κακὸν ἐξιάσηται· κἂν τούτῳ τιμῶν ἡμῶν τὸ ἀρχαῖον τοῦ αὐτεξουσίου ἀξίωμα, καὶ ἵνα ὅπως εἴη τὰ ἀγαθὸν, τῇ αὐτοῦ μὲν ἐξειργασμένον τοκαθόλου εὐδοκίᾳ καὶ χάριτι· τῆς δὲ ἡμετέρας σπουδῆς καὶ ἐπιμελείας λογίζοιτο τὸ κατόρθωμα· κἀκεῖνος μὲν, εἰ καὶ Θεὸς Βέστι καὶ Δεσπότης, ἀλλ᾿ οὖν ἅπαν τὰ ἑαυτοῦ πεποίηκε· πάντας γὰρ καὶ ὁμοίως ἔπλασε, καὶ ὡσάυτως ὑπὲρ πάντων ἀπέθανε, ἵνα ἐπίσης σώσῃ τοὺς ἅπαντας. Ἐν ἡμῖν δὲ ἀπελείφθη τὸ προσελθεῖν, τῇ πιστεῦσαι, τὸ οἰκειωθῆναι, τὸ μετὰ φόβου, καὶ σπουδῆς, καὶ ἀγάπης λατρεύειν τῷ ὄντως ἀγαπήσαντι ἡμᾶς φιλανθρώπῳ Δεσπότῃ, καὶ κηδεμόνι. ὥστε καὶ θάνατον ἐθελῆσαι ὑπενεγκεῖν ἑκουσίως ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν, καὶ θάνατον ἐπονείδιστον, ἵνα ἡμᾶς τῆς τοῦ διαβόλου καὶ ἀρχεκάκου ἐχθροῦ ἀπαλλάξῃ τυραννίδος, καὶ τῷ Πατρὶ καὶ Θεῷ καταλλάξῃ· καὶ κληρονόμους μὲν Θεοῦ, συγκληρονόμους δὲ αὐτοῦ ἀπεργάσηται, τὸ παραδοξότατον, καὶ μακαριώτατον· μὴ δὴ διὰ μικρᾶς καὶ βραχείας ῥαθυμίας, καὶ ἀμελείας, καὶ ἐπιπλάστου ἡδονῆς οἱασοῦν, τῶν τασούτων σῶν ἡλίκων ἀποξενώσωμεν ἑαυτοὺς ἀγαθῶν καὶ γερῶν, καὶ ἀπολαύσεως· ἀλλὰ πάντα πράξωμεν, καὶ πραγματευώμεθα· καὶ αὐτῆς, εἰ δέοι, τῆς ζωῆς, ὑπὲρ αὐτοῦ μὴ φεισώμεθα, ὡς κἀκεῖνος δι᾿ ἡμᾶς, καίτοι Θεὸς ὢν ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν πεποίηκεν, ἵν᾿ οὕτως καὶ τῶν ἀπάρτι, καὶ τῶν ἀπάντων δωρεῶν καὶ στεφάνων καταξιωθῶμεν· ὧν γένοιτο πάντας ἡμᾶς ἐπιτυχεῖν, εὐδοκίᾳ καὶ χάριτι αὐτοῦ τοῦ ὑπεραγάθου καὶ ἐλεήμονος, τοῦ Κυρίου, καὶ Θεοῦ, καὶ Σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, τοῦ ταπεινώσαντος ἑαυτὸν τοσοῦτον ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν, καὶ αὐτοῦ χάριν ἀπὸ τοῦ νῦν ἐνεργῶς πλουσίως ἐπιδαψιλεύοντος· ὅτι αὐτῷ πρέπει πᾶσα ἡ δόξα, καὶ ἡ τιμή, καὶ ἡ προσκύνησις, ἅμα τῷ ἀνάρχῳ καὶ ἀχράντῳ αὐτοῦ Πατρί· καὶ τῷ συναΐδίῳ, καὶ παναγίῳ, καὶ ἀγαθῷ, καὶ ζωοποιῷ αὐτοῦ Πνεύματι· νῦν καὶ ἀεί, καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Ἀμήν.
METHOD AND MOST ACCURATE RULE OF CALLISTUS AND IGNATIUS XANTHOPULUS, THE MONKS, WITH GOD
Also containing the testimonies of the saints, concerning those who have chosen to live peacefully and monastically; regarding their instruction, their manner of life, and their regimen; and how many and how great are the good things that stillness provides to those who approach it with understanding.
The present treatise of the discourse is divided into one hundred chapters. The preface of the discourse, which also bears the number of the first chapter, is concerning the divine and supernatural gift and grace existing in the faithful through the Holy Spirit.
1. We ought, indeed, according to the divine oracles, to be taught by God, inasmuch as we bear about the new law ineffably inscribed upon our hearts, shining more clearly than a torch, and are steered by the good and most upright Spirit, as children and heirs of God, and joint-heirs with Christ, to live in a manner imitating the angels, and to be in no need at all of one to teach us, "Know the Lord." But now, our turning away from good from our earliest youth, and our inclination toward evil; furthermore, the deception of the dreadful Belial and the relentless tyranny that he exercises against us, have disposed us to run far from the saving and god-working commandments, and to rush toward soul-destroying precipices. And, what is more miserable, he provokes us both to think and to act against these commandments; whence also, according to the divine utterance, "There is none that understandeth, there is none that seeketh after God; for all have turned aside, together we have become unprofitable," and for this reason we have become flesh, deprived of the light and of divine grace, and we are in need of mutual excitation and aid toward the good.
That this argument was explained out of the inquiry of a certain brother, and in accordance with his desire, and for the observance of the Fathers' precepts.
2. Since, however, you, out of longing, in accordance with the Lord's word, have often demanded of us—unworthy as we are—a discourse and a written rule for the sake of your own profit, and perhaps also for that of others, as you yourself say, that you might search the divine and life-bestowing Scriptures and be instructed securely; and since, if not before, at any rate now, by the help of God, we have judged it necessary to fulfill your praiseworthy and heartfelt desire—forgetting our own innate indolence for the sake of charity and your profit, but rather admiring your ardor for good things and your persistent love of study, spiritual and most beloved son, and before all these things, fearing the judgment of God which has dreadfully threatened the one who hides his talent; and fulfilling also the paternal command which our Fathers and spiritual teachers laid upon us, that we should trust and hand down to other friends of God those things which they taught us. May God, therefore, the Father of charity and the unfailing Bestower of all good things, grant to us, who are so slow and endowed with such a thin voice, a timely discourse upon the opening of our mouth—He who often inspired voices into irrational animals—for the profit of the hearers; and may He grant to you, and to all who come upon these things, according to your desire, an ear to hear them wisely and properly and to fulfill them faithfully according to His mind; because without Him, as it is written, we can do nothing useful or saving, and because "unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it have labored in vain." And these things by this manner.
That the end precedes every matter; therefore, the end of the present treatise is to learn what the foundation is.
3. Since the end precedes every matter; and the purpose of both—ours, indeed, to explain to you what tends to spiritual growth; and yours, to live sincerely according to what is said—it behooves us, before anything else, to examine what sort of perfection of the house of Christ we are intending by laying a useful foundation; then, as the occasion invites us, or rather as we are abundantly favored by aid from above, we may be enabled to place a roof worthy of the architecture of the Spirit.
That the beginning of every life according to God consists in acting according to the commandments of the Savior; but the end is the return to the perfect grace of the most holy and life-giving Spirit, given to us from the beginning through divine baptism.
4. The beginning, therefore, of every life according to God, to grasp it in summary, is that we hasten
in every way and with all our strength to conduct our lives according to the ordinance of all the deifying commandments of the Savior. And the end is that, through the keeping of these, we may return to that perfect and spiritual transformation and conformation of grace, given to us from above and from the very beginning through the holy pool—or, if it pleases you to call this gift such—stripping off the old Adam along with his deeds and desires, and putting on the new and spiritual One, who is the Lord Jesus Christ, as the most divine Paul says: "My little children, of whom I travail in birth again until Christ is formed in you," and, "As many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ."
On the question of what grace is, and how we might attain it; and what things cloud it, and what things, in turn, cleanse it again.
5. But as to what grace is, and how we might attain it, and which things cloud it and which in turn cleanse it, he who is more radiant than any gold in soul and tongue shall declare to you, saying thus in regard to that which is written: "What is intended by the words, 'beholding the glory of the Lord, we are transformed into the same image'?" "This was shown more clearly when the gifts of the Spirit were working through signs, yet even now it is not difficult for one who has faithful eyes to perceive it. For, as soon as we are baptized, our soul shines brighter than the sun, being cleansed by the Spirit, and we not only look upon the glory of God, but we also receive from thence a certain radiance. For just as pure silver, if it be placed before the rays of the sun, sends forth rays itself, not only from its own nature, but also from the solar brilliance; so also the soul, being cleansed and having become brighter than any silver, receives a ray from the glory of the Spirit into the glory which is being generated, and such as is fitting to be received from the Lord the Spirit." And a little further on: "Do you wish that I manifest this to you more vividly from the apostles as well? Consider Paul, whose garments performed works; Peter, whose shadows possessed power. For they would not have had such power in their garments and shadows if they did not bear the image of the King, and if their splendors were not inaccessible. For the garments of a king are terrible even to robbers. Do you wish to see this radiance also shining through the body? 'Looking steadfastly,' it says, 'at the face of Stephen, they saw it as the face of an angel.' But this is nothing compared to the glory that shines within. For that which Moses once had upon his face, these men carried within their soul; nay, indeed, something much greater. For that of Moses was sensory, but this is incorporeal. And just as flaming colors flowing from radiant bodies onto those things which are near communicate their own brilliance to them, so indeed does it befall the faithful; and because of this, those who experience this are released from the earth and dream of the things that are in heaven, alas! For it is beautiful even to sigh with longing, because, while enjoying such nobility, we do not...
even know what is spoken of, because we quickly destroy these things, and are beside ourselves for the sake of sensible things. "For this glory, which is unassailable and fearsome, remains in us for a day or two, but thereafter we extinguish it, bringing upon ourselves the winter of the concerns of this life, and by the thickness of the clouds, we repel the rays." And again elsewhere: "The bodies of those who have pleased God will be clothed in such glory that it cannot be seen even by these eyes." And God has prepared for us certain signs and faint traces of these things, both in the Old Testament and in the New: for there, the face of Moses shone at that time with such glory that it was inaccessible to the eyes of the Israelites. But in the New, the face of Christ shone forth with much more than this. Have you heard the words of the Spirit? Have you understood the power of the mystery? Have you learned what kind of offspring the perfect spiritual formation within us is, which proceeds from the holy font? What, then, will be the yields of the fruits, what the fullness, what the rewards? And how is it in our power to both increase and diminish—that is, to brighten and to dim—this supernatural grace in the present life? From this arise the storm of the affairs of this life and the moonless night of passions born from them, which, like a winter storm or a wild torrent, rush upon us, and, submerging the soul, do not allow it to breathe or look toward that truly beautiful and blessed One, for the sake of whom it was made, but rather, darkening it entirely with the surge and smoke of pleasures, having become powerful and bitter, they submerge it. Just as, therefore, the things contrary to these—that is, those born through the deifying commandments—are beneficial and saving for those who walk not according to the flesh but according to the spirit ("For walk in the Spirit," he says, "and you shall not fulfill the lust of the flesh" [Gal. 5:16]), and, like a ladder, lead to that crowning point and the highest of the steps, which is love, which is God.
That in holy baptism we receive the divine grace as a gift through it, but having obscured it by passions, we cleanse it again by the fulfillment of the commandments.
6. But while we originally receive in the divine womb—that is, in the holy font—the entire [gift], perfect divine grace as a gift, if, however, we later, by the misuse of temporal things and by the care for the affairs of this life and by the mist of the passions, have, as we ought not to have, obscured it, it is permitted to us, even so, through repentance and the fulfillment of the deifying commandments, to recover such supernatural brightness and to regain it, and to behold its manifestation most clearly. Yet the appearance of this is revealed according to the measure and strength of each person's faith, and before these, by the help and good pleasure of the Lord Jesus Christ, as the holy Mark says: "Christ, who is perfect God, has bestowed on the baptized the perfect grace of the Holy Spirit, in no...
wise receiving an addition from us, but being revealed and manifested to us according to the proportion of our working of the commandments, and providing for us an increase of faith, until we all attain to the unity of the faith, to the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ." If, therefore, we make any addition, having been regenerated in Him, that too is from Him, and was hidden within us from Him.
That he who labors according to God must fulfill all His commandments, but must attribute the greatest part of his work to the first and, as it were, general ones
7. Since, therefore, the beginning and root of this entire undertaking, as we have said, is to live according to the saving commandments, and the end and fruit is to return to the perfect grace of the Spirit which was first bestowed upon us by baptism—which exists in us (for the gifts of God, it is said, are without repentance), but was buried by the passions, and is revealed through the working of the divine commandments—it behooves us, by the fulfillment of all such commandments as far as we are able, to hasten by every means to cleanse that manifestation of the Spirit which is in us, and to behold it most clearly. "For Your law, O Lord," says the blessed David, "is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths, and the commandment of the Lord is bright, enlightening the eyes," and "I was directed to all Your commandments." And he who reclined upon the breast of Christ says: "He who keeps His commandments abides in Him, and He in him; and His commandments are not grievous." And the Lord Himself says: "He who has My commandments and keeps them, he it is who loves Me; and he who loves Me shall be loved by My Father, and I will love him, and will manifest Myself to him." And, "If anyone loves Me, he will keep My word, and My Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our abode with him." And, "He who does not love Me does not keep My words." We ought, therefore, to apply the greatest part of our work to the first and more general of these commandments, and in a way to those which are as it were the mothers of the rest; for thus, with God, we may unerringly attain the proposed goal, namely, the beautiful beginning, and the end of our desire, which is the manifestation of the Spirit.
That the beginning of every God-pleasing work is the invocation with faith of the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, and with it, the peace and love that spring from it
8. The beginning, however, of every God-pleasing work is the invocation with faith of the saving name of our Lord Jesus Christ, because He Himself declared: "Without Me you can do nothing." And with it, peace. For, it is said, one ought to pray "without anger and disputing." And love; because God is love, and he who abides in love abides in God, and God in him. This peace and love not only make prayer acceptable, but from prayer itself [they are renewed].
born and rise, like twin divine rays, and they grow and are perfected.
*That through each of these, and simultaneously through all three, the store of all good things is lavished upon us.*
9. From these, or rather through each of them, and simultaneously through all three, the store of all good things is lavished and overflows upon us. For by the invocation of the name of our Lord Jesus Christ in faith, we firmly hope to receive mercy and true life hidden in Him; as if from another ever-flowing divine spring, it pours these forth abundantly into our breasts, when the name of the Lord Jesus Christ is purely invoked. By her, however, who possesses the whole mind, the peace, we are deemed worthy to be united with God and with other men. By charity, truly, whose glory is incomparable, since it is the end and sum of the law and the prophets, and since God Himself is named charity, we are wholly united with God, our sins being abolished by the justice of God, and that grace which makes us sons wonderfully working in us through charity. For charity, he says, will cover a multitude of sins; and charity bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things; charity never fails.
*That our Lord Jesus Christ also, at the time of His saving passion, left these to His disciples as a kind of final commandment and divine testament, and likewise after the resurrection.*
10. Whence also our all-good and most sweet Lord Jesus Christ, both when He arrived at His voluntary passion for our sake, and when, after the resurrection, He was seen by the apostles; and indeed also when He was about to return to Him who is Father to Him by nature and to us by grace—as a true and most loving father—he left all these to all His own as a kind of final command, and gentle consolations, and most sweet and solid, so to speak, pledges; or rather, as an indelible divine testament. And indeed, entering upon His saving passion, He said to His disciples: "Whatever you ask the Father in my name, I will do." And, "Amen, amen, I say to you, that whatever you ask the Father in my name, He will give you. Hitherto you have asked nothing in my name; ask, and you shall receive, that your joy may be full." And, "On that day you will ask in my name." And again, after His resurrection, He said: "And these signs shall follow those who have believed: in my name they shall cast out demons, they shall speak in new tongues," and so forth. Consistent with these, he who reclined upon His breast also declares: "Many other signs therefore Jesus did in the sight of His disciples, which are not written in this book; but these are written, that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that..."
believing you may have life in His name.” And the inspired Paul says, “In the name of Jesus every knee shall bow,” and so forth. And therefore, in the Acts of the Apostles it is written thus: “Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, said: ‘Be it known to you all, and to all the people of Israel, that in the name of Jesus of Nazareth, whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead, by Him this man stands before you whole.’” And after a few words: “And there is no salvation in any other; for there is no other name under heaven given among men, by which we must be saved.” And again, the Savior says, “All authority has been given to Me in heaven and on earth.” And again, as to what the God-man Lord said to His apostles before the crucifixion: “Peace I leave with you; My peace I give to you. These things I speak to you, that in Me you may have peace.” And, “This is My commandment, that you love one another.” And, “By this all will know that you are My disciples, if you have love for one another; as the Father loved Me, I also have loved you; abide in My love. If you keep My commandments, you will abide in My love, just as I have kept My Father’s commandments and abide in His love.” And again, after the resurrection, He appears at various times and frequently gives peace, manifesting Himself to His own and saying, “Peace to you.” And to Peter, to whom He entrusted the governance of the disciples, He shows that the care of the flock is a sort of requital for his fiery love for the Lord Jesus Christ Himself, saying in this way for the third time, “If you love Me, Peter, more than these, feed My sheep.” One might perhaps say, and not without reason, that through these three great things which we have shown, three other excellent things are born to us—namely, the purification of the soul, illumination, and perfection.
That all virtues are woven together in these three.
11. But if anyone wishes to examine accurately, he will clearly find that in this triple-braided and, so to speak, unbroken cord, all the abundant and God-fashioned purple of the virtues is suspended and woven. For the life according to God is as a precious chain, and a rope variegated with gold, connecting one virtue to another and reducing all to a consolidated unity. Indeed, many things bring about this one work—namely, the deification of the man who sincerely lives a life in accordance with the virtues—so that, bound by such knots and ties, through faith, if he wills, and hope, and humility, he may deserve to be named by the beloved and saving name of the Lord Jesus Christ, and attain peace and charity. This is truly the thrice-perfect tree, the planting of God, bearing the fruit of life; in which, once grafted, man in this life, having become a participant in it in a manner befitting him, does not reap death, as the first-formed one did, but eternal life and a
life that does not perish.
That the gift and arrival of the Holy Spirit to the faithful, through God the Father, is granted in Christ Jesus and in His holy name.
12. Indeed, the gift and arrival of the Holy Spirit to the faithful, through God the Father, is granted in Christ Jesus and in His holy name, as the most divine and loving Lord Jesus Christ Himself says to the apostles: "It is expedient for you that I go away; for if I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you." And, "But when the Paraclete comes, whom I shall send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father." And again: "But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name."
That it has rightly been ordained by our holy Fathers, that we should pray to our Lord B Jesus Christ with the Holy Spirit dwelling in them, and seek mercy from Him.
13. For this reason, then, our renowned guides and teachers, quite wisely and with the Holy Spirit dwelling in them, teach us that before every other good work and exercise—especially if we wish to dedicate ourselves to the arena of deifying stillness, to be set apart for God, to be severed from the world, and to live in stillness according to reason—we must pray in the Lord and seek mercy from Him without wavering, and hold His most holy and sweet name as an unceasing work and meditation. And we must carry this in our heart, and in our mind, and on our lips without interruption, and in Him and with Him breathe, and live, and sleep, and keep watch, and move, and eat, and drink, and, so to speak, strive to do all things in like manner. For just as when He is absent, every evil rushes in—or rather, nothing of what is useful is present to us—so when He is present within us, every contrary thing is driven away, and above all, nothing of the good is lacking to us, nor is anything opposed to our improvement; just as our Lord Himself declares: "He who abides in me, and I in him, he bears much fruit; for without me you can do nothing." Therefore, having invoked in faith this work and name—which is to be feared and revered by every creature, and which is above every work and name—and having altogether unfurled the sails of this present discourse upon it, we thus begin to speak and to proceed further.
That he who wishes to walk without stumbling must, before all else, choose the Lord's path of stillness along with total renunciation and perfect obedience.
14. In the name of the great God our Savior Jesus Christ, who said: "I am the light, the life, and the truth, and the way, and the door to God the Father, and through me if anyone enters, he shall be saved," and D
he shall enter and go out, and he shall find pasture, that is to say, salvation. Apply your mind to what we are saying, and we sincerely offer you counsel: above all, choose for yourself, in accordance with the universal divine declaration, renunciation and unconditional, perfect submission; that is, strive to seek and find a guide and teacher who does not err. And that which is unerring will be found if he presents the testimony of the holy Scriptures in the things he says, if he has the Holy Spirit within himself, leading a life that conforms to his actions; if he is lofty in contemplation but humble in mindset, and in all other ways good, and such a one as the divine words define a teacher according to Christ to be. But once you have found him, remain attached to him, as a most loving son to a true father, with both body and spirit; remain whole by walking according to his commandments, looking toward him as if toward Christ himself, and not toward a man, casting all disbelief and doubt far from you; and indeed, even your own mindset and your own appetites together with your will; thus, simply and without curiosity, follow the footsteps of the teacher as if you possessed some mirror, for clear conviction and supreme obedience, regarding your own conscience. And if at any time the devil, who hates virtue, should sow anything contrary into your mind, jump away from it as you would from fornication and fire, and wisely talk back to the deceiving tempter, saying that the one being led does not direct the one leading, but the one leading directs the one being led; and "I do not sit in judgment of my master, nor has my master accepted my judgment; nor am I his judge, but he has been constituted as my judge," as he who takes his name from the *Ladder* says, and reply with other things of this sort.
For there is nothing, without a doubt, more certain by such direction—that is, by submission—to one who has chosen to, for him to tear up the handwritings of his own transgressions and be inscribed in the divine record of those who are saved. For if, according to the blessed Paul, the Son of God and our God, the Lord Jesus, became as we are for our sake, and while wisely managing the Father's good pleasure, he was seen travelling such a path, through which he was deemed worthy of the paternal proclamation, even for the sake of his good pleasure according to man? "For he humbled himself," he says, "becoming obedient unto death, even the death of the cross. Wherefore God also highly exalted him, and gave him a name," and the rest. D Who then will hope with pride, not to say foolishly, that he will attain the glory of the Lord and God and Savior Jesus Christ and the paternal rewards, if he does not choose to walk the same path as our leader and teacher, Jesus Christ? For it is necessary for the disciple, if he wishes to become like the teacher, to gaze incessantly, as if upon an exemplar and most beautiful archetype, with the whole force of his soul, unswervingly, toward the life and conduct of his tutor; and daily to attempt to imitate him. Furthermore, concerning our Lord Jesus Christ himself, it is written: "And he was subject to his father and mother." And the Savior himself says:
I came not to be ministered unto, but to minister."» And there is another who wishes to live in a different way, that is, self-pleasingly and of his own authority, and without a guide. Does such a man think that he is walking in the manner of a life according to God? By no means; not at all; he is like one leaping over cliffs. And the one of the Ladder says: "Just as he who has no guide easily wanders on the road, so also he who walks the monastic path by his own authority easily perishes, even if he understands all the wisdom of the world." For this reason, many, not to say all, who are not subject and do not walk with counsel, though they labor and sweat greatly while dreaming, truly reap the very least. But some, alas, instead of grain, gather tares, as they walk, according to what has been said, in self-will and a self-pleasing mindset, than which there is nothing worse. And witness to this is the author of the Ladder, who writes thus: "As many of you as have undertaken to strip for the arena of mental confession; as many of you as wish to place the yoke of Christ upon your own necks; as many of you as are eager to lay your own burdens upon the neck of another; as many of you as are hastening voluntarily to write your own lives, and wish to have freedom rendered to you in return for them; as many of you as are being lifted up by the hands of others and are swimming across this great sea; know that you have chosen to walk a short and rough path, having only the error in itself; and this is called 'self-will' (idiorrhythmia). For he who has renounced this entirely, before he even walks, has reached the goods that seem spiritual and pleasing to God. For obedience is to distrust oneself in all good things until the end of life." When you, therefore, having studied these things with understanding and desiring to practice the good portion and the inalienable peace of the heaven-bound stillness, follow the laws which have been well-proclaimed, as has been shown to you, and first eagerly embrace obedience, then in this way, peace. For just as practice is a step toward contemplation, so is obedience to stillness. And do not wish to move the boundaries, as it is written, which the Fathers have set. Woe to the solitary! For in this way, by laying a beautiful foundation, as time advances, you will place a most glorious roof upon the architecture of the Spirit. For just as he whose beginning is, as it has been said, without glory, will have his whole work rejected, so conversely, he whose beginning is glorious, his whole work will be acceptable and well-arranged, even if its opposite sometimes happens; and this, however, happens to come about through our own purpose and will.
What are the signs of true subjection, by which he who is instructed might be truly subject.
15. But since the discourse concerning such a way of life is extensive and difficult to navigate, from which it follows that those who undergo it do so in different ways, it is fitting also to indicate a few things about it, as it were, as signs, which...
you may keep as an infallible rule and balance, in order to live most purely. And this we say: He who is truly subject must necessarily pursue these five virtues. First, faith, that is to say, to have pure and sincere faith in him by whom he is directed, to such a degree that he believes that Christ himself is observing him and that he is obeying Him, as the Lord Jesus says: "He that heareth you, heareth me; and he that despiseth you, despiseth me; and he that despiseth me, despiseth him that sent me." And whatsoever is not of faith, according to him who derives his name from the Ladder, is sin. Second, truth: it is necessary for him to be truthful both in deed and word, and in the accurate confession of his thoughts. "For the beginning of thy words is truth," as it is written, "and the Lord requireth truth." And Christ also says: "I am the truth"; and indeed He is called Truth itself. Third, not to follow one’s own will. For it is a loss, he says, for one who is subject, to do his own will, but he must always willingly submit it, and not allow himself to be compelled by his own Father. Fourth, not to contradict nor to contend at all, since contradiction and contention are not characteristics of the pious. And the most holy Paul writes: "But if any man seem to be contentious, we have no such custom, neither the churches of God." If then it is so simply and commonly forbidden to all Christians, by much more so to monks, and this according to the Lord, to whom they have promised to be accurately subject. Contradiction, however, and emulation have their origin in a mind teeming with pride and unbelief, as it has been said: A proud monk contradicts vehemently; just as the opposite, that is to say, not to contradict and not to contend, proceeds from a faithful and humble disposition. And fifth, he must guard this virtue, namely to have an accurate and sincere confession toward his superior, just as we did at our tonsure, as if we were standing before the fearful judgment seat of Christ, in the sight of God and the holy angels, where we gave our promise to hold fast to the beginning and the end, along with our other promises and covenants made to the Lord, and to confess the secrets of our heart. It has been said also by the most holy David: "I said, I will confess against myself my iniquity to the Lord, and thou hast forgiven," etc. And by the same Author of the Ladder: "Stripes, if they triumph, will not advance to the worse, but shall be healed."
Whoever wisely and ardently guards this fivefold number of virtues which we have shown, let him know without doubt that he will attain, as if by a down payment, the blessedness of the righteous. And these indeed are the properties of this magnificent subjection, and are as it were the root and the foundation. But hear also what the branches are, and the fruit, and the top.
From subjection, the same Author of the Ladder says again, comes humility; from humility, discretion; from discretion, perspicacity; and from this, foresight; which is solely the work of God, and to those who successfully act according to God, a gift
bestowed by Him, excellent and supernatural. A Furthermore, let this also be known to you: that according to the measure of your submission, humility will sprout within you; and again, according to the measure of humility, likewise discretion; and so on for the rest of the virtues. And strive with all your might to run the course of obedience without stumbling. For in this way, you will advance without danger to the things that lie before you. But if you should limp by some fault in the pursuit of submission, know that you will not successfully finish the remaining race of the course of the, as we say, life according to Christ; nor will you be crowned with the wreath given to the victors. Therefore, take obedience to be your own and what we have called its properties, so that it may show you the way, just as those who sail are guided by the stars, so that they do not wander across the seas; so that, always looking to it, you may be able to cross the great ocean of the virtues and thus reach the tranquil harbor of detachment. But if some storm and tossing should come upon you, this too will happen because of your disobedience. For the true obedient one, according to the Fathers, not even the devil himself is able to harm. But that we may show you in a few words how sublime and honorable true obedience is, let us record one more oracle of a holy Father.
Therefore, the most radiant light of the life according to Christ, and the new Beseleel of the heavenly Ladder, says again: “The Fathers define armor to be psalmody; a wall, prayer; but a bath, blameless tears; yet they judge blessed obedience to be a confession, without which no one among those subject to the passions will see the Lord.” These things are indeed sufficient, as it seems to us, for the most evident declaration and praise of the inimitable imitation of thrice-blessed obedience. We can still learn and discern this by experience if we look back to the things before, and inquire what was the cause of our destruction and mortality, since we were not created such from the beginning; and what is the cause of our renewal and immortality. We find, then, that the cause of the former, that is, of corruption, was the first Adam’s self-reliance, his self-will, and his disobedience; from which arose the rejection and transgression of the divine commandment. But of the latter, that is, of incorruption, the author was the second Adam, even God and our Savior Jesus Christ, through His subjection to the Father, from which came the observance of His commandment. “For I,” says the Savior, “have not spoken of myself; but the Father who sent me, He gave me a commandment, what I should say and what I should speak. And I know that His commandment is eternal life. Therefore, what I speak, as the Father has said to me, so I speak.” As, therefore, in the forefather and those who act according to him, self-conceit is the root and mother of all evils; so in the new God-man Jesus Christ, and in those who strive to live according to Him, the beginning, and fountain, and foundation of all good things, is humility. Such a state and order, and which is above us, we see that of the divine Angels observing; this, indeed, the earthly
Church, and those of us who turn aside from such regulations, and wishing—not to speak arrogantly—to live differently, we remember and believe that they are severed from God, and from that brilliant heavenly inheritance and the catholic Church, and are cast out and sent down into the darkness and the fire of Gehenna. And we say that those who behaved wickedly toward the East, and who in the times of the heretics spoke vain things, suffered this, as the divinely written oracles have shown, who, because of their self-sufficiency and pride, were miserably cast out from the divine glory, as it is said, and joy, and the holy assembly. B It has also been said by one of the wise that "contraries are the cures for contraries." Since, therefore, the cause of all gloomy things is disobedience and arrogance, while that of joyful things is obedience and contrition, it is necessary that he who desires to live securely should subject himself to a prudent Father, versed in the way, who, by experience of time and knowledge of divine things, possesses authority, and whose life is adorned with a garland of virtues; and he should hear his precepts and counsels as the voice and counsel of God. "For safety is in much counsel," he says. And, "A man without counsel is an enemy to himself." And if it happened that some of the Fathers, even without this exercise of subjection, attained divine peace and that perfection which is according to God, this was by divine revelation and happened rarely. It is also written that the rare is not the law of the Church, just as neither does one swallow make spring. But do you, believing true obedience to be the preliminary introduction to the most excellent tranquility, leave aside those things which once happened by divine dispensation, and walk according to those things that were pleasing to the venerable Fathers. Thus will you be worthy of the reward due to those who live lawfully. What then? Would one not tread an obvious path if he had not yet experienced it, without an expert guide? Nor would he traverse the Ocean without an expert pilot; nor attempt any art or science without an infallible master; and yet, the art of arts, the science of sciences, the path leading to God, and the infinite ocean of the mind,—namely, the monastic life, which is compared to the life of the angels—would anyone dare to approach it, and hope to attain its end, without a leader, and pilot, and prudent and sincere master? In reality, whoever he is, he deceives himself, and errs, not even laying any foundation, since he is exercised outside the rule; just as, on the contrary, he who obeys the oracles of the Fathers has anticipated the end even before he walks. For from where else can we learn how we ought to fight against the flesh, as is fitting, or how the war against desires and demons is to be undertaken? For together with the virtues, as it is written, grow the vices, and they stand in a certain way near the door. But how shall we chastise the senses of the body and order the virtues of the soul as in a threshing floor? Or rather, how will it be permitted to us to discern voices, and revelations, and divine exhortations and contemplations, and the guilts, errors, and oracles of the demon? And, to speak in one word, how are we to attain to that union with God, to that divine perfection, to the mysteries, when—
without the leading of a true and enlightened mystagogue? It is not possible, indeed, it is not possible. For when we see that chosen vessel, the most blessed Paul, that instructor in the ineffable, the mouth of Christ, the light of the world, the common sun, the teacher of the entire inhabited earth, sharing and deliberating on the Gospel with his fellow apostles—and the reason, he says, is lest I might be running, or have run, in vain—and indeed when we hear Wisdom herself, our Lord Jesus Christ, speaking of Himself, that "I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of Him who sent me, the Father," and concerning the all-holy and life-giving Spirit, that "He will not speak on His own authority, but whatever He hears, He will speak;" by reason of the utility of this order, which holds together both heavenly and earthly things, we are seized with horror, stupor, and anguish when we attend to our own weakness and infirmity, and to those who dementedly choose to live obliquely, dangerously, by their own whim and caprice. For in truth, that struggle is terrible, and the robbers are countless, and the stratagems of the tempters are six hundredfold. And the shipwrecks cannot be numbered; whence even out of the many, barely a few escape. But let them walk as they please; "For every man’s work, as it is written, the fire will test," and that "You will render to each according to his works." But especially, may Christ grant to all to understand not simply how they wish, but how it is necessary to both will and live. As for you, and whoever wishes to live according to Christ, as if taking hold of a hem of these words, seize the golden and spiritual path of blessed obedience, and hasten, as has been indicated beforehand, to find a learned and perfect master; for perfect, according to the divine apostle Paul, is solid food; that is, for those who by reason of habit have their senses trained to discern good and evil. And in this way, namely, by seeking with labor and faith, you will not miss your proposed goal. "For everyone, says divine Scripture, who asks, receives, and he who seeks, finds, and to him who knocks it will be opened." And he will initiate you successively and by order into those things which are to be done and which please God, or rather, he himself will take you by the hand to those things which are pleasing and spiritual to God, and by most people considered intolerable; when he sees you truly rejoicing in mediocrity, humility, and simplicity, whether in food, or in clothing, or in cloak; and being content with those things which for the time are useful and opportune and necessary; and not with those superfluous, idle things, nor those things which, indulging in trifles and insane splendor, men deem great and draw a sword against themselves and their own salvation. For even the great Apostle says: "Having food and clothing, with these we shall be content." But you desire and wish to learn from us in writing what things pertain to the beginning, the inception, and the end of this Christian life? However much your question is to be commended, it is truly laborious to suddenly answer you
nevertheless, with Christ guiding our hand, we shall endeavor to fulfill your request, building, as upon a firm and unshakable foundation, upon that perfect and in every way reward-worthy obedience, this house celebrated by the speech of all, which we call the divine peace of all spiritual building. And surely we speak, supported by the oracles of the Fathers and the Holy Spirit as by most firm pillars.
That he who wishes to have true and divine peace must take care to be full of good works along with orthodox faith; and that faith is double; and that he who is at peace must be peaceable, undistracted, free from care—that is, unconcerned—silent, quiet, thankful in all things, conscious of his own weakness, and must bear temptations nobly, hope in God, and accept from Him what is useful.
16. The Savior says: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ shall enter the kingdom of heaven; but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven.” And you, therefore, beloved, if you love this God-making stillness not only with empty words—which, to those who sincerely enter into it, even now provides clearly the impressions of the kingdom of heaven and of God, and in the future, more fully and perfectly—but if you love it in truth and in deed, take care to be, alongside your orthodox faith, full of good works. Then, let your manner be peaceable with all, undistracted, free from care—that is, entirely unconcerned—silent, quiet, thankful in all things, and conscious of your own weakness. And in all, keep an eye wakeful and sober against the various and manifold temptations that occur to you each day; fighting with obedience and magnanimity against the waves and the affliction that may come upon you from any side.
Concerning the first and the second—that is, that you ought to be adorned with good works along with orthodox faith—that illustrious brother of the Lord admonishes you openly, saying: “Faith without works is dead; just as works are without faith,” and, “Show me your faith by your works.” And before him, the instructor and master of all, our Lord Jesus Christ, said to His disciples: “Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to keep all that I have commanded you.” And the Theologian also says that God seeks these three things from every man who has baptism: right faith from the soul, self-control from the body, and truth from the tongue.
That faith is twofold.
2. Note that faith, according to the God-given oracles, is twofold. One is general, common to all orthodox Christians, into which we were baptized from the beginning and in which we must depart from this world. The other belongs to the few, namely to those who, through the fulfillment of the commandments of the deifying passions, have returned to the image and likeness, and thus, having been enriched by the divine light of grace, have anchored all their hope in the Lord. And so great—oh, the dignity of it!—is this, that they no way, according to the Lord’s word, waver at the time of prayer in their requests to God; but rather, they ask with faith and thus readily receive what is beneficial. For this reason the blessed ones have possessed this faith, confirmed by sincere works, as having cast away all knowledge, discernment, hesitation, and anxiety from themselves, and having been totally and completely immersed in the divine intoxication of faith, hope, and love toward God, and thus transformed by the better and blessed transformation of the right hand of the Most High, as the divine David says.
But to speak at length about the first faith is not for the present time; however, to speak about the second, which blossoms and is born like a flower from the first, is very timely. For faith is like a root and principle of the namesake deifying stillness. For if you do not believe, says the author of the *Ladder*, how will you be still? The divine David therefore says: "I believed, therefore I spoke" (Ps. CXV, 10). And the great apostle Paul says: "Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen" (Heb. XI, 1); and "The just shall live by faith" (Heb. X, 38), etc. And the Savior, to the disciples asking him to increase their faith, speaks thus: "If you have faith as a grain of mustard seed, you would say to this mulberry tree, ‘Be plucked up by the roots and be planted in the sea,’ and it would obey you" (Luke XVII, 6). And: "If you have faith and do not doubt, you will not only do what was done to the fig tree, but even if you say to this mountain, ‘Be removed and be cast into the sea,’ it will be done" (Matt. XXI, 21). And: "All things whatever you ask in prayer, believing, you will receive" (Matt. XXI, 22). And: "Your faith has saved you" (Matt. IX, 22). The holy Isaac also writes: "Faith is sharper than knowledge, as knowledge is [sharpened regarding] sensible things." For all the saints, having been deemed worthy to find this manner of life—which is an amazement toward God—live in the power of faith, in the delights of that life which is above nature.
We do not mean by faith that by which one believes in the distinction of the adorable and divine persons, and in the excellent and proper nature of the Divinity Itself, and in the wonderful economy which is accomplished in humanity, in the assumption of our nature—although that faith is indeed very high. Rather, we mean the faith which arises from the light of grace in the soul, by the testimony of the mind, establishing the heart unshakeably—far removed from any mere opinion. It does not show itself by the mere hearing of the ears, but looks with the eyes of the spirit upon the mysteries hidden in the soul, and those hidden and divine riches which are separated from the eyes of the children of the flesh and are revealed through the Spirit only to those who recline at the table of Christ and meditate upon his laws, just as
at the assurance of hope, which is removed from all conceit; and it shows itself not in the increase of the hearing of the ears, but in the spiritual eyes, the mysteries hidden in the soul; and the hidden and divine wealth, which is hidden from the eyes of the sons of the flesh, and is revealed in the Spirit to those who dwell at the table of Christ, in the meditation of his laws, as he said: “If you keep my commandments, I will send you the Paraclete, the Spirit of truth, which the world cannot receive; and he will teach you all truth,” and so forth. And again: “Until that comes which is the fullness of the mysteries, and we are deemed worthy of the manifestation of them, faith serves between God and the holy ones, mysteries [of which may we be deemed worthy through the grace of his Christ], here indeed as in a pledge, but there in the substance of truth, in the kingdom of the heavens, with those who love him.”
That you must be peaceable.
C. Concerning the third, namely that you must have peace with all, the exhortation is evident from the oracle of David; and indeed even more so from that of the Christ-bearing Paul, which rings out clearer than a trumpet: the former says, “Great peace have they that love thy law; and there is no stumbling-block for them.” – “And with them that hated peace I was peaceable.” And: “Seek peace, and pursue it.” The latter says, “Follow peace with all men, and holiness, without which no man shall see the Lord.” And: “As far as it is possible for you, being at peace with all men.”
That you must not be distracted.
D. As for the fourth, namely that you must be undistracted, that holy man Isaac will teach you, saying: “If desire,” he says, “is the fruit of the senses, then let those keep silent henceforth who claim that peace of mind can be preserved alongside distraction; and do not associate with those who are distracted.”
That you must be free of anxiety and care.
E. Concerning the fifth, namely that you should not be anxious or concerned for any reason, whether from reasonable or unreasonable causes, you shall have as a document that which the Lord says in the Gospels: “Therefore I say to you, do not be anxious for your life, what you shall eat; nor for your body, what you shall put on. Is not the soul more than meat, and the body than clothing? Behold the birds of the heaven, that they do not sow, neither do they reap, nor gather into barns; and your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not much better than they? Which of you by being anxious can add one cubit to his stature? And why are you anxious for clothing?” And a little later: “Do not be anxious, therefore, saying, ‘What shall we eat?’ or ‘What shall we drink?’ or ‘Wherewith shall we be clothed?’ For all these things the nations seek after. For your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things. But seek first the kingdom of...
and His righteousness, and all these things shall be added unto you. Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof.” St. Isaac also says: “Unless you are free from anxiety, do not seek for light, nor for tranquility and stillness, in the slackness of your senses.” And the author of the *Climax* says: “A single hair torments the eye, and a little care banishes stillness. For stillness is the setting aside of thoughts and the denial of reasonable anxieties. He who has truly grasped stillness will not even be concerned about his own flesh.” For He who promised is truthful.
That you must be a lover of silence.
6. Furthermore, the theme of the sixth point—namely, that you must be silent—compels me to speak. Regarding this, the holy Isaac also says: “He who keeps his mouth from backbiting preserves his heart from the passions; and he who cleanses his heart from the passions beholds the Lord at every hour. And if you place all the works of the way of life on one side of the scale, and silence on the other, you will find that silence has more weight.” And: “Love silence above all things, because it brings you near to the fruit. For the tongue is powerless to explain it. Let us first force ourselves to be silent, and then something will be born in us from silence, guiding us to silence itself. May God grant you to perceive something born in you from silence! But if you begin in this way of life, I do not know how great a light will rise for you from it.” And again: “Silence is the mystery of the world to come, but words are the instruments of this world.” And to the holy Arsenius, the divine voice prescribed for the second time: “Arsenius, flee, be silent, be still, and you shall be saved.”
That you must be tranquil.
7. Likewise, regarding the seventh point—namely, that you must live a tranquil life—the great Basil and again the holy Isaac are trustworthy witnesses to present. The former says: “Tranquility is the beginning of the purification of the soul”; the latter says: “The definition of tranquility is silence from all things.” The one indicates its beginning, the other its end, through these words, as if in brief. And in the Old Testament it is said: “Have you sinned? Be tranquil.” And: “Be still, and know that I am God.” The author of the *Climax* also says: “The primary work of tranquility is to care for nothing, whether concerning things that are rational and agreeable, or contraries. For he who opens the door to the former will immediately fall into the latter: a fearless prayer, and then the most perfect work of the heart.” It is impossible for one who has not learned letters to study on tablets; it is still more impossible for those who have not attained the first to attain the two others. And again the holy Isaac says: “The desire for tranquility is the continuous expectation of death. He who enters into tranquility without this exercise cannot endure what we must patiently bear and endure in every way.”
That one must give thanks in everything.
Likewise, concerning the eighth, that is, that you ought to give thanks in everything, you have an excellent guide in the divine apostle Paul, who instructs us thus: "In everything give thanks." And the holy Isaac says: "The gratitude of the receiver incites the giver to bestow greater gifts than the former ones. He who does not give thanks for smaller things is a liar and unjust regarding greater ones. And the heart that directs the gifts of God toward man is a heart moved toward unceasing thanksgiving; the intention that directs temptation toward the soul is the thought of murmuring, which is always stirred up in the heart; but the mouth that gives thanks continually receives a blessing from the Lord, and the grace of God is poured out upon the heart that perseveres in gratitude."
That one must acknowledge one's own infirmity.
How much profit is gathered by him who proceeds to know his own infirmity (which is indeed the ninth in number), you will learn by applying your mind to the sixth psalm of the divine David, where he says: "Have mercy on me, O Lord, for I am infirm." And elsewhere: "I am a worm and no man, a reproach of men and the outcast of the people." And the holy Isaac says: "Blessed is the man who knows his own infirmity, because this knowledge becomes for him a foundation and the beginning of all goodness. For when someone learns and in truth senses his own infirmity, then he protects his soul from the pride that weakens knowledge, and he stores up a defense for himself." And: "The man who has attained to knowing the measure of his own infirmity, this one has reached the perfection of humility."
That one must manfully resist temptation.
There remains that chapter which constitutes the tenth number, namely that you must manfully, patiently, and long-sufferingly sustain the diverse and manifold temptations that supervene upon you. Hear, therefore, what is written in the divine Scriptures concerning this; for the apostle of Christ, Paul, says: "Our struggle is not against blood and flesh, but against principalities and powers, against the world-rulers of this darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places." And: "If you are without discipline, of which all have become partakers, then you are illegitimate and not sons." And: "Whom the Lord loves, He disciplines; and He scourges every son whom He receives." And the brother of the Lord: "A man who is not tempted is unapproved." And the holy Elias, that just man, says: "It is permitted for every Christian who truly believes in God not to be anxious, but to wait for and receive temptation from every side, so that when it comes, he may not be startled nor troubled, but, giving thanks, may endure the blows of affliction, and consider what he says while chanting with the Prophet: 'Test me, O Lord, and try me';" he does not say:
Your discipline has destroyed me," but A "He has straightened me to the end." Furthermore, do not seek after the causes of temptations, nor from whence they come; but only pray to God to be able to bear them with gratitude, as the holy Mark says: "When a temptation has come, do not seek why, or through whom it has come, but rather how you might endure it with gratitude and without resentment." And again: "If it is not easy to find one who has been pleasing [to God] without temptations, one must give thanks to God for every occurrence." And: "Every affliction tests the inclination of the will, whether it leans to the right or to the left; for this reason, the affliction that befalls one is called a temptation, as it provides to the participant a trial of hidden volitions." And the holy Isaac, among many other things, also says this: "Temptation is useful to every person; for if it is useful to Paul, every mouth shall be stopped, and all the world shall be held accountable to God." Those who struggle are tempted so that they may add to their wealth; the proud are tempted, that they may preserve themselves from those who do them harm; the drowsy are tempted, that they may be instructed to awaken; those who are far away, that they may draw near to God; and those who are familiar, that they may dwell in [His] presence with boldness. Every son who is not trained does not receive the wealth of his father's house, so as to be helped by it; and for this reason, God first tempts and afflicts, then shows the gift. Glory to the Lord, who brings us the delights of health through bitter remedies! There is no one who, in the time of training, is not burdened, and there is no one to whom the time in which he is given the poison of temptations to drink does not seem bitter. For without these, it is impossible to acquire a strong constitution; and to endure, moreover, is not our own. For how could a vessel made of clay sustain the nature of water, if the divine fire did not solidify it? If we be submissive, praying in humility with constant desires, we, too, shall receive all things in patience, in Christ Jesus our Lord. It is said also in the Wisdom of Sirach: "My son, if you come forward to serve the Lord your God, prepare your soul for temptation, and set your heart straight, and endure, and do not be hasty in the time of affliction."
That one ought to hope in God, and to expect from Him what is beneficial.
Fasten the anchor of hope upon God who is able to save you, and wait for the outcome of temptations from Him at the opportune time. "For faithful," he says, "is God, who will not suffer us to be tempted beyond what we are able, but will, along with the temptation, also make the issue." And that "affliction produces patience; and patience, probation; and probation, hope; and hope does not put to shame." And, "He who endures to the end, this one shall be saved"; and, "In your patience, possess your souls." And the brother of the Lord also speaks thus: "Count it all joy, my brethren, when you fall into various temptations, knowing that the testing of your faith produces patience;
and patience has its perfect work, that you may be perfect and entire, lacking in nothing. And, "Blessed is the man who endures temptation, for when he has been approved, he will receive the crown of life which the Lord has promised to those who love Him." And, "The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us." And, "I waited patiently for the Lord, and He inclined to me, and heard my cry, and brought me up out of a horrible pit, and out of the miry clay, and set my feet upon a rock, and established my steps; and He has put a new song in my mouth, a hymn to our God." And the blessed Simeon Metaphrastes also writes: "A soul caught in the bonds of divine love deems suffering as nothing, but rejoices in evils and flourishes in hardships; and when it suffers nothing painful for the sake of its Beloved, then it believes that it suffers most of all, and flees from ease as if it were a punishment."
Concerning the fear of God, that it is twofold: the fear of beginners and the fear of the perfect.
17. We must not hesitate now to make mention of the twofold fear according to God, although, by our own arbitrary choice, by speaking of the perfect fear after we had finished the ten chapters we indicated, we have disturbed the order of the first fear; for after faith, fear is ordained by the holy Fathers.
Concerning the first fear, which is that of beginners.
Know then, most beloved, that the fear of God is twofold: one indeed of beginners, the other of the perfect. Concerning the former, it is written: "The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord"; and, "Come, you children, listen to me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord"; and, "By the fear of the Lord everyone turns away from evil"; and, "Where there is fear of God, there is the fulfillment of the commandments." And the pious Isaac also says: "The fear of God is the beginning of virtue." It is said to be the fruit of faith, and it is sown in the heart when the mind is separated from the distraction of the world, for the gathering of its thoughts that are wandering from instability, in the contemplation of the future restoration. And, "The beginning of the true life of man is the fear of God; and this cannot remain in the souls of some men along with instability of mind"; and, "Take care that on your journey you lay as a foundation the fear of the Lord, and you may be able to arrive at the gates of the kingdom after a few days, without the detours of the road."
Concerning the second and perfect fear of God.
Concerning the second, namely the perfect fear of God, it is thus said: "Blessed is the man who fears the Lord, who delights greatly in His commandments"; and, "Blessed are all who fear the Lord, who walk in His ways"; and, "Fear the Lord, all you His saints, for there is no want to those who fear Him"; and, Behold
so shall the man be blessed who fears the Lord; and, "The fear of the Lord is pure, enduring for ever and ever." Saint Peter of Damascus also writes: "The sign of the first fear is hatred and anger against sin, as if one were wounded by a beast; but of the perfect fear, it is the love of virtue and the fear of change." And he adds that no one is immutable, and that in all actions of life we must fear lest we fall. Wherefore, you too, understanding these things prudently, endeavor with all the aforementioned to keep that first fear within yourself ceaselessly; for it is the safest treasury of every good work. For having it thus, your steps will be directed toward the practice of all the commandments of our Lord Jesus Christ; and proceeding on this way, you will also attain to the perfect and pure fear, through the desire for virtues, and through the mercy of our good God.
That for the sake of the commandments and the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, when the occasion is urgent, we ourselves must not spare our own life.
18. In addition to what has been said, you ought also to observe this, that for the sake of the life-giving commandments, and the faith in our Lord Jesus Christ according to them, we ought, when the occasion demands it, to gladly lose our very soul; that is, not even to spare our own life. As our Lord Jesus Christ himself says regarding this: "He who loses his soul for my sake and the Gospel's, he will save it"; believing without doubt and without hesitation that the God-man, Jesus the Savior, is both resurrection and life, and everything that is salvific, as He Himself said: "I am the resurrection and the life; he who believes in me, even if he die, shall live"; and, "Everyone who lives and believes in me shall never die for eternity"; and, "For God so loved the world that He gave His only-begotten Son, that everyone who believes in Him should not perish, but have eternal life"; and, "I came that they may have life, and have it abundantly." Having yourself thus, and always forgetting the things behind and stretching out to the things before, as it is said, run with Christ Jesus our Lord, without turning back, in this way your course. It is good, however, as it seems to us, and very useful, to set forth first the natural method of the most blessed Nicephorus the Great, regarding the interior heart through the entrance of breathing by the nostrils, which contributes somehow also to the recollection of the intellect; so that thus, by a well-disposed path, with God, the present treatise may proceed. That divine man therefore says, with many others, having the authority from the recorded testimonies of the saints, the following:
natural method regarding the interior of the heart through the inspiration of the nostrils, and the prayer that operates with it, which is: "Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me." Such a method also contributes to the gathering of the mind.
19. A “You know, brother, that the breath which we breathe is this air; and we breathe it not for any other reason, but for the sake of the heart; for this is the cause of life and of the warmth in the body. The heart therefore draws in the spirit, in order that it may expel the heat outward through the expiration, and provide itself with a good temperament. The cause, or rather the minister, of such a process is the lungs, which, created fragile by the Creator, like a bellows painlessly draw in and send out the surrounding air. Thus, therefore, the heart, by drawing in the cool air and expelling the warm, inviolably maintains the order for which it was created for the preservation of the living creature. You, therefore, sitting in a quiet cell and gathering your mind, introduce it—that is, the mind—into the path of the nostrils, where the spirit enters into the heart, and urge it, and force it to descend with the inhaled spirit into the heart. And when it has entered there, what will happen to you afterwards will not be without joy, nor without delight; but as a man who is away from his own house, when he returns, does not know what to do for joy because he has been deemed worthy to meet with his children and his wife, so also the mind, when it is united with the soul, is filled with ineffable joy and gladness. Therefore, brother, accustom the mind not to leave that place quickly; for at the beginning it suffers much because of the confinement and narrowness. But when it becomes accustomed, it no longer desires the roamings outside. For the kingdom of heaven is within us; and he who looks at it there, and seeks it through pure prayer, detests and hates all things outside.” And a little later: “You must also learn this, that when your mind is in that state, you ought not to leave it idle and silent, but take care that it meditate on this: ‘Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me,’ and that it meditate assiduously, and never cease from this meditation. For this work, holding the mind firmly, renders it insuperable and inexpugnable to the blows of the enemy, and leads it daily to the love and desire of God.” These, then, are the words of that blessed Father, having as his primary aim that, by the operation of this natural method in some way, the mind might return from its accustomed wandering, captivity, and instability to attention, and through attention might be joined to itself, and thus be united to prayer, and that from then on it might descend into the heart—with the prayer itself, clearly—and remain always within it, just as another of the men full of divine wisdom, as if explaining the oracle previously set forth, as one who is experienced in such a sacred work, declares the following. And
On the method of natural inspiration through the nostrils, and the invocation of our Lord Jesus Christ that accompanies it.
20. It is necessary to make this manifest to those who love learning: that if we train our intellect to descend, during the intake of the breath, along with it, then we would accurately understand that the intellect, having descended, does not depart—or rather, it does not begin to depart—before it has cast off every reasoned thought and has become single and naked, clinging to no other memory save for the invocation of our Lord Jesus Christ; but when it departs from there again and goes to external things, it is divided, even against its will, toward a multiform memory.
That the divine Chrysostom, as also others of the ancient holy Fathers, decrees that we must pray in Christ Jesus our Lord; and within the heart; and he speaks of this prayer: "Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me."
21. Also the great Chrysostom says: "I entreat you, brothers, never trample upon or despise the rule of prayer." And a little later: "The monk ought, whether he is eating, or drinking, or sitting, or serving, or traveling, or doing anything else, to cry out unceasingly: 'Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me.'" And after a little: "In order that the name of the Lord Jesus, descending into the depth of the heart, may humble the dragon that has seized the pastures, and may save and vivify the soul." "Therefore, remain unceasingly with the name of the Lord Jesus, in order that the heart may swallow the Lord, and the Lord the heart, and the two may become one." And again: "Do not separate your heart from God, but persevere, and protect it with the memory of our Lord Jesus Christ always, until the name of the Lord is implanted deep within the heart, and it thinks of nothing else, so that Christ may be magnified in you."
Further, regarding that memory of Jesus, with attention, within the heart through the inspiration of the nostrils.
22. Also, the author of the [i] Ladder [/i] writes: "Let the memory of Jesus be joined to your breath, and then you shall know the benefit of stillness." And the holy Hesychius says: "If you truly desire to cast shame upon your thoughts, and to live in stillness and tranquility, and to watch over your heart with ease, let the prayer of Jesus be joined to your breath; and in a few days you shall see this accomplished."
That it is necessary for one who wishes to watch over his mind spiritually, and especially the beginner, to sit during the time of prayer in a quiet and dark cell, because in this way the intellect and thought are naturally, in part, gathered together.
23. Whence, along with the things declared, as being from above, and as decreed by the great holy Fathers, in accordance with the testimonies set forth for us concerning praying through the inspiration of the nostrils and within the heart—both in our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, and in his holy and saving name—and regarding the exercise, and the watchfulness, and the petitioning for mercy from him; there must be added also this, namely that always, but especially
at the appointed time of prayer, and indeed in a dark corner, one should sit who is striving to watch mentally within his heart, and this is even more applicable to the beginner, as those holy Fathers and teachers who have had experience of such a most blessed work instruct and command. For the gaze and vision of the eyes are naturally apt to divide and separate the mind toward things seen and observed, and indeed to distract and change it. But when one is shut in, as has been said, in a quiet and dark room, he ceases from this distraction and change which occur through sight and appearance; and thus, whether willingly or unwillingly, the mind dwells in peace and is accustomed to be gathered to itself, as the great Basil says: "A mind not distracted toward external things, nor diffused over the world by the senses, returns to itself."
That before all things, through our Lord Jesus Christ and the invocation of his holy name with faith in the heart, constancy is provided to the mind; and the natural method through the inspiration of the nostrils, and the remaining in a quiet and dark place, and the like, cooperate with it in a certain way in the heart.
24. And before these, or rather before all things, such a struggle is brought to perfection for the mind by the cooperation of divine grace, which supervenes upon the single-word invocation of our Lord Jesus Christ, performed with a pure heart and without turning about in faith, and not by that method we have set forth—by the inspiration of the nostrils or staying in a quiet and dark place—far from it! For such things were not devised by the holy Fathers for any other purpose than that these might serve as aids to the recollection of the mind and to its return from its accustomed wandering to itself and to attention, as we have said. Through all of which, a continuous, and pure, and constant prayer is generated in the mind. As St. Nilus says, the attention that prayer seeks, it will find. For prayer follows attention—if anything else does—which is why it must be sought. And these things have been said.
