But you, my son, who wish to live and desire to see good days, and to live in the body as if without a body, live under such a rule and standard.
How one who is quiet ought to pass the interval which separates evening from dawn; and the beginning of the instruction according to width.
25. When the sun has set, after you have invoked our Lord Jesus Christ, the all-good and omnipotent, for his aid, sit on a couch in a quiet and dark cell, and gathering your mind from its external, accustomed roaming and wandering, and gently pushing it into the interior of your heart, through the inspiration of the nostrils hold the prayer, namely: "Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me"; at the same time, of course, drawing in with your breath in a unified way the words of the prayer, just as the holy Hesychius says: "Unite the watchfulness of your [heart] to the inspiration of your nostril, and the name of Jesus, and the certain care for death, and humility." D
For you know that both these things are helpful: having, along with prayer and the other things mentioned to you, the memory of the judgment and of the recompense for good and evil deeds; and—strictly deeming yourself, in your soul, to be the most sinful of all men, and more unclean than the demons themselves—on account of this, consider that you are to be eternally punished. In whatever line of reasoning among those mentioned you find compunction, sorrow, and tears, dwell specifically on that one as long as these alone continue. But if you have not yet been deemed worthy of the gift of tears, strive and ask with a humble mind to attain it. For through these we are cleansed of passions and stains, and we become partakers of good and saving things, as the one of the Ladder says: "Just as fire consumes straw, so pure tears consume every stain, both visible and invisible." And another Father says: "He who wishes to cast out malice, casts it out by weeping; and he who wishes to acquire virtues, acquires them by weeping. And if you do not have compunction, know that you have vainglory; for this does not allow the soul to be pricked." If tears do not come, sit and attend to these thoughts, along with prayer, for one hour; then, having risen, chant the Little Compline with attention, and sitting down again, hold to the prayer as much as you are able, purely and without distraction—that is, free from anxiety, from any kind of thought, and from any imagination—with great vigilance for half an hour, according to the one who says: "Without breath and food, be outside all other things in prayer, if you wish to become with the mind alone." Then, having sealed yourself with the sign of the precious and life-giving cross, and likewise your bed, and having sat upon it, enter into contemplation concerning future enjoyments, we say, and punishments; [also] of the fleeting and deceptive nature of temporal things; and indeed also of the sudden and common debt—namely, death; and of the fearful judgment that is after the end, and [that which is] before the end; and having remembered your transgressions in general, as in a summary, and having fervently asked for forgiveness for these, and having examined yourself accurately as to how you passed the previous day, lie down, holding also to the prayer, according to the one who says: "Let the memory of Jesus sleep with you," sleep for five or six hours; or rather, according to the interval of the night, sleep yourself in proportion.
How one ought to pass the time of the dawn, even until the morning.
26. Having become awake, and having glorified God, and again having called upon Him for your help, begin the first of your first works, that is, to pray in your heart without distraction and purely, for one hour; for at that time the mind is generally calm and unperturbed. Nevertheless, we are commanded to offer to God the first and foremost things; that is, to extend our first thought, as much as possible, unswervingly, through pure prayer of the heart, toward our Lord Jesus Christ. And the holy Nilus says: "This one performs prayer, who always [keeps] his primary thought..."
offered to God. After this, chant the midnight office. But if, because you are not yet suited for more perfect stillness, you are unable, as we have said, to begin, or perhaps for some other reason—as often tends to happen to those just starting such a work, and indeed rarely even to those who are progressing and have not yet attained perfection (for the perfect can do all things in Christ who strengthens them)—rise from sleep, and as far as you are able, having become vigilant, chant first the midnight office with all attention and understanding. Then, sitting down, pray purely and unswervingly in your heart, as has been indicated, for one hour; or rather, as the Giver of good things shall grant you. For the author of the *Ladder* says: "By night, give most of your time to prayer; [give] but a little to psalmody; and when day returns, prepare yourself according to your strength." If, however, even after struggling in this way, you are still negligent and despondent, and you find your mind troubled by some occurrence, rise, bestir yourself, as you know how, and occupy yourself with prayer.
Then sitting down, hasten to pray, as has been written, constantly taking care that through pure prayer you may commune with the pure God. Then rising, chant with understanding the Six Psalms, the fiftieth, and whatever canon you wish. Then sitting down after this and keeping watch, pray with sincerity for half an hour. And again, rising, chant the praises [of God], the customary doxology, and the first hour. And after these things, conclude. Let the words spoken by your lips be raised to such a height that they are audible only to your own ears; since we are commanded to offer the fruit of our lips to God; with all our soul and mind giving thanks to the benevolent and provident and all-wise God of ours, who, according to His great mercy, has granted us to pass safely through the expanse of the past night, and to behold the bright course of the present day; and fervently entreating Him likewise that He may grant us to pass the day without tumult, through the dark and savage storm of demons and passions, and that He may have mercy upon us.
How one should conduct oneself from morning until the midday meal.
27. Again, from the morning until the midday meal, as much as you can, offering yourself wholly to the whole God, and praying to Him with a contrite heart that He might help you—as you are weak, frail, and feeble—pass the time thus in constant prayer of the heart; when reading, read the Psalms, the Apostle, and the Gospel while standing; doing likewise in your prayers to our Lord Jesus Christ and the most pure Theotokos; but sitting during the remaining readings of the Holy Scriptures. After these things, chant with your mind the customary hours, which have been most wisely arranged by the fathers of the Church, driving away idleness with all your will, as the mother of all malice.
along with the passions and their occasions, even if they seem to be small and appear harmless.
On guarding against idleness; and that it is necessary even for the one who lives in tranquility to observe the ecclesiastical tradition.
28. As the holy Isaac says: "Guard yourselves, dearly beloved, against idleness; for in it most certain death is concealed, so that without it, it is not possible to fall into the hands of those who hasten to capture the monk." God will judge us on that day not for the psalms, nor for sloth in prayer, but for the fact that through their omission, an entrance is given to the demons. And once they have found room and entered in, and have closed the doors of our eyes, then they will fill us tyrannically and impurely, just as the divine sentence comprehends its fellow-workers with the most violent vengeance; and we become their servants, because we have neglected the small things which, for Christ’s sake, are worthy of care, as it has been written by the most wise: "He who does not subject his own will to God, will be subjected to His adversary." Thus, these things that seem small to you should be reckoned as walls for you against those who lie in wait for us, the perfection of which has been wisely established within the cell by those who hold the magistracy of the Church, for the guarding of our life in the spirit of revelation, the neglect of which is considered trivial by the unwise, who do not reckon the damage that follows from them. Of these men, the beginning and the middle of the way is untaught liberty, which is the mother of the passions. For it is better to struggle not to neglect small things, than to give a place to sin by neglecting them. For the end of this untimely liberty is bitter servitude. And again: "O how sweet are the beginnings of the passions!" For while one can sometimes cut off the passions and become tranquil by their removal, and rejoice when they cease, yet he cannot abandon their causes; therefore, we are tempted even against our will, and are bound by the passions, but we prefer their principles to reside within us. We do not desire the sins, but we receive with joy the causes that bring them to us. For this reason, the latter become, by their own efficacy, the causes of the former. He who loves the beginnings of the passions is subject to them against his will and desire, and is made a slave to the passions. He who hates his own sins will cease from them; and he who has confessed them will find forgiveness. However, it is impossible for anyone to abandon the habit of sin before he has conceived hatred for it, and to attain forgiveness before he has confessed his transgressions; the former is the cause of true humility, the latter of compunction, which follows in the heart with shame. And again: "There is no sin that is irremissible, except that which is not corrected." But enough has been said on these matters. You, however, after the psalmody of the stated hours, eat; while occupying yourself in prayer during the eating, so that by doing this you may arrive at the habit, by the power of grace, of praying unceasingly, according to our Lord's
commandment. But let the discourse concerning the food that sustains the body, according to the ineffable wisdom of its Creator, wait a little; and let the discourse concerning that which sustains and vivifies the soul be set forward, which is, according to the saints, the holy and deifying prayer. And very rightly so, since the soul is also more precious than the body.
Concerning prayer, and that one ought to pray always.
29. Just as this body of ours, if the soul is absent, is dead and exhales a foul odor, so too the soul, if it does not move itself toward prayer, is dead, and wretched, and foul. And that it is fitting to believe that the lack of prayer is worse than any death, the great prophet Daniel teaches us well, who deemed it better to die than to be deprived of prayer for a single moment of an hour. The divine Chrysostom also teaches us well: "Whoever prays, converses with God. How great a good it is for a man to converse with God, no one among all is ignorant; but to demonstrate this honor in words, no one could. For this honor transcends even the magnificent state of the angels." And further: "Prayer is the common work of angels and men alike. There is no longer, regarding prayer, any medium between either nature. It separates you from the brute beasts; it joins you to the angels. C Quickly would one pass over into their way of life, and manner of living, and conversation, and honor, and nobility, and wisdom, and understanding, if he would zealously spend his whole life in prayers and in the worship of God." And further: "When the devil sees a soul fenced about with virtues, he does not dare to draw near to it, fearing the strength and power which prayers provide, which nourish the soul more than corn nourishes the body." And further: "Prayers are the nerves of the soul. For just as the body is held together by nerves, and is knit up, and stands, and lives, and is made solid; but if anyone should cut these, he dissolves the whole harmony of the body; so souls are harmonized and knit together through holy prayers, and they run the course of piety happily. If, however, you deprive yourself of prayer, you do the same thing as if you were to take a fish out of the water. For just as water is life to it, so is prayer to you; through it, you may fly through the air, as if through water, and ascend into the heavens, and draw near to God." And further: "Prayer and supplication render men the temples of God; and just as gold, and precious stones, and marble make the houses of kings, so also does prayer make men the temples of Christ. What greater eulogy of prayer could there be than that it makes us temples of God? And He whom the heavens do not contain, this One enters into the soul that lives in prayers." And further: "From this one may know the virtue of holy prayer, that Paul, who runs throughout the whole earth as if winged, and dwells in prison, and endures lashes and sorrows, and lives amidst bloodshed and dangers, casts out demons, raises the dead, and throughout all the habitable [next page begins: ...world...]
area, he did not rely on any of these things for the salvation of men, but fortified his soul with prayers; and after the signs and the resurrection of the dead, he ran to his prayers just as an athlete runs to the wrestling ground for his crown. For prayer is the provider of the resurrection of the dead and of all other things. For as water has power over trees, so do prayers have power over the life of the holy ones. Furthermore: Prayer is the occasion of salvation, the procurer of immortality, the unbreachable wall of the Church, an asylum and guardian, fearful to the demons but saving to us the pious. Furthermore: Just as when a queen enters a city, it is necessary that all wealth follow her, so too, when prayer enters into a soul, the whole of virtue enters with it. Furthermore: What the foundation is to a house, that is prayer to the soul; and it is necessary to stake this down first like a base and root in the soul, and then to build upon it eagerly both temperance, and provision for the poor, and all the laws of Christ. Furthermore: Prayer with fervor is the light of the intellect and the soul; a light unquenchable and perpetual. For this reason the wicked one casts countless swarms of thoughts into our minds; and things we never even contemplated, he gathers together and pours over our soul at the time of prayer. Furthermore: Prayer is a great weapon; a great security. And the Theologian says: “One must remember God and breathe God.” And again: “Think of God more continuously than you breathe.” And the holy Isaac says: “Without unceasing prayer, you cannot draw near to God.” And: “After the labor of prayer, to cause the intellect to occupy itself with another care brings about a dispersion of the mind.” And: “Every prayer in which the body is not labored and the heart is not crushed is considered an abortion; for that prayer is without a soul.” And the one of the Ladder says: “Prayer is, according to its essence, the communion and union of man and God; but according to its operation, it is the consistency of the world, reconciliation with God, the mother of tears and again their daughter, the expiation of sins, a rampart against temptations, a middle wall against affliction, the healing of wars, the work of the angels, the food of all incorporeal beings, future joy, infinite activity, the fountain of virtues, the origin of gifts, invisible progress, food for the soul, enlightenment of the intellect, an axe for despair, the demonstration of hope, the cleansing of filth, the riches of monks, the treasure of the hesychasts, the mitigation of anger, a mirror of progress, the showing of measures, the declaration of a state, the revelation of things to come, a token of glory. Prayer is, to those who truly pray, a tribunal and judgment seat, before the future judgment seat is established. And again: “Prayer is nothing other than an alienation from the visible and invisible world.” And the holy Nilus says: “If you desire to pray, renounce all things, so that you may inherit the All.” Furthermore: Prayer is...
the communion of the mind with God. Furthermore: Just as bread is nourishment for the body, and virtue for the soul, so too is spiritual prayer the nourishment of the mind. And so much for these things; it is timely now to set forth, as briefly as possible, regarding bodily diet, both as to weight, quantity, and quality thereof.
On bodily regimen: how he who is tranquil ought to nourish himself.
30. It is written: “Son of man, thou shalt eat thy bread by weight, and drink thy water by measure, that by these, he who wishes to struggle according to God may live, having sufficient nourishment.” For unless you give blood, as it is said, you shall not receive spirit. But also the great Paul says: “I chastise my body, and bring it into subjection, lest perhaps when I have preached to others, I myself should become a castaway.” And the divine David: “My knees are weakened through fasting, and my flesh is changed for oil.” And the Theologian: “By nothing else, as by suffering evil, is God worshiped, and his mercy poured out through tears.” And holy Isaac: “As a mother cares for her child, so Christ cares for the afflicted body, and is perpetually near to this body.” And again: “In a belly that is full, there is no knowledge of the mysteries of God.” And: “As to those who sow in tears, sheaves of rejoicing arise, so joy follows that affliction of the body which is according to God.” And Macarius: “He who removes himself from all delights which separate him from his Creator.” And again: “Being tempted for a long time on the right and on the left, and having often tested myself in these two ways, and having received countless blows from the enemy, and having been deemed worthy of great secret gifts, I have gained experience for myself from the long passage of years; and in probation, and by the grace of God, I have learned these things: namely, that the foundation of all good things, and the liberation of the soul from the captivity of the enemy, and the way leading to light and to life, are these two methods: to gather oneself into one place, and to always fast; that is to say, to regulate oneself in temperance of the belly, wisely and prudently, in an immovable seat, in incessant tranquillity, and in the meditation of God. For from thence arises the subjection of the senses; thence the vigilance of the mind; thence those raging desires which are stirred in the body are restrained; thence the sweetness of reasonings; thence the luminous motion of thought; thence the ardor for the divine works of virtue; thence sublime and delicate thoughts; thence incessant tears, which flow perpetually; thence the memory of death; thence the pure wisdom which is removed from every phantasy that hinders thought; thence the sharpness of sight and the vigor of the knowledge of things that are far off. Thence those deeper mystical senses which thought grasps in the power of the divine oracles, and the interior motions which are produced in the soul, and the difference and the discernment of spirits and of holy powers and of true vision and vain imaginations, and thence the fear of the ways and paths—
that are stirred up in the sea of the mind, which cuts off sloth and negligence; and the flame of zeal, which transcends every danger and passes over every fear; and the warmth, which scorns every desire and wipes it out from the mind, and produces oblivion of all memory of things that pass away along with the rest. And, to speak briefly, the freedom of the true man, and the joy of the soul, and the resurrection, and the rest with Christ in the kingdom of heaven, come from this. If anyone is negligent in these two, let him know that he not only deprives himself of all the things aforementioned, but also shakes the foundation of all virtues by his contempt for these two virtues. And just as these are in the soul the beginning and head of divine operation, and the door and way to Christ, if anyone takes hold of them and perseveres in them, so also if anyone withdraws from them and leaps away from them, he arrives at the two things that are contrary to these—I mean, to be puffed up in the body, and to indulge in gluttony lawlessly, and the rest. And in others: "And some, being slothful and lax at their beginnings, are not only terrified and troubled by these and such-like struggles, but also by the rustling of the leaves of a tree; and they are overcome and cast down and turn backward by a small necessity that arises from the discomfort of hunger, and by a small infirmity. But the sincere and approved ones are not even sated with the grass of herbs; nor, nourished by the roots of dry plants, do they dare to taste anything of them before the appointed hour of food. But they lie upon the ground in the infirmity and weakness of the body; and their eyes have dim vision, because their body is excessively empty. And if they are in such a state from necessity that they are about to depart from the body, not even then do they give their hands to be overcome and succumb, so strong is their will. For they desire and wish to do violence to themselves for the sake of the love of God; and they prefer to labor for the sake of virtue than to have a transient life and all the rest that is in it. And when temptations come upon them, they rejoice more that they are perfected in them, that is, they become perfect. But neither do they doubt in the love of God because of the harsh afflictions that occur in them; but until they have departed from this life, they desire to undertake labors generously, and they do not yield, because they become perfect in them." Following then in these and such-like things, and also being obedient to Him who said: "Walk in the royal way, and do not turn aside to the right or to the left," we also set forth for you an example and a rule of the mean, which indeed has this definition.
How one who struggles ought to be nourished on the second, fourth, and sixth days.
31. As for the three days of the week, that is, the second, fourth, and sixth, observe them perpetually; that is, eat once a day, taking six ounces of bread, taking a sufficient amount of dry foods temperately; and of water, if you wish, three or four...
of the apostles, who says: "If a bishop, or presbyter, or deacon, or reader, or chanter does not fast during the holy quadragesima of Pascha, or the fourth day, or the preparation day (Friday), let him be deposed, unless he is hindered by bodily infirmity. But if a layman, let him be excommunicated." And the second day has likewise been regulated by the holy Fathers.
How one must eat on the third and fifth day
32. On these two days again, namely the third and the fifth, eat twice in the day: at the midday meal, sustain yourself with six ounces of bread, eating temperately of cooked food and some of the dry foods, and drinking wine mixed with water—up to three or four cups, if you wish. Toward evening, take three ounces of bread and some dry foods or certain fruits; take wine mixed with water, one cup, or at most two, when violent thirst urges you. For thirst cooperates vehemently in tears, having wakefulness as a companion, as the author of the *Ladder* says: "Thirst and wakefulness have wrung out the heart; and when the heart was afflicted, waters have gushed forth." And the blessed Isaac says: "Thirst for God's sake, that He may fill you with His love." But if you prefer to eat only once on these two days, you shall do well. For fasting and temperance are the first, and mother, and root, and fountain, and foundation of all good things. A certain one among the profane says: "Choose the best life; habit will make it sweet." And the great Basil: "Where there is choice, there is no obstacle." And another of the saintly ones: "The beginning of fruit is the flower, and the beginning of the active life is temperance." But these things may perhaps seem difficult, nay even impossible, to those who wish to follow them; yet he who considers the thriving fruitfulness that blossoms from them, and contemplates what great glory they are wont to generate, will judge them tractable, and by the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ and his own zeal according to his strength, he will proclaim them most easy in words and deeds, and will seal them with sanction. And the holy Isaac says: "Simple bread from a clean table cleanses the soul of the eater from every passion." And: "From the table of those who fast and keep vigil and labor in the Lord, take for yourself a remedy of life, and stir up the dormant soul of yours; because the Beloved reclines in their midst, sanctifying the foods, and transforms their bitterness into His own ineffable sweetness. And His spiritual and celestial ministers overshadow them and their holy food." And: "The odor of the one who fasts is most sweet, and his encounter gladdens the hearts of those who have discernment." And: "The life of the temperate man is most dear to God."
How one must eat on the Sabbath; and concerning vigils, and how one must eat during their time
33. On every Sabbath, except the Great Sabbath, it behooves you to eat twice, as has been indicated for the third and
fifth, both because of the definition of the holy canons, and because you ought to possess this custom on all the Sundays of the entire year, except for the vigil during the week of Tyrophagy, unless perhaps a vigil for one of the great Feasts of the Lord or one of the greatest Saints should fall then; in which case, having celebrated that, you may omit the Sunday vigil. Nevertheless, whatever the case may be, eat twice on the Sabbaths. It is useful, however, that you constantly compel yourself to the labor of the nocturnal vigil. Whence, even if by chance a vigil occurs in the middle of the week, it is most profitable for you to keep the vigil also on Sunday, and you will quickly receive great gain from it; nay more, your morning light will thus break forth, according to that which was said: “And your garments [in other copies: your healings] shall soon rise.” The holy Isaac also says: “For every struggle against sin and desire, the labor of the vigil and of fasting is the beginning, and especially for him who fights against the sin within us. And the sign of hatred for sin and its desire is manifest from this to those who gird themselves for this invisible war. And almost all the impulses of the passions begin to diminish in fasting. And after fasting, the night vigil cooperates with the exercise. He who in all his life loves the yoke of this combined discipline, this man becomes a friend of prudence; just as the delights of the belly are the principle of all evils, and the abundance of sleep, which favors the desire of fornication: so the holy way of God and the foundation of every virtue is fasting, and the vigil, and alertness in the service of God.” And again: “A soul that is brightened by the memory of God and by sleepless vigil, day and night: there the Lord builds for its security, a cloud overshadowing it by day, and a fire of light illuminating the night; and in its darkness, light will shine.” And further: “Choose for yourself the operation of delights, the continuous vigil in the nights: in which all the Fathers put off the old man, and were deemed worthy of the renewal of the mind. In these hours the soul perceives that immortal life; and in the perception of it, it puts off the darkness of the passions, and receives the Holy Spirit.” And again: “Honor the operation of the vigil, so that you may find consolation in your soul.” And further: “Do not think, O man, that in any of the monastics’ work, there is any conduct greater than the nocturnal vigil.” And: “Do not look upon a monk who persists in the vigil, with discernment of mind, as one clothed in flesh; for this work is truly of the angelic order.” And further: “A soul laboring in this angelic conduct of the vigil will have cherubic eyes, to look constantly and behold the heavenly contemplation.” You shall spend these vigils, namely, in prayer, psalmody, and reading, purely and steadfastly and with compunction, alone, or with a pious and like-minded assembly. After any vigil of yours, perform a small refreshment, because of the labor brought on by the vigil, eating and drinking, at the time of the meal: to wit, eat three ounces of bread; add a little dry food, which will suffice for you: drink wine with water, three cups. See to it, however, that you do not push your vigil into the day.
through to the ninth hour, having kept vigil, and perhaps because of the vigil, break your ninth hour fast. For it is necessary to do this, and not leave the other undone. For the Word has prescribed that you perform the prayer of thanksgiving once the vigil is finished.
How one ought to eat on Sundays; and concerning certain other things; and furthermore, concerning toil and humility.
34. Likewise, on all Sundays, eat twice in the day, just as you do on Saturdays; and let this rule be kept safe and sound, barring sickness; for these days have been granted by the holy Fathers and relaxed, owing to long custom and certain more recent causes—we speak of divine ones, or even others. For on these days we neither eat once, nor do we partake of dry food; but we partake of all that is useful and irreproachable, and herbs: yet temperately, and with the determined quantity; for it is always best to practice temperance in all things. But in bodily infirmities, as we have said, we must without blushing partake of all things useful and lawful which support the body; for the holy Fathers have taught us to be slayers of the passions, not slayers of the body. Likewise, it is fitting for you to taste a little bit of all things that are allowed, that is, whatever is permitted by the profession, for the glory and thanksgiving of God, and to avoid pride. But repel whatever is superfluous. “For the scarcity of things,” as Saint Isaac says, “teaches a man temperance, even against his will and desire; for when we have an abundance and plenty of them, we cannot restrain ourselves.” Do not love bodily rest. For the soul that loves God, according again to the holy Isaac, possesses its rest in God alone. Rather, choose to live with toil and hardship and humility. For toil and humility, as some saint writes, possess Jesus.
How one ought to live and conduct oneself during the holy Lenten seasons, and especially during the Great Lent.
35. Regarding the manner of life and order during the holy Lenten seasons, we consider it superfluous to explain it in detail and minutely. For as it has been previously determined for you to live on the days on which you perform the ninth hour, so it is allowed for you to work during the holy Lenten seasons, except for Saturdays and Sundays. Indeed, if possible, even more accurately and more vigilantly, and especially during the holy and Great Lent, as it is the tithe of the whole year, and it provides the rewards of the contests, through the Lord’s divine and illustrious day of Resurrection, to those who have been victorious according to Christ.
Concerning discernment, in part, and that there is no honor in mediocre work; and concerning obedience.
36. Furthermore, these things, and those similar to these,
you must approach with accurate discernment, for the harmony of the double composite being and for a peaceful state. "For with wisdom," he says, "is a house built, and with understanding it is set aright; and by sense are the storehouses filled with all precious and beautiful wealth." And the divine Thalassius writes: "Need and straitness, when joined with reason, are the royal road; so that indiscriminate mortification or irrational self-abasement are unprofitable, as both happen contrary to reason." And the holy Isaac says: "There follows after the loosening of the members a disarray and confusion of the thoughts; and after immoderate labor, listlessness; and after listlessness, rapture (ecstasis). But one rapture differs from another: for upon the first rapture there follows the war of fornication; but upon the second, the abandonment of one's own cell, and migration from place to place. Moreover, for work that is moderate and remains painful, there is no honor; for the reduction of these things increases pleasure, but immoderation causes rapture." And the great Maximus says: "Do not spend all your leisure time on the flesh; but set for it an exercise according to your strength, and turn your whole mind toward the interior things. For bodily exercise profits a little, but godliness [profits] in all things," and so forth. If the scales of the flesh somehow pull back, and tyrannize, and weigh down the scales of the soul, drawing it toward disorderly and soul-corrupting movements and impulses, as it is written: "The flesh lusts against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh," you yourself must curb it with the bridle of self-control, and mortify it until, even against its will, it becomes manageable and obeys the better part, mindful of the great Paul, who says: "As much as our outward man is perishing, so much is the inward man being renewed day by day." And the holy Isaac says: "Give yourself to die in the contests, and do not live in neglect; for not only are those who have accepted death for the sake of faith in Christ martyrs, but also those who die for the sake of the observance of His commandments. And it is better for us to die in the struggle than to live in transgression." And before all things, be with counsel and inquiry, doing everything according to your spiritual Father in the Lord. For thus, by the grace of Christ, even things that are burdensome and uphill will seem light to you, and as if you were being carried over a flat plain. But we must return to where we started.
How the one who is struggling ought to pass the time between the meal and the setting of the sun; and that one ought to believe that, according to the labor and the measure of our work, the distribution of divine gifts is granted to us.
37. After having dined, as the one who is struggling ought to do—according to the divine Paul, who teaches that he who struggles exercises self-control in all things—read, while sitting, in the watchful writings of the Fathers, sufficiently. And thereafter sleep for one hour, if the days are long. Then, having risen, perform a little manual labor, while also engaging in prayer. After
these things, pray, as has been indicated beforehand; read, meditate, and strive that you may be humbled and hold yourself beneath all men. “For he who exalts himself,” he says, “will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted.” And: “Let him who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall.” And, “God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” And: “The beginning of pride is to not know the Lord.” And: “The proud have transgressed exceedingly.” And: “Do not mind high things, but associate with the humble.” The divine Chrysostom also says: “This man is most truly one who knows himself, he who thinks himself to be nothing. For nothing is so dear to God as to count oneself among the lowest.” And holy Isaac says: “To the humble-minded the mysteries are revealed.” And: “Where humility blossoms, there the glory of God also springs forth.” And, that “Humility runs before grace, and conceit runs before instruction.” And holy Barsanuphius says: “If you truly wish to be saved, listen in deed: take your feet off the earth, and lead your mind up into heaven, and let your meditation be there night and day; and as much as you have strength, seek to be despised; striving to see yourself beneath every man. This is the true way; outside of this, there is no other for him who wishes to be saved through Him who strengthens him, Christ. Let him who wills run; let him who wills run; let him who wills run, so that he may attain—I testify before the living God, and the willing One—to share eternal life with everyone who so wills.” And the author of the *Ladder* says: “I have not fasted, I have not kept vigil, I have not slept on the ground, but I was humbled, and He saved me quickly,” pursuing before all else the state of being unreckoned, as holy Barsanuphius says: for freedom from anxiety regarding every matter causes you to approach the city; and not being appraised among men causes you to dwell in the city; and dying to every man causes you to inherit the city, and its treasures. And if you wish to be saved, hold fast to being unreckoned, and run toward the goal set before you. It is, moreover, according to his student, the venerable John, what being unreckoned is: not to consider oneself equal to anyone, and not to say concerning a good work, “I also did this.” Then again, sitting down, pray purely and steadfastly until the evening arrives, and so chant the customary vespers, and conclude, believing with a sincere heart that for our labor and the sorrow on account of virtue and the measure of our work, the distribution and declaration and consolation of gifts and rewards will be brought about by God; as the divine Psalmist says: “According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your consolations have gladdened my soul.” And the Savior: “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” And the great Paul: “If we suffer with Christ, that we may also be glorified with him; for I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory which shall be revealed in us.” And the divine and wise Maximus says concerning these things: “The measure of each man’s faith is said to be the cause of the distribution of divine blessings; just as
we believe, so too do we have an increase of zeal for acting. Thus, he who acts, in proportion to his action, demonstrates the measure of his faith, receiving the measure of grace as he has believed. But he who does not act, in proportion to his inaction, demonstrates the measure of his unbelief, receiving, as he has disbelieved, the privation of grace. Therefore, the envious man does ill to begrudge those who are making progress, for the choice of believing and acting, and of receiving the grace that comes according to the measure of faith, lies clearly with him, and is not placed in another. Let us then, with all our soul, pray that we may remain in this state for the rest of our time. And may the very ends of our life be Christian, free of pain, unashamed, and peaceful; and in addition to these, may we render a good account, standing before the fearful judgment seat of our Lord, and God, and Savior Jesus Christ.
That pure prayer is greater than every work.
B 38. In addition to the things declared, know this also, brother, that every method, and every rule, and, if you will, every different practice, has been fashioned and regulated in this way, because we are not yet able to pray in our hearts purely and without distraction. For if we have perfectly attained, through the benevolence and grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and have abandoned those many, various, and fleeting things, we are united immediately, beyond reason, with Him who is one and simple and has the power of union, as was said by the illustrious Theologian: “God being united with and known by divine men”; which is that interior illumination in the heart, through the Holy Spirit, which is born, as has been said, from the aforementioned pure and undistracted prayer of the heart. But this is rare, and hardly one in a thousand is deemed worthy, by the grace of Christ, to progress to this state. But to pass even beyond this, and to be deemed worthy of spiritual prayer, and to obtain the revelation of the mysteries of the age to come, is given to very few, and they are found from generation to generation, by the benevolence of grace, just as the holy Isaac writes: “Just as with difficulty one is found out of ten thousand men who has fulfilled the commandments and the ordinances without any small lack, and has reached the purity of the soul, so one in a thousand is found who is deemed worthy to reach, with great vigilance, to pure prayer, and to break through this limit, and to obtain that mystery. For many were not at all deemed worthy of pure prayer; but few. But he who has reached that mystery which is after it and beyond it, is found with difficulty from generation to generation, by the grace of Christ.” And a little later: “And if with difficulty someone prays with purity, what shall we say about spiritual prayer? For all spiritual prayer is free from movement. And that which inclines even a little is below the spiritual.” Therefore, if you yourself wish to be deemed worthy of such new mysteries in Christ Jesus, by work and deed, that is, by experience itself, hasten to pray in your heart at every time and every hour and in all your work, purely and without distraction; so that from
an infant nursing you may progress to a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ, and with the faithful and prudent servant may attain blessedness and the crown, as you direct your words in judgment—that is, acting according to reason—whence you shall not be shaken for eternity. As the holy Philemon writes concerning this: "Brother, whether by night or by day, may God deem you worthy to pray with a pure mind without distraction; do not cling to your own rule, but as much as you are able, strive to be united with God; and He Himself will illuminate your heart concerning spiritual labor." And one of the God-bearing ones says: "If you wish to serve God in the body as if without a body, possess unceasing prayer secretly in your heart, and before death your soul shall become as an angel." The holy Isaac writes in agreement with these things. For when asked by someone what the summit of all the fruits of this work—that is, of hesychia—was, so that anyone reaching it might know that he had attained the perfection of life, he answered thus: "When one is deemed worthy of the abiding of prayer; for when he reaches this, he has reached the summit of all virtues, and henceforth has become a dwelling-place of the Holy Spirit." For if someone has not perfectly received the grace of the Paraclete, he cannot accomplish perseverance in prayer in leisure. For the Spirit, he says, when He dwells in a certain man, does not cease to pray. For the Spirit Himself prays always. Then, neither in sleep nor in waking does prayer fail from his soul; but whether he eats, or drinks, or sleeps, or does anything else, and even in deep sleep, the sweet fragrance and breathings of prayer gush forth without labor; and then prayer has no division; but at all hours, even if such a one's prayer is tranquil externally, yet again it serves him in secret. For a certain saint calls the silence of the perfect ones prayer; since their thoughts are certain divine movements; and the movements of a pure heart and mind are gentle voices, with which they chant in secret to the hidden God. And many other holy men, initiated by divine grace itself, have set forth many such things worthy of admiration; which we have omitted on account of the length of our discourse.
On the number of genuflections per the space of a day and night.
39. As for the number of genuflections, we know that three hundred are prescribed by our divine Fathers, which we ought to perform throughout the space of a day and night during the five days of the week; for on every Sabbath and every Sunday, and also on other days designated by custom and in weeks, according to certain mystical and unspeakable reasons, we are commanded to be at leisure from these. There are, however, some who exceed this number. And some who do not reach it, each according to his strength or preference. And you, therefore, do according to your ability; yet indeed blessed is he who in all things that are according to God offers violence to himself.
“For the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent take it by force.”
That not only, as has been said before, is the distribution of divine gifts granted according to the struggle and the measure of our exertion, but also according to our habit, our aptitude, and our faith, and the natural disposition present within us.
40. And this, therefore, must be known: that not only, as we have said before, is the distribution of divine gifts granted to us according to the struggle and the measure of our exertion, but also according to the habit and aptitude of our way of life, and indeed, according to our faith regarding the things set before us, and the natural disposition fittingly present within us. And holy Maximus says: “The mind is the organ of wisdom; the reason, of knowledge; the natural persuasion regarding both is of the faith that consists through both; but for the gift of healings, it is natural compassion.” For every divine gift has something in us that is fitting and appropriate, as a power, or a habit, or a disposition, an organ capable of receiving it: for example, he who has made his mind pure from all sensible images receives wisdom; and he who has made his reason master of the innate passions—I mean anger and desire—receives knowledge; and he who has an unshakeable assurance regarding the Divine, according to his mind and reason, receives the faith that can do all things; and he who has perfected natural compassion, after the complete removal of self-love, receives the gifts of healings. And these things are so. But beware that no one may know your work, except the one who admonishes and guides you; praying for us who are unworthy, who speak indeed, but do not do the good, so that we may be deemed worthy to do first the things pleasing to God, and then to speak and persuade others. For he who has done and taught, according to the divine oracle, this one shall be called great. May the almighty and all-merciful Lord strengthen and guide you again, to understand these things intelligently, and to do them with all longing. For “not the hearers of the law are just before God,” according to the divine Paul, “but the doers [of the law]”; may the Lord lead you to every good and salutary work, and may He take you by the hand to the spiritual purpose and holy work in the Spirit, by the prayers of the saints. Amen.
But since we have spoken before concerning the practical discernment, it is now opportune to say a few words, as we are able, concerning the discernment that is universal and most perfect, since according to our renowned Fathers it is greater than all the virtues.
On the universal and most perfect discernment; and who it is that lives contrary to nature and carnally; and who it is that lives according to nature and psychologically; and who it is that conducts himself above nature and spiritually.
41. He who lives and conducts himself carnally and contrary to nature has completely lost his own power of discernment; but he who has refrained from evils, and rejects the beginning of doing well, as...
it is written: “Depart from evil and do good” [Ps. XXXVI, 27], he as a beginner, and one who yields to instruction, bends his head just a little towards a certain sense of discernment, such as is appropriate for the novice. But he who lives according to nature and psychically, as one performing acts within the mind and living according to reason—who is also called the “middle” one—he, according to his own measure, sees and discerns both that which concerns himself and that which concerns those like him. But he who lives above nature and spiritually, he—as one who has surpassed the passionate state, the beginning stage, and the boundaries of the middle state, and who has progressed by Christ’s grace to the perfect state, that is to say, to the essential illumination and the most perfect discernment—he sees himself and discerns most clearly. And indeed, he sees and discerns all things purely, while he himself is seen, looked into, and judged by no one; nay, he is judged as the one who is and is named a spiritual man. “Not with writings and ink, but by deed and grace,” as the divine Apostle says: “The spiritual man judges all things, but he himself is judged by no one” [I Cor. II, 15].
Further concerning discernment, by way of example.
42. The first of these is like one who walks in a deep, dark, and gloomy night, whence, wandering and covered in impenetrable darkness, he not only does not see or discern himself, but does not even know where he is going or walking, as the Savior says: “He who walks in darkness does not know where he is going” [John XII, 35]. The second is like one who moves in a night that is clear and illuminated by the stars, whence, being slightly brightened by the twinkling of the stars, he walks little by little, often striking his feet against the stones of undiscerning-ness, and suffering frequent falls. This man, therefore, sees and discerns himself a little, but as if in a shadow, as it is written: “Awake, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine upon you” [Ephes. V, 14]. The third is like him who makes his way in a quiet night illuminated by the brightness of the moon; whence, being directed also by the lunar rays, he travels more unerringly and moves forward. He sees himself, as if in a mirror, and discerns at the same time those who are traveling with him, as it has been said: “You do well, paying attention to the law, as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts” [II Pet. I, 19]. The fourth is like him who walks at high noon, firm and most pure, illuminated by the shining rays of the sun; and therefore such a one sees himself sincerely in the solar light, and discerns, and judges others—or rather, indeed, all men, in accordance with the divine Apostle; and indeed, all things that occur to him from everywhere and in any way, walking himself without error and leading those who follow him without stumbling toward the true Light, and the Life, and the Truth, concerning whom it is also written: “You are the light of the world” [Matt. V, 14]. And the most divine Paul also says: “God who said light should shine out of darkness, he has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” [II Cor. IV, 6]. And the blessed D
David: “The light of thy countenance, O Lord, is signed upon us” [Ps. IV, 7]. And: “In thy light shall we see light” [Ps. XXXV, 10]. And the Lord: “I am the light of the world; he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life” [John VIII, 12].
On conversion and change in the individual, and on the eminent glory of humility.
43. We wish you to know this also: that even those who have attained to perfection through purification and illumination, in accordance with their powers—for there is no complete perfection in this imperfect age, but rather an incomplete perfection—do not always possess unchangeability with them, both because of natural infirmity and because of the opinion that sometimes creeps in. Indeed, they sometimes suffer changes and thefts for the sake of testing, and then again receive greater succors; and the Fathers define those who are contrary to these as being a portion of the wolves. For firmness and unchangeability are reserved for the age to come; but in the present, it is now a time of purity, peace, and divine consolation, and now a time of defilement, tempest, and sadness, and this is in proportion to each person’s manner of life and progress, and in accordance with the judgments of the Lord, which He alone knows; and indeed, so that through these things we may judge our own infirmity. “For blessed,” he says, “is he who knows his own infirmity, that we may not be confident in ourselves, according to Paul, but in Him who raises the dead” [cf. II Cor. I, 9]; and thus we may run continuously to God in humility, repentance, and confession. And the holy Isaac says: “Again and again do some happen to transgress, and yet by repentance they bring a remedy to their souls; and grace enters in unto them.” For in every reasonable nature, change has its place quite often. Changes attend every human being at all hours of his life; from these, one who has the power of discernment can understand this matter. And the trials which he experiences within himself every day can do much to make him wise, if he be vigilant: that he may observe himself in his intellect, and learn how great a change of gentle-mindedness and kindness his mind receives each day; and how, from its own peace, it is suddenly turned into confusion, when there is no cause from the place for it to be turned; and how he finds himself in great and unspeakable danger. And this is what the blessed Macarius wrote clearly, with much care and zeal, for the memory and instruction of the brethren, so that they might not fall into despair at the time of the change of contrary things, teaching that to those standing in the place of purity it happens that they fall—just as it happens to the air to grow cold—and this even without them being in carelessness or laxity. Nay rather, even when they are proceeding according to their order, falls occur to them, contrary to the aim of their own will. And continuing, he says: “What, then, is it now? Changes,” he says, “happen to every person just as they do to the air.” But understand that in each one. For nature is verily one. Do not believe that he is speaking of the weaker and more fragile
beings and only the smallest ones, and that, consequently, the perfect are free from change and stand unswervingly in one order, without impassioned thoughts, as the Euchites say. This is why he added, “in each one.” How then, O Macarius, is this so? Yet you yourself say: cold, and a little later, heat; and perhaps hail, and after a while, clear weather. And in our life it is likewise: war and the receiving of grace, and at times the soul lies in a tempest, and horrendous waves rise up against it. And again, a change occurs, with grace protecting and filling the heart with joy and divine peace, and with sensible and peaceful thoughts. These counsels of prudence he joins together, exhorting those who were previously brutish and impure, and he rouses them, saying: “If, therefore, after these counsels of prudence and gentleness, calamity follows, let us not be saddened nor despair.” And in the rest of grace, again, let us not become proud, but in the time of joy, let us accept affliction. And continuing, he says: “Know that all the saints were in this operation. As long as we are in this world, consolation abounds for us with afflictions. Therefore, daily and every hour, the proof of divine love is sought from you in the struggle and fight against temptations: which is that you not be saddened, nor be negligent in the struggle.” And thus your way is directed. “But he who wishes to be cast out from these and to decline from this, he is of the portion of the wolves.” O marvelous word of this man! C How in a few words he confirmed that oracle, and showed it to be full of meaning, and perfectly drove doubt from the mind of the reader! “But that man,” he says, “who declines from these, and is made a part of the wolves, wishes to walk upon an untrodden path, and has set it in his mind to gain this fate, and wishes to walk in private paths, not trodden by the Fathers.” And a little later: “Humility without works admits many sins: but works without humility are altogether useless.” And a little after: “As salt is to food, so is humility to every virtue; and it can crush the power of all sins; beyond it, it is necessary that we be saddened unceasingly according to the mind in humiliation and sorrow of judgment; and if we possess it, it makes us children of God; and without good works it presents us to God; and thus, without it, all our works are vain, and all virtues and all operations. But God desires the change of the mind.” And: “By the mind we become better: it alone can stand before God without help, and speak for us.” He says furthermore: “One of the saints said: When the sense of pride comes to you, saying to you: ‘Remember your virtues,’ say: ‘Elder, look to your fornication.’”
On penance, purity, and perfection
44. The perfection of every course is in these three things: in penance, and in purity, and in perfection. What then is penance? To leave behind former things and to be saddened over them. And what is meant by purity, in brief? The heart…
that is merciful over the whole of created nature. And what is perfection? A depth of humility, which is the leaving behind of all things, both visible and invisible—visible, that is, all sensible things; invisible, that is, those that are intelligible—and being free, furthermore, from the anxiety regarding them. Moreover, penance is a twofold death voluntarily undergone for all things. A merciful heart is a burning of the heart for the whole of creation, for men and for birds and for animals and for demons and for every creature. And again, as long as we are left in this world and in the flesh, even if we were to be raised up to the vault of the heavens, it is not possible for us to be without works and toil, or to be in a state of freedom from care; this is what perfection is. Pardon me; that which is beyond this is solicitation, that is to say, it is without reason. And Saint Maximus: “Philosophy according to virtue is naturally able to produce the tranquility of the mind, not nature; through which spiritual tranquility, the joy of divine grace enters into the mind.” And again: “He who has experienced the sorrow and pleasure of the flesh might be called proven, inasmuch as he has been tempted by the zeal or the weariness of carnal acts; but perfect is he who has mastered the pleasure or pain of the flesh by the virtue of reason; and he is entirely a victor who has maintained the habits of action and contemplation with steadfastness towards God. By these things, indeed, discernment is demonstrated to be greater than all virtues, so that in those in whom it is born, once they are illumined by the divine light, it is permitted to discern accurately both divine and human matters, and mystical and hidden visions. It is time, therefore, in order, to show you as much as I am able the beginning of the holy and deifying peace which we have announced, so that it may be manifest; and may God direct even these things which we are about to say.
Concerning the five operations of the first and, as it were, introductory peace of beginners: namely prayer, psalmody, reading, meditation, and manual labor.
45. Through these five operations, by which God is worshiped, the beginner in stillness ought to pass the day and night; namely, in prayer, that is to say, in the memory of the Lord Jesus Christ, continuously introduced [in another manuscript: invoked], as has been said before, through the breath of the nose into the heart gently, and again in this manner brought forth, with lips closed, without any other thought or imagination—which, through the temperate control of the belly, we say, of sleep and of other sensible things, is accomplished within the cell with sincere humility—in psalmody, in reading from the holy Psalter, the Apostle, and the holy Gospels, and from the writings of the God-bearing and holy Fathers, and especially the chapters on prayer and watchfulness, and in addition the other divine oracles of the Holy Spirit, in the laborious memory of sins of the heart, and in the meditation upon the judgment of God, or of death, or of punishment, or of delight, and the like; and in light manual labor, as a muzzle for sloth, and again to return [45 cont.] to prayer, even if...
the matter has force until the mind becomes accustomed to cast aside its own wandering easily through complete contemplation toward the Lord Jesus Christ, and through constant memory, and through a continuous inclination to the inward treasury, that is, the hidden space of the heart, and through firm rootedness. For the holy Isaac also writes: "Make haste to enter into thy treasury within, and thou shalt see the heavenly treasury; for this and that are one, and in one entry thou beholdest both." And the holy Maximus: "The heart directs the whole organ, and when grace has taken hold of the pastures of the heart, it governs all thoughts and members. For there is the mind, and all the thoughts of the soul; there, therefore, it behooves us to watch, whether the grace of the Holy Spirit has inscribed its laws." There—where? In the leading organ, in the throne of grace, where the mind is, and all the thoughts of the soul, that is to say, in the heart.
Whence those who desire to live in peace according to reason must begin, and what is the beginning, and the increase, and the advancement, and the perfection.
46. This is the work of the ancient monks, the first, and as it were introductory for those who choose to live in peace according to reason, beginning from the fear of God, and the fulfillment of all the deifying commandments according to their strength; from freedom from the cares of reasonable and unreasonable things, and above all from faith and from the utter flight of things contrary to it, and from a pure disposition toward Him who truly Is, as has been said; but as they grow in unashamed hope, and advance to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ, through prayer of the heart—pure, and becoming unwavering, and occurring through a complete, divinely inspired, and fervent love, and thus being perfected—through motionless and unceasing spiritual prayer, and through that which wells up from perfect love toward Him alone, by a direct ecstasy, and by the rapture and union of the highest object of desire, which is the unerring advancement and resurrection [or, uplifting] from action toward contemplation, which the ancestor of God, David, also suffered, and being changed by that blessed change, he cried out loudly: "I said in my ecstasy, Every man is a liar." And another of those who shone in the Old Testament: "Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither hath it entered into the heart of man, what God hath prepared for them that love Him." And the great Paul, concluding this, adds: "But to us God has revealed it through His Spirit; for the Spirit searcheth all things, even the deep things of God."
On the order of stillness for beginners.
47. The beginner, then, as we have said, must not constantly depart from his cell, nor converse with others, and must refrain from all outward looking, unless there is great necessity, and then with attention and safety, and rarely, as the divine Isaac says: "In everything, let this memory remain in thee, that the help which arises from guarding is better than the help which comes from works." And not only for beginners, but also for those who have already...
progressed, such things cause scattering and distraction, as the same holy Isaac says again, that "Rest harms only the young, but relaxation harms both the young and the old; and peace mortifies the external senses, but excites the internal movements; while external conversation does the opposite of these things, that is, it excites the external senses and mortifies the internal movements." And he indeed indicates action, or rather the way of peace, by these words; while the *Ladder* signifies him who acts and walks well along this path by what follows, writing: "The hesychast is one who strives to enclose the incorporeal in a bodily house, which is a most paradoxical thing; and the hesychast is he who said: 'I sleep, and my heart watcheth;' and he shuts indeed the door of the cell to the body, and the door of the tongue to speech, and the door of the spirit within." He is peaceful who strives to determine the incorporeal in a bodily house, which is worthy of the greatest praise; and peaceful is he who said: "I sleep, but my heart watcheth"; and he has indeed closed the door of the cell to the body, and the door of the tongue to sound, and within he has closed the door of the spirit.
Of prayer which is performed with attention and the vigilance of the heart, and of its operation.
48. Prayer which is performed with attention and vigilance within the heart, as has been said, without any other cogitation and imagination, clearly, is performed through these words: "Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God," and through the memory of the Lord Jesus Christ Himself, the mind is extended immaterially and utterance-lessly; but through the "Have mercy on me," it returns and is moved toward itself, as if unable to endure not praying for itself; but having progressed toward charity through experience, it is turned singular-ly toward the Lord Jesus Christ Himself, for it has received manifest persuasion of the second.
How the divine Fathers have delivered to us to say the prayer, and that it is done differently, and what prayer is.
49. Therefore, not all the divine Fathers appear to have delivered the prayer in its entirety; but one indeed [delivered it] whole, another half; another in part, and another in a different way, according to the powers and state of the one praying. And the divine Chrysostom indeed delivered it in its entirely, thus saying: "I exhort you, brethren, never to trample upon or despise the rule of prayer. For I once heard the Fathers saying: 'Who is that monk who would despise or trample upon the rule? But he ought, whether he eats, or drinks, or sits, or serves, or travels, or does any other thing, incessantly to cry out: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me,' so that this memory of the name of our Lord Jesus Christ may stir him to fight against the enemy. For the soul that uses force can find everything through memory, whether evil things or good things. But first it is permitted to see the evil within his heart, and then the good; for memory can stir the dragon, and memory can humble him; memory can detect the sin dwelling in us, and memory can destroy it and stir up all the power of the enemy in the heart, and memory can overcome and eradicate it by parts; so that the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, descending into the depths of the heart...
may humble the dragon that holds its pastures, and save and vivify the soul. Persistently, therefore, remain with the name of the Lord Jesus, that the heart may swallow the Lord, and the Lord the heart, and the two become one. But this task is not of one day, or two, but of much time; for much struggle and much time are needed, so that the enemy may be cast out, and Christ may dwell within. And again: "It is necessary to strengthen and rein in the mind, and put a bridle upon it, and to chastise every thought and every energy of the wicked one through the invocation of our Lord Jesus Christ." And where the body stands, there let the mind also be, that between God and the heart nothing else may be found as an intermediate wall, or a partition darkening the heart, and separating the mind from God. If at any time it carries the mind away, you must not linger on the thoughts, so that the assent to these thoughts may not be reckoned to his account on the day of judgment before the Lord, when God shall judge the hidden things of men. Be at leisure, therefore, always, and cleave to the Lord our God, until He has mercy upon you, and seek nothing else, but only mercy from the Lord of glory. And seeking mercy, seek it with a humble and wretched heart, and cry from morning until evening, and if possible, even the whole night, "Lord Jesus Christ, have mercy on me," and force your mind to this task even unto death; for this task requires much violence, because "narrow is the gate and strait the way which leads to life, and the violent enter into it"; for the kingdom of heaven belongs to the violent. I exhort you, therefore, do not separate your hearts from God, but cleave to Him and guard them always and everywhere with the memory of our Lord Jesus Christ, until the name of the Lord is planted within in the heart, and it thinks of nothing else, so that Christ may be magnified in you. C Before this, however, the great Paul, putting forward the Lord Jesus, says: "If you confess with your mouth the Lord Jesus, and believe in your heart that God has raised Him from the dead, you will be saved; for with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation." And again: "No one says that Jesus is Lord, except by the Holy Spirit." And he adds "by the Holy Spirit," that is, when the heart receives the power of the Holy Spirit, through which it also prays, which belongs to those who have made progress, and who have become rich in Christ, who manifestly dwells within them. Consistently with this, the holy Diadochus also says: "The mind demands from us, when we have blocked all its exits with the memory of God, a task which can satisfy its diligence. Therefore, we must give it this: 'Lord Jesus,' solely for the entire operation, which tends toward the goal. For no one can say the Lord Jesus, except by the Holy Spirit. But let him contemplate this word strictly in his inner treasuries, lest he wander into some fantasies. For whoever meditates on that glorious and lovable name continuously in the profound heart, they are able also to perceive the light of the mind at times; for by strict study, having been occupied with thought, it burns up all the filth emerging in the soul. For God...
He says, is a consuming fire; whence also the Lord finally calls the soul to great love of His glory. For that glorious and lovable name, abiding through the memory of the mind in the warmth of the heart, begets in us a habit of completely loving His goodness, with nothing left to hinder it. For this is the precious pearl, which anyone having sold all his wealth can purchase, and have inexpressible joy at its finding. The holy Hesychius, writing thus about Christ Jesus, adds: "The soul flying through death in the air to the gates of heaven, having Jesus with it and above it, will not fear its enemies there, but with confidence, as now, so then at the gates will speak to them, provided that at its exit it does not cease to cry out to the Lord Jesus Christ day and night; and He Himself will perform its vengeance speedily, according to His own and God’s promise, which He expressed concerning the judge of iniquity; and I say to you truly, He will do it both in the present life and after its soul has departed from the body." And the one of the Ladder, saying Jesus alone: "With the name of Jesus whip the enemies; for there is no weapon stronger in heaven and on earth," and he adds nothing else. And again he says: "Let the memory of Jesus be united to your breath, and then you will know the benefit of stillness."
Item, that not only among the aforementioned holy Fathers, but also from the very foremost of the apostles, Peter, and Paul, and John, are found the words of the holy and life-giving prayer somehow mystically signified in the Spirit.
V. Not only by these aforementioned God-bearing Fathers, and those after them, will one find such words of holy prayer somehow mystically signified, but certainly before them, even from the first and foremost apostles themselves, we mean those around Peter, and Paul, and John. For one says, as we have mentioned before: "No one can say 'Lord Jesus' except in the Holy Spirit," and another: "Every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is of God." And the chief of the disciples of Christ, to the question directed by the Savior and Master to the apostles themselves, "Who do people say that I am?" bringing forward that most blessed confession, answered: "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God." For this reason also those who came after them, our glorious instructors, and rather those who pursued the life without yoke, and the eremitic and quiet life, gathered such utterances scattered here and there, and part by part, in these three pillars of the holy Church, proclaimed in advance as divine voices put forth according to revelation in the Holy Spirit, and for these three men worthy of faith, as most things declare and testify, "In the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall be established," those heavenly men, gathering them into one and with the Spirit dwelling in them,
. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . climantes, they have announced the column of prayer, and have commended those who followed them to occupy and keep it in the same manner. Observe, therefore, the order and consequence, which stands out greatly with divine wisdom. One, indeed, says "Jesus," another "Jesus Christ," but the third "Christ the Son of God," as if one were following another, and they held together among themselves by the concord and bond of such words. For you may see each one of them taking the voice which is at the end in the next, and the matter being so regarding the third. And you will see the same regarding the addition of the Holy Spirit. For the blessed Paul saying: "No one can say 'Lord Jesus,' except in the Holy Spirit," at this final word, namely the Holy Spirit, he who has a voice like thunder, John, began in his usage, saying: "Every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is of God." They have placed these before all things, not spontaneously nor of themselves, but led by the hand of the most holy Spirit. For indeed the confession of the divine Peter was made through revelation in the Holy Spirit. "For all these," he says, "works one and the same Spirit, dividing to each one as He wills." And thus, therefore, the context and stitching of the life-giving thread of prayer, having been applied and unbroken, has been most wisely and learnedly constructed, and has reached down to us, keeping the same method.
The addition, therefore, of this voice, "Have mercy on me," the Fathers who followed them have made and ordered with these saving words, namely "Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God," and especially because of those who are still infants in virtue, namely the beginners and the imperfect. For those who have progressed and are perfect in Christ, through each one of those oracles, "Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God," or even sometimes through the sole invocation of "Jesus," are sufficient for themselves, and they embrace and apply it as the universal work of prayer, and through it are filled with a joy ineffable and surpassing all sight and hearing. And thus, therefore, these most blessed men, dwelling outside the flesh and the world, imposing silence upon their senses, raised by the gift and grace into the most ardent and happiest love for the Divine which dwells within them, are cleansed and illuminated, and are made perfect, inasmuch as they look accurately at the supernatural and eternal and uncreated grace of the supersubstantial Godhead, in the part of a pledge, obscurely as in a mirror, contented by memory alone and meditation, as has been said, with one or another appellation of the Word of God and Man, through this they are lifted up into raptures and knowledge and revelation, which they experience in the Spirit without speech. In manifestation of which and most evident faith, our sweetest and most loving Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, whose words, acts, and deeds are, according to Him, Spirit and life to us, clearly revealed, saying: "Without me you can do nothing." And, "If you ask anything in my name, I will do it." And those things which follow and have been handed down to us.
That it is permitted even for beginners to pray at times with the entire words of the prayer, and at times with a part of it, yet always within the heart, and that one should not continually change the words.
51. It is permitted even for beginners to pray at times with the entire words of the prayer, and at times with a part of it, yet within the heart and perpetually; for according to the holy Diadochus, "He who always dwells in his own heart departs from the things of this beautiful life." For one who walks in the Spirit cannot know the desires of the flesh, since he henceforth conducts his walk within the fortress of the virtues, having these virtues as it were the gatekeepers of the citadel of purity. Therefore, the schemes of the demons become henceforth ineffectual against him. And the holy Isaac also writes: "The heart of him who keeps watch over his soul every hour rejoices in revelations; and he who gathers his contemplation within himself beholds the radiance of the Spirit." Whoever has loathed all distraction beholds his Master within the depths of his heart, and one must not continually change the phrases of prayer, lest the mind, having become accustomed to constant change and shifting—to a kind of instability and wavering—remain unsteady and unfruitful, like trees that are constantly moved and transplanted.
That the fruit of praying within the heart also requires much time, and struggle, and violence, and that every good thing is accomplished through much toil and time.
52. And this praying always within the heart, and likewise the things that go beyond it, are not accomplished simply, or as it happens, or through brief and momentary toil. Even if this is indeed found rarely in some by an ineffable providence, it requires much time, and labor, and struggle of both body and soul, and much violence, and intensified effort for its accomplishment. For according to the portion of the gift of grace that we hope to be granted in participation, it behooves us to exert our own struggles in proportion to our strength, and to measure out the hours; and this is, according to the holy Fathers, to cast out the enemy from the pastures of the heart and to establish Christ clearly within it. For the holy Isaac also says: "He who wishes to see the Lord makes an effort to cleanse his heart with the uninterrupted memory of God, and thus in the radiance of his intellect he shall behold the Lord at every hour." And the holy Barsanuphius says: "Unless the inward operation united with God helps a man, he toils in vain in outward things. For the inward operation brings purity along with the labor of the heart; and purity, in turn, [brings] true
stillness of heart, and this stillness brings humility, and humility makes man a dwelling-place of God. And from this dwelling-place, the demons are cast out along with the passions, and thus man becomes a temple of God, full of sanctification, full of illumination, and of purity and grace. Blessed, then, is he who beholds his own Lord in the inner sanctum of the heart, pouring out his prayer with weeping before His goodness. And the pious John of Karpathos [says]: "Much struggle and time is needed in prayers, so that we may find in the undisturbed state of the mind another heavenly space within the heart, where Christ dwells, as the Apostle says: B 'Or do you not realize that Jesus Christ is in you? Unless indeed you fail to meet the test!' And the great Chrysostom [says]: "Incessantly cleave to the name of the Lord Jesus, that the heart may swallow the Lord, and the Lord the heart, and the two may become one." But this work is not of one day or two, but of long and much time; for much struggle and time is needed so that the enemy may be cast out and Christ may dwell within. And so much for these things; let the discourse return to what was proposed in order.
Concerning prayer of the heart that is not [yet] pure, and how one comes to pure and constant prayer.
53.
