From adhering to the aforementioned method of interior and pure and constant prayer—even if it is not perhaps otherwise pure and constant—it is manifest that the one who struggles, despite the phantasies and thoughts that obstruct his prayer, comes to a habit of praying without violence and inconstancy, and [prays] purely and truly. That is, by keeping (the mind) in the heart, and not with force and contempt through the inspiration introducing and again extracting [the mind], but by always adhering to it and thus praying perpetually. For the holy Hesychios says: "He who does not have prayer free from thoughts has no weapon for battle; and by prayer I mean that which is ceaselessly active in the inner sanctum of the heart, so that by the invocation of Jesus Christ, the one who fights in secret may be scourged and the enemy may be burned." And again: "Blessed is he who is thus joined to the prayer of Jesus in his understanding, and invokes Him unceasingly in his heart, just as air is united to our bodies, or as flame to wax." And again: "And as the sun, passing over the earth, makes the day, so the holy and venerable name of the Lord Jesus, shining continuously in the understanding, will generate unnumbered sun-like thoughts."
Concerning constant and pure prayer of the heart, and the ardor born from it.
54. This is and is called prayer of the heart—pure and constant, as has been said—from which a certain ardor is born in the heart, according to that: "My heart was warmed within me, and in my meditation, a fire shall be kindled." (Ps. XXXVIII, 4).
This is the fire which the Lord Jesus Christ came to cast into the earth of our hearts, which previously bore thorns because of the passions, but now by grace brings forth the Spirit, as our Lord Jesus Christ says: "I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what will I, if it be already kindled?" (Luc. XII, 49). This fire, having once warmed and burned those about Cleopas, caused them to cry out to one another in ecstasy: "Was not our heart burning within us in the way?" (Luc. XXIV, 32). The great John of Damascus also says, in one of his hymns to the all-holy Theotokos: "The fire which lies hidden in the heart draws me to sing of the love of the Virgin."
St. Isaac also writes: "From intense labor is born the immeasurable warmth, which is kindled in the heart from the ardent desires that have newly come upon the intellect. This labor and watchfulness thin out the mind with their warmth and provide it with vision; and as it progresses, the outpouring of tears is born from this warmth which arises from the grace of contemplation. After a little, the soul receives peace of thoughts from the unceasing tears. From the peace of thoughts, it is raised to the purity of the mind; through the purity of the mind, man comes to see the mysteries of God."
And after a few words: "After these things, the mind arrives at seeing revelations and signs, just as the prophet Ezekiel saw." And further: "Tears and the beating of the head in prayer, and rolling about with warmth, awaken the warmth of their sweetness within the heart; and with praised ecstasy, the heart flies toward God and cries: 'My soul hath thirsted after the strong, living God; when shall I come and appear before the face of God?' (Ps. XLI, 3), and so on."
And [the author] of the Ladder: "Fire having settled in the heart, it has awakened prayer; this having been aroused and caught up into heaven, a descent of fire in the upper room of the soul has come to pass."
Further: "Who then is the faithful and wise monk, who has kept his own warmth unquenchable, and until his departure, day by day, adding fire to fire, and warmth to warmth, and desire to desire, and zeal to zeal, has not ceased?"
And St. Elias the Ecdicus: "When the soul, having desisted from external things, is joined to the Soul, then, like a flame surrounding it—just as fire [affects] iron—it renders it entirely ignited. It is indeed the same soul, but no longer touchable. For the ignited iron can no longer be grasped."
And further: "Blessed is he who in this life is deemed worthy to be seen as such; and having seen that his own sculpted form, by nature earthen, has by grace been made fiery!"
That warmth also has a different origin, and the one from pure prayer of the heart is more sovereign.
55. Know also that such warmth has the origin of its existence in us in various and manifold ways.
And this is evident from the oracles of the saints set forth, but we hesitate to say [it comes] from the action itself; yet there is a way in which the warmth resulting from pure prayer of the heart is more sovereign than these. Progressing continuously with it, and increasing, it brings one to the subsistent light, that is, it renders the one in such a state enlightened in a subsistent manner, according to the Fathers.
What is the work of the warmth of the heart?
56. Such warmth immediately drives away the things that hinder the prior, pure prayer from being accomplished perfectly. For our God is a fire, and a fire consuming the wickedness of the demons and of our passions. For the holy Diadochus also says: "When the heart receives the arrows of the demons with a certain sharp pain, such that it imagines it is the enemy himself bringing these weapons, then the soul, as if beginning to be cleansed, hates the passions with pain." Therefore, if one does not suffer greatly over the impudence of sin, one will not be able to rejoice richly in the goodness of righteousness. He, then, who wishes to purify his heart, let him inflame it perpetually with the memory of Jesus Christ, having this alone as his meditation and unceasing work. For it is not the case that those who wish to cast out their own corruption ought to pray at one time and not at another; but rather, they must always be occupied with prayer in the custody of the mind, even if they should happen to be lodging somewhere outside the houses of prayer. For just as he who wishes to purify gold, if he allows the fire beneath the furnace to be extinguished even for a little while, causes the material to become hard again; so too he who remembers God at one time, but at another does not, loses through idleness what he seems to have acquired through prayer. It is, however, the characteristic of a man who is a lover of virtue to use the memory of God to consume the earthly element of the heart, so that in this way, with the evil being gradually consumed by the fire of the memory of the good, the soul may return perfectly to its natural brightness with greater glory. And so, the mind remaining in the heart without hindrance, prays purely and without error, according to the holy one who says: "Then is prayer true and unerring, when the mind guards the heart while praying." And the holy Hesychius also writes: "This is a monk who is truly such, he who perfects watchfulness, and thus he is truly sober, who is a monk in the heart."
Concerning the longing and love that arises from fervent attention and prayer.
57. In such warmth, and with attention and prayer—that is, pure prayer—there is born in the heart a desire and divine love and charity toward the Lord Jesus Christ, who is always being remembered, as it is written: "Young maidens have loved me, they have drawn me," and that "I am wounded with love." And the holy Maximus also says: "All the virtues cooperate with the mind toward divine love, but most of all
pure prayer. For by this the mind, taking wing toward God, is established outside of all things."
On tears of the heart; and further on divine desire and love.
58. From this heart, a tear for the most part flows forth, cleansing and fattening him who has acquired these things through charity, but not softening and drying them. For this is what they work: the one from divine fear, and the other from divine love, through an intense and unrestrained desire and love for the remembered Lord Jesus Christ. And the soul, inspired, cries out: "You have charmed me with desire, O Christ, and have changed me with your divine love." And: "You are the whole, O Savior, sweetness; you are all desire and yearning; you are wholly beyond comprehension; you are wholly indescribable beauty." And with Paul, the herald of Christ, it cries out: "The charity of God compasses us," and: "Who shall separate us from the charity of Christ? Shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or hunger, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword?" And again: "I am sure that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature shall be able to separate us from the charity of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord."
Exhortation not to seek anything beyond measure; and also an incitement to the continuous memory of our Lord Jesus Christ in the heart.
59. If, therefore, one is to be deemed worthy of these things, and of all that follows—which it is not timely to speak of now—do not seek, it says, for what pertains to the season before the season. And good is not good when it is not done well. And according to the holy Mark, it is not profitable to know things that come later before the performance of things that come earlier; for knowledge puffs up on account of idleness, but charity edifies by enduring all things. One must hasten and always strive, as has been said, to carry the memory of the Lord Jesus Christ continuously in the depth of the heart, and not outwardly or superficially, as the same blessed Mark also says concerning this: "Unless the inmost and hidden and sincere space of our heart be opened through universal and intellectual hope, it is not possible to know firmly Him who dwells within, nor to know whether our rational sacrifices have been accepted or not."
On ardent zeal, and the divine appearance within us, and the substantial illumination of grace.
60. For thus one will readily turn away, not only from evil works, but also from passionate thoughts and unseemly fantasies, as it is written: "Walk in the spirit, and you shall not fulfill the desires of the flesh." Nay rather, he will depart from every thought and every fantasy, as burning them up with an ardent zeal for virtue, so to speak, and expelling every act of malice, whether through the senses or through the mind, which previously operated within him, together with the leaders of these things, the demons who rejoice in alien evil.
Terrible is he to the demons and beloved of God and His angels, who with burning zeal eradicates the thorns planted within him by the enemy. And he will reach a state of progress so as to have from this a certainty of the love for Him, and of the manifest appearance, and indwelling of the substantial and most divine light of grace. Or, if you wish to express it this way, he will quite brightly run back to that nobility and spiritual adoption given to us from above through the grace of baptism. And again, holy Isaac says: «This is Jerusalem, and the kingdom of God, which is hidden within us according to the word of the Lord. This place is the cloud of the glory of God, into which only the pure in heart shall enter to behold the face of their own Master.» Only let him not seek the appearance of God, lest he receive the one who is truly darkness, and pretends to be light.
On divine operation, and that which is contrary.
61. When, however, his mind sees light not seeking it, let him not accept it immediately, nor yet reject it, as the holy Mark says, for «There is an operation of grace unknown to the infant. And there is another [operation] of malice, very similar to the truth. It is good for those who are not erring not to contemplate such things, nor to curse them for the sake of truth; but in all things to take refuge in God through hope. For He Himself knows what is useful in both cases; but let him ask the one who has grace and power before God to teach him, and to discern.»
On the illuminated and unerring master.
62. And if he finds one who can teach, not only as he has known from the divine Scripture, but as he himself has also blessedily experienced the divine illumination, thanks be to God. If not, it is better not to accept [it], but to take refuge in God in humility, deeming himself unworthy of such high merit and contemplation with a sincere heart; just as it has been said, and from those things which will be said, and as we have been initiated, by the grace of Christ, from lips that do not lie, moved and speaking by the Holy Spirit; and from the God-inspired Scriptures and from personal experience.
On true and false light, that is, on divine and evil light.
63. For even if, in some of their writings, our glorious Fathers give us the signs of unerring light and of that which is of deception, as indeed the thrice-blessed Paul did when he spoke to a disciple of his who asked him about such a matter, that "the light of the opposing power is like fire, smoky, and conforms to material fire; and when a soul that is a friend of virtue and pure sees it, it is without joy and rejects it. But the light of the good is good, and most pleasing, and pure; and as it comes it sanctifies, and fills the soul with light and joy and serenity, and makes it gentle and merciful." And others say similar things. But nevertheless, you hear the aforesaid things also from one delivering them by living voice,
and so you shall likewise hear about this in due time; for now is not the time.
On base and noble phantasia, and how one must approach them.
A 64. Since a little while ago we mentioned phantasia, and base phantasia, it is most useful, as it seems to us, to speak briefly about it, or rather about all phantasia, as far as is possible. For this cursed thing resists the pure and heart-felt prayer, and the singular and unerring activity of the mind, with great intensity. Whence the divine Fathers express themselves many times about it and against it. This multi-form phantasia, then—like the fabled Daedalus, and many-headed like the Hydra—has been called by the saints a kind of bridge for the demons. For through it, the murderous spirits pass across and cross over, communicating and mingling with the soul, making it a hive of drones and a dwelling-place of fruitless and passionate thoughts. This phantasia, then, is to be rejected altogether; unless perhaps you wish, for the sake of repentance, and contrition, and mourning, and humility—and above all, for the meditation on the things that are—to set a noble phantasia against a base one, and to weigh them against each other; and by mixing that with this, and acting in opposition, and like a deserter having basely cast off his shield, having fallen defeated and cast down, you may be able to celebrate a triumph. And so, by acting in this way, you would be the author not only of causing no harm, but even of profit to yourself, as one who directs his own affairs with steady judgment, destroying the base phantasia with a noble one, and striking and killing these enemies with the weapons of their opposites, just as divine David of old did to Goliath.
That not only base phantasia, but also noble phantasia, is to be rejected by the saints for pure prayer and for the simple and singular activity of the mind.
65. This, however, is a struggle for those who are still infants, that is, for beginners. For those who have advanced in time cast away the base phantasia altogether along with the noble one, and make them vanish—burning them up and dissolving them like wax before the face of fire—because of pure prayer, and the unformed stripping away and nakedness of the mind from all things, for the sake of the simple approach to God; or if you will, for the sake of receiving [Him], and of that unconfigured and singular union. For the holy Hesychius also says: "Every thought is a phantasia in the mind of some sensible thing." For the Assyrian, that is the spirit, is not able to deceive in any other way unless he uses the things that are sensible and familiar to us. And the holy Diadochus: "Since every thought enters the heart through the phantasia of certain sensible things, then the blessed light of the Godhead shines upon it when it has completely found rest from all things, and has become unconfigured from them, if indeed the splendor of that Light appears to the pure mind through the privation of all thoughts." And the great Basil:
"Just as the Lord does not dwell in temples made by hands, so neither does He dwell in certain configurations and mental images." For these are cast forth as barriers to the soul that has been corrupted, which is not able to gaze purely toward the truth, but is still held by the mirror and the enigma. And the divine Evagrius: "God is said to sit there, where He is known; hence the pure mind is called the throne of God." The thought of God, therefore, will not be found in the thoughts that configure the mind, but in thoughts that do not configure it. Wherefore, he who prays must be separated entirely from the thoughts that configure the mind; for the mind will be configured in one way when it contemplates the mind, and will be disposed in another way when it contemplates the Word of God. B From this we learn how spiritual knowledge detaches the mind from the thoughts that configure it, and, rendering it unconfigured, presents it to God. And holy Maximus in the *Scholia* on the great Dionysius: "Phantasy is one thing, and thought—that is, the concept—is another. For they arise from different faculties, and they differ in the nature of their movement. For thought is a kind of efficacy and action; but phantasy is a passion and a figurative representation that brings news of something sensible, or as of something sensible. And sense perception perceives beings according to an obtuse formation. But the mind touches—that is, perceives—beings in another way, and not as sense perception does. Concerning, then, the corporeal or the spiritual, in which we previously said the senses also exist, the movement is passive and figurative. But judgment and intellect are to be granted to the soul and to the mind. Imagination, therefore, must be removed from this intellect of the mind. Imagination is divided into three parts: the first is the capacity for imaging that provides the sensible form to the things that cause the perception; the second is that which fashions a type from the residues remaining from these things, which does not have images resting upon anything, which they properly call 'phantastic'; the third is that in which all pleasure and the imagination of what is thought to be good, or the sadness of that which seems evil, is composed. No phantasy, therefore, as has been said, has a place in God; for He is, once and for all, simply beyond thought and transcends it. And again the great Basil: "The mind that is not dissipated upon external things, nor scattered toward the world through the senses, returns to itself; and through itself it ascends to the thought of God, and, being illuminated by that beauty, it receives a forgetting of its own nature." You, therefore, knowing these things, strive at all hours to pray to God without phantasy, without figure, and without form, as a whole with the whole, with a pure mind and with a pure soul; for holy Maximus also speaks thus.
Concerning the mind, soul, and heart that are pure and perfect.
§ 66. Concerning the pure mind.—A pure mind is that which has been separated from ignorance, and is illuminated by the divine light.
Concerning a pure soul.
—A pure soul is that which has been liberated from the passions, and is incessantly gladdened by divine love.
Concerning a pure heart.
—A pure heart is that which presents itself to God entirely without form and unconfigured; it is ready to be impressed only by His own types, through which He is naturally accustomed to manifest Himself. Following these, let the following also be added.
Concerning a perfect mind.
—A perfect mind is that which, through true faith, has known the One who cannot be penetrated, and has contemplated His works [i.e., the universe]; and has received from God, as far as is possible for a human being, the comprehensive knowledge of the providence and judgment that are in them.
Concerning a perfect soul.
—A soul is perfect whose passive faculty has inclined entirely toward God.
Concerning a perfect heart.
—A perfect heart is, perhaps, called that which has no natural movement of any kind toward anything whatsoever; in it, as if on a polished tablet, because of its extreme simplicity, God arrives and inscribes His own laws.
Concerning the pure [mind].
—Furthermore, to cleanse the mind, according to the holy Diadochus, belongs to the Holy Spirit alone; furthermore, to make the mind stand still, according to the [i] Climax [/i], belongs to the Holy Spirit alone. The holy Nilus also says: "If anyone wishes to see the state of the mind, let him divest himself of all thoughts, and then he will see it appearing like a sapphire or a heavenly color." And again: "The state of the mind is an intellectual height similar to a heavenly color, to which the light of the most holy Trinity comes at the time of prayer." And the holy Isaac [says]: "When the mind has stripped off the old man and put on the new man of grace, then it will see its own purity to be similar to the heavenly hue, which was named the place of God by the council of the children of Israel when He appeared to them on the mountain." Thus, therefore, by acting as has been said—that is, by praying purely, without fantasy, and without forms—you will be following in the footsteps of the saints. But if not, you will become a visionary instead of a hesychast, and instead of grapes you will harvest thorns. May this not happen to you!
How the prophets had visions.
67. If any assume that the visions, configurations, and revelations of the prophets occurred through fantasy and natural sequence, let them know that they have wandered far from the right goal and the truth. For the prophets—and now our mystagogues—did not see and have visions of what they saw and envisioned through some natural operation, order, or fantasy, but divinely and beyond nature, being configured and having visions by the ineffable power and grace of the Holy Spirit, as the great Basil says: "By an ineffable power they have visions, and having a mind that is undistracted and pure, they have as it were the Word of God resounding within them." And again: "The prophets saw, in the Spirit who directed them, the types..."
of the governing mind." And the Theologian Gregory says: "This (that is, the Holy Spirit) operated previously in the angelic and celestial powers." And a little later: "Then in the Fathers and the prophets: some of whom represented God to themselves and knew Him, while others foretold the future; they had the governing mind molded by the Spirit, and were present to future things as if they were actually there."
Still further concerning phantasies, and the many and various contemplations.
68. If there are some who still doubt, as they accept phantasies and many and various contemplations, and resist us—thinking that they are adhering to the footsteps of the saints, and contending that the Theologian means that God is only shadowed forth by the mind, not from those things that are in Him, but from those things that are around Him, by a phantasy gathered from one thing to another into one certain image of truth, and so on; and that the divine Maximus says that the mind cannot become without passion from actions alone, unless it receives many and various images; and that similarly other saints say things equal to these—let such persons know that these words of those blessed ones do not refer to the operation which is according to reception and the grace of knowledge and vision, which through experience itself joins man to God, but rather to that which is through effort [conatum], namely, that which proceeds from wisdom and from that contemplation which gathers together the analogies and harmonies of things, and inclines in some way, albeit obscurely, to the thought of God—which is easy of access and thought for the many, or rather for all. So that whoever examines such oracles of the saints with reflection will clearly perceive that it was written: "From the greatness and beauty of created things, the Creator is proportionately perceived" [Wisd. 13:5], that is, from that profane, verbose, vain, and laborious knowledge of the world. For that, as an obscure handmaid, and one puffed up with learned sophistical and demonstrative thought, not following evangelical faith and humility and true assent, is driven far from the sacred doors. Our discourse now, however, is about the perfect and substantial illumination, just as the chosen apostles who, ascending the mountain of Tabor with Jesus, underwent an ineffably beautiful and truly blessed transformation, and were accounted worthy to behold the invisible kingdom and Divinity, their sense of sight having been prepared for something more divine—that is, having been made spiritual by the right hand of the all-holy Spirit. For as far as the east is from the west, and heaven from earth, and as the soul excels the body, by so much does the operation and grace through reception excel that which is through effort. The latter, to be sure—that which is through effort—is profane, as we have said, and has its progress through the well-ordered motions of things, and the order and collection of images following one from another, and is extended to God in faith. The former, however—that which is through reception—is accustomed to be produced immediately by God Himself, substantially within the heart; and sometimes it even makes the body a participant in its own illumination and most divine light, which is above thought, by a supernatural illumination of the heart.
according to the most wise Maximus, not generating the unbegotten deification. For this saint says: "I call unbegotten deification that illumination which comes to pass according to the essential form of the Divinity; which has no generation, but an inconceivable manifestation in those who are worthy." The great Dionysius also speaks in harmony with what has been said: "One must know that our mind possesses a power for thinking, by which it perceives intelligible things; but it also possesses a union which transcends the nature of the mind, by which it is joined to things that are beyond itself." And the holy Isaac says: "We possess two psychic eyes, as the Fathers say, and the usefulness of the contemplation through each is not the same. For with one eye we see the things hidden in natures, that is, the power of God, and His wisdom, and His providence towards us, which is perceived from the holiness of His governance towards us; and with the other eye we behold the glory of His holy nature, whenever God deigns to lead us into spiritual mysteries." And the divine Diadochus says: "Wisdom and knowledge are gifts of the one Holy Spirit, as are all divine gifts, but each has its own proper energy. Wherefore the Apostle testifies that to one is given wisdom, and to another knowledge, by the same Spirit. For knowledge unites man to God by experience, without moving the soul to reasonings about things. Therefore, some of those who pursue the monastic life are indeed illuminated by it in sense, but they do not arrive at divine reasonings. But wisdom, if it be given to someone with fear (and this is rare), manifests the very energies of knowledge; since the one is accustomed to illuminate by energy, the other by reason. And prayer, along with much tranquility and complete freedom from care, brings knowledge. But the unvain study of the oracles of God brings wisdom, and first the grace of the God who gives." And furthermore, the holy Maximus says in the Scholia: "The well of Jacob is Scripture; the water is the knowledge which is in Scripture; the deep is the difficult contemplation of the Scriptural enigmas; the drawing is the instruction through the letters of the divine Word, which the Lord did not have, since He was the Word Himself, and He gave to those who believe not the knowledge from instruction and meditation, but the ever-flowing, spiritual wisdom from grace, which never ceases, bestowing it upon the worthy. For the drawing, that is to say the instruction, receiving the smallest part of knowledge, leaves the whole, being unable by any reason to grasp it. But knowledge according to grace has the whole, and without meditation, it brings forth such wisdom as is appropriate for men, for various needs." And again the holy Diadochus: "Our mind, for the most part, is moved with difficulty toward prayer; because, indeed, the volitional virtue is too narrow and constricted; but theology freely offers itself, because divine contemplation is broad and unconstrained. But let us not give ourselves the will to say many things, and let us not think to fly beyond measure, for cheerfulness, prayer, and psalmody...
and the reading of the holy Scriptures, to which we devote our time, should not allow us to neglect the discipline of learned men, the faith of whom is known through their writings. And while doing this, let us not permit the mind to mix its own words with the words of grace, nor to be distracted by vainglory, dispersed by excessive joy and talkativeness; but let us guard it far from every fantasy at the time of contemplation, and let us cultivate in it, from this, all tearful thoughts. For the one who rests in times of quiet, and who delights especially in the sweetness of prayer, not only remains free from the aforementioned faults, but is more and more renewed, so that he may cast himself vividly and without labor into divine thoughts by degrees, and abound in the knowledge of discernment with much humility. It must be known, however, that prayer excels every latitude; but it belongs only to those who are filled in every sense and faith with the grace of God. Have you heard? There is, he says, a prayer surpassing all latitude, which belongs only to those who, within and in the heart, in every sense and faith, are substantially and supernaturally flooded with the divine light of grace. The holy Isaac calls this "unsealed memory," meaning formless and imageless and simple. And other holy Fathers speak of it in other ways.
On the Five Powers of the Soul; and likewise also concerning the fantasies peculiar to the soul and the mind, and that it is necessary to flee entirely from fantasy, and figures, and types, and forms, in pure prayer and in the simple and unified operation of the mind.
69. But, since it has been demonstrated that the soul can imagine not only from demons but also naturally from itself through its five powers—namely the mind, the intellect, opinion, fantasy, and sense, just as the body has five senses: sight, smell, hearing, taste, and touch—and since fantasy is, as we have said, one of the soul's powers through which the soul is possessed of the faculty of imagining, it is necessary to govern and temper it well in those things which pertain to it, to incite those powers which most closely join it to God, both in the present age and in the future, and to direct them toward God; but as for the rest, it is necessary to care for them as is fitting, and to use them, and to do them. It must be inquired, therefore, what the Fathers have said concerning all these things, and what seems probable. And the holy Maximus says: "Since the soul by itself, that is, through its own substance, is rational and intellectual, and altogether subsists by itself. And if it subsists by itself, it will act by itself and according to itself naturally, and with the body, naturally thinking and reasoning, and never naturally granting rest to the spiritual powers inherent within it; for those things which by nature belong to any substance [remain]..."
as long as it exists and subsists, cannot be taken away. The soul, therefore, which from the moment it was created has always existed and subsisted through God who created it, always thinks, reasons, and knows—both by itself and with the body—through itself and its own nature. Thus, no argument will be found capable of separating the soul from those things that naturally belong to it, nor through the body, after its dissolution. Since, therefore, we know—and are instructed by the holy ones—that the mind and the intellect are moved and operate toward God both in the present age and in the one to come, while the other powers do so in the present age alone as being proper to this age, it is necessary, therefore, that the soul, as a skilled governor and naturally ruling over them, should not only in the present age, as we have said, direct and move its labor, mind, and thought completely and ardently toward God, and unite with Him during the time of pure, spiritual, single, and simple prayer; but it is necessary, I say, that it completely separate them from fantasy and from the other powers. For as Saint Nilus says: "The order of prayer is a state without passion, which with most ardent love snatches the philosopher and spiritual mind to spiritual height." For by acting in this way, the soul will preserve the dignity that befits and adorns it.
Further concerning the mind.
70. Likewise, it is necessary that the mind itself, being an indivisible, simple, and self-sufficient substance, clean and luminous, should keep and guard itself untainted and separated from that—namely, from fantasy; for the mind inherently possesses a natural power to return to itself, to attend to itself, and to be moved. For this is the rest of the mind, which is granted to it by divine grace, as the Climacicus says: "To make the mind rest is nothing but [the work] of the Holy Spirit." For even if, in that it is a power of the soul, the mind is moved and exists in some way from it, yet it is and is called its eye, and it possesses its own natural power that is self-subsistent, as we have said. Therefore, when the mind remains disposed relative to the soul and its powers, it is then as a potential mind, and is called the natural man. But if it recovers its own natural, simple, and essential dignity—the splendor that is indivisible, self-sufficient, and self-governing—that is, if it is delivered from bodily and psychic natural relations and movements, and if it is deemed worthy to transition from being a potential mind to becoming a mind in act, that is, if it rises to the supernatural and spiritual man, then it always returns to itself without straying, and through itself ascends firmly and constantly to the thought of God. This thought has neither form nor figure, but is simple, as the Great Basil says: "The mind that is not scattered upon external things, nor diffused over the world by the senses, returns to itself, and through itself ascends to the thought of God; and, glowing and illumined by that beauty, it receives the knowledge of His nature." And thus, therefore, the image of God
and His likeness, being a mind, and through itself immediately and intellectually being united and joined to the divine, that is to say, to God. This operation is the motion in a circle, that is, the return and turning of the mind to itself, and its union, and the union through itself to God, which alone is truly unerring and faultless, as it is a union that is disengaged, immediate, beyond thought, and a vision beyond sight. And the great Dionysius says: “The motion of the soul is indeed circular, that is, its entry into itself from external things; and the simple involution of its intellectual powers, as in a circle, which provides it with unerringness, and turns it from many things from without, and gathers it first into itself, and then, having become uniform, unites it to the powers that are unified simply, and thus leads it to the Beautiful and Good, which is above all things that exist, and is one and the same, and unbegotten and immortal and eternal. But the soul is moved in a circle in as much as it is properly illuminated by divine knowledge; not mentally and unitively, but logically and periodically, and as though by mixed and transitive faculties. But the straight way is when it does not enter into itself, and is not moved by a single intellect (for that is posterior, as I said, to the motion in a circle), but proceeds to things around it, and is led from external things, as from various complex and manifold symbols, to simple and unified contemplation.” And the holy Maximus says: “Having received an immediate union with God, the mind is able to be entirely empty and free from thinking and from being thought of. When, therefore, it lets go of this faculty, thinking of something of those things that are after God, it is convicted of breaking the union that is above thought, through which, so long as it is with God, as though supernatural and by participation itself become God, it transgresses the law of its nature as an immovable end.” And again: “A pure mind has received a relationship regarding the Cause in a union beyond thought, according to which, having brought to a rest its manifold natural motion and relationship toward things after the Cause, it clings only unknowably, having become, in the unspeakable outcome, partaker of the most blessed silence that is above thought, which neither speech nor thought can fully manifest, but only experience through participation, of those who have been deemed worthy of the enjoyments beyond thought; of which a sign, easy to see and manifest to all, is the soul’s total insensibility and rest regarding its disposition toward this present age.” To this, therefore, the mind, neither being assisted by the soul—that is, to be always moved toward God—nor by itself attaining and performing what is its own—that is, returning to itself and thus ascending disengagedly to the thought of God—or rather not reaping this from either part, but being joined to fantasy, is now henceforth made manifold, and is far distant from God.
Still concerning pure prayer.
A 71. And saint Nilus says: "Strive to keep your mind quiet and silent at the time of prayer, and thus you will be able to pray; furthermore, I will say my own [thought], which I have also said to the younger ones: Blessed is the mind which at the time of prayer has acquired a perfect formlessness." And saint Philotheos: "It is rare to find those who act in peace regarding reason; and it belongs only to those who strive to have divine joy and consolation within themselves through this thing perpetually." And the great Basil: "A good prayer is that which forms an effective thought of God in the soul; and this is the indwelling of God, namely, to hold God in oneself through memory, when the continuity of memory is not interrupted by earthly cares, nor is the mind disturbed by unexpected passions, but the lover of God, escaping all these, departs toward God."
That the apatheia of the mind is one thing, and true prayer another, which is even greater.
72. It must be known, therefore, this also, that, if even according to saint Maximus, "The mind cannot become free from passion through action alone without desire, unless many and varied contemplations receive it," yet again, according to the most divine Nilus, it is possible for one who has become free from passion not to pray truly, but to be made manifold, and to be far distant from God. For this Father says concerning such a matter thus: "Even if the mind is above bodily contemplation, it has not yet contemplated the perfect place of God; for it can be in the knowledge of thoughts, and be made manifold toward it." And further: "He who has attained apatheia does not yet pray truly; for he can be in mere thoughts, and be distracted by their histories, and be far distant from God." And further: "Not because the mind lingers in the mere thoughts of things, has it already reached the place of prayer; for it can be in the contemplation of things and chatter in their arguments; which, even if they are mere words, but as theorems belonging to things, they mold the mind, and lead it far away from God." And the one of the Ladder also says: "If the mind has learned to pray truly, these speak to the Lord dominantly and face to face, as those who speak words toward the king's ear." From these and such things, you can accurately understand the difference of both types, and by comparison their dissimilarity, since the one is through reception, and the other through effort. For of the one, the work is cares, and many and varied contemplations. D Of the other, the work is true prayer. Moreover, that the apatheia of the mind is one thing, and true prayer another. Furthermore, that he who possesses true prayer, according to the saints, is by every necessity also naturally disposed to possess a mind free from passion, but he who possesses only a mind free from passion has not been able to possess also true prayer. And these things are thus; but let the discourse return to what is proposed to us. Since not only those things which we have said, but also the memory of good and evil things itself, frequently are accustomed to mold the mind and lead it to fantasy;
of this—for this, too, we must speak a little—is the memory of both good and evil, which is wont, in a certain way, to present itself suddenly to the mind and provoke fantasy. It is therefore necessary to say a little about this as well.
Still concerning fantasies, and the images of the mind, and the signs of error and of truth; and what are the signs of error.
B 75. If you are living in stillness and wish to be alone with God alone, never receive any sensible or intelligible thing that you may see, whether inside or outside yourself, even if it be the supposed form of Christ, or an angel, or the appearance of a saint, or a manifestation of light that appears to the mind. But remain incredulous and heavy/wary toward it—even if it seems good—before you have asked those who are experienced, as we have said. For this is most useful, and most dear and acceptable to God. Always keep your mind without color, without form, without image, without quality, and without quantity. Cleave only to the words of prayer, and apply and contemplate them within the movements of the heart, as the Climacus says: “The beginning of prayer is to pursue the words throughout their preludes by means of soliloquy; the middle is to have the mind attentive to what is being said; and the end is a rapture toward the Lord.” And Saint Nilus likewise says: “The supreme prayer of the perfect is a certain rapture of the mind, a total withdrawal from all things that are according to the senses, with the spirit communing with God through ineffable groanings—He who looks upon the disposition of the heart as an inscribed book, opened up, showing its will in silent signs.” Just as Paul was rapt up to the third heaven, not knowing whether he was in the body or out of the body; similarly, Peter went up to the roof to pray and saw the vision of the sheet. The second prayer, after the first, is to pronounce the words while the mind follows with a subsequent compunction, knowing to whom it addresses its petition. But prayer that is interrupted and dissipated by bodily thoughts has departed from the state of the one who is praying. Remain, therefore, in these things and do not accept others until you have attained peace and have asked those who are experienced, as has been said. These are the signs of error that we have announced, and others similar to them. But see also what are the signs of truth. The signs of truth, and of the good and life-giving Spirit, are love, joy, peace, long-suffering, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, temperance, and the rest, as the divine Apostle says, calling them all fruits of the Holy Spirit. He says also again: “Walk as children of light. For the fruit of the Spirit is in all goodness and justice and truth,” of which error possesses the direct opposite. And one of the wise men, being asked by someone, says: “Concerning the secure way of salvation, beloved, as you have said, there are many ways that lead to life, and many that lead to death.” And proceeding further: “You have one way that leads to life: the observance of the commandments of Christ. In these commandments you will find every form of virtue, but especially these three: humility, charity, and mercy, without which no one will see the Lord.” And a little later: “These three are the invincible weapons against the demons, which the Holy Trinity has bestowed upon us: I mean humility and charity and
mercy, against which even the whole swarm of demons cannot look. For there is not among them the slightest trace of humility, since they were blinded by pride and eternal fire was prepared for them. Where is there among them, or even a shadow of, charity or mercy—they who have fostered unceasing hatred toward the human race and do not cease to wage war against it? Let us then be armored with these weapons, which whoever puts on becomes invincible to his enemies.” And a little later: “This triple-woven cord, which the Holy Trinity wove and joined together, we see to be both three and one; three, indeed, in names, or if you will, also in persons; but one in power and efficacy, and in that closeness, inclination, and familiarity which it has with God.” Concerning these the Master said: “My yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matt. xi, 30). And the disciple whom he loved: “And his commandments are not heavy” (I John v, 3). And after a few words: “For this reason, the soul that is mingled with God through purity of soul, and through the keeping of the commandments, and possesses these three weapons, which are God Himself, puts on God Himself and becomes god by participation, through humility, mercy, and charity, and having passed beyond the material dyad and having transcended the head of the law—I mean charity—is joined to the supersubstantial and life-creating Trinity, conversing with her immediately, adding light to light and being suffused with ceaseless and eternal joy.” But enough has been said regarding these things. It is worth while, however, just as we have mentioned from a part of the signs and fruits of error and truth (whence, from these very fruits, according to the divine Paul, we may know those who are at work, of what spirit they are), so also to discourse briefly from the Fathers concerning both kinds of excitation—that is, regarding the divine and true grace, and the false and contrary one. Thus, therefore, does the divine Diadochus speak concerning this.
Concerning divine and false excitation.
“When our mind begins to perceive the consolation of the Holy Spirit, then Satan also, in some pleasant sensory way, in the silence of the night, when one is coming into the inclination of a very light sleep, excites the soul. If, therefore, the mind is found to be holding the holy name of the Lord Jesus with very fervent memory, and uses that holy and glorious name as a weapon against the deception, the deceiver of guile withdraws, but henceforth he kindles a manifest war against the soul. Whence, recognizing the deception of the evil one accurately, the mind progresses further into the experience of discernment.” And again: “The good consolation occurs while the body is awake, or also when it is about to come into some semblance of sleep, when one is in fervent memory of God, and as it were glued to His charity; but that of the deception occurs when, as I said, the wrestler has come into some light sleep, with a middling memory
of God. For the one, as being from God, clearly wishes to urge the souls of those who wrestle in piety, in a great outpouring of soul, toward His love. But the other, since it is accustomed to toss the soul in some wind of delusion, attempts to steal, through the sleep of the body, the experience of the sense of the healthy mind, especially when it is lukewarm regarding the memory of God. If, therefore, the mind is found, as I said, cautiously remembering the Lord Jesus Christ, it scatters that sweet-seeming breeze of the enemy, and rejoicing, moves to war against him, as having, beyond grace, a second successful weapon: the boasting derived from experience. And again: If by a certain motion, free from images and doubt, the soul is kindled toward the love of God, drawing its body as well into the depths of that ineffable charity—whether the body be awake or, in the way I have mentioned, entering into sleep—being led by the holy grace, and thinking of nothing else at all save only that toward which it is moved, one must know that this is the activity of the Holy Spirit. For, being thoroughly suffused with this ineffable sweetness, it can think of nothing else, since it rejoices in a joy that is never remitted. If, however, the mind conceives any ambiguous or sordid thought while engaged in this, even if it uses the holy name for defense against the evil one, and not rather solely for the love of God, one must understand that such an excitation is from the deceiver, in the guise of joy. But that joy is qualitatively and structurally chaotic, for it is the enemy wishing to seduce the soul. For when he sees the mind precisely boasting in the experience of his own sensation, then, as I said, he invites the soul with certain fair-seeming excitations, so that, as it is distracted by that shallow and liquid sweetness, the mixing of the deceiver may remain unknown to it. From this, therefore, we shall know the spirit of truth and the spirit of delusion. It is impossible, however, for anyone to taste the divine goodness sensibly, or to experience the wickedness of the demons sensibly, unless one first persuades himself that grace truly resides in the depths of the mind, whereas evil spirits dwell in the parts of the heart—a thing the demons never wish for men to believe, lest the mind, knowing this precisely, should arm the memory of God against them. You have now enough on this subject, and you should be content; for one should not cross beyond the Pillars of Gades, and if you find honey, eat but a little, lest, having had your fill, you vomit it up.
On divine pleasure, which springs from the heart.
66. Or rather, it is more timely and appropriate to say: Who shall announce the sweetness of honey to those who have not yet tasted it, and much more, incomparably, the divine pleasure and supernatural joy, life-giving and ever-flowing, which springs from a pure and true heart, and leaps up with perpetual streams? As the God-man Jesus says: "Whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him, shall not thirst forever; but the
water that I will give him shall become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life." And again: "If anyone thirsts, let him come to Me and drink." "He who believes in Me, as the Scripture has said, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water." But He said this concerning the Spirit, says the Theologian, which those believing in Him were about to receive; and the great Paul: "God has sent forth the Spirit of His Son into our hearts, crying: Abba, Father."
That this spiritual joy is manifold, and nameless.
76. This spiritual joy is supernatural, lifegiving, and substantial splendor; it is called, mystically, the darkness that is above light, and the inexplicable beauty, and the greatest of things desired, and inspection, and the vision of God, and deification; but it remains unnamed after it has been named, and unknown after it has been known, and inconceivable after it has been conceived. And the great Dionysius says: "According to this, we pray to reach the super-luminous darkness, and through blindness and ignorance to see and to know Him who is beyond vision and knowledge—that is, to see and to know this very thing, that He is not visible and not knowable; for this is indeed to see and to know, and to praise the Supersubstantial supersubstantially through the removal of all beings." And further: "The divine darkness is the inaccessible light in which God is said to dwell; and it is invisible on account of its superabundant splendor, and inaccessible on account of the excess of its supersubstantial effusion. In this light is he who is deemed worthy to know and see God; by this very fact of not seeing and not knowing, he truly enters into that which is beyond vision and knowledge; knowing this very thing, that He is beyond all things sensible and intelligible." And the great Basil says: "The flashes of divine beauty are altogether ineffable and indescribable; speech cannot express them, nor hearing receive them. Even if you mention the splendors of the morning star, or the brightness of the moon, or the light of the sun, all are vile in comparison to that glory, and fall further short in comparison to the true light than deep night and gloomy darkness fall short of the purest midday. This beauty is invisible to eyes of flesh, but graspable by the soul and mind alone. And if at any time it has shone upon any of the saints, it has left behind in them an unendurable sting of longing, so that, exulting with joy for the future life, they would say: 'Woe is me, that my sojourning is prolonged!' and 'My soul thirsted for God, the strong, the living; when shall I come and appear before the face of my God?' And, 'To depart and be with Christ is far better.' And, D 'Now dismiss your servant, Master, according to your word, in peace'; considering this present life a prison-house. For they, since they could not be sated with the contemplation of the divine beauty, wished that, through all eternal life, the contemplation of the splendor of the Lord might be extended along with it. And the Theologian says: 'Whose fear is the keeping of the commandments,
is the cleansing of the flesh, which surrounds the soul like a cloud, and does not permit it to see the divine rays; whose inundation is illumination, and illumination is the fulfillment of desire for those who desire the greatest things, or the Greatest [God] Himself, or things beyond the great.' And the divine Gregory of Nyssa says: 'If you should empty out, through the care of a virtuous life, the grime that has formed on your heart, divine beauty will shine forth for you, as is wont to happen with iron. For when, through the whetstone, that which was just before black is stripped of its rust, it sends forth from itself certain rays and shines with brightness toward the sun; so also the inner man, whom the Lord calls heart, once it has scrubbed off the poisonous grime that has sprouted upon its form through evil corruption, will again retrieve its likeness to the archetype, and will be good; for good follows in every way upon that which is good.' And saint Nilus: 'Blessed is he who embraces the ignorance which is inseparable from prayer.' And the [author] of the Ladder: 'The abyss of mourning beheld consolation, the cleansing of the heart received illumination; illumination is an ineffable operation, glimpsed invisibly and understood unknowingly.' For this reason, those who like the ancient Mary have chosen this good portion and way of life — the spiritual and unstealable one — are thrice-blessed and deemed worthy of such God-befitting good fortune, so that with great and ecstatic joy, it is permitted to them, along with the divine Paul, to be inspired openly and to cry out together: 'But when the kindness and the philanthropy of God our Savior appeared, not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to His mercy He saved us, through the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, which He poured out on us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Savior, that being justified by His grace, we should become heirs according to the hope of eternal life' (Tit. III, 4-7); and again: 'Who also has anointed us and sealed us, and given us the earnest of the Spirit in our hearts' (II Cor. I, 21-22); and: 'But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us' (II Cor. IV, 7). And those men were such; but may it be for us also, by their prayers to the Lord that persuade God, to share partly, like them, in mercy and in grace.
That it is necessary by all means for him to be of a gentle heart who desires to live in peace absolutely.
77. But this, O child, you must know now in due time before all else, and along with all else, that just as he who wishes to learn to shoot an arrow well does not aim his bow without marks, so he who wishes to learn to live in peace must have, as his mark, to be always gentle of heart. And saint Isidore says: 'It is not sufficient for virtue to practice, but it is necessary to be moderate in the practice as well. For if, starting the contest of gentleness, we fight with a troubled mind, it is nothing other than wishing indeed to attain salvation, but not wishing to do the things that contribute to it.' And before him the divine David: 'He will guide the meek in judgment; He will teach—
the meek His ways. And the son of Sirach: 'To the meek are mysteries revealed.' And the sweetest Jesus: 'Learn from me, for I am meek and lowly in heart, and you shall find rest for your souls.' And: 'To whom shall I look, but to him who is meek and quiet, and who trembles at My words?' And: 'Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth,' that is, the heart, bringing forth fruit by grace: thirty, sixty, and a hundred-fold, according to the order of the beginners, the intermediate, and the perfect. For that man will not be troubled, nor will he be troubled by others, if the discourse is not yet concerning piety.
How meekness is achieved in us, and concerning the tripartite soul: the irascible, the desiderative, and the rational.
You can easily achieve this, if you turn away from everything at once and move your soul toward love, remaining silent for the most part, eating moderately, and always praying, as it has been said to the Fathers: 'Bridle the irascible part of the soul with love; mortify its desiderative part with temperance; and give wings to its rational part with prayer: and the light of the mind will never be dimmed.' And: 'The bridle of anger is timely silence; of irrational desire, measured food; of the stubborn mind, one-thought prayer.' And again: 'There are three virtues which provide light to the mind always: not knowing the malice of any man; bearing what happens without disturbance; and doing good to those who do evil. These three virtues beget three other virtues greater than themselves: not knowing the malice of man begets love; bearing what happens without disturbance begets meekness; and doing good to those who do evil grants peace.' And again: 'There are three moral states, more general among monks: the first is not to sin in action; the second, not to let passionate thoughts linger in the soul; and the third, to view the forms of women and of those who cause sorrow, without passion, in the mind.'
That one must repent quickly for accidental lapses, and thus wisely secure oneself for the future.
79. But if it should happen at some time that you are disturbed, or that you slip into some fault, and miss the mark of what is proper, you must immediately be reconciled with the person you have grieved or who has grieved you; and you must repent from the soul, mourn and weep, and reproach yourself. And thus, for the future, you must be heedful and secure yourself most wisely, as the Lord Jesus teaches: 'If you offer your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go, first be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.' And the apostle Paul: 'All bitterness and wrath...'
and anger, and clamor, and blasphemy, be put away from you, with all malice. And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you.' And: 'Be ye angry, and sin not.' And: 'Let not the sun go down upon your wrath.' And: 'Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath.' And: 'Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good.' And this indeed is said concerning mutual reconciliation.
Of slipping and repentance.
Concerning slipping, St. Isaac says: "We should not grieve when we slip in something, but when we remain in it. For slipping happens often even to the perfect; but remaining in it is complete destruction. The sorrow, however, that we feel for our own slips is reckoned to us, by grace, as a place of pure work. He who slips a second time in the hope of repentance walks before God with craftiness; upon him death falls unexpectedly, and he does not reach the time of his hope to fulfill the works of virtue." And further: "It is necessary," he says, "for us to know at every hour that in these twenty-four hours of night and day we are in need of repentance. The understanding of the name 'repentance,' as we have known it from the true nature of things, is this: it is a stretch of supplication at every hour, in prayer filled with compunction, approaching God for the remission of past things; and sorrow for the guarding of those to come." And again: "Grace upon grace, repentance has been given to men. For repentance is a second regeneration from God, and the pledge which we received from faith, through repentance we receive as His grace. Repentance is the door of mercy, which is opened to those who seek it. Through this door we enter into the divine mercy, and outside this entrance, we shall not find mercy. Because all have sinned, according to the divine Scripture, justified freely by His grace. Repentance is the second grace, and it is born in the heart from faith and fear. And fear is the paternal rod which steers us until we reach the spiritual paradise; and when we have reached it, it leaves us and turns back. Paradise is the love of God, in which is the delight of all blessings." And again: "Just as it is impossible to cross the great sea without a ship and a boat, so no one can cross to love without fear. We can pass through the foul sea that is spread between us and the spiritual paradise by the boat of repentance, which holds the rowing-oars of fear. But if the rowing-oars of fear do not steer this boat of repentance, through which we pass the sea of this world toward God, we are submerged in that foul sea."
81. Repentance is a ship; fear is its helmsman; charity is the divine harbor. Fear therefore establishes us in the ship of repentance and sends us across the foul sea of this life; and it leads us to the divine harbor, which is charity, into which all those who toil and are burdened through repentance arrive. And when we reach charity, we have reached God, and our journey is finished, and we have crossed over to the island which is beyond this world, where the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit are. Concerning sorrow according to God, the Savior speaks thus: "Blessed are they that mourn, for they shall be comforted."
Further concerning tears, the holy Isaac writes this: "Tears during prayer are a sign of the mercy of God, of which the soul has been deemed worthy in its repentance; they indicate that it has been accepted and has begun to enter into the plain of purity through tears. For unless thoughts of what is passing away are cast off, and they cast from themselves the hope of the world, and there is stirred up within them contempt for it, and they begin to prepare good provisions for their departure from the world, and thoughts of certain things that are there in heaven begin to be moved in the soul, the eyes cannot weep. For tears are multiplied and increase more and more from pure and constant converse, from many and continuous thoughts, and from those that come readily and from the memory of some slight thing formed in the mind, and the heart grieving from the memory of it, and from these [things] tears are increased and grow yet more." And he of the Ladder says: "As fire consumes stubble, so the pure tear consumes every defilement, whether apparent or conceptual." Further: "Let us acquire pure and sincere tears for our own dissolution; for in them there is no theft or conceit; rather, there is purification, progress in charity toward God, the washing away of sin, and the deprivation of passions." Further: "Do not trust your springs before perfect purification; for wine that is enclosed in casks immediately from the winepress does not have stability." Further: "Tears which proceed from fear possess within themselves their own safeguard; but those of charity, before charity is perfect, are in some cases exposed to those who would plunder them, unless perhaps the fire which is to be ever-remembered, at the time of its operation, has entirely kindled the heart. And it is a wondrous thing how that which is more humble is more secure in the time of its fire." Further: "A tear of departure has brought forth fear; but when fear has brought forth security, joy has appeared; and as inexpressible joy has ceased, the flower of holy charity has sprouted."
Regarding self-reproach, the great Antony says: "This is the great work of a man, that he should cast his own fault upon himself before God, and expect temptation until his very last breath." And another holy Father, being asked, "What is the greater thing you have found, Father, in this way?" replied saying, "To reproach oneself in all things." This, the one who had asked approved, and said to him, "There is no other way than this." And Abbot Poemen […]
said: "All the virtues entered this world with a sigh. Take away one virtue, and outside of it, a man stands with toil." And they asked him, "What is this one?" And he says: "That a man should reproach himself at all times." He said again: "He who reproaches himself, whatever may happen to him, whether loss, or disgrace, or any affliction whatsoever, has anticipated it by judging himself worthy of it, and he is never disturbed."
On attention and the need to be wisely confirmed.
82. In like manner, regarding attention and confirmation, the divine Paul writes: "See how carefully you walk; not as unwise, but as wise, redeeming the time, because the days are evil" (Eph. v, 15). And holy Isaac says: "O wisdom, how admirable you are, and how you foresee all things from afar! Blessed is he who finds you; for he has been delivered from the sloth of youth. If anyone trades through a small profit—that is, provision—the healing of great passions, he does well. For this is wisdom, that one should always be vigilant even in the smallest and least things being done by him. For he treasures up great rest for himself, and does not sleep, lest anything contrary happen to him; but he cuts off the causes of evil before the time, and through the briefest matters sustains a small sadness, through it dissipating the greater ones and advancing. Therefore also the Wise Man says: 'Be vigilant and attentive for your life; for sleep is a relative of thought, and an image of the true immortal.' The Hierophant Basil also says: 'Whoever is slothful in small things, do not trust him to excel in matters of greatness.'"
That one ought to act seriously in all the things aforementioned; but above all, that we should be tranquil and gentle, and that it is necessary to invoke the Lord Jesus Christ purely within the heart, if we desire to act in peace.
83. Because of all these things, set yourself to work seriously on the things aforementioned; but above all, that you may be tranquil and gentle, and with a clean conscience, invoke the Lord Jesus Christ in the depths of the heart, as we have said. For in this way, advancing by this path, you will possess divine grace resting in your soul. For the Climacus also says: "He who is encumbered by anger and conceit, and hypocrisy and the memory of injuries, will never dare to see the trace of tranquility, lest he should thereby gain an ecstasy; but if one is pure from these, he will eventually know what is advantageous; though I think not even he." And indeed, you will not only have grace resting in your soul, but also having your soul resting completely from those things that formerly troubled it, namely demons and passions. For even if they trouble it again, they do not succeed, because it does not cling to them, nor does it desire the pleasure that comes from them.
On good and ecstatic love, and on divine beauty.
84. For the whole longing of such a one, and the inward
disposition of his soul, gazes toward the supreme beauty, which the Fathers have called the sum of all desirable things. And the great Basil says: “When the love of piety takes hold of the soul, every form of warfare is for it a laughing-stock, and all those who tear it apart for the sake of the One whom it loves, benefit rather than strike it.” And again: “What is more wonderful than the divine beauty? What thought is more pleasant than divine magnificence? What yearning of the soul is as vehement and as unbearable as that which is produced by God in a soul purged of all malice, and which, from a true disposition, says: ‘I am wounded by love’?”
On warfare, and on instructive withdrawal,
and on abandonment by aversion.
85. Now, war is waged by way of instructive withdrawal, not by way of abandonment through aversion. Why? So that his mind may not be exalted on account of the good it has found; but, being warred upon and instructed, it always puts on humility, by which alone it not only conquers those who arrogantly wage war against it, but is also continuously deemed worthy of greater gifts, progressing as much as human nature allows, bound and weighed down by necessary cords and the burden of the flesh, and journeying toward the perfection and impassibility that is in Christ. And Saint Diadochus says: “The Lord Himself says that Satan has fallen like lightning from the heavens, so that the deformed one might not look upon the habitations of the holy angels.” How, then, can the human mind, which is not deemed worthy of the communion of good servants, have a common dwelling-place with God? But they will say that this happens by way of withdrawal, and they will say nothing more. For instructive withdrawal in no way deprives the soul of the divine light; it only hides, as I have already said many times, the presence of grace from the mind, so that it may be urged forward—just as the soul, through the bitterness of the demons, is urged, because of all fear and great humility, to seek out the help that comes from God, recognizing bit by bit the malice of its enemy. Just as if a mother were to briefly push away from her arms a child who is unruly regarding the laws of breastfeeding, so that, being terrified by some repulsive men standing around him, or by any wild beasts whatever, he might return to his mother’s bosom with great fear and tears. But the withdrawal that occurs by way of aversion delivers the soul that does not wish to have God to the demons, as if it were a prisoner. We, however, are not children of abandonment—may it never be!—but we believe ourselves to be true infants of the grace of God, nourished by it with small withdrawals and frequent consolations, so that, through the goodness of God, we may hasten to arrive at a perfect man, unto the measure of age. And again: “The instructive withdrawal indeed brings much sorrow and humility, and a diffidence proportionate to the soul, so that its ambitious and dauntless part may fittingly come to humility; but straightway it brings the fear of God and tears of confession into the heart, and a vehement desire for the best silence. But the abandonment that comes by way of aversion to God is filled with desperation, and diffidence, and anger
and permits the soul to be filled with pride. We must, therefore, know the experience of both kinds of abandonment, and according to the manner of each, we must approach God. In the former case, we owe Him thanksgiving along with our apology, inasmuch as He chastised the intemperance of our mind by the delay of consolation, so that, as a good Father, He might teach us the difference between virtue and vice. But in the latter case, we owe unending confession of sins, incessant tears, and more complete withdrawal, so that we might thereby be able, by the addition of labors, to appease God at last, so that He might look again, as before, into our hearts.
Nevertheless, it must be known that, when the battle between the soul and Satan takes place by way of a providential encounter—I mean by the instructional abandonment—grace withdraws itself, as I have already said; yet it cooperates secretly with the soul by its assistance, so that it may show the victory to be that of the soul alone against its enemies. And Saint Isaac says: "It is impossible for a man, without those temptations that occur by divine permission, to become wise in spiritual wars, and to know his own Provider, and to sense his God, and to be strengthened in His faith secretly, unless he receives it by the power of the experience which he has undergone. And when grace sees that conceit has begun in his mind even a little, and he has begun to think great things about himself, it immediately permits temptations to be strengthened and to prevail against him, until he learns his own infirmity, and flees, and possesses God in humility. And in these things man comes to the measure of a perfect man, in the faith and hope of the Son of God, and is exalted toward love."
For the love of God toward man is known to be admirable when he happens to be in the midst of circumstances that cut off his hope; and therein God shows His power in the salvation that He brings upon him. For man never learns the divine power in rest and relief; and God never showed His own energy perceptibly except in a place of stillness, and in the desert, and in places devoid of the encounters and the tumult of living alongside men.
On Apathy, and what human apathy is.
86. Further, it is necessary here to add a word from a part on apathy and perfection, and after a little, to put an end to the present treatise. Hear what the great Basil says: "He who has become a lover of God, and desires to grasp even the smallest portion of His apathy, and of His spiritual holiness, and of that tranquility, and freedom from disturbance, and gentleness, and of the happiness and joy that is born from these, strives to withdraw his thoughts far from every material passion that defiles the soul. He looks upon divine things with a pure and unobscured eye; he is filled inexhaustibly with the light that rises from thence; and after he has exercised his soul into such a habit and state, he becomes, as far as is possible, similar to God, and loves and desires Him, inasmuch as he
has sustained a great and difficult struggle and, being freed from the commixture of matter, is able, with a mind pure and separated from the intermingling of bodily passions, to commune with God. And this is concerning *apatheia* (dispassion). But concerning what human *apatheia* is, the holy Isaac writes as follows: "Apatheia is not the failure to feel the passions, but the failure to accept them. For from the many and varied virtues, both manifest and hidden, which one has acquired, the passions have become weak within them, and they cannot easily rise up against the soul; and the intellect does not need to pay attention to them at all times. For at every moment it is filled with its own thoughts, through meditation and the conversation of the best ways of life, which move in the understanding within the mind. And when the passions begin to be moved and to be troubled, the intellect is suddenly snatched away from their proximity, by a certain understanding that looks down into the mind; and the passions are left idle in it, as the blessed Mark said: 'The mind, fulfilling the acts of the virtues by the grace of God, and abounding in knowledge, feels little of the evil and irrational part of the soul.' For its knowledge snatches it up to the heights and alienates it from all things that are in the world; and because of the purity, subtilty, lightness, and keenness of their mind, and because of their continued exercise, their mind is cleansed and shown to be clear, because their flesh has been withered by the leisure of stillness (*hesychia*) and the long persistence therein. For this reason, contemplation is easily and quickly attached to each one, and the theory within them leads them, to their own astonishment; and in this they are multiplied a hundredfold in theories; and their intellect never lacks material for understanding; and they are never outside those things which the fruit of the Spirit produces in them. And through long-accustomed habit, those memories that move the passions in the soul are erased from their hearts, as is the strength of the power of the devil. For when the soul does not dally with the passions, nor associate with them in their meditation, by being held fast by another care without ceasing, the strength of the claws of the passions is unable to take hold of its spiritual senses." And the divine Diadochus says: "Apatheia is not the state of not being attacked by demons—for then we would have to depart from the world, according to the Apostle—but the state of remaining unvanquished while being attacked by them. For those steel-clad soldiers are indeed shot at by their adversaries, and they hear the sound of the archery, and they even see the very arrows being sent against them, but they are not struck because of the solidity of their martial garments. But while those men, armored in iron, remain unvanquished while under attack, we, however, armored with the light of the holy all-
armor, and with the helmet of the Savior, having armed ourselves with all that is good, let us break the dark phalanxes of the demons. For it is not the mere ceasing to do evil that brings purity, but also the total abolition of evil through diligence in good deeds.» And Saint Maximus also divides apathia in four ways, saying this: «I call the first apathia the motionlessness of the body regarding sin in its operation. I call the second apathia the complete casting away of passionate thoughts in the soul, through which the motion of the passions, which the first apathia extinguishes, is withered away, having no passionate thoughts to ignite it into action. I call the third apathia the total stillness of desire regarding the passions, through which the second also naturally comes to be, established by the purity of the thoughts. I call the fourth apathia the complete discarding of all sensible images in the intellect, through which the third takes its origin, as it no longer possesses the images of sensible things that give form in it to the icons of the passions.» Further: «Apathia is a peaceful state of the soul whereby it becomes difficult to move toward wickedness.»
Further concerning apathia and perfection
87. And indeed, Saint Ephrem also, concerning apathia and perfection, declares thus: «Those who are passionless, reaching out insatiably toward the supreme desirable object, make their perfection unfinishable; for there is no end to eternal goods. And it is perfect, insofar as it relates to the measure of human capacity. Yet it is unfinishable, as it always surpasses itself with daily additions, and is elevated continuously in its ascents toward God.» Similarly, Saint Nilus also speaks thus concerning perfection: «Two perfections must be understood: one temporal, and the other eternal; concerning which the Apostle writes: 'When that which is perfect is come, then that which is in part shall be abolished' (1 Cor. xiii, 10).
