For when it says 'when that which is perfect is come,' it signifies that here we are unable to attain divine perfection.» Further: «The divine Paul recognizes two perfections; and he knows the same man to be both perfect and not perfect: insofar as he relates to the present life, the man is called perfect; but as he relates to Him who is truly perfect, he is not perfect. Therefore he says, 'Not that I have already attained, or am already perfected' (Philipp. iii, 12). And a little later he says: 'Let us therefore, as many as are perfect, be thus minded' (Ibid. 15).»
Concerning the passionate, the sweetly-passionate, the strongly-passionate, and the lack of passion
88. Saint Elias the Ekdikos also says: «Evil matter: of the body—passion; of the soul—sweet-passion; of the mind—strong-passion. It is indicted, the first by touch; the second by the remaining senses; the last by a contrary disposition.» Further: «The sweetly-passionate one is near to the passionate one; the strongly-passionate one to the sweetly-passionate; but far from both is the passionless one.»
What it is to experience the passionate, the sweetly-passionate, the strongly-passionate, and the passionless; and concerning the cure of each
89. One is passionate who possesses the sinful [act]
more violently than the thought, even if for the time being he does not sin outwardly. One is sweetly-passionate who possesses the operation of sin weaker than the thought, even if he suffers [it] outwardly. One is strongly-passionate who inclines more to the freedom than to the servitude of the intermediate things. One would be passionless, who is ignorant of the difference between all these things. Likewise, however, concerning the cure of both, he declares the following: corporeal passion is cast out from the soul through fasting and prayer; the sweetly-passionate, through vigils and silence; the strongly-passionate, through stillness and attention; and passionlessness consists in the memory of God.
On faith, hope, and love.
8. But since faith, hope, and love are the beginning, the middle, and the end of all good things—or, if you would prefer to say, the leader and the guide—that threefold cord, and God-woven, and above all, love, because God is and is called love, it is not right not to complete by these also what is lacking in the present treatise. Or rather, since even according to holy Isaac one receives the perfection of the many fruits of the Spirit when he is accounted worthy of perfect love.
Let us mention a little about it also. For indeed, the author of the *Ladder* writes: “Now finally, after all that has been said, these three remain, binding fast and holding the bond of all: faith, hope, love; but the greatest of these is love, for God is named [by it].” I, however, see the one as a ray, the other as light, the third as a circle, but all as one radiance and brightness. For the one can do and create all things; the second, the mercy of God encircles, and makes it unashamed; and the third never falls, nor ceases to run, nor allows him whom it has wounded to rest from that blessed madness. And further: “The discourse about love is known to the angels, and to them, according to the operation of illumination, love is God.” He who wishes to state the limit of this is like a blind man measuring the sand in an abyss. Love, according to its quality, is a likeness of God, as far as is possible for mortals; according to its operation, it is an intoxication of the soul; according to its property, it is a fountain of faith, an abyss of long-suffering, a sea of humility. Love is truly the repulsion of every contrary thought, since love does not imagine evil. Love, and passionlessness, and adoption are distinguished by names only; as light, and fire, and flame run together into one operation, so also think concerning these. And the holy Diadochus: “Let faith, hope, and love, my brothers, lead every spiritual contemplation, but love most of all. For the former teach one to despise visible goods, but love joins the soul itself to the virtues of God, investigating the invisible God with an intellectual sense.” And further: “There is one love of the soul, the natural one, and another which is brought about in it from the holy Spirit. For the former is stirred proportionally by our own will when we wish, and therefore it is easily snatched away by evil spirits when we do not violently master our own inclination.”
And it so inflames the soul toward the love of God that all the parts of the soul are then gathered into an immense disposition of simplicity, for the mind, being then as it were pregnant from the spiritual energy, gushes forth a certain fountain of love and joy. And Saint Isaac says: “Charity which arises from certain things is like a small lamp, nourished by oil, and thus its light is maintained, or like a torrent flowing from rain, the flow of which ceases when the material that produces it fails. But that charity which has God as its author is like a springing fountain, and its waves are never interrupted; for He alone is the source of charity, and its unfailing substance.” And again, when asked what the perfection of the manifold fruits of the Spirit is, he answered: “When someone is deemed worthy of the perfect charity of God.” And being asked again how one knows that one has reached this, he said: “When the memory of God is stirred in his consciousness, his heart is immediately moved in His love, and his eyes pour forth tears abundantly; for it is the custom of love to draw tears from the memory of those things which are loved, and such a one is never lacking in tears. For he never lacks the material which carries him into the memory of God, so that even in his sleep he converses with God; for such is the custom of love, to do these things, and this is the perfection of men in this life of theirs.” And furthermore: “The charity of God is hot by nature, and when it falls upon someone beyond measure, it makes that soul ecstatic. For this reason the heart of the one who has felt it cannot contain it or endure it, but according to the measure of the quality and the charity that has come upon him, an unusual change is seen in him. And these are its sensible signs: the man’s face becomes fiery and joyful, and his body is warmed, fear and shame depart from him, and he becomes as it were ecstatic, and the faculty that gathers the mind flees from him, and he becomes as one out of his mind, counting even terrible death as joy, and the contemplation of his mind never suffers any interruption from the thought of heavenly things. And though absent, he converses as if present, though unseen by anyone. His knowledge and natural vision pass away, and he is not sensibly aware of his own movement by which he moves among things. And if he does anything, he does not feel it at all, having his mind hovering in this contemplation, and his reflection always converses with another. Apostles and martyrs were once inebriated with this spiritual drunkenness; and some, traveling around the whole world, labored and were burdened with injuries; others, with mangled limbs, poured out their blood like water, and while suffering the most terrible things, did not flag, but endured them generously. And although wise, they were held as foolish, and others wandered in deserts and mountains, and in caves and in the holes of the earth; and in such turmoil, they were not perturbed. May God grant us to attain this foolishness.
On Holy Communion; and on the good things that the continuous reception of this, with a pure conscience, provides for us.
A 91. Nothing contributes and helps us so much toward the purification of the soul, the illumination of the mind, the sanctification of the body, and the transformation and immortality of both toward that which is more divine—nay, more, toward the repulsion of passions and demons, or, to speak more appropriately, toward union and a supernatural conjunction and blending with God—as the continuous reception and communion, with a pure heart and upright disposition, as far as is possible for man, of the holy, immaculate, immortal, and life-giving mysteries; we speak of that very venerable body and blood of our Lord and God and Savior, Jesus Christ. Therefore, it is most necessary that we also set forth some things concerning this, and devote time to this care, and thus bring our discourse to an end.
And this, therefore, is manifest, not only from what the saints say, but much more manifest from the very words of the Author of life and truth. For He says: «I am the bread of life» C; and, «This is the bread which comes down from heaven, that if anyone eats of it, he will not die. I am the living bread which came down from heaven; if anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever. And the bread that I shall give is My flesh for the life of the world.» And, «Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man, and drink His blood, you have no life in you; he who eats My flesh and drinks My blood has eternal life.» And further: «For My flesh is food indeed, and My blood is drink indeed; he who eats My flesh and drinks My blood abides in Me, and I in him. As the living Father sent Me, and I live because of the Father, so he who eats Me, he also will live because of Me. This is the bread which came down from heaven; and he who eats this bread will live forever.» And Christ’s disciple Paul says these things: «Brethren, I received from the Lord that which also I delivered to you, that the Lord Jesus in the same night in which He was betrayed took bread, and when He had given thanks, He broke it and said, Take, eat; this is My body which is broken for you: do this in remembrance of Me. In the same manner also the cup, after supper, saying, This cup is the new Testament in My blood; do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of Me. For as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death till He comes. Therefore, whoever eats this bread or drinks this cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread and drink of that cup. For he who eats and drinks in an unworthy manner eats and drinks judgment to himself, not discerning the Lord’s body. Therefore, among you many are weak and infirm...
and many are asleep. If we judged ourselves, we would not surely be judged. But when we are judged, we are chastened by the Lord, that we may not be condemned with this world.”
What it is necessary to learn regarding the miracle of the sacred mysteries; and what it is, and why it is given, and what its utility is.
92. Chrysostom writes: “It is necessary to learn what the miracle of the mysteries is, and why it is given, and what the utility of this matter is. We are one body and members, from the flesh of our Lord Jesus Christ, and from his bones. But let those who have been initiated give ear to what is said, so that we may not only become this according to charity, but may in very reality be blended into that same flesh; this is effected by the food which He has bestowed upon us, wishing to show us the love which He has for us. Therefore He has mingled Himself with us and implanted His body in us, so that we might become one, as a body united to a head. For this belongs to those who love vehemently. Hinting at this, Job spoke of his servants, to whom he was passionately desirable, for in showing their love, they said: ‘Who would give us to be filled with his flesh?’ Therefore Christ also has done this, leading us to a greater friendship and manifesting His love for us, not only offering Himself to be seen by those who desire Him, but also to be touched and eaten; and He willed that we should be united and connected to His flesh, and that our entire desire should be fulfilled.” And further: “Those who partake of this most holy body and venerated blood stand with angels and archangels and the heavenly powers, clothed in the royal garment of Christ itself and holding heavenly weapons. But they have not yet said anything; for they have put on the King Himself. But just as it is great and awesome and marvelous, so if you approach with purity, you have approached unto salvation; but if with an evil conscience, unto condemnation and punishment. For he who eats and drinks unworthily, eats and drinks judgment to himself. For if those who defile the royal purple are punished no less than those who have torn it, it is altogether consistent that those who receive the body with a defiled conscience should undergo the same punishment as those who pierced it with nails. See, therefore, how Paul revealed this punishment, saying: ‘He who has despised the law of Moses, without mercy, on the testimony of two or three witnesses, dies. Of how much worse punishment do you think he will be worthy, who has trampled underfoot the Son of God, and has considered the blood of the covenant common, in which he was sanctified?’ D Whoever, therefore, we are who partake of this body, whoever we are who taste this blood, consider that we are tasting Him who sits on high, who is worshipped by the angels, who is near the omnipotent power. Oh! How many ways are opened unto us for salvation! He has made us His body, He has rendered us participants of His body, and none of these things draws us back from evil! O, the indolence!"
O, the insensibility! And again: “A certain wonderful old man told me that he had been accounted worthy to see and hear such a thing: that those who are about to depart from hence, if they have happened to be partakers of the mysteries with a pure conscience, when they are on the point of death, the angels, escorting them on account of that which was received, lead them away from hence.”
And the divine John Damascene says: “Since we are twofold and composite, it behooves us that our birth and likewise our nourishment should be twofold and composite. Our birth, therefore, is given to us through water and the Spirit, but our food is the bread of life itself, our Lord Jesus Christ, who descended from heaven. And just as in baptism, since it is the custom for men to be washed with water and anointed with oil, He joined the grace of the Spirit to the water and oil and made them a laver of regeneration, so, since it is our custom to eat bread and to drink water and wine, He joined His own divinity to these and made them His body and blood, so that through things habitual and natural we might attain to things supernatural.”
The body is truly joined to the divinity, *the body born of the holy Virgin, not that that body which we receive descends from heaven, but that the bread itself and the wine are changed into the body and blood of God. But if you inquire into the manner of how this comes to pass, it suffices for you to hear that it is through the Holy Spirit—just as from the holy Theotokos, through the Holy Spirit, the Lord took flesh unto Himself and in Himself—and we know nothing more. But because the Word of God is true and effectual and omnipotent, while the mode is inscrutable, it becomes, therefore, to those who receive it worthily with faith, for the remission of sins and for eternal life, and for the preservation of soul and body; but to those who partake in unbelief and unworthily, it becomes for punishment and torment, just as the death of the Lord. And the bread and the wine are not a figure of the body and blood of Christ—God forbid!—but the body of Christ itself, deified, and the blood itself. “For my flesh,” He says, “is food indeed, and my blood is drink indeed.”
It is the body and blood of Christ, descending into the substance of our soul and body, not being consumed, not corrupting, not passing into the draught, but into our substance and preservation, a cleanser of all filth; and even if it finds gold alloyed with dross, it cleanses it through the refining fire that we may not be condemned in the future with the world. Cleansed through it, we are united to the body of Christ and to His Spirit, and we become the body of Christ. This bread is the beginning of the future bread, which is the supersubstantial bread; for “supersubstantial” signifies either that which is future, that is to say, of the future age, or that which is taken for the preservation of our substance. The flesh of the Lord is a life-giving spirit, because it was conceived from the life-giving Spirit; for that which is born of the Spirit is spirit. This
however, is spoken of as antitypes of things to come, not as though it were not truly the body and blood of Christ, but because now, through these, we partake of Christ’s divinity, whereas then, we shall do so mentally through vision alone. And the most divine Macarius says: "Just as wine is infused into all the limbs of the one drinking, and the wine becomes in him, and he in the wine, so too, he who drinks the blood of Christ is watered by the Spirit of Divinity, and it is infused into the perfected soul, and the soul into it; and thus, having been sanctified, it becomes worthy of the Lord." For all, he says, have been given that same Spirit to drink; and through the Eucharist of the bread, those who partake of the Holy Spirit in truth are counted worthy to become partakers, and thus the soul, being worthy, can live for ages. And just as for the body, life is not from itself, but from without, that is to say from the earth, so too did God B will for the soul to have—not from its own nature, but from His own Divinity, from His own Spirit and light—food, drink, and clothing, which is the true life of the soul. For the divine nature has also the bread of life, He who said, "I am the bread of life," and living water, and wine that gladdens, and the oil of gladness. And Saint Isidore says: "The reception of the divine mysteries is called communion, because it grants us union with Christ and makes us partakers of His kingdom." And the venerable Nilus says: "It is impossible for the faithful to be saved in any other way, and to receive the remission of sins, and to attain the kingdom of heaven, unless he receives with fear, faith, and desire the mystical and immaculate body and blood of Christ." Likewise, the great Basil writes in his letter to the patrician Caesaria: "And to communicate and receive the holy body and blood of Christ every day is good and beneficial, the Lord Himself saying, 'He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him, and has eternal life.' For who doubts that to partake of life continuously is nothing other than to live in many ways? We, however, communicate four times every week: on the Lord's Day, on Wednesday, on Friday, and on Saturday, and on other days if the memorial of some saint occurs; on which days, I think, the saint also celebrated. For he could not do so daily, being burdened by so many cares." And Saint Apollo also said that "a monk ought, if possible, to communicate in the mysteries of Christ every day. For he who keeps himself away from these, keeps himself away from God; but he who does this continuously receives the flesh continuously. For the saving voice says: 'He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him.' It is incumbent, therefore, upon monks to make a perpetual remembrance of the saving passion. They must, therefore, always be prepared and so dispose themselves that they may be worthy to receive the sacred mysteries, since in this way we are made worthy of the remission of sins." And Climax also says: "If another body, when touching a body, is changed in its efficacy, how shall he not be changed who touches the body of God with innocent hands?" And it is written in the Geronticon: "John of Bostra, a holy man and one having power over unclean spirits, demons
who were dwelling in certain girls who were mad and being wickedly acted upon by them, asked, 'What things do you fear from the Christians?' They replied: 'You truly have three great things: one which you wear about your neck, and one which you wash in at the Church, and one which you eat in the communion.' And when questioned again, 'Of these three, which do you fear more?' they answered: 'If you guard well what you receive, none of us is able to harm a Christian. But there are things which our enemies fear more than the others: the Cross, Baptism, and Communion.'"
The end of all the matters explored in detail, and a specific exhortation to the one who asked.
93. See now, most beloved child, your request has been fulfilled, with God. Whether it is in accordance with your intent and purpose, we do not know precisely; but it is in accordance with our power, and what is according to one’s power is pleasing to God. See to it, therefore, that your eagerness to learn and your zeal do not stop at this, but that you may also appear eager and fervent in works. For the illustrious brother of the Lord says: "My beloved brethren, be doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves. For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he is like a man observing his natural face in a mirror; for he observed himself, went away, and immediately forgot what kind of man he was. But he who looked into the perfect law of liberty and continued in it, and is not a forgetful hearer but a doer of the work, this one will be blessed in what he does."
How one ought to hear and receive the spiritual sayings of the Fathers.
94. And before all these things, in order that you may faithfully and with the proper reverence receive and listen to the holy and spiritual sayings of the Fathers, remember what holy Macarius says: "Spiritual things are unreachable to the inexperienced; but the communion of the Holy Spirit and the heavenly treasures of the Spirit take hold of a holy and faithful soul, and they become manifest only to him who has experienced them; but to the uninitiated, it is not even possible to conceive of them at all." Listen, therefore, to the Fathers regarding these things religiously, until it befalls you, as you believe, to be deemed worthy of attaining them. For then you will know by the very experience of the eyes of the soul what good things and mysteries the souls of Christians are able to commune with even here. For if you are in this state, you will most quickly gather the fruit and benefit of the things written and heard, and from both learning and acting, you will progress so as to be able to exhort others and lead them by that same experience to things more divine and to those unknown to the many. May this come to pass for you, relying upon and guided by the most powerful hand of the Lord Jesus Christ! Amen. Since, however, satiety of speech is hostile to the ears, just as too much food is to the body, and since every measure is indeed best, we must be satisfied
with having avoided that satiety, and embracing moderation as the best course, having lingered only a little while in the discourse, and having sketched out a sort of summary of the present treatise, thus to cast the anchor of our discourse there.
Recapitulation, and how one ought to pray, and concerning true illumination and divine power.
B 95. The Fathers say: He who desires to be vigilant in speech must constantly hasten to pray purely and undistractedly within his heart through the inhalation of his nostrils, attending only to the words of the prayer, and meditating and pondering the phrases—namely: "Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me"—until the time of the illumination of the mind in the heart, as the holy Diadochus says: "Whoever meditates ceaselessly in the depth of their heart upon the glorious and much-desired name of the Lord Jesus, these are able at some point to see the light of the mind." Once this has happened, by the impulse of God, from that time forward we shall walk the remainder of the course of our life according to God as if in the light, or rather, having become sons of light, we shall proceed without wandering and without stumbling, as Jesus, the Giver of Light, says: "While you have the light, believe in the light, that you may become sons of light; and: I am the light of the world; he who follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life." And David cries out such things to the Lord: "In your light we shall see light." And the most divine Paul: "God, who said light shall shine out of darkness, he has shone in our hearts." For through Him, as through an inextinguishable and most brilliant lamp, those who are truly faithful are guided and proceed beyond the sensible realm; and for them, being pure in heart, the heavenly gate is opened, which is the gate of this life, a life similar to that of the angels and of this sublime state. And again, for these persons, as if from a solar disc, it rises, and they are enabled to investigate, to judge, to discern, to foresee, and things like these. And altogether through Him there shines before their eyes the revelation and manifestation of the hidden mysteries; they are filled in the Holy Spirit with supernatural and divine power; and through this spiritual power their burden is lightened, or rather the heaviness of the flesh is diminished, lifted up, and they fly over it. By the grace of the power of this Holy Spirit who illuminates, although they were still clothed in flesh, certain holy Fathers, as if void of matter and body, crossed inaccessible lights and boat-traversed seas without sinking, and carried out long journeys of many days in an instant, and performed other extraordinary things in heaven, on earth, in the sun, in the sea, in the deserts, in cities, in every place and region, among beasts and among reptiles, and in a word in all creation and in all the elements; and they were glorified through all things, and while they stood in prayer, their holy and venerable bodies were raised from the earth as if they had wings; and by that divine and consuming and imma-
immaterial fire of grace, they were incinerated of their bodily thickness and weight, and enabled to be lifted up lightly. O wonderful thing! Transformed and reshaped toward what is more divine, by the wonder-working hand of the power and grace dwelling within them. And after death, the bodies of some remain holy and incorruptible, manifestly testifying to the supernatural grace and power that dwelt in them and dwells in all sincere believers. After the common and universal resurrection, through the same power shining in the Spirit, as if they had acquired wings, they will be caught up in the clouds to meet the Lord, as the most divine Paul, teacher of secrets, says: “And so they will always be with the Lord.” To these things also the Spirit-inspired David sings: “O Lord, in the light of thy countenance they shall walk, and in thy name they shall rejoice all the day”—that is, the eternal one—“and in thy righteousness they shall be exalted, for thou art the boast of their strength.” And, “In thy good pleasure our horn shall be exalted.” And again: “The strong ones of God were raised up highly from the earth.” And the most loud-voiced Isaiah thus declares: “They that wait upon the Lord shall put forth wings; they shall renew their strength.” And Saint Macarius says: “Every soul which through faith and the zeal of all the virtues has been rendered worthy of being perfectly clothed with Christ in power and faith thenceforth, and has been united with the celestial light of the incorruptible image, is found worthy to receive substantial knowledge of the heavenly mysteries. And on the day of the resurrection, by the same celestial image of glory, the body, being glorified together with the soul and snatched up into the heavens by the Spirit, according to that which is written, to meet the Lord in the air, having been found worthy to be conformed to the body of his glory, shall reign together with the soul for ages.”
Another recapitulation
26. The beginning and origin of these new and ineffable words is the previously mentioned state of total freedom from care, stillness, attention, and prayer; these possess as a foundation—as it were a firmament and an impregnable rampart—the fulfillment of all the divinizing commandments according to one’s power. From this freedom from care, stillness, attention, and prayer, we say, comes the movement and fervor in the heart which burns up the passions and the demons, and purifies the heart as if in a furnace; and from this ardor follows the desire for the Lord Jesus Christ, and an unceasing love. From this, the sweet outflow of tears of the heart flows in streams, through which the soul and the body, as if by hyssop, are cleansed and nourished by repentance, charity, and thanksgiving and confession. From these things come the calm and peace of thoughts, which has no limit, as it surpasses every mind. From these things follows the snow-bright illumination; and finally, as far as it is possible for man, apathy; and the resurrection of the soul before the resurrection of the body, and the...
image and likeness of the posterior; and through action and contemplation, through faith and hope and love, a reformation and conversion. A direction toward God and an immediate union with Him, an ecstasy, and a cessation, a perfect rest, in the present time indeed as in a mirror and in an enigma and in a pledge; but in the future, a vision face to face, and the perfect and complete participation of God, and His eternal enjoyment.
That this is truly the unerring, and true, and tradition-bearing, and godly way of life, namely the stillness born of obedience; which is also called by the saints, and rightly so, the life hidden in Christ.
97. This is the way, and the godly spiritual life, and the sacred operation of those who are truly Christians; it is the true, and unerring, and unadulterated, and clearly the life hidden in Christ. This the God-Man and most sweet Jesus opened up and initiated; the divine apostles traversed it; and after them followed those who were their successors, our illustrious leaders and teachers; who from the beginning, from the very first presence of Christ on earth, and down to our own day, have shone like luminaries in the world, with the brightness of their life-giving words and with their wonder-working deeds; who have handed down to those even in our time this good seed, this sacred leaven, the holy first-fruits, the inviolable deposit, the grace, the power from on high, the precious pearl, the divine inheritance of the Father, the treasure hidden in the field, the pledge of the Holy Spirit, the royal seal, the living and leaping water, the divine fire, the venerable salt, the charisma, the seal, the light, and things similar to these; which shall also be given as an inheritance, and mystically transmitted through generations of generations, until the very second presence of Christ on earth. For He who promised is truthful, saying, “And behold, I am with you all the days, even unto the end of the age.” Amen.
That even if there be other ways of salvation, yet this one is pre-eminent, and the queen, and leads to adoption.
98. Even if there are other ways and manner of life, and if you will, good works that serve to guide toward salvation and bring to rest the one who follows them, just as indeed there are, and lead to servitude or mercenary labor, and end there, just as it has been said that there are many mansions with the Father given by the Savior; yet this one is the queen and most excellent, and superior to all works, as the soul is superior to the body; inasmuch as it renews one into the adoption of God from earth and dust, and wonderfully makes the man who enters into it a god in the Spirit, as the great Basil says: “When the Holy Spirit has come upon the soul of man, He gave life, He gave immortality, He raised up the one lying fallen.” And that which is moved by the Holy Spirit with an eternal motion has become a holy living being, and man has received the dignity of the Holy Spirit in
him, of prophet, apostle, angel, and of God; though he was previously mere earth and ashes.
That because of the excellence of its operation, this way of life bears many names.
99. Therefore, the divine Fathers have celebrated it with many and various glorious names. They have called it a learned way, an action worthy of praise, and ingenious contemplation; a prayer excelling all breadth; watchfulness of the mind; spiritual work; the work of the age to come; the angelic life; the heavenly way of acting; divine conversation; the region of the living; mystical intuition; the spiritual table; the divine paradise; heaven; the heavenly palace; the kingdom of God; the light-transcending darkness; a life hidden in Christ; the supernatural vision of God; and names similar to these. Following these divine Fathers—while we live in clay and brick, with evil and impure thoughts, words, and works—we have ardently determined to fulfill your request, most beloved one; truly, just as you have asked, we have not hesitated to speak even beyond our measure, on account of our love for you and the command of the Fathers. The leader of this angelic life is the new and ineffable providence and incarnation of the Word and Son of God, the good pleasure of the unbegotten Father, and the cooperation of the Holy Spirit.
ETHICON
That with the help and grace of God, it behooves us to hasten and struggle as much as we can, so that we may be deemed worthy even now, as if by a pledge, of such supernatural and most great gifts; and that we may not, through a little sloth, lose these—alas!—which God forbid.
100. Since such and so great goods are set before us, beloved, not only in hopes and in promises to be fulfilled in the future, but in truth and in reality already, let us hasten, we implore you, while we have time; let us run, let us struggle, so that we too, through a small and temporary zeal and brief toil—and, for the most part, by the gift and grace of God—may be deemed worthy of them. “For the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the glory that shall be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII, 18), as that divine herald Paul says; let us listen to him. Nay, rather, by hastening from now on, even we shall find it as if in the beginning and by way of a pledge. For if those who are chosen for royal kinship and for communion from a lowly station do everything—in work, word, and intent, and by reaching for even those things unreachable—and yet often despise their very lives for the sake of such glory and honor, which is fleeting and temporary, and which sometimes leads to total destruction rather than to any usefulness, how much more does it behoove us to strive and hasten, who are invited to the communion, and marriage, and union of God, the King of all kings and Creator, and the only One incorruptible and existing eternally, and [Who gives] His glory and bo-
honor to His own, glorious and lasting; and furthermore, that we have received the power to become children of God. "For as many," He says, "as received Him, to them He gave the power to become children of God, to those who believe in His name." He gives power; He does not draw us tyrannically nor force us against our own will. For tyranny always arms the one who is oppressed against the oppressor, so that evil may be cured by evil. But in this way He honors the preeminent dignity of our free will, so that the good may be brought about entirely by the benevolence and grace of the working God, while yet the act is also one of our own will and care. And He, although He is God and Lord, did whatever was necessary for Him to do; for He created all alike, and died for all, so that He might save all equally. To us, however, was left the freedom to approach, to believe, to enter into friendship, and with fear and fervor and love to serve that merciful Lord who truly and solicitously loved us; so that for our sake He willingly consented to undergo death, and indeed a shameful death, that He might deliver us from the tyranny of the devil, that ancient enemy, and reconcile us to the Father and God, making us heirs of God and joint-heirs with Himself—a thing most paradoxical and most blessed. B Let us not, then, through small and brief despondency, and carelessness, and worldly pleasure, of whatever kind, cast ourselves away from such and so great goods, and honors, and enjoyments; but let us do everything, and let us work; and if need be, let us not spare even our life for His sake, just as He, though being God, did for our sake, so that we may thus be deemed worthy of all these gifts and crowns, both now and forever. May all of us be granted to attain these, by the benevolence and grace of Him, the all-good and merciful One, our Lord and God and Savior Jesus Christ, who humbled Himself so much for our sake, and who effectively and abundantly bestows His supernatural and deifying grace from then on even to those who are humble in such a way; for to Him is due all glory, and honor, and worship, together with His unbegotten and most pure Father, and His co-eternal, and all-holy, and good, and life-giving Spirit, now and ever, and to the ages of ages. Amen.
CHAPTERS ON PRAYER


[635] {#pg.147.635}
METHOD AND MOST ACCURATE RULE OF CALLISTUS AND IGNATIUS XANTHOPULUS, THE MONKS, WITH GOD
Also containing the testimonies of the saints, concerning those who have chosen to live peacefully and monastically; regarding their instruction, their manner of life, and their regimen; and how many and how great are the good things that stillness provides to those who approach it with understanding.
The present treatise of the discourse is divided into one hundred chapters. The preface of the discourse, which also bears the number of the first chapter, is concerning the divine and supernatural gift and grace existing in the faithful through the Holy Spirit.
1. We ought, indeed, according to the divine oracles, to be taught by God, inasmuch as we bear about the new law ineffably inscribed upon our hearts, shining more clearly than a torch, and are steered by the good and most upright Spirit, as children and heirs of God, and joint-heirs with Christ, to live in a manner imitating the angels, and to be in no need at all of one to teach us, "Know the Lord."   But now, our turning away from good from our earliest youth, and our inclination toward evil; furthermore, the deception of the dreadful Belial and the relentless tyranny that he exercises against us, have disposed us to run far from the saving and god-working commandments, and to rush toward soul-destroying precipices. And, what is more miserable, he provokes us both to think and to act against these commandments; whence also, according to the divine utterance, "There is none that understandeth, there is none that seeketh after God; for all have turned aside, together we have become unprofitable," and for this reason we have become flesh, deprived of the light and of divine grace, and   we are in need of mutual excitation and aid toward the good.


[637] {#pg.147.637}
That this argument was explained out of the inquiry of a certain brother, and in accordance with his desire, and for the observance of the Fathers' precepts.
2. Since, however, you, out of longing, in accordance with the Lord's word, have often demanded of us—unworthy as we are—a discourse and a written rule for the sake of your own profit, and perhaps also for that of others, as you yourself say, that you might search the divine and life-bestowing Scriptures and be instructed securely; and since, if not before, at any rate now, by the help of God, we have judged it necessary to fulfill your praiseworthy and heartfelt desire—forgetting our own innate indolence for the sake of charity and your profit, but rather admiring your ardor for good things and your persistent love of study, spiritual and most beloved son, and before all these things, fearing the judgment of God which has dreadfully threatened the one who hides his talent; and fulfilling also the paternal command which our Fathers and spiritual teachers laid upon us, that we should trust and hand down to other friends of God those things which they taught us. May God, therefore, the Father of charity and the unfailing Bestower of all good things, grant to us, who are so slow and endowed with such a thin voice, a timely discourse upon the opening of our mouth—He who often inspired voices into irrational animals—for the profit of the hearers; and may He grant to you, and to all who come upon these things, according to your desire, an ear to hear them wisely and properly and to fulfill them faithfully according to His mind; because without Him, as it is written, we can do nothing useful or saving, and because "unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it have labored in vain." And these things by this manner.
That the end precedes every matter; therefore, the end of the present treatise is to learn what the foundation is.
3. Since the end precedes every matter; and the purpose of both—ours, indeed, to explain to you what tends to spiritual growth; and yours, to live sincerely according to what is said—it behooves us, before anything else, to examine what sort of perfection of the house of Christ we are intending by laying a useful foundation; then, as the occasion invites us, or rather as we are abundantly favored by aid from above, we may be enabled to place a roof worthy of the architecture of the Spirit.
That the beginning of every life according to God consists in acting according to the commandments of the Savior; but the end is the return to the perfect grace of the most holy and life-giving Spirit, given to us from the beginning through divine baptism.
4. The beginning, therefore, of every life according to God, to grasp it in summary, is that we hasten


[639] {#pg.147.639}
in every way and with all our strength to conduct our lives according to the ordinance of all the deifying commandments of the Savior. And the end is that, through the keeping of these, we may return to that perfect and spiritual transformation and conformation of grace, given to us from above and from the very beginning through the holy pool—or, if it pleases you to call this gift such—stripping off the old Adam along with his deeds and desires, and putting on the new and spiritual One, who is the Lord Jesus Christ, as the most divine Paul says: "My little children, of whom I travail in birth again until Christ is formed in you," and, "As many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ."
On the question of what grace is, and how we might attain it; and what things cloud it, and what things, in turn, cleanse it again.
5. But as to what grace is, and how we might attain it, and which things cloud it and which in turn cleanse it, he who is more radiant than any gold in soul and tongue shall declare to you, saying thus in regard to that which is written: "What is intended by the words, 'beholding the glory of the Lord, we are transformed into the same image'?" "This was shown more clearly when the gifts of the Spirit were working through signs, yet even now it is not difficult for one who has faithful eyes to perceive it. For, as soon as we are baptized, our soul shines brighter than the sun, being cleansed by the Spirit, and we not only look upon the glory of God, but we also receive from thence a certain radiance.   For just as pure silver, if it be placed before the rays of the sun, sends forth rays itself, not only from its own nature, but also from the solar brilliance; so also the soul, being cleansed and having become brighter than any silver, receives a ray from the glory of the Spirit into the glory which is being generated, and such as is fitting to be received from the Lord the Spirit." And a little further on: "Do you wish that I manifest this to you more vividly from the apostles as well? Consider Paul, whose garments performed works; Peter, whose shadows possessed power. For they would not have had such power in their garments and shadows if they did not bear the image of the King, and if their splendors were not inaccessible. For the garments of a king are terrible even to robbers. Do you wish to see this radiance also shining through the body? 'Looking steadfastly,' it says, 'at the face of Stephen, they saw it as the face of an angel.' But this is nothing compared to the glory that shines within. For that which Moses once had upon his face, these men carried within their soul;   nay, indeed, something much greater. For that of Moses was sensory, but this is incorporeal. And just as flaming colors flowing from radiant bodies onto those things which are near communicate their own brilliance to them, so indeed does it befall the faithful; and because of this, those who experience this are released from the earth and dream of the things that are in heaven, alas! For it is beautiful even to sigh with longing, because, while enjoying such nobility, we do not...


[641] {#pg.147.641}
A even know what is spoken of, because we quickly destroy these things, and are beside ourselves for the sake of sensible things. "For this glory, which is unassailable and fearsome, remains in us for a day or two, but thereafter we extinguish it, bringing upon ourselves the winter of the concerns of this life, and by the thickness of the clouds, we repel the rays." And again elsewhere: "The bodies of those who have pleased God will be clothed in such glory that it cannot be seen even by these eyes." And God has prepared for us certain signs and faint traces of these things, both in the Old Testament and in the New: for there, the face of Moses shone at that time with such glory that it was inaccessible to the eyes of the Israelites. But in the New, the face of Christ shone forth with much more than this. Have you heard the words of the Spirit? Have you understood the power of the mystery? Have you learned what kind of offspring the perfect spiritual formation within us is, which proceeds from the holy font? What, then, will be the yields of the fruits, what the fullness, what the rewards? And how is it in our power to both increase and diminish—that is, to brighten and to dim—this supernatural grace in the present life? From this arise the storm of the affairs of this life and the moonless night of   passions born from them, which, like a winter storm or a wild torrent, rush upon us, and, submerging the soul, do not allow it to breathe or look toward that truly beautiful and blessed One, for the sake of whom it was made, but rather, darkening it entirely with the surge and smoke of pleasures, having become powerful and bitter, they submerge it. Just as, therefore, the things contrary to these—that is, those born through the deifying commandments—are beneficial and saving for those who walk not according to the flesh but according to the spirit ("For walk in the Spirit," he says, "and you shall not fulfill the lust of the flesh" [Gal. 5:16]), and, like a ladder, lead to that crowning point and the highest of the steps, which is love, which is God.
That in holy baptism we receive the divine grace as a gift through it, but having obscured it by passions, we cleanse it again by the fulfillment of the commandments.
6. But while we originally receive in the divine womb—that is, in the holy font—the entire [gift], perfect divine grace as a gift, if, however, we later, by the misuse of temporal things and by the care for the affairs of this life and by the mist of the passions, have, as we ought not to have, obscured it, it is   permitted to us, even so, through repentance and the fulfillment of the deifying commandments, to recover such supernatural brightness and to regain it, and to behold its manifestation most clearly. Yet the appearance of this is revealed according to the measure and strength of each person's faith, and before these, by the help and good pleasure of the Lord Jesus Christ, as the holy Mark says: "Christ, who is perfect God, has bestowed on the baptized the perfect grace of the Holy Spirit, in no...


[643] {#pg.147.643}
wise receiving an addition from us, but being revealed and manifested to us according to the proportion of our working of the commandments, and providing for us an increase of faith, until we all attain to the unity of the faith, to the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ." If, therefore, we make any addition, having been regenerated in Him, that too is from Him, and was hidden within us from Him.   That he who labors according to God must fulfill all His commandments, but must attribute the greatest part of his work to the first and, as it were, general ones
7. Since, therefore, the beginning and root of this entire undertaking, as we have said, is to live according to the saving commandments, and the end and fruit is to return to the perfect grace of the Spirit which was first bestowed upon us by baptism—which exists in us (for the gifts of God, it is said, are without repentance), but was buried by the passions, and is revealed through the working of the divine commandments—it behooves us, by the fulfillment of all such commandments as far as we are able, to hasten by every means to cleanse that manifestation of the Spirit which is in us, and to behold it most clearly. "For Your law, O Lord," says the blessed David, "is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths, and the commandment of the Lord is bright, enlightening the eyes," and "I was directed to all Your commandments." And he who reclined upon the breast of Christ says: "He who keeps His commandments abides in Him, and He in him; and His commandments are not grievous." And the Lord Himself says: "He who has My commandments and keeps them, he it is who loves Me; and he who loves Me shall be loved by My Father, and I will love him, and will manifest Myself to him." And, "If anyone loves Me, he will keep My word, and My Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our abode with him." And, "He who does not love Me does not keep My words."   We ought, therefore, to apply the greatest part of our work to the first and more general of these commandments, and in a way to those which are as it were the mothers of the rest; for thus, with God, we may unerringly attain the proposed goal, namely, the beautiful beginning, and the end of our desire, which is the manifestation of the Spirit.   That the beginning of every God-pleasing work is the invocation with faith of the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, and with it, the peace and love that spring from it
8. The beginning, however, of every God-pleasing work is the invocation with faith of the saving name of our Lord Jesus Christ, because He Himself declared: "Without Me you can do nothing." And with it, peace. For, it is said, one ought to pray "without anger and disputing." And love; because God is love, and he who abides in love abides in God, and God in him. This peace and love not only make prayer acceptable, but from prayer itself [they are renewed].


[645] {#pg.147.645}
born and rise, like twin divine rays, and they grow and are perfected. *That through each of these, and simultaneously through all three, the store of all good things is lavished upon us.*
9. From these, or rather through each of them, and simultaneously through all three, the store of all good things is lavished and overflows upon us. For by the invocation of the name of our Lord Jesus Christ in faith, we firmly hope to receive mercy and true life hidden in Him; as if from another ever-flowing divine spring, it pours these forth abundantly into our breasts, when the name of the Lord Jesus Christ is purely invoked.   By her, however, who possesses the whole mind, the peace, we are deemed worthy to be united with God and with other men. By charity, truly, whose glory is incomparable, since it is the end and sum of the law and the prophets, and since God Himself is named charity, we are wholly united with God, our sins being abolished by the justice of God, and that grace which makes us sons wonderfully working in us through charity. For charity, he says, will cover a multitude of sins; and charity bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things; charity never fails.
*That our Lord Jesus Christ also, at the time of His saving passion, left these to His disciples as a kind of final commandment and divine testament, and likewise after the resurrection.*   10. Whence also our all-good and most sweet Lord Jesus Christ, both when He arrived at His voluntary passion for our sake, and when, after the resurrection, He was seen by the apostles; and indeed also when He was about to return to Him who is Father to Him by nature and to us by grace—as a true and most loving father—he left all these to all His own as a kind of final command, and gentle consolations, and most sweet and solid, so to speak, pledges; or rather, as an indelible divine testament. And indeed, entering upon His saving passion, He said to His disciples: "Whatever you ask the Father in my name, I will do." And, "Amen, amen, I say to you, that whatever you ask the Father in my name, He will give you.   Hitherto you have asked nothing in my name; ask, and you shall receive, that your joy may be full." And, "On that day you will ask in my name." And again, after His resurrection, He said: "And these signs shall follow those who have believed: in my name they shall cast out demons, they shall speak in new tongues," and so forth. Consistent with these, he who reclined upon His breast also declares: "Many other signs therefore Jesus did in the sight of His disciples, which are not written in this book; but these are written, that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that..."


[647] {#pg.147.647}
believing you may have life in His name.”   And the inspired Paul says, “In the name of Jesus every knee shall bow,” and so forth. And therefore, in the Acts of the Apostles it is written thus: “Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, said: ‘Be it known to you all, and to all the people of Israel, that in the name of Jesus of Nazareth, whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead, by Him this man stands before you whole.’” And after a few words: “And there is no salvation in any other; for there is no other name under heaven given among men, by which we must be saved.” And again, the Savior says, “All authority has been given to Me in heaven and on earth.” And again, as to what the God-man Lord said to His apostles before the crucifixion: “Peace I leave with you; My peace I give to you. These things I speak to you, that in Me you may have peace.” And, “This is My commandment, that you love one another.” And, “By this all will know that you are My disciples, if you have love for one another; as the Father loved Me, I also have loved you; abide in My love. If you keep My commandments, you will abide in My love, just as I have kept My Father’s commandments and abide in His love.” And again, after the resurrection, He appears at various times and frequently gives peace, manifesting Himself to His own and saying, “Peace to you.”   And to Peter, to whom He entrusted the governance of the disciples, He shows that the care of the flock is a sort of requital for his fiery love for the Lord Jesus Christ Himself, saying in this way for the third time, “If you love Me, Peter, more than these, feed My sheep.” One might perhaps say, and not without reason, that through these three great things which we have shown, three other excellent things are born to us—namely, the purification of the soul, illumination, and perfection.
That all virtues are woven together in these three.
11. But if anyone wishes to examine accurately, he will clearly find that in this triple-braided and, so to speak, unbroken cord, all the abundant and God-fashioned purple of the virtues is suspended and woven. For the life according to God is as a precious chain, and a rope variegated with gold, connecting one virtue to another and reducing all to a consolidated unity.   Indeed, many things bring about this one work—namely, the deification of the man who sincerely lives a life in accordance with the virtues—so that, bound by such knots and ties, through faith, if he wills, and hope, and humility, he may deserve to be named by the beloved and saving name of the Lord Jesus Christ, and attain peace and charity. This is truly the thrice-perfect tree, the planting of God, bearing the fruit of life; in which, once grafted, man in this life, having become a participant in it in a manner befitting him, does not reap death, as the first-formed one did, but eternal life and a


[649] {#pg.147.649}
A life that does not perish.
That the gift and arrival of the Holy Spirit to the faithful, through God the Father, is granted in Christ Jesus and in His holy name.
12. Indeed, the gift and arrival of the Holy Spirit to the faithful, through God the Father, is granted in Christ Jesus and in His holy name, as the most divine and loving Lord Jesus Christ Himself says to the apostles: "It is expedient for you that I go away; for if I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you." And, "But when the Paraclete comes, whom I shall send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father." And again: "But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name."
That it has rightly been ordained by our holy Fathers, that we should pray to our Lord   Jesus Christ with the Holy Spirit dwelling in them, and seek mercy from Him.
13. For this reason, then, our renowned guides and teachers, quite wisely and with the Holy Spirit dwelling in them, teach us that before every other good work and exercise—especially if we wish to dedicate ourselves to the arena of deifying stillness, to be set apart for God, to be severed from the world, and to live in stillness according to reason—we must pray in the Lord and seek mercy from Him without wavering, and hold His most holy and sweet name as an unceasing work and meditation. And we must carry this in our heart, and in our mind, and on our lips without interruption, and in Him and with Him breathe, and live, and sleep, and keep watch, and move, and eat, and drink, and, so to speak, strive to do all things in like manner. For just as when He is absent, every evil rushes in—or rather, nothing of what is useful is present to us—so when He is present within us, every contrary thing is driven away, and above all, nothing of the good is lacking to us, nor is anything opposed to our improvement; just as our Lord Himself declares: "He who abides in me, and I in him, he bears much fruit; for without me you can do nothing." Therefore, having invoked in faith this work and name—which is to be feared and revered by every creature, and which is above every work and   name—and having altogether unfurled the sails of this present discourse upon it, we thus begin to speak and to proceed further.
That he who wishes to walk without stumbling must, before all else, choose the Lord's path of stillness along with total renunciation and perfect obedience.
14. In the name of the great God our Savior Jesus Christ, who said: "I am the light, the life, and the truth, and the way, and the door to God the Father, and through me if anyone enters, he shall be saved," and


[651] {#pg.147.651}
he shall enter and go out, and he shall find pasture, that is to say, salvation. Apply your mind to what we are saying, and we sincerely offer you counsel: above all, choose for yourself, in accordance with the universal divine declaration, renunciation and unconditional, perfect submission; that is, strive to seek and find a guide and teacher who does not err. And that which is unerring will be found if he presents the testimony of the holy Scriptures in the things he says, if he has the Holy Spirit within himself, leading a life that conforms to his actions; if he is lofty in contemplation but humble in mindset, and in all other ways good, and such a one as the divine words define a teacher according to Christ to be. But once you have found him, remain attached to him, as a most loving son to a true father, with both body and spirit; remain whole   by walking according to his commandments, looking toward him as if toward Christ himself, and not toward a man, casting all disbelief and doubt far from you; and indeed, even your own mindset and your own appetites together with your will; thus, simply and without curiosity, follow the footsteps of the teacher as if you possessed some mirror, for clear conviction   and supreme obedience, regarding your own conscience. And if at any time the devil, who hates virtue, should sow anything contrary into your mind, jump away from it as you would from fornication and fire, and wisely talk back to the deceiving tempter, saying that the one being led does not direct the one leading, but the one leading directs the one being led; and "I do not sit in judgment of my master, nor has my master accepted my judgment; nor am I his judge, but he has been constituted as my judge," as he who takes his name from the *Ladder* says, and reply with other things of this sort.
For there is nothing, without a doubt, more certain by such direction—that is, by submission—to one who has chosen to, for him to tear up the handwritings of his own transgressions   and be inscribed in the divine record of those who are saved. For if, according to the blessed Paul, the Son of God and our God, the Lord Jesus, became as we are for our sake, and while wisely managing the Father's good pleasure, he was seen travelling such a path, through which he was deemed worthy of the paternal proclamation, even for the sake of his good pleasure according to man? "For he humbled himself," he says, "becoming obedient unto death, even the death of the cross. Wherefore God also highly exalted him, and gave him a name," and the rest.   Who then will hope with pride, not to say foolishly, that he will attain the glory of the Lord and God and Savior Jesus Christ and the paternal rewards, if he does not choose to walk the same path as our leader and teacher, Jesus Christ? For it is necessary for the disciple, if he wishes to become like the teacher, to gaze incessantly, as if upon an exemplar and most beautiful archetype, with the whole force of his soul, unswervingly, toward the life and conduct of his tutor; and daily to attempt to imitate him. Furthermore, concerning our Lord Jesus Christ himself, it is written: "And he was subject to his father and mother." And the Savior himself says:


[653] {#pg.147.653}
"I came not to be ministered unto, but to minister."»   And there is another who wishes to live in a different way, that is, self-pleasingly and of his own authority, and without a guide. Does such a man think that he is walking in the manner of a life according to God? By no means; not at all; he is like one leaping over cliffs. And the one of the Ladder says: "Just as he who has no guide easily wanders on the road, so also he who walks the monastic path by his own authority easily perishes, even if he understands all the wisdom of the world."   For this reason, many, not to say all, who are not subject and do not walk with counsel, though they labor and sweat greatly while dreaming, truly reap the very least. But some, alas, instead of grain, gather tares, as they walk, according to what has been said, in self-will and a self-pleasing mindset, than which there is nothing worse. And witness to this is the author of the Ladder, who writes thus: "As many of you as have undertaken to strip for the arena of mental confession; as many of you as wish to place the yoke of Christ upon your own necks; as many of you as are eager to lay your own burdens upon the neck of another; as many of you as are hastening voluntarily to write your own lives, and wish to have freedom rendered to you in return for them; as many of you as are being lifted up by the hands of others and are swimming across this great sea; know that you have chosen to walk a short and rough path, having only the error in itself; and this is called 'self-will' (idiorrhythmia). For he who has renounced this entirely, before he even walks, has reached the goods that seem spiritual and pleasing to God. For obedience is to distrust oneself in all good things until the end of life."   When you, therefore, having studied these things with understanding and desiring to practice the good portion and the inalienable peace of the heaven-bound stillness, follow the laws which have been well-proclaimed, as has been shown to you, and first eagerly embrace obedience, then in this way, peace. For just as practice is a step toward contemplation, so is obedience to stillness. And do not wish to move the boundaries, as it is written, which the Fathers have set. Woe to the solitary! For in this way, by laying a beautiful foundation, as time advances, you will place a most glorious roof upon the architecture of the Spirit. For just as he whose beginning is, as it has been said, without glory, will have his whole work rejected, so conversely, he whose beginning is glorious, his whole work will be acceptable and well-arranged, even if its opposite   sometimes happens; and this, however, happens to come about through our own purpose and will.
What are the signs of true subjection, by which he who is instructed might be truly subject.
15. But since the discourse concerning such a way of life is extensive and difficult to navigate, from which it follows that those who undergo it do so in different ways, it is fitting also to indicate a few things about it, as it were, as signs, which...


[655] {#pg.147.655}
you may keep as an infallible rule and balance, in order to live most purely. And this we say: He who is truly subject must necessarily pursue these five virtues. First, faith, that is to say, to have pure and sincere faith in him by whom he is directed, to such a degree that he believes that Christ himself is observing him and that he is obeying Him, as the Lord Jesus says: "He that heareth you, heareth me; and he that despiseth you, despiseth me; and he that despiseth me, despiseth him that sent me." And whatsoever is not of faith, according to him who derives his name from the Ladder, is sin. Second, truth: it is necessary for him to be truthful both in deed and word, and in the accurate confession of his thoughts. "For the beginning of thy words is truth," as it is written, "and the Lord requireth truth." And Christ also says: "I am the truth"; and indeed He is called Truth itself. Third, not to follow one’s own will. For it is a loss, he says, for one who is subject, to do his own will, but he must always willingly submit it, and not allow himself to be compelled by his own Father. Fourth, not to contradict nor to contend at all, since contradiction and contention are not characteristics of the pious. And the most holy Paul writes: "But if any man seem to be contentious, we have no such custom, neither the churches of God." If then it is so simply and commonly forbidden to all Christians, by much more so to monks, and this according to the Lord, to whom they have promised to be accurately subject. Contradiction, however, and emulation have their origin in a mind teeming with pride and unbelief, as it has been said: A proud monk contradicts vehemently;   just as the opposite, that is to say, not to contradict and not to contend, proceeds from a faithful and humble disposition. And fifth, he must guard this virtue, namely to have an accurate and sincere confession toward his superior, just as we did at our tonsure, as if we were standing before the fearful judgment seat of Christ, in the sight of God and the holy angels, where we gave our promise to hold fast to the beginning and the end, along with our other promises and covenants made to the Lord, and to confess the secrets of our heart. It has been said also by the most holy David: "I said, I will confess against myself my iniquity to the Lord, and thou hast forgiven," etc. And by the same Author of the Ladder: "Stripes, if they triumph, will not advance to the worse, but shall be healed."
Whoever wisely and ardently guards this fivefold number of virtues which we have shown, let him know without doubt that he will attain, as if by a down payment, the blessedness of the righteous. And these indeed are the properties of this magnificent subjection, and are as it were the root and the foundation. But hear also what the branches are, and the fruit, and the top.
From subjection, the same Author of the Ladder says again, comes humility; from humility, discretion; from discretion, perspicacity; and from this, foresight;   which is solely the work of God, and to those who successfully act according to God, a gift


[657] {#pg.147.657}
bestowed by Him, excellent and supernatural. A Furthermore, let this also be known to you: that according to the measure of your submission, humility will sprout within you; and again, according to the measure of humility, likewise discretion; and so on for the rest of the virtues. And strive with all your might to run the course of obedience without stumbling. For in this way, you will advance without danger to the things that lie before you. But if you should limp by some fault in the pursuit of submission, know that you will not successfully finish the remaining race of the course of the, as we say, life according to Christ; nor will you be crowned with the wreath given to the victors. Therefore, take obedience to be your own and what we have called its properties, so that it may show you the way, just as those who sail are guided by the stars, so that they do not wander across the seas; so that, always looking to it, you may be able to cross the great ocean of the virtues and thus reach the tranquil harbor of detachment. But if some storm and tossing should come upon you, this too will happen because of your   disobedience. For the true obedient one, according to the Fathers, not even the devil himself is able to harm. But that we may show you in a few words how sublime and honorable true obedience is, let us record one more oracle of a holy Father.
Therefore, the most radiant light of the life according to Christ, and the new Beseleel of the heavenly Ladder, says again: “The Fathers define armor to be psalmody; a wall, prayer; but a bath, blameless tears; yet they judge blessed obedience to be a confession, without which no one among those subject to the passions will see the Lord.” These things are indeed sufficient, as it seems to us, for the most evident declaration and praise of the inimitable imitation of thrice-blessed obedience. We can still learn and discern this by experience   if we look back to the things before, and inquire what was the cause of our destruction and mortality, since we were not created such from the beginning; and what is the cause of our renewal and immortality. We find, then, that the cause of the former, that is, of corruption, was the first Adam’s self-reliance, his self-will, and his disobedience; from which arose the rejection and transgression of the divine commandment. But of the latter, that is, of incorruption, the author was the second Adam, even God and our Savior Jesus Christ, through His subjection to the Father, from which came the observance of His commandment. “For I,” says the Savior, “have not spoken of myself; but the Father who sent me, He gave me a commandment, what I should say and what I should speak. And I know   that His commandment is eternal life. Therefore, what I speak, as the Father has said to me, so I speak.” As, therefore, in the forefather and those who act according to him, self-conceit is the root and mother of all evils; so in the new God-man Jesus Christ, and in those who strive to live according to Him, the beginning, and fountain, and foundation of all good things, is humility. Such a state and order, and which is above us, we see that of the divine Angels observing; this, indeed, the earthly


[659] {#pg.147.659}
Church, and those of us who turn aside from such regulations, and wishing—not to speak arrogantly—to live differently, we remember and believe that they are severed from God, and from that brilliant heavenly inheritance and the catholic Church, and are cast out and sent down into the darkness and the fire of Gehenna. And we say that those who behaved wickedly toward the East, and who in the times of the heretics spoke vain things, suffered this, as the divinely written oracles have shown, who, because of their self-sufficiency and pride, were miserably cast out from the divine glory, as it is said, and joy, and the holy assembly.   It has also been said by one of the wise that "contraries are the cures for contraries." Since, therefore, the cause of all gloomy things is disobedience and arrogance, while that of joyful things is obedience and contrition, it is necessary that he who desires to live securely should subject himself to a prudent Father, versed in the way, who, by experience of time and knowledge of divine things, possesses authority, and whose life is adorned with a garland of virtues; and he should hear his precepts and counsels as the voice and counsel of God. "For safety is in much counsel," he says. And, "A man without counsel is an enemy to himself." And if it happened that some of the Fathers, even without this exercise of subjection, attained divine peace and that perfection which is according to God, this was by divine revelation and happened rarely. It is also written that the rare is not the law of the Church, just as neither does one swallow make spring. But do you, believing   true obedience to be the preliminary introduction to the most excellent tranquility, leave aside those things which once happened by divine dispensation, and walk according to those things that were pleasing to the venerable Fathers. Thus will you be worthy of the reward due to those who live lawfully. What then? Would one not tread an obvious path if he had not yet experienced it, without an expert guide? Nor would he traverse the Ocean without an expert pilot; nor attempt any art or science without an infallible master; and yet, the art of arts, the science of sciences, the path leading to God, and the infinite ocean of the mind,—namely, the monastic life, which is compared to the life of the angels—would anyone dare to approach it, and hope to attain its end, without a leader, and pilot, and prudent and sincere master? In reality, whoever he is, he deceives himself, and errs, not even laying any foundation, since he is exercised outside the rule; just as, on the contrary, he who obeys the oracles of the Fathers has anticipated the end   even before he walks. For from where else can we learn how we ought to fight against the flesh, as is fitting, or how the war against desires and demons is to be undertaken? For together with the virtues, as it is written, grow the vices, and they stand in a certain way near the door. But how shall we chastise the senses of the body and order the virtues of the soul as in a threshing floor? Or rather, how will it be permitted to us to discern voices, and revelations, and divine exhortations and contemplations, and the guilts, errors, and oracles of the demon? And, to speak in one word, how are we to attain to that union with God, to that divine perfection, to the mysteries, when—


[661] {#pg.147.661}
without the leading of a true and enlightened mystagogue? It is not possible, indeed, it is not possible. For when we see that chosen vessel, the most blessed Paul, that instructor in the ineffable, the mouth of Christ, the light of the world, the common sun, the teacher of the entire inhabited earth, sharing and deliberating on the Gospel with his fellow apostles—and the reason, he says, is lest I might be running, or have run, in vain—and indeed when we hear Wisdom herself, our Lord Jesus Christ, speaking of Himself, that "I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of Him who sent me, the Father," and concerning the all-holy and life-giving Spirit, that "He will not speak on His own authority, but whatever He hears, He will speak;"   by reason of the utility of this order, which holds together both heavenly and earthly things, we are seized with horror, stupor, and anguish when we attend to our own weakness and infirmity, and to those who dementedly choose to live obliquely, dangerously, by their own whim and caprice. For in truth, that struggle is terrible, and the robbers are countless, and the stratagems of the tempters are six hundredfold. And the shipwrecks cannot be numbered; whence even out of the many, barely a few escape. But let them walk as they please; "For every man’s work, as it is written, the fire will test," and that "You will render to each according to his works."   But especially, may Christ grant to all to understand not simply how they wish, but how it is necessary to both will and live. As for you, and whoever wishes to live according to Christ, as if taking hold of a hem of these words, seize the golden and spiritual path of blessed obedience, and hasten, as has been indicated beforehand, to find a learned and perfect master; for perfect, according to the divine apostle Paul, is solid food; that is, for those who by reason of habit have their senses trained to discern good and evil. And in this way, namely, by seeking with labor and faith, you will not miss your proposed goal.   "For everyone, says divine Scripture, who asks, receives, and he who seeks, finds, and to him who knocks it will be opened." And he will initiate you successively and by order into those things which are to be done and which please God, or rather, he himself will take you by the hand to those things which are pleasing and spiritual to God, and by most people considered intolerable; when he sees you truly rejoicing in mediocrity, humility, and simplicity, whether in food, or in clothing, or in cloak; and being content with those things which for the time are useful and opportune and necessary; and not with those superfluous, idle things, nor those things which, indulging in trifles and insane splendor, men deem great and draw a sword against themselves and their own salvation. For even the great Apostle says: "Having food and clothing, with these we shall be content." But you desire and wish to learn from us in writing what things pertain to the beginning, the inception, and the end of this Christian life? However much your question is to be commended, it is truly laborious to suddenly answer you


[663] {#pg.147.663}
nevertheless, with Christ guiding our hand, we shall endeavor to fulfill your request, building, as upon a firm and unshakable foundation, upon that perfect and in every way reward-worthy obedience, this house celebrated by the speech of all, which we call the divine peace of all spiritual building. And surely we speak, supported by the oracles of the Fathers and the Holy Spirit as by most firm pillars.   That he who wishes to have true and divine peace must take care to be full of good works along with orthodox faith; and that faith is double; and that he who is at peace must be peaceable, undistracted, free from care—that is, unconcerned—silent, quiet, thankful in all things, conscious of his own weakness, and must bear temptations nobly, hope in God, and accept from Him what is useful.
16.
