The Savior says: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ shall enter the kingdom of heaven; but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven.” And you, therefore, beloved, if you love this God-making stillness not only with empty words—which, to those who sincerely enter into it, even now provides clearly the impressions of the kingdom of heaven and of God, and in the future, more fully and perfectly—but if you love it in truth and in deed, take care to be, alongside your orthodox faith, full of good works. Then, let your manner be peaceable with all, undistracted, free from care—that is, entirely unconcerned—silent, quiet,   thankful in all things, and conscious of your own weakness. And in all, keep an eye wakeful and sober against the various and manifold temptations that occur to you each day; fighting with obedience and magnanimity against the waves and the affliction that may come upon you from any side.
Concerning the first and the second—that is, that you ought to be adorned with good works along with orthodox faith—that illustrious brother of the Lord admonishes you openly, saying: “Faith without works is dead; just as works are without faith,” and, “Show me your faith by your works.” And before him, the instructor and master of all, our Lord Jesus Christ, said to His disciples: “Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to keep all that I have commanded you.” And the Theologian also says that God seeks these three things from every man who has baptism: right faith from the soul, self-control from the body, and truth from the tongue.


[665] {#pg.147.665}
That faith is twofold.
2. Note that faith, according to the God-given oracles, is twofold. One is general, common to all orthodox Christians, into which we were baptized from the beginning and in which we must depart from this world. The other belongs to the few, namely to those who, through the fulfillment of the commandments of the deifying passions, have returned to the image and likeness, and thus, having been enriched by the divine light of grace, have anchored all their hope in the Lord. And so great—oh, the dignity of it!—is this, that they no way, according to the Lord’s word, waver at the time of prayer in their requests to God; but rather, they ask with faith and thus readily receive what is beneficial. For this reason the blessed ones have possessed this faith, confirmed by sincere works, as having cast away all knowledge, discernment, hesitation, and anxiety from themselves, and having been totally and completely immersed in the divine intoxication of faith, hope, and love toward God, and thus transformed by the better and blessed transformation of the right hand of the Most High, as the divine David says.
But to speak at length about the first faith is not for the present time; however, to speak about the second, which blossoms and is born like a flower from the first, is very timely. For faith is like a root and principle of the namesake deifying stillness. For if you do not believe, says the author of the *Ladder*, how will you be still?   The divine David therefore says: "I believed, therefore I spoke" (Ps. CXV, 10). And the great apostle Paul says: "Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen" (Heb. XI, 1); and "The just shall live by faith" (Heb. X, 38), etc. And the Savior, to the disciples asking him to increase their faith, speaks thus: "If you have faith as a grain of mustard seed, you would say to this mulberry tree, ‘Be plucked up by the roots and be planted in the sea,’ and it would obey you" (Luke XVII, 6). And: "If you have faith and do not doubt, you will not only do what was done to the fig tree, but even if you say to this mountain, ‘Be removed and be cast into the sea,’ it will be done" (Matt. XXI, 21). And: "All things whatever you ask in prayer, believing, you will receive" (Matt. XXI, 22). And: "Your faith has saved you" (Matt. IX, 22). The holy Isaac also writes: "Faith is sharper than knowledge, as knowledge is [sharpened regarding] sensible things."   For all the saints, having been deemed worthy to find this manner of life—which is an amazement toward God—live in the power of faith, in the delights of that life which is above nature.
We do not mean by faith that by which one believes in the distinction of the adorable and divine persons, and in the excellent and proper nature of the Divinity Itself, and in the wonderful economy which is accomplished in humanity, in the assumption of our nature—although that faith is indeed very high. Rather, we mean the faith which arises from the light of grace in the soul, by the testimony of the mind, establishing the heart unshakeably—far removed from any mere opinion. It does not show itself by the mere hearing of the ears, but looks with the eyes of the spirit upon the mysteries hidden in the soul, and those hidden and divine riches which are separated from the eyes of the children of the flesh   and are revealed through the Spirit only to those who recline at the table of Christ and meditate upon his laws, just as


[667] {#pg.147.667}
at the assurance of hope, which is removed from all conceit; and it shows itself not in the increase of the hearing of the ears, but in the spiritual eyes, the mysteries hidden in the soul; and the hidden and divine wealth, which is hidden from the eyes of the sons of the flesh, and is revealed in the Spirit to those who dwell at the table of Christ, in the meditation of his laws, as he said: “If you keep my commandments, I will send you the Paraclete, the Spirit of truth, which the world cannot receive; and he will teach you all truth,” and so forth. And again: “Until that comes which is the fullness of the mysteries, and we are deemed worthy of the manifestation of them, faith serves between God and the holy ones, mysteries [of which may we be deemed worthy through the grace of his Christ], here indeed as in a pledge, but there in the substance of truth, in the kingdom of the heavens, with those who love him.”
That you must be peaceable.
C. Concerning the third, namely that you must have peace with all, the exhortation is evident from the oracle of David; and indeed even more so from that of the Christ-bearing Paul, which rings out clearer than a trumpet: the former says, “Great peace have they that love thy law; and there is no stumbling-block for them.” – “And with them that hated peace I was peaceable.” And: “Seek peace, and pursue it.” The latter says, “Follow peace with all men, and holiness, without which no man shall see the Lord.” And: “As far as it is possible for you, being at peace with all men.”
That you must not be distracted.
D. As for the fourth, namely that you must be undistracted, that holy man Isaac will teach you, saying: “If desire,” he says, “is the fruit of the senses, then let those keep silent henceforth   who claim that peace of mind can be preserved alongside distraction; and do not associate with those who are distracted.”
That you must be free of anxiety and care.
E. Concerning the fifth, namely that you should not be anxious or concerned for any reason, whether from reasonable or unreasonable causes, you shall have as a document that which the Lord says in the Gospels: “Therefore I say to you, do not be anxious for your life, what you shall eat; nor for your body, what you shall put on. Is not the soul more than meat, and the body than clothing? Behold the birds of the heaven, that they do not sow, neither do they reap, nor gather into barns; and your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not much better than they? Which of you by being anxious can add one cubit to his stature? And why are you anxious for clothing?” And a little later: “Do not be anxious, therefore, saying, ‘What shall we eat?’ or ‘What shall we drink?’ or ‘Wherewith shall we be clothed?’ For all these things the nations seek after. For your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things. But seek first the kingdom of...


[669] {#pg.147.669}
and His righteousness, and all these things shall be added unto you. Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof.” St. Isaac also says: “Unless you are free from anxiety, do not seek for light, nor for tranquility and stillness, in the slackness of your senses.” And the author of the *Climax* says: “A single hair torments the eye, and a little care banishes stillness. For stillness is the setting aside of thoughts and the denial of reasonable anxieties. He who has truly grasped stillness will not even be concerned about his own flesh.” For He who promised is truthful.
That you must be a lover of silence.
6. Furthermore, the theme of the sixth point—namely, that you must be silent—compels me to speak. Regarding this, the holy Isaac also says: “He who keeps his mouth from backbiting preserves his heart from the passions; and he who cleanses his heart from the passions beholds the Lord at every hour. And if you place all the works of the way of life on one side of the scale, and silence on the other, you will find that silence has more weight.” And: “Love silence above all things, because it brings you near to the fruit. For the tongue is powerless to explain it. Let us first force ourselves to be silent, and then something will be born in us from silence, guiding us to silence itself. May God grant you to perceive something born in you from silence! But if you begin in this way of life, I do not know how great a light will rise for you from it.” And again: “Silence is the mystery of the world to come, but words are the instruments of this world.” And to the holy Arsenius, the divine voice prescribed for the second time: “Arsenius, flee, be silent, be still, and you shall be saved.”
That you must be tranquil.
7. Likewise, regarding the seventh point—namely, that you must live a tranquil life—the great Basil and again the holy Isaac are trustworthy witnesses to present. The former says: “Tranquility is the beginning of the purification of the soul”; the latter says: “The definition of tranquility is silence from all things.” The one indicates its beginning, the other its end, through these words, as if in brief. And in the Old Testament it is said: “Have you sinned? Be tranquil.” And: “Be still, and know that I am God.” The author of the *Climax* also says: “The primary work of tranquility is to care for nothing, whether concerning things that are rational and agreeable, or contraries. For he who opens the door to the former will immediately fall into the latter: a fearless prayer, and then the most perfect work of the heart.” It is impossible for one who has not learned letters to study on tablets; it is still more impossible for those who have not attained the first to attain the two others. And again the holy Isaac says: “The desire for tranquility is the continuous expectation of death. He who enters into tranquility without this exercise cannot endure what we must patiently bear and endure in every way.”


[671] {#pg.147.671}
That one must give thanks in everything. A Likewise, concerning the eighth, that is, that you ought to give thanks in everything, you have an excellent guide in the divine apostle Paul, who instructs us thus: "In everything give thanks." And the holy Isaac says: "The gratitude of the receiver incites the giver to bestow greater gifts than the former ones. He who does not give thanks for smaller things is a liar and unjust regarding greater ones. And the heart that directs the gifts of God toward man is a heart moved toward unceasing thanksgiving; the intention that directs temptation toward the soul is the thought of murmuring, which is always stirred up in the heart; but the mouth that gives thanks continually receives a blessing from the Lord, and the grace of God is poured out upon the heart that perseveres in gratitude."
That one must acknowledge one's own infirmity.  How much profit is gathered by him who proceeds to know his own infirmity (which is indeed the ninth in number), you will learn by applying your mind to the sixth psalm of the divine David, where he says: "Have mercy on me, O Lord, for I am infirm." And elsewhere: "I am a worm and no man, a reproach of men and the outcast of the people." And the holy Isaac says: "Blessed is the man who knows his own infirmity, because this knowledge becomes for him a foundation and the beginning of all goodness. For when someone learns and in truth senses his own infirmity, then he protects his soul from the pride that weakens knowledge, and he stores up a defense for himself." And: "The man who has attained to knowing the measure of his own infirmity, this one has reached the perfection of humility."
That one must manfully resist temptation.  There remains that chapter which constitutes the tenth number, namely that you must manfully, patiently, and long-sufferingly sustain the diverse and manifold temptations that supervene upon you. Hear, therefore, what is written in the divine Scriptures concerning this; for the apostle of Christ, Paul, says: "Our struggle is not against blood and flesh, but against principalities and powers, against the world-rulers of this darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places." And: "If you are without discipline, of which all have become partakers, then you are illegitimate and not sons." And: "Whom the Lord loves, He disciplines; and He scourges every son whom He receives." And the brother of the Lord: "A man who is not tempted is unapproved."   And the holy Elias, that just man, says: "It is permitted for every Christian who truly believes in God not to be anxious, but to wait for and receive temptation from every side, so that when it comes, he may not be startled nor troubled, but, giving thanks, may endure the blows of affliction, and consider what he says while chanting with the Prophet: 'Test me, O Lord, and try me';" he does not say:


[673] {#pg.147.673}
"Your discipline has destroyed me," but A "He has straightened me to the end." Furthermore, do not seek after the causes of temptations, nor from whence they come; but only pray to God to be able to bear them with gratitude, as the holy Mark says: "When a temptation has come, do not seek why, or through whom it has come, but rather how you might endure it with gratitude and without resentment." And again: "If it is not easy to find one who has been pleasing [to God] without temptations, one must give thanks to God for every occurrence." And: "Every affliction tests the inclination of the will, whether it leans to the right or to the left; for this reason, the affliction that befalls one is called a temptation, as it provides to the participant a trial of hidden volitions."   And the holy Isaac, among many other things, also says this: "Temptation is useful to every person; for if it is useful to Paul, every mouth shall be stopped, and all the world shall be held accountable to God." Those who struggle are tempted so that they may add to their wealth; the proud are tempted, that they may preserve themselves from those who do them harm; the drowsy are tempted, that they may be instructed to awaken; those who are far away, that they may draw near to God; and those who are familiar, that they may dwell in [His] presence with boldness. Every son who is not trained does not receive the wealth of his father's house, so as to be helped by it; and for this reason, God first tempts and afflicts, then shows the gift. Glory to the Lord, who brings us the delights of health through bitter remedies! There is no one who, in the time of training, is not burdened, and there is no one to whom the time in which he is given the poison of temptations to drink does not seem bitter. For without these, it is impossible to acquire a strong constitution; and to endure, moreover, is not our own. For how could a vessel made of clay sustain the nature of water,   if the divine fire did not solidify it? If we be submissive, praying in humility with constant desires, we, too, shall receive all things in patience, in Christ Jesus our Lord. It is said also in the Wisdom of Sirach: "My son, if you come forward to serve the Lord your God, prepare your soul for temptation, and set your heart straight, and endure, and do not be hasty in the time of affliction."
That one ought to hope in God, and to expect from Him what is beneficial.
Fasten the anchor of hope upon God who is able to save you, and wait for the outcome of temptations from Him at the opportune time. "For faithful," he says, "is God, who will not suffer us to be tempted beyond what we are able, but will, along with the temptation, also make the issue." And that "affliction produces patience; and patience, probation; and probation, hope; and hope does not put to shame." And, "He who endures to the end, this one shall be saved"; and, "In your patience, possess your souls." And the brother of the Lord also speaks thus: "Count it all joy, my brethren, when you fall into various temptations, knowing that the testing of your faith produces patience;


[675] {#pg.147.675}
and patience has its perfect work, that you may be perfect and entire, lacking in nothing. And, "Blessed is the man who endures temptation, for when he has been approved, he will receive the crown of life which the Lord has promised to those who love Him." And, "The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us." And, "I waited patiently for the Lord, and He inclined to me, and heard my cry, and brought me up out of a horrible pit, and out of the miry clay, and set my feet upon a rock, and established my steps; and He has put a new song in my mouth, a hymn to our God."   And the blessed Simeon Metaphrastes also writes: "A soul caught in the bonds of divine love deems suffering as nothing, but rejoices in evils and flourishes in hardships; and when it suffers nothing painful for the sake of its Beloved, then it believes that it suffers most of all, and flees from ease as if it were a punishment."
Concerning the fear of God, that it is twofold: the fear of beginners and the fear of the perfect.
17. We must not hesitate now to make mention of the twofold fear according to God, although, by our own arbitrary choice, by speaking of the perfect fear after we had finished the ten chapters we indicated, we have disturbed the order of the first fear; for after faith, fear is ordained by the holy Fathers.
Concerning the first fear, which is that of beginners.
Know then, most beloved, that the fear of God is twofold: one indeed of beginners, the other of the perfect. Concerning the former, it is written:   "The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord"; and, "Come, you children, listen to me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord"; and, "By the fear of the Lord everyone turns away from evil"; and, "Where there is fear of God, there is the fulfillment of the commandments." And the pious Isaac also says: "The fear of God is the beginning of virtue." It is said to be the fruit of faith, and it is sown in the heart when the mind is separated from the distraction of the world, for the gathering of its thoughts that are wandering from instability, in the contemplation of the future restoration. And, "The beginning of the true life of man is the fear of God; and this   cannot remain in the souls of some men along with instability of mind"; and, "Take care that on your journey you lay as a foundation the fear of the Lord, and you may be able to arrive at the gates of the kingdom after a few days, without the detours of the road."
Concerning the second and perfect fear of God.
Concerning the second, namely the perfect fear of God, it is thus said: "Blessed is the man who fears the Lord, who delights greatly in His commandments"; and, "Blessed are all who fear the Lord, who walk in His ways"; and, "Fear the Lord, all you His saints, for there is no want to those who fear Him"; and, Behold


[677] {#pg.147.677}
so shall the man be blessed who fears the Lord; and, "The fear of the Lord is pure, enduring for ever and ever." Saint Peter of Damascus also writes: "The sign of the first fear is hatred and anger against sin, as if one were wounded by a beast; but of the perfect fear, it is the love of virtue and the fear of change." And he adds that no one is immutable, and that in all actions of life we must fear lest we fall. Wherefore, you too, understanding these things prudently, endeavor with all the aforementioned to keep that first fear within yourself ceaselessly; for it is the safest treasury of every good work. For having it thus, your steps will be directed toward the practice of all the commandments of our Lord Jesus Christ; and proceeding on this way, you will also attain to the perfect and pure fear, through the desire for virtues, and through the mercy of our good God.
That for the sake of the commandments and the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, when the occasion is urgent, we ourselves must not spare our own life.
18. In addition to what has been said, you ought also to observe this, that for the sake of the life-giving commandments, and the faith in our Lord Jesus Christ according to them, we ought, when the occasion demands it, to gladly lose our very soul; that is, not even to spare our own life. As our Lord Jesus Christ himself says regarding this: "He who loses his soul for my sake and the Gospel's, he will save it"; believing without doubt and without hesitation that the God-man, Jesus the Savior, is both resurrection and life, and everything that is salvific, as He Himself   said: "I am the resurrection and the life; he who believes in me, even if he die, shall live"; and, "Everyone who lives and believes in me shall never die for eternity"; and, "For God so loved the world that He gave His only-begotten Son, that everyone who believes in Him should not perish, but have eternal life"; and, "I came that they may have life, and have it abundantly." Having yourself thus, and always forgetting the things behind and stretching out to the things before, as it is said, run with Christ Jesus our Lord, without turning back, in this way your course. It is good, however, as it seems to us, and very useful, to set forth first the natural method of the most blessed Nicephorus the Great, regarding the interior heart through the   entrance of breathing by the nostrils, which contributes somehow also to the recollection of the intellect; so that thus, by a well-disposed path, with God, the present treatise may proceed. That divine man therefore says, with many others, having the authority from the recorded testimonies of the saints, the following:


[679] {#pg.147.679}
A natural method regarding the interior of the heart through the inspiration of the nostrils, and the prayer that operates with it, which is: "Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me." Such a method also contributes to the gathering of the mind.
19. A “You know, brother, that the breath which we breathe is this air; and we breathe it not for any other reason, but for the sake of the heart; for this is the cause of life and of the warmth in the body. The heart therefore draws in the spirit, in order that it may expel the heat outward through the expiration, and provide itself with a good temperament. The cause, or rather the minister, of such a process is the lungs, which, created fragile by the Creator, like a bellows painlessly draw in and send out the surrounding air. Thus, therefore, the heart, by drawing in the cool air and expelling the warm, inviolably maintains the order for which it was created for the preservation of the living creature. You, therefore, sitting in a quiet cell and gathering your mind, introduce it—that is, the mind—into the path of the nostrils, where the spirit enters into the heart, and urge it, and force it to descend with the inhaled spirit into the heart.   And when it has entered there, what will happen to you afterwards will not be without joy, nor without delight; but as a man who is away from his own house, when he returns, does not know what to do for joy because he has been deemed worthy to meet with his children and his wife, so also the mind, when it is united with the soul, is filled with ineffable joy and gladness. Therefore, brother, accustom the mind not to leave that place quickly; for at the beginning it suffers much because of the confinement and narrowness. But when it becomes accustomed, it no longer desires the roamings outside. For the kingdom of heaven is within us; and he who looks at it there, and seeks it through pure prayer, detests and hates all things outside.” And a little later:   “You must also learn this, that when your mind is in that state, you ought not to leave it idle and silent, but take care that it meditate on this: ‘Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me,’ and that it meditate assiduously, and never cease from this meditation. For this work, holding the mind firmly, renders it insuperable and inexpugnable to the blows of the enemy, and leads it daily to the love and desire of God.” These, then, are the words of that blessed Father, having as his primary aim that, by the operation of this natural method in some way, the mind might return from its accustomed wandering, captivity, and instability to attention, and through attention might be joined to itself, and thus be united to prayer, and that from then on it might descend into the heart—with the prayer itself, clearly—and remain always within it, just as another of the men full of divine wisdom, as if explaining the oracle previously set forth, as one who is experienced in such a sacred work, declares the following. And


[681] {#pg.147.681}
On the method of natural inspiration through the nostrils, and the invocation of our Lord Jesus Christ that accompanies it.
20. It is necessary to make this manifest to those who love learning: that if we train our intellect to descend, during the intake of the breath, along with it, then we would accurately understand that the intellect, having descended, does not depart—or rather, it does not begin to depart—before it has cast off every reasoned thought and has become single and naked, clinging to no other memory save for the invocation of our Lord Jesus Christ; but when it departs from there again and goes to external things, it is divided, even against its will, toward a multiform memory.
That the divine Chrysostom, as also others of the ancient holy Fathers, decrees that we must pray in Christ Jesus our Lord; and within the heart; and he speaks of this prayer: "Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me."
21. Also the great Chrysostom says: "I entreat you, brothers, never trample upon or despise the rule of prayer." And a little later: "The monk ought, whether he is eating, or drinking, or sitting, or serving, or traveling, or doing anything else, to cry out unceasingly: 'Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me.'" And after a little: "In order that the name of the Lord Jesus, descending into the depth of the heart, may humble the dragon that has seized the pastures, and may save and vivify the soul."   "Therefore, remain unceasingly with the name of the Lord Jesus, in order that the heart may swallow the Lord, and the Lord the heart, and the two may become one." And again: "Do not separate your heart from God, but persevere, and protect it with the memory of our Lord Jesus Christ always, until the name of the Lord is implanted deep within the heart, and it thinks of nothing else, so that Christ may be magnified in you."
Further, regarding that memory of Jesus, with attention, within the heart through the inspiration of the nostrils.
22. Also, the author of the Ladder writes: "Let the memory of Jesus be joined to your breath, and then you shall know the benefit of stillness." And the holy Hesychius says: "If you truly desire to cast shame upon your thoughts, and to live in stillness and tranquility, and to watch over your heart with ease, let the prayer of Jesus be joined to your breath; and in a few days you shall see this accomplished."
That it is necessary for one who wishes to watch over his mind spiritually, and especially the beginner, to sit during the time of prayer in a quiet and dark cell, because in this way the intellect and thought are naturally, in part, gathered together.
23. Whence, along with the things declared, as being from above, and as decreed by the great holy Fathers, in accordance with the testimonies set forth for us concerning praying through the inspiration of the nostrils and within the heart—both in our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, and in his holy and saving name—and regarding the exercise, and the watchfulness, and the petitioning for mercy from him; there must be added also this, namely that always, but especially


[683] {#pg.147.683}
at the appointed time of prayer, and indeed in a dark corner, one should sit who is striving to watch mentally within his heart, and this is even more applicable to the beginner, as those holy Fathers and teachers who have had experience of such a most blessed work instruct and command. For the gaze and vision of the eyes are naturally apt to divide and separate the mind toward things seen and observed, and indeed to distract and change it. But when one is shut in, as has been said, in a quiet and dark room, he ceases from this distraction and change which occur through sight and appearance; and thus, whether willingly or unwillingly, the mind dwells in peace and is accustomed to be gathered to itself, as the great Basil says: "A mind not distracted toward external things, nor diffused over the world by the senses, returns to itself."   That before all things, through our Lord Jesus Christ and the invocation of his holy name with faith in the heart, constancy is provided to the mind; and the natural method through the inspiration of the nostrils, and the remaining in a quiet and dark place, and the like, cooperate with it in a certain way in the heart.
24. And before these, or rather before all things, such a struggle is brought to perfection for the mind by the cooperation of divine grace, which supervenes upon the single-word invocation of our Lord Jesus Christ, performed with a pure heart and without turning about in faith, and not by that method we have set forth—by the inspiration of the nostrils or staying in a quiet and dark place—far from it! For such things were not devised by the holy Fathers for any other purpose than that these might serve as aids to the recollection of the mind and to its return from its accustomed wandering to itself and to attention, as we have said. Through all of which, a continuous, and pure, and constant prayer   is generated in the mind. As St. Nilus says, the attention that prayer seeks, it will find. For prayer follows attention—if anything else does—which is why it must be sought. And these things have been said. But you, my son, who wish to live and desire to see good days, and to live in the body as if without a body, live under such a rule and standard.
How one who is quiet ought to pass the interval which separates evening from dawn; and the beginning of the instruction according to width.
25. When the sun has set, after you have invoked our Lord Jesus Christ, the all-good and omnipotent, for his aid, sit on a couch in a quiet and dark cell, and gathering your mind from its external, accustomed roaming and wandering, and gently pushing it into the interior of your heart, through the inspiration of the nostrils hold the prayer, namely: "Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me"; at the same time, of course, drawing in with your breath   in a unified way the words of the prayer, just as the holy Hesychius says: "Unite the watchfulness of your [heart] to the inspiration of your nostril, and the name of Jesus, and the certain care for death, and humility."


[685] {#pg.147.685}
For you know that both these things are helpful: having, along with prayer and the other things mentioned to you, the memory of the judgment and of the recompense for good and evil deeds; and—strictly deeming yourself, in your soul, to be the most sinful of all men, and more unclean than the demons themselves—on account of this, consider that you are to be eternally punished. In whatever line of reasoning among those mentioned you find compunction, sorrow, and tears, dwell specifically on that one as long as these alone continue. But if you have not yet been deemed worthy of the gift of tears, strive and ask with a humble mind to attain it. For through these we are cleansed of passions and stains, and we become partakers of good and saving things, as the one of the Ladder says: "Just as fire consumes straw, so pure tears consume every stain, both visible and invisible."   And another Father says: "He who wishes to cast out malice, casts it out by weeping; and he who wishes to acquire virtues, acquires them by weeping. And if you do not have compunction, know that you have vainglory; for this does not allow the soul to be pricked." If tears do not come, sit and attend to these thoughts, along with prayer, for one hour; then, having risen, chant the Little Compline with attention, and sitting down again, hold to the prayer as much as you are able, purely and without distraction—that is, free from anxiety, from any kind of thought, and from any imagination—with great vigilance for half an hour, according to the one who says: "Without breath and food, be outside all other things in prayer, if you wish to become with the mind alone." Then, having sealed yourself with the sign of the precious and life-giving cross, and likewise your bed, and having sat upon it, enter into contemplation concerning future enjoyments, we say, and punishments; [also] of the fleeting and deceptive nature of temporal things; and indeed also of the sudden and common debt—namely, death; and of the fearful judgment that is after the end, and [that which is] before the end; and having remembered your transgressions in general, as in a summary, and having fervently asked for forgiveness for these, and having examined yourself accurately as to how you passed the previous day, lie down, holding also to the prayer, according to the one who says: "Let the memory of Jesus sleep with you," sleep for five or six hours; or rather, according to the interval of the night, sleep yourself in proportion.
How one ought to pass the time of the dawn, even until the morning.
26. Having become awake, and having glorified God, and again having called upon Him for your help, begin the first of your first works, that is, to pray in your heart without distraction and purely, for one hour; for at that time the mind is generally calm and unperturbed. Nevertheless, we are commanded to offer to God the first and foremost things; that is, to extend our first thought, as much as possible, unswervingly, through pure prayer of the heart, toward our Lord Jesus Christ.   And the holy Nilus says: "This one performs prayer, who always [keeps] his primary thought..."


[687] {#pg.147.687}
A offered to God. After this, chant the midnight office. But if, because you are not yet suited for more perfect stillness, you are unable, as we have said, to begin, or perhaps for some other reason—as often tends to happen to those just starting such a work, and indeed rarely even to those who are progressing and have not yet attained perfection (for the perfect can do all things in Christ who strengthens them)—rise from sleep, and as far as you are able, having become vigilant, chant first the midnight office with all attention and understanding. Then, sitting down, pray purely and unswervingly in your heart, as has been indicated, for one hour; or rather, as the Giver of good things shall grant you. For the author of the *Ladder* says: "By night, give most of your time to prayer; [give] but a little to psalmody; and when day returns, prepare yourself according to your strength." If, however, even after struggling in this way, you are still negligent and despondent, and you find your mind troubled by some occurrence, rise, bestir yourself, as you know how, and occupy yourself with prayer.
Then sitting down, hasten to pray, as has been written,   constantly taking care that through pure prayer you may commune with the pure God. Then rising, chant with understanding the Six Psalms, the fiftieth, and whatever canon you wish. Then sitting down after this and keeping watch, pray with sincerity for half an hour. And again, rising, chant the praises [of God], the customary doxology, and the first hour. And after these things, conclude. Let the words spoken by your lips be raised to such a height that they are audible only to your own ears; since we are commanded to offer the fruit of our lips to God; with all our soul and mind giving thanks to the benevolent and provident and all-wise God of ours, who, according to His great mercy, has granted us to pass safely through the expanse of the past night, and to behold the bright course of the present day; and fervently entreating Him likewise that He may grant us to pass the day without tumult, through the dark and savage storm of demons and passions, and that He may have mercy upon us.
How one should conduct oneself from morning until the midday meal.
27. Again, from the morning until the midday meal, as much as you can, offering yourself wholly to the whole God, and praying to Him with a contrite heart that He might help you—as you are weak, frail, and feeble—pass the time thus in constant prayer of the heart; when reading, read the Psalms, the Apostle, and the Gospel while standing; doing likewise in your prayers to our Lord Jesus Christ and the most pure Theotokos; but sitting during the remaining readings of the Holy Scriptures. After these things, chant with your mind the customary hours, which have been most wisely arranged by the fathers of the Church, driving away idleness with all your will, as the mother of all malice.


[689] {#pg.147.689}
along with the passions and their occasions, even if they seem to be small and appear harmless.
On guarding against idleness; and that it is necessary even for the one who lives in tranquility to observe the ecclesiastical tradition.
28. As the holy Isaac says: "Guard yourselves, dearly beloved, against idleness; for in it most certain death is concealed, so that without it, it is not possible to fall into the hands of those who hasten to capture the monk." God will judge us on that day not for the psalms, nor for sloth in prayer, but for the fact that through their omission, an entrance is given to the demons. And once they have found room and entered in, and have closed the doors of our eyes,   then they will fill us tyrannically and impurely, just as the divine sentence comprehends its fellow-workers with the most violent vengeance; and we become their servants, because we have neglected the small things which, for Christ’s sake, are worthy of care, as it has been written by the most wise: "He who does not subject his own will to God, will be subjected to His adversary." Thus, these things that seem small to you should be reckoned as walls for you against those who lie in wait for us, the perfection of which has been wisely established within the cell by those who hold the magistracy of the Church, for the guarding of our life in the spirit of revelation, the neglect of which is considered trivial by the unwise,   who do not reckon the damage that follows from them. Of these men, the beginning and the middle of the way is untaught liberty, which is the mother of the passions. For it is better to struggle not to neglect small things, than to give a place to sin by neglecting them. For the end of this untimely liberty is bitter servitude. And again: "O how sweet are the beginnings of the passions!" For while one can sometimes cut off the passions and become tranquil by their removal, and rejoice when they cease, yet he cannot abandon their causes; therefore, we are tempted even against our will, and are bound by the passions, but we prefer their principles to reside within us. We do not desire the sins, but we receive with joy the causes that bring them to us.   For this reason, the latter become, by their own efficacy, the causes of the former. He who loves the beginnings of the passions is subject to them against his will and desire, and is made a slave to the passions. He who hates his own sins will cease from them; and he who has confessed them will find forgiveness. However, it is impossible for anyone to abandon the habit of sin before he has conceived hatred for it, and to attain forgiveness before he has confessed his transgressions; the former is the cause of true humility, the latter of compunction, which follows in the heart with shame. And again: "There is no sin that is irremissible, except that which is not corrected." But enough has been said on these matters. You, however, after the psalmody of the stated hours, eat; while occupying yourself in prayer during the eating, so that by doing this you may arrive at the habit, by the power of grace, of praying unceasingly, according to our Lord's


[691] {#pg.147.691}
A commandment. But let the discourse concerning the food that sustains the body, according to the ineffable wisdom of its Creator, wait a little; and let the discourse concerning that which sustains and vivifies the soul be set forward, which is, according to the saints, the holy and deifying prayer. And very rightly so, since the soul is also more precious than the body.
Concerning prayer, and that one ought to pray always.
29. Just as this body of ours, if the soul is absent, is dead and exhales a foul odor, so too the soul, if it does not move itself toward prayer, is dead, and wretched, and foul. And that it is fitting to believe that the lack of prayer is worse than any death, the great prophet Daniel teaches us well,   who deemed it better to die than to be deprived of prayer for a single moment of an hour. The divine Chrysostom also teaches us well: "Whoever prays, converses with God. How great a good it is for a man to converse with God, no one among all is ignorant; but to demonstrate this honor in words, no one could. For this honor transcends even the magnificent state of the angels." And further: "Prayer is the common work of angels and men alike. There is no longer, regarding prayer, any medium between either nature. It separates you from the brute beasts; it joins you to the angels.   Quickly would one pass over into their way of life, and manner of living, and conversation, and honor, and nobility, and wisdom, and understanding, if he would zealously spend his whole life in prayers and in the worship of God." And further: "When the devil sees a soul fenced about with virtues, he does not dare to draw near to it, fearing the strength and power which prayers provide, which nourish the soul more than corn nourishes the body." And further: "Prayers are the nerves of the soul. For just as the body is held together by nerves, and is knit up, and stands, and lives, and is made solid; but if anyone should cut these, he dissolves the   whole harmony of the body; so souls are harmonized and knit together through holy prayers, and they run the course of piety happily. If, however, you deprive yourself of prayer, you do the same thing as if you were to take a fish out of the water. For just as water is life to it, so is prayer to you; through it, you may fly through the air, as if through water, and ascend into the heavens, and draw near to God." And further: "Prayer and supplication render men the temples of God; and just as gold, and precious stones, and marble make the houses of kings, so also does prayer make men the temples of Christ. What greater eulogy of prayer could there be than that it makes us temples of God? And He whom the heavens do not contain, this One enters into the soul that lives in prayers." And further: "From this one may know the virtue of holy prayer, that Paul, who runs throughout the whole earth as if winged, and dwells in prison, and endures lashes and sorrows, and lives amidst bloodshed and dangers, casts out demons, raises the dead, and throughout all the habitable


[693] {#pg.147.693}
area, he did not rely on any of these things for the salvation of men, but fortified his soul with prayers; and after the signs and the resurrection of the dead, he ran to his prayers just as an athlete runs to the wrestling ground   for his crown. For prayer is the provider of the resurrection of the dead and of all other things. For as water has power over trees, so do prayers have power over the life of the holy ones. Furthermore: Prayer is the occasion of salvation, the procurer of immortality, the unbreachable wall of the Church, an asylum and guardian, fearful to the demons but saving to us the pious. Furthermore: Just as when a queen enters a city, it is necessary that all wealth follow her, so too, when prayer enters into a soul, the whole of virtue enters with it. Furthermore: What the foundation is to a house, that is prayer to the soul; and it is necessary to stake this down first like a base and root in the soul, and then to build upon it eagerly both temperance, and provision for the   poor, and all the laws of Christ. Furthermore: Prayer with fervor is the light of the intellect and the soul; a light unquenchable and perpetual. For this reason the wicked one casts countless swarms of thoughts into our minds; and things we never even contemplated, he gathers together and pours over our soul at the time of prayer. Furthermore: Prayer is a great weapon; a great security. And the Theologian says: “One must remember God and breathe God.” And again: “Think of God more continuously than you breathe.” And the holy Isaac says: “Without unceasing prayer, you cannot draw near to God.” And: “After the labor of prayer, to cause the intellect to occupy itself with another care brings about a dispersion of the mind.” And: “Every prayer in which the body is not labored and the heart is not crushed is considered an abortion; for that prayer is without a soul.” And the one of the Ladder says:   “Prayer is, according to its essence, the communion and union of man and God; but according to its operation, it is the consistency of the world, reconciliation with God, the mother of tears and again their daughter, the expiation of sins, a rampart against temptations, a middle wall against affliction, the healing of wars, the work of the angels, the food of all incorporeal beings, future joy, infinite activity, the fountain of virtues, the origin of gifts, invisible progress, food for the soul, enlightenment of the intellect, an axe for despair, the demonstration of hope, the cleansing of filth, the riches of monks, the treasure of the hesychasts, the mitigation of anger, a mirror of progress, the showing of measures, the declaration of a state, the revelation of things to come, a token of   glory. Prayer is, to those who truly pray, a tribunal and judgment seat, before the future judgment seat is established. And again: “Prayer is nothing other than an alienation from the visible and invisible world.” And the holy Nilus says: “If you desire to pray, renounce all things, so that you may inherit the All.” Furthermore: Prayer is...


[695] {#pg.147.695}
the communion of the mind with God. Furthermore: Just as bread is nourishment for the body, and virtue for the soul, so too is spiritual prayer the nourishment of the mind. And so much for these things; it is timely now to set forth, as briefly as possible, regarding bodily diet, both as to weight, quantity, and quality thereof.
On bodily regimen: how he who is tranquil ought to nourish himself.
30. It is written: “Son of man, thou shalt eat thy bread by weight, and drink thy water by measure, that by these, he who wishes to struggle according to God may live, having sufficient nourishment.” For unless you give blood, as it is said, you shall not receive spirit. But also the great Paul says: “I chastise my body, and bring it into subjection, lest perhaps when I have preached to others, I myself should become a castaway.” And the divine David: “My knees are weakened through fasting, and my flesh is changed for oil.” And the Theologian: “By nothing else, as by suffering evil, is God worshiped, and his mercy poured out through   tears.” And holy Isaac: “As a mother cares for her child, so Christ cares for the afflicted body, and is perpetually near to this body.” And again: “In a belly that is full, there is no knowledge of the mysteries of God.” And: “As to those who sow in tears, sheaves of rejoicing arise, so joy follows that affliction of the body which is according to God.” And Macarius: “He who removes himself from all delights which separate him from his Creator.” And again: “Being tempted for a long time on the right and on the left, and having often tested myself in these two ways, and having received countless blows from the enemy, and having been deemed worthy   of great secret gifts, I have gained experience for myself from the long passage of years; and in probation, and by the grace of God, I have learned these things: namely, that the foundation of all good things, and the liberation of the soul from the captivity of the enemy, and the way leading to light and to life, are these two methods: to gather oneself into one place, and to always fast; that is to say, to regulate oneself in temperance of the belly, wisely and prudently, in an immovable seat, in incessant tranquillity, and in the meditation of God. For from thence arises the subjection of the senses; thence the vigilance   of the mind; thence those raging desires which are stirred in the body are restrained; thence the sweetness of reasonings; thence the luminous motion of thought; thence the ardor for the divine works of virtue; thence sublime and delicate thoughts; thence incessant tears, which flow perpetually; thence the memory of death; thence the pure wisdom which is removed from every phantasy that hinders thought; thence the sharpness of sight and the vigor of the knowledge of things that are far off. Thence those deeper mystical senses which thought grasps in the power of the divine oracles, and the interior motions which are produced in the soul, and the difference and the discernment of spirits and of holy powers and of true vision and vain imaginations, and thence the fear of the ways and paths—


[697] {#pg.147.697}
that are stirred up in the sea of the mind, which cuts off sloth and negligence; and the flame of zeal, which transcends every danger and passes over every fear; and the warmth, which scorns every desire and wipes it out from the mind, and produces oblivion of all memory of things that pass away along with the rest. And, to speak briefly, the freedom of the true man, and the joy of the soul, and the resurrection, and the rest with Christ in the kingdom of heaven, come from this. If anyone is negligent in these two, let him know that he not only deprives himself of all the things aforementioned, but also shakes the foundation of all virtues by his contempt for these two virtues.   And just as these are in the soul the beginning and head of divine operation, and the door and way to Christ, if anyone takes hold of them and perseveres in them, so also if anyone withdraws from them and leaps away from them, he arrives at the two things that are contrary to these—I mean, to be puffed up in the body, and to indulge in gluttony lawlessly, and the rest. And in others: "And some, being slothful and lax at their beginnings, are not only terrified and troubled by these and such-like struggles, but also by the rustling of the leaves of a tree; and they are overcome and cast down and turn backward by a small necessity that arises from the discomfort of hunger, and by a small infirmity. But the sincere and approved ones are not even sated with the grass of herbs; nor, nourished by the roots of dry plants, do they dare to taste anything of them before the appointed hour of food. But they lie upon the ground in the infirmity and weakness of the body; and their eyes have dim vision,   because their body is excessively empty. And if they are in such a state from necessity that they are about to depart from the body, not even then do they give their hands to be overcome and succumb, so strong is their will. For they desire and wish to do violence to themselves for the sake of the love of God; and they prefer to labor for the sake of virtue than to have a transient life and all the rest that is in it. And when temptations come upon them, they rejoice more that they are perfected in them, that is, they become perfect. But neither do they doubt in the love of God because of the harsh afflictions that occur in them; but until they have departed from this life, they desire to undertake labors generously, and they do not yield, because they become perfect in them." Following then in these and such-like things, and also being obedient to Him who said:   "Walk in the royal way, and do not turn aside to the right or to the left," we also set forth for you an example and a rule of the mean, which indeed has this definition.
How one who struggles ought to be nourished on the second, fourth, and sixth days.
31. As for the three days of the week, that is, the second, fourth, and sixth, observe them perpetually; that is, eat once a day, taking six ounces of bread, taking a sufficient amount of dry foods temperately; and of water, if you wish, three or four...


[699] {#pg.147.699}
of the apostles, who says: "If a bishop, or presbyter, or deacon, or reader, or chanter does not fast during the holy quadragesima of Pascha, or the fourth day, or the preparation day (Friday), let him be deposed, unless he is hindered by bodily infirmity. But if a layman, let him be excommunicated." And the second day has likewise been regulated by the holy Fathers. A How one must eat on the third and fifth day
32. On these two days again, namely the third and the fifth, eat twice in the day: at the midday meal, sustain yourself with six ounces of bread, eating temperately of cooked food and some of the dry foods, and drinking wine mixed with water—up to three or four cups, if   you wish. Toward evening, take three ounces of bread and some dry foods or certain fruits; take wine mixed with water, one cup, or at most two, when violent thirst urges you. For thirst cooperates vehemently in tears, having wakefulness as a companion, as the author of the *Ladder* says: "Thirst and wakefulness have wrung out the heart; and when the heart was afflicted, waters have gushed forth." And the blessed Isaac says: "Thirst for God's sake, that He may fill you with His love." But if you prefer to eat only once on these two days, you shall do well. For fasting and temperance are the first, and mother, and root, and fountain, and foundation of all good things. A certain one among the profane says: "Choose the best life; habit will make it sweet." And the great Basil:   "Where there is choice, there is no obstacle." And another of the saintly ones: "The beginning of fruit is the flower, and the beginning of the active life is temperance." But these things may perhaps seem difficult, nay even impossible, to those who wish to follow them; yet he who considers the thriving fruitfulness that blossoms from them, and contemplates what great glory they are wont to generate, will judge them tractable, and by the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ and his own zeal according to his strength, he will proclaim them most easy in words and deeds, and will seal them with sanction. And the holy Isaac says: "Simple bread from a clean table cleanses the soul of the eater from every passion." And: "From the table of those who fast and keep vigil and labor in the Lord, take for yourself a remedy of life, and stir up   the dormant soul of yours; because the Beloved reclines in their midst, sanctifying the foods, and transforms their bitterness into His own ineffable sweetness. And His spiritual and celestial ministers overshadow them and their holy food." And: "The odor of the one who fasts is most sweet, and his encounter gladdens the hearts of those who have discernment." And: "The life of the temperate man is most dear to God."
How one must eat on the Sabbath; and concerning vigils, and how one must eat during their time
33. On every Sabbath, except the Great Sabbath, it behooves you to eat twice, as has been indicated for the third and


[701] {#pg.147.701}
A fifth, both because of the definition of the holy canons, and because you ought to possess this custom on all the Sundays of the entire year, except for the vigil during the week of Tyrophagy, unless perhaps a vigil for one of the great Feasts of the Lord or one of the greatest Saints should fall then; in which case, having celebrated that, you may omit the Sunday vigil. Nevertheless, whatever the case may be, eat twice on the Sabbaths.   It is useful, however, that you constantly compel yourself to the labor of the nocturnal vigil. Whence, even if by chance a vigil occurs in the middle of the week, it is most profitable for you to keep the vigil also on Sunday, and you will quickly receive great gain from it; nay more, your morning light will thus break forth, according to that which was said: “And your garments [in other copies: your healings] shall soon rise.”   The holy Isaac also says: “For every struggle against sin and desire, the labor of the vigil and of fasting is the beginning, and especially for him who fights against the sin within us. And the sign of hatred for sin and its desire is manifest from this to those who gird themselves for this invisible war. And almost all the impulses of the passions begin to diminish in fasting. And after fasting, the night vigil cooperates with the exercise. He who in all his life loves the yoke of this combined discipline, this man becomes a friend of prudence; just as the delights of the belly are the principle of all evils, and the abundance of sleep, which favors the desire of fornication: so the holy way of God and the foundation of every virtue is fasting, and the vigil, and alertness in the service of God.” And again:   “A soul that is brightened by the memory of God and by sleepless vigil, day and night: there the Lord builds for its security, a cloud overshadowing it by day, and a fire of light illuminating the night; and in its darkness, light will shine.” And further: “Choose for yourself the operation of delights, the continuous vigil in the nights: in which all the Fathers put off the old man, and were deemed worthy of the renewal of the mind. In these hours the soul perceives that immortal life; and in the perception of it, it puts off the darkness of the passions, and receives the Holy Spirit.” And again: “Honor the operation of the vigil, so that you may find consolation in your soul.” And further: “Do not think, O man, that in any of the monastics’ work, there is any conduct greater than the nocturnal vigil.” And: “Do not look upon a monk who persists in the vigil, with discernment of mind, as one clothed in flesh; for this work is truly of the angelic order.” And further: “A soul laboring in this angelic conduct of the vigil will have cherubic eyes, to look constantly and behold the heavenly contemplation.” You shall spend these vigils, namely, in prayer, psalmody, and reading, purely and steadfastly and with compunction, alone, or with a pious and like-minded assembly. After any vigil of yours, perform a small refreshment, because of the labor brought on by the vigil, eating and drinking, at the time of the meal: to wit, eat three ounces of bread; add a little dry food, which will suffice for you: drink wine with water, three cups. See to it, however, that you do not push your vigil into the day.


[703] {#pg.147.703}
through to the ninth hour, having kept vigil, and perhaps because of the vigil, break your ninth hour fast. For it is necessary to do this, and not leave the other undone. For the Word has prescribed that you perform the prayer of thanksgiving once the vigil is finished.
How one ought to eat on Sundays; and concerning certain other things; and furthermore, concerning toil and humility.
34. Likewise, on all Sundays, eat twice in the day, just as you do on Saturdays; and let this rule be kept safe and sound, barring sickness; for these days have been granted by the holy Fathers and relaxed, owing to long custom and certain more recent causes—we speak of divine ones, or even others. For on these days we neither eat once, nor do we partake of dry food; but we partake of all that is useful and irreproachable, and herbs: yet temperately, and with the determined quantity; for it is always best to practice temperance in all things. But in bodily infirmities, as we have said, we must without blushing partake of all things useful and lawful which support the body; for the holy Fathers have taught us to be slayers of the passions, not slayers of the body. Likewise, it is fitting for you to taste a little bit of all things that are allowed, that is, whatever is permitted by the profession, for the glory and thanksgiving of God, and to avoid pride. But repel whatever is superfluous. “For the scarcity of things,” as Saint Isaac says, “teaches a man temperance, even against his will and desire; for when we have an abundance and plenty of them, we cannot restrain ourselves.” Do not love bodily rest. For the soul that loves God, according again to the holy Isaac, possesses its rest in God alone. Rather, choose to live with toil and hardship and humility. For toil and humility, as some saint writes, possess Jesus.
How one ought to live and conduct oneself during the holy Lenten seasons, and especially during the Great Lent.
35. Regarding the manner of life and order during the holy Lenten seasons, we consider it superfluous to explain it in detail and minutely. For as it has been previously determined for you to live on the days on which you perform the ninth hour, so it is allowed for you to work during the holy Lenten seasons, except for Saturdays and Sundays. Indeed, if possible, even more accurately and more vigilantly, and especially during the holy and Great Lent, as it is the tithe of the whole year, and it provides the rewards of the contests, through the Lord’s divine and illustrious day of Resurrection, to those who have been victorious according to Christ.
Concerning discernment, in part, and that there is no honor in mediocre work; and concerning obedience.
36. Furthermore, these things, and those similar to these,


[705] {#pg.147.705}
you must approach with accurate discernment, for the harmony of the double composite being and for a peaceful state. "For with wisdom," he says, "is a house built, and with understanding it is set aright; and by sense are the storehouses filled with all precious and beautiful wealth." And the divine Thalassius writes: "Need and straitness, when joined with reason, are the royal road; so that indiscriminate mortification or irrational self-abasement are unprofitable, as both happen contrary to reason." And the holy Isaac says: "There follows after the loosening of the members a disarray and confusion of the thoughts; and after immoderate labor, listlessness; and after listlessness, rapture (ecstasis). But one rapture differs from another: for upon the first rapture there follows the war of fornication; but upon the second, the abandonment of one's own cell, and migration from place to place. Moreover, for work that is moderate and remains painful, there is no honor; for the reduction of these things increases pleasure, but immoderation causes rapture." And the great Maximus says: "Do not spend all your leisure time on the flesh; but set for it an exercise according to your strength, and turn your whole mind toward the interior things. For bodily exercise profits a little, but godliness [profits] in all things," and so forth. If the scales of the flesh somehow pull back, and tyrannize, and weigh down the scales of the soul, drawing it toward disorderly and soul-corrupting movements and impulses, as it is written: "The flesh lusts against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh," you yourself must curb it with the bridle of self-control, and mortify it until, even against its will, it becomes manageable and obeys the better part, mindful of the great Paul, who says: "As much as our outward man is perishing, so much is the inward man being renewed day by day." And the holy Isaac says: "Give yourself to die in the contests, and do not live in neglect; for not only are those who have accepted death for the sake of faith in Christ martyrs, but also those who die for the sake of the observance of His commandments. And it is better for us to die in the struggle than to live in transgression." And before all things, be with counsel and inquiry, doing everything according to your spiritual Father in the Lord. For thus, by the grace of Christ, even things that are burdensome and uphill will seem light to you, and as if you were being carried over a flat plain. But we must return to where we started.
How the one who is struggling ought to pass the time between the meal and the setting of the sun; and that one ought to believe that, according to the labor and the measure of our work, the distribution of divine gifts is granted to us.
37. After having dined, as the one who is struggling ought to do—according to the divine Paul, who teaches that he who struggles exercises self-control in all things—read, while sitting, in the watchful writings of the Fathers, sufficiently. And thereafter sleep for one hour, if the days are long. Then, having risen, perform a little manual labor, while also engaging in prayer. After


[707] {#pg.147.707}
these things, pray, as has been indicated beforehand; read, meditate, and strive that you may be humbled and hold yourself beneath all men. “For he who exalts himself,” he says, “will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted.” And: “Let him who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall.” And, “God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” And: “The beginning of pride is to not know the Lord.” And: “The proud have transgressed exceedingly.” And: “Do not mind high things, but associate with the humble.” The divine Chrysostom also says: “This man is most truly one who knows himself, he who thinks himself to be nothing. For nothing is so dear to God as to count oneself among the lowest.” And holy Isaac says: “To the humble-minded the mysteries are revealed.” And: “Where humility blossoms, there the glory of God also springs forth.” And, that “Humility runs before grace, and conceit runs before instruction.” And holy Barsanuphius says:   “If you truly wish to be saved, listen in deed: take your feet off the earth, and lead your mind up into heaven, and let your meditation be there night and day; and as much as you have strength, seek to be despised; striving to see yourself beneath every man. This is the true way; outside of this, there is no other for him who wishes to be saved through Him who strengthens him, Christ. Let him who wills run; let him who wills run; let him who wills run, so that he may attain—I testify before the living God, and the willing One—to share eternal life with everyone who so wills.” And the author of the *Ladder* says: “I have not fasted, I have not kept vigil, I have not slept on the ground, but I was humbled, and He saved me quickly,” pursuing before all else the state of being unreckoned, as holy Barsanuphius says: for freedom from anxiety regarding every matter causes you to approach the city; and not being appraised among men causes you to dwell in the city; and dying to every man causes you to inherit the city, and its treasures. And if you wish to be saved, hold fast to being unreckoned, and run toward the goal set before you. It is, moreover, according to his student,   the venerable John, what being unreckoned is: not to consider oneself equal to anyone, and not to say concerning a good work, “I also did this.” Then again, sitting down, pray purely and steadfastly until the evening arrives, and so chant the customary vespers, and conclude, believing with a sincere heart that for our labor and the sorrow on account of virtue and the measure of our work, the distribution and declaration and consolation of gifts and rewards will be brought about by God; as the divine Psalmist says: “According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your consolations have gladdened my soul.” And the Savior: “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” And the great Paul: “If we suffer with Christ,   that we may also be glorified with him; for I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory which shall be revealed in us.” And the divine and wise Maximus says concerning these things: “The measure of each man’s faith is said to be the cause of the distribution of divine blessings; just as


[709] {#pg.147.709}
we believe, so too do we have an increase of zeal for acting.   Thus, he who acts, in proportion to his action, demonstrates the measure of his faith, receiving the measure of grace as he has believed. But he who does not act, in proportion to his inaction, demonstrates the measure of his unbelief, receiving, as he has disbelieved, the privation of grace. Therefore, the envious man does ill to begrudge those who are making progress, for the choice of believing and acting, and of receiving the grace that comes according to the measure of faith, lies clearly with him, and is not placed in another. Let us then, with all our soul, pray that we may remain in this state for the rest of our time. And may the very ends of our life be Christian, free of pain, unashamed, and peaceful; and in addition to these, may we render a good account, standing before the fearful judgment seat of our Lord, and God, and Savior Jesus Christ.
That pure prayer is greater than every work.
38. In addition to the things declared, know this also, brother, that every method, and every rule, and, if you will, every different practice, has been fashioned and regulated in this way, because we are not yet able to pray in our hearts purely and without distraction. For if we have perfectly attained, through the benevolence and grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and have abandoned those many, various, and fleeting things, we are united immediately, beyond reason, with Him who is one and simple and has the power of union, as was said by the illustrious Theologian: “God being united with and known by divine men”; which is that interior illumination in the heart, through the Holy Spirit, which is born, as has been said, from the aforementioned pure and undistracted prayer of the heart.   But this is rare, and hardly one in a thousand is deemed worthy, by the grace of Christ, to progress to this state. But to pass even beyond this, and to be deemed worthy of spiritual prayer, and to obtain the revelation of the mysteries of the age to come, is given to very few, and they are found from generation to generation, by the benevolence of grace, just as the holy Isaac writes: “Just as with difficulty one is found out of ten thousand men who has fulfilled the commandments and the ordinances without any small lack, and has reached the purity of the soul, so one in a thousand is found who is deemed worthy to reach, with great vigilance, to pure prayer, and to break through this limit, and to obtain that mystery. For many were not at all deemed worthy   of pure prayer; but few. But he who has reached that mystery which is after it and beyond it, is found with difficulty from generation to generation, by the grace of Christ.” And a little later: “And if with difficulty someone prays with purity, what shall we say about spiritual prayer? For all spiritual prayer is free from movement. And that which inclines even a little is below the spiritual.” Therefore, if you yourself wish to be deemed worthy of such new mysteries in Christ Jesus, by work and deed, that is, by experience itself, hasten to pray in your heart at every time and every hour and in all your work, purely and without distraction; so that from


[711] {#pg.147.711}
an infant nursing you may progress to a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ, and with the faithful and prudent servant may attain blessedness and the crown, as you direct your words in judgment—that is, acting according to reason—whence you shall not be shaken for eternity. As the holy Philemon writes concerning this: "Brother, whether by night or by day, may God deem you worthy to pray with a pure mind without distraction; do not cling to your own rule, but as much as you are able, strive to be united with God; and He Himself will illuminate your heart concerning spiritual labor." And one of the God-bearing ones says: "If you wish to serve God in the body as if without a body, possess unceasing prayer secretly in your heart, and before death your soul shall become as an angel." The holy Isaac writes in agreement with these things. For when asked by someone what the summit of all the fruits of this work—that is, of hesychia—was, so that anyone reaching it might know that he had attained the perfection of life, he answered thus: "When one is deemed worthy of the abiding of prayer; for when he reaches this, he has reached the summit of all virtues, and henceforth has become a dwelling-place of the Holy Spirit." For if someone has not perfectly received the grace of the Paraclete, he cannot accomplish perseverance in prayer in leisure. For the Spirit, he says, when He dwells in a certain man, does not cease to pray. For the Spirit Himself prays always. Then, neither in sleep nor in waking does prayer fail from his soul; but whether he eats, or drinks, or sleeps, or does anything else, and even in deep sleep, the sweet fragrance and breathings of prayer gush forth without labor; and then prayer has no division; but at all hours, even if such a one's prayer is tranquil externally, yet   again it serves him in secret. For a certain saint calls the silence of the perfect ones prayer; since their thoughts are certain divine movements; and the movements of a pure heart and mind are gentle voices, with which they chant in secret to the hidden God. And many other holy men, initiated by divine grace itself, have set forth many such things worthy of admiration; which we have omitted on account of the length of our discourse.
On the number of genuflections per the space of a day and night.
39. As for the number of genuflections, we know that three hundred are prescribed by our divine Fathers, which we ought to perform throughout the space of a day and night during the five days of the week; for on every Sabbath and every Sunday, and also on other days designated by custom and in weeks, according to certain mystical and unspeakable reasons, we are commanded to be at leisure from these. There are, however, some who exceed this number. And some who do not reach it, each according to his strength or preference. And you, therefore, do according to your ability; yet indeed blessed is he who in all things that are according to God offers violence to himself.


[713] {#pg.147.713}
A “For the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent take it by force.”
That not only, as has been said before, is the distribution of divine gifts granted according to the struggle and the measure of our exertion, but also according to our habit, our aptitude, and our faith, and the natural disposition present within us.
40.   And this, therefore, must be known: that not only, as we have said before, is the distribution of divine gifts granted to us according to the struggle and the measure of our exertion, but also according to the habit and aptitude of our way of life, and indeed, according to our faith regarding the things set before us, and the natural disposition fittingly present within us. And holy Maximus says: “The mind is the organ of wisdom; the reason, of knowledge; the natural persuasion regarding both is of the faith that consists through both; but for the gift of healings, it is natural compassion.” For every divine gift has something in us that is fitting and appropriate, as a power, or a habit, or a disposition, an organ capable of receiving it: for example, he who has made his mind pure from all sensible images receives wisdom; and he who has made his reason master of the innate passions—I mean anger and desire—receives knowledge; and he who has an unshakeable assurance regarding the Divine, according to his mind and reason, receives the faith that can do all things; and he who has perfected natural compassion, after the complete removal of self-love, receives the gifts of healings. And these things are so.   But beware that no one may know your work, except the one who admonishes and guides you; praying for us who are unworthy, who speak indeed, but do not do the good, so that we may be deemed worthy to do first the things pleasing to God, and then to speak and persuade others. For he who has done and taught, according to the divine oracle, this one shall be called great. May the almighty and all-merciful Lord strengthen and guide you again, to understand these things intelligently, and to do them with all longing. For “not the hearers of the law are just before God,” according to the divine Paul, “but the doers [of the law]”; may the Lord lead you to every good and salutary work, and may He take you by the hand to the spiritual purpose and holy work in the Spirit, by the prayers of the saints. Amen.
But since we have spoken before concerning the practical discernment, it is now opportune to say a few words, as we are able, concerning the discernment that is universal and most perfect, since according to our renowned Fathers it is greater than all the virtues.
On the universal and most perfect discernment; and who it is that lives contrary to nature and carnally; and who it is that lives according to nature and psychologically; and who it is that conducts himself above nature and spiritually.
41. He who lives and conducts himself carnally and contrary to nature has completely lost his own power of discernment; but he who has refrained from evils, and rejects the beginning of doing well, as...


[715] {#pg.147.715}
it is written: “Depart from evil and do good” [Ps. XXXVI, 27], he as a beginner, and one who yields to instruction, bends his head just a little towards a certain sense of discernment, such as is appropriate for the novice. But he who lives according to nature and psychically, as one performing acts within the mind and living according to reason—who is also called the “middle” one—he, according to his own measure, sees and discerns both that which concerns himself and that which concerns those like him. But he who lives above nature and spiritually, he—as one who has surpassed the passionate state, the beginning stage, and the boundaries of the middle state, and who has progressed by Christ’s grace to the perfect state, that is to say, to the essential illumination and the most perfect discernment—he sees himself and discerns most clearly.
