And indeed, he sees and discerns all things purely, while he himself is seen, looked into, and judged by no one; nay, he is judged as the one who is and is named a spiritual man. “Not with writings and ink, but by deed and grace,” as the divine Apostle says: “The spiritual man judges all things, but he himself is judged by no one” [I Cor. II, 15].
Further concerning discernment, by way of example.
42. The first of these is like one who walks in a deep, dark, and gloomy night, whence, wandering and covered in impenetrable darkness, he not only does not see or discern himself, but does not even know where he is going or walking, as the Savior says: “He who walks in darkness does not know where he is going” [John XII, 35]. The second is like   one who moves in a night that is clear and illuminated by the stars, whence, being slightly brightened by the twinkling of the stars, he walks little by little, often striking his feet against the stones of undiscerning-ness, and suffering frequent falls. This man, therefore, sees and discerns himself a little, but as if in a shadow, as it is written: “Awake, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine upon you” [Ephes. V, 14]. The third is like him who makes his way in a quiet night illuminated by the brightness of the moon; whence, being directed also by the lunar rays, he travels more unerringly and moves forward. He sees himself, as if in a mirror, and discerns at the same time those who are traveling with him, as it has been said: “You do well, paying attention to the law, as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts” [II Pet. I, 19]. The fourth is like him who   walks at high noon, firm and most pure, illuminated by the shining rays of the sun; and therefore such a one sees himself sincerely in the solar light, and discerns, and judges others—or rather, indeed, all men, in accordance with the divine Apostle; and indeed, all things that occur to him from everywhere and in any way, walking himself without error and leading those who follow him without stumbling toward the true Light, and the Life, and the Truth, concerning whom it is also written: “You are the light of the world” [Matt. V, 14]. And the most divine Paul also says: “God who said light should shine out of darkness, he has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” [II Cor. IV, 6]. And the blessed


[717] {#pg.147.717}
David: A “The light of thy countenance, O Lord, is signed upon us” [Ps. IV, 7]. And: “In thy light shall we see light” [Ps. XXXV, 10]. And the Lord: “I am the light of the world; he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life” [John VIII, 12].
On conversion and change in the individual, and on the eminent glory of humility.
43. We wish you to know this also: that even those who have attained to perfection through purification and illumination, in accordance with their powers—for there is no complete perfection in this imperfect age, but rather an incomplete perfection—do not always possess unchangeability with them, both because of natural infirmity and because of the opinion that sometimes creeps in. Indeed, they sometimes suffer changes and thefts for the sake of testing, and then again receive greater succors; and the Fathers define those who are contrary to these as being a portion of the wolves.   For firmness and unchangeability are reserved for the age to come; but in the present, it is now a time of purity, peace, and divine consolation, and now a time of defilement, tempest, and sadness, and this is in proportion to each person’s manner of life and progress, and in accordance with the judgments of the Lord, which He alone knows; and indeed, so that through these things we may judge our own infirmity. “For blessed,” he says, “is he who knows his own infirmity, that we may not be confident in ourselves, according to Paul, but in Him who raises the dead” [cf. II Cor. I, 9]; and thus we may run continuously to God in humility, repentance, and confession. And the holy Isaac says: “Again and again do some happen to transgress,   and yet by repentance they bring a remedy to their souls; and grace enters in unto them.” For in every reasonable nature, change has its place quite often. Changes attend every human being at all hours of his life; from these, one who has the power of discernment can understand this matter. And the trials which he experiences within himself every day can do much to make him wise, if he be vigilant: that he may observe himself in his intellect, and learn how great a change of gentle-mindedness and kindness his mind receives each day; and how, from its own peace, it is suddenly turned into confusion, when there is no cause from the place for it to be turned;   and how he finds himself in great and unspeakable danger. And this is what the blessed Macarius wrote clearly, with much care and zeal, for the memory and instruction of the brethren, so that they might not fall into despair at the time of the change of contrary things, teaching that to those standing in the place of purity it happens that they fall—just as it happens to the air to grow cold—and this even without them being in carelessness or laxity. Nay rather, even when they are proceeding according to their order, falls occur to them, contrary to the aim of their own will. And continuing, he says: “What, then, is it now? Changes,” he says, “happen to every person just as they do to the air.” But understand that in each one. For nature is verily one. Do not believe that he is speaking of the weaker and more fragile


[719] {#pg.147.719}
A beings and only the smallest ones, and that, consequently, the perfect are free from change and stand unswervingly in one order, without impassioned thoughts, as the Euchites say. This is why he added, “in each one.” How then, O Macarius, is this so? Yet you yourself say: cold, and a little later, heat; and perhaps hail, and after a while, clear weather. And in our life it is likewise: war and the receiving of grace, and at times the soul lies in a tempest, and horrendous waves rise up against it. And again, a change occurs, with grace protecting and filling the heart with joy and divine peace, and with sensible and peaceful thoughts. These counsels of prudence he joins together, exhorting those who were previously brutish and impure,   and he rouses them, saying: “If, therefore, after these counsels of prudence and gentleness, calamity follows, let us not be saddened nor despair.” And in the rest of grace, again, let us not become proud, but in the time of joy, let us accept affliction. And continuing, he says: “Know that all the saints were in this operation. As long as we are in this world, consolation abounds for us with afflictions. Therefore, daily and every hour, the proof of divine love is sought from you in the struggle and fight against temptations: which is that you not be saddened, nor be negligent in the struggle.” And thus your way is directed. “But he who wishes to be cast out from these and to decline from this, he is of the portion of the wolves.” O marvelous word of this man!   How in a few words he confirmed that oracle, and showed it to be full of meaning, and perfectly drove doubt from the mind of the reader! “But that man,” he says, “who declines from these, and is made a part of the wolves, wishes to walk upon an untrodden path, and has set it in his mind to gain this fate, and wishes to walk in private paths, not trodden by the Fathers.” And a little later: “Humility without works admits many sins: but works without humility are altogether useless.” And a little after: “As salt is to food, so is humility to every virtue; and it can crush the power of all sins; beyond it, it is necessary that we be saddened unceasingly according to the mind in humiliation and sorrow of judgment; and if we possess it, it makes us children of God; and without good works it presents us to God;   and thus, without it, all our works are vain, and all virtues and all operations. But God desires the change of the mind.” And: “By the mind we become better: it alone can stand before God without help, and speak for us.” He says furthermore: “One of the saints said: When the sense of pride comes to you, saying to you: ‘Remember your virtues,’ say: ‘Elder, look to your fornication.’”
On penance, purity, and perfection
44. The perfection of every course is in these three things: in penance, and in purity, and in perfection. What then is penance? To leave behind former things and to be saddened over them. And what is meant by purity, in brief? The heart…


[721] {#pg.147.721}
that is merciful over the whole of created nature. And what is perfection? A depth of humility, which is the leaving behind of all things, both visible and invisible—visible, that is, all sensible things; invisible, that is, those that are intelligible—and being free, furthermore, from the anxiety regarding them. Moreover, penance is a twofold death voluntarily undergone for all things. A merciful heart is a burning of the heart for the whole of creation, for men and for birds and for animals and for demons and for every creature. And again, as long as we are left in this world and in the flesh, even if we were to be raised up to the vault of the heavens, it is not possible for us to be without works and toil, or to be in a state of freedom from care; this is what perfection is. Pardon me; that which is beyond this is solicitation, that is to say, it is without reason. And Saint Maximus: “Philosophy according to virtue is   naturally able to produce the tranquility of the mind, not nature; through which spiritual tranquility, the joy of divine grace enters into the mind.” And again: “He who has experienced the sorrow and pleasure of the flesh might be called proven, inasmuch as he has been tempted by the zeal or the weariness of carnal acts; but perfect is he who has mastered the pleasure or pain of the flesh by the virtue of reason; and he is entirely a victor who has maintained the habits of action and contemplation with steadfastness towards God. By these things, indeed, discernment is demonstrated to be greater than all virtues, so that in those in whom it is born, once they are illumined by the divine light, it is permitted to discern   accurately both divine and human matters, and mystical and hidden visions. It is time, therefore, in order, to show you as much as I am able the beginning of the holy and deifying peace which we have announced, so that it may be manifest; and may God direct even these things which we are about to say.
Concerning the five operations of the first and, as it were, introductory peace of beginners: namely prayer, psalmody, reading, meditation, and manual labor.
45. Through these five operations, by which God is worshiped, the beginner in stillness ought to pass the day and night; namely, in prayer, that is to say, in the memory of the Lord Jesus Christ, continuously introduced [in another manuscript: invoked], as has been said before, through the breath of the nose   into the heart gently, and again in this manner brought forth, with lips closed, without any other thought or imagination—which, through the temperate control of the belly, we say, of sleep and of other sensible things, is accomplished within the cell with sincere humility—in psalmody, in reading from the holy Psalter, the Apostle, and the holy Gospels, and from the writings of the God-bearing and holy Fathers, and especially the chapters on prayer and watchfulness, and in addition the other divine oracles of the Holy Spirit, in the laborious memory of sins of the heart, and in the meditation upon the judgment of God, or of death, or of punishment, or of delight, and the like; and in light manual labor, as a muzzle for sloth, and again to return to prayer, even if...


[723] {#pg.147.723}
the matter has force until the mind becomes accustomed to cast aside its own wandering easily through complete contemplation toward the Lord Jesus Christ, and through constant memory, and through a continuous inclination to the inward treasury, that is, the hidden space of the heart, and through firm rootedness. For the holy Isaac also writes: "Make haste to enter into thy treasury   within, and thou shalt see the heavenly treasury; for this and that are one, and in one entry thou beholdest both." And the holy Maximus: "The heart directs the whole organ, and when grace has taken hold of the pastures of the heart, it governs all thoughts and members. For there is the mind, and all the thoughts of the soul; there, therefore, it behooves us to watch, whether the grace of the Holy Spirit has inscribed its laws." There—where? In the leading   organ, in the throne of grace, where the mind is, and all the thoughts of the soul, that is to say, in the heart.
Whence those who desire to live in peace according to reason must begin, and what is the beginning, and the increase, and the advancement, and the perfection.
46. This is the work of the ancient monks, the first, and as it were introductory for those who choose   to live in peace according to reason, beginning from the fear of God, and the fulfillment of all the deifying commandments according to their strength; from freedom from the cares of reasonable and unreasonable things, and above all from faith and from the utter flight of things contrary to it, and from a pure disposition toward Him who truly Is, as has been said; but as they grow in unashamed hope, and advance to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ, through prayer of the heart—pure, and becoming unwavering, and occurring through a complete, divinely inspired, and fervent love, and thus being perfected—through motionless and unceasing spiritual prayer, and through that which wells up from perfect love toward Him alone, by a direct ecstasy, and by the rapture and union of the highest object of desire, which is the unerring advancement and resurrection [or, uplifting] from action toward contemplation, which the ancestor of God, David, also suffered, and being changed by that blessed change, he cried out loudly: "I said in my ecstasy, Every man is a liar." And another of those who shone in the Old Testament: "Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither hath it entered into the heart of man, what God hath prepared for them that love Him." And the great Paul, concluding this, adds: "But to us God has revealed it through His Spirit; for the Spirit searcheth all things, even the deep things of God."
On the order of stillness for beginners.
47. The beginner, then, as we have said, must not constantly depart from his cell, nor converse with others, and must refrain from all outward looking, unless there is great necessity, and then with attention and safety, and rarely, as the divine Isaac says: "In everything, let this memory remain in thee, that the help which arises from guarding is better than the help which comes from works." And not only for beginners, but also for those who have already...


[725] {#pg.147.725}
progressed, such things cause scattering and distraction, as the same holy Isaac says again, that "Rest harms only the young, but relaxation harms both the young and the old; and peace mortifies the external senses, but excites the internal movements; while external conversation does the opposite of these things, that is, it excites the external senses and mortifies the internal movements."   And he indeed indicates action, or rather the way of peace, by these words; while the *Ladder* signifies him who acts and walks well along this path by what follows, writing: "The hesychast is one who strives to enclose the incorporeal in a bodily house, which is a most paradoxical thing; and the hesychast is he who said: 'I sleep, and my heart watcheth;' and he shuts indeed the door of the cell to the body, and the door of the tongue to speech, and the door of the spirit within."   He is peaceful who strives to determine the incorporeal in a bodily house, which is worthy of the greatest praise; and peaceful is he who said: "I sleep, but my heart watcheth"; and he has indeed closed the door of the cell to the body, and the door of the tongue to sound, and within he has closed the door of the spirit.
Of prayer which is performed with attention and the vigilance of the heart, and of its operation.
48. Prayer which is performed with attention and vigilance within the heart, as has been said, without any other cogitation and imagination, clearly, is performed through these words: "Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God," and through the memory of the Lord Jesus Christ Himself, the mind is extended immaterially and utterance-lessly; but through the "Have mercy on me," it returns and is moved toward itself, as if unable to endure not praying for itself; but having progressed toward charity through experience, it is turned singular-ly toward the Lord Jesus Christ Himself, for it has received manifest persuasion of the second.   How the divine Fathers have delivered to us to say the prayer, and that it is done differently, and what prayer is.
49. Therefore, not all the divine Fathers appear to have delivered the prayer in its entirety; but one indeed [delivered it] whole, another half; another in part, and another in a different way, according to the powers and state of the one praying. And the divine Chrysostom indeed delivered it in its entirely, thus saying: "I exhort you, brethren, never to trample upon or despise the rule of prayer. For I once heard the Fathers saying: 'Who is that monk who would despise or trample upon the rule? But he ought, whether he eats, or drinks, or sits, or serves, or travels, or does any other thing, incessantly to cry out: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me,'   so that this memory of the name of our Lord Jesus Christ may stir him to fight against the enemy. For the soul that uses force can find everything through memory, whether evil things or good things. But first it is permitted to see the evil within his heart, and then the good; for memory can stir the dragon, and memory can humble him; memory can detect the sin dwelling in us, and memory can destroy it and stir up all the power of the enemy in the heart, and memory can overcome and eradicate it by parts; so that the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, descending into the depths of the heart...


[727] {#pg.147.727}
may humble the dragon that holds its pastures, and save and vivify the soul. Persistently, therefore, remain with the name of the Lord Jesus, that the heart may swallow the Lord, and the Lord the heart, and the two become one. But this task is not of one day, or two, but of much time; for much struggle and much time are needed, so that the enemy may be cast out, and Christ may dwell within.   And again: "It is necessary to strengthen and rein in the mind, and put a bridle upon it, and to chastise every thought and every energy of the wicked one through the invocation of our Lord Jesus Christ." And where the body stands, there let the mind also be, that between God and the heart nothing else may be found as an intermediate wall, or a partition darkening the heart, and separating the mind from God. If at any time it carries the mind away, you must not linger on the thoughts, so that the assent to these thoughts may not be reckoned to his account on the day of judgment before the Lord, when God shall judge the hidden things of men. Be at leisure, therefore, always, and cleave to the Lord our God, until He has mercy upon you, and seek nothing else, but only mercy from the Lord of glory. And seeking mercy, seek it with a humble and wretched heart, and cry from morning until evening, and if possible, even the whole night, "Lord Jesus Christ, have mercy on me," and force your mind to this task even unto death; for this task requires much violence, because "narrow is the gate and strait the way which leads to life, and the violent enter into it"; for the kingdom of heaven belongs to the violent. I exhort you, therefore, do not separate your hearts from God, but cleave to Him and guard them always and everywhere with the memory of our Lord Jesus Christ, until the name of the Lord is planted within in the heart, and it thinks of nothing else, so that Christ may be magnified in you.   Before this, however, the great Paul, putting forward the Lord Jesus, says: "If you confess with your mouth the Lord Jesus, and believe in your heart that God has raised Him from the dead, you will be saved; for with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation." And again: "No one says that Jesus is Lord, except by the Holy Spirit." And he adds "by the Holy Spirit," that is, when the heart receives the power of the Holy Spirit, through which it also prays, which belongs to those who have made progress, and who have become rich in Christ, who manifestly dwells within them. Consistently with this, the holy Diadochus also says: "The mind demands from us, when we have blocked all its exits with the memory of God, a task which can satisfy its diligence. Therefore, we must give it this: 'Lord Jesus,' solely for the entire operation, which tends toward the goal. For no one can say the Lord Jesus, except by the Holy Spirit. But let him contemplate this word strictly in his inner treasuries,   lest he wander into some fantasies. For whoever meditates on that glorious and lovable name continuously in the profound heart, they are able also to perceive the light of the mind at times; for by strict study, having been occupied with thought, it burns up all the filth emerging in the soul. For God...


[729] {#pg.147.729}
He says, is a consuming fire; whence also the Lord finally calls   the soul to great love of His glory. For that glorious and lovable name, abiding through the memory of the mind in the warmth of the heart, begets in us a habit of completely loving His goodness, with nothing left to hinder it. For this is the precious pearl, which anyone having sold all his wealth can purchase, and have inexpressible joy at its finding. The holy Hesychius, writing thus about Christ Jesus, adds: "The soul flying through death in the air to the gates of heaven, having Jesus with it and above it, will not fear its enemies there, but with confidence, as now, so then at the gates will speak to them, provided that at its exit it does not cease to cry out to the Lord Jesus Christ day and night; and He Himself will perform its vengeance speedily, according to His own and God’s promise, which He expressed concerning the judge of iniquity; and I say to you truly, He will do it both in the present life and after its soul has departed from the body." And the one of the Ladder, saying Jesus alone: "With the name of Jesus whip the enemies; for there is no weapon stronger in heaven and on earth," and he adds nothing else. And again he says: "Let the memory of Jesus be united to your breath, and then you will know the benefit of stillness."
Item, that not only among the aforementioned holy Fathers, but also from the very foremost of the apostles, Peter, and Paul, and John, are found the words of the holy and life-giving prayer somehow mystically signified in the Spirit.
V. Not only by these aforementioned God-bearing Fathers, and those after them, will one find such words of holy prayer somehow mystically signified, but certainly before them, even from the first and foremost apostles themselves, we mean those around Peter, and Paul, and John. For one says, as we have mentioned before: "No one can say 'Lord Jesus' except in the Holy Spirit," and another: "Every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is of God." And the chief of the disciples of Christ, to the question directed by the Savior and Master to the apostles themselves, "Who do people say that I am?" bringing forward that most blessed confession, answered: "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God." For this reason also those who came after them, our glorious instructors, and rather those who pursued the life without yoke, and the eremitic and quiet life, gathered such utterances scattered here and there, and part by part, in these three pillars of the holy Church, proclaimed in advance as divine voices put forth according to revelation in the Holy Spirit,   and for these three men worthy of faith, as most things declare and testify, "In the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall be established," those heavenly men, gathering them into one and with the Spirit dwelling in them,


[731] {#pg.147.731}
climantes, they have announced the column of prayer, and have commended those who followed them to occupy and keep it in the same manner. Observe, therefore, the order and consequence, which stands out greatly with divine wisdom. One, indeed, says "Jesus," another "Jesus Christ," but the third "Christ the Son of God," as if one were following another, and they held together among themselves by the concord and bond of such words. For you may see each one of them taking the voice which is at the end in the next, and the matter being so regarding the third. And you will see the same regarding the addition of the Holy Spirit. For the blessed Paul saying: "No one can say 'Lord Jesus,' except in the Holy Spirit,"   at this final word, namely the Holy Spirit, he who has a voice like thunder, John, began in his usage, saying: "Every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is of God." They have placed these before all things, not spontaneously nor of themselves, but led by the hand of the most holy Spirit. For indeed the confession of the divine Peter was made through revelation in the Holy Spirit. "For all these," he says, "works one and the same Spirit, dividing to each one as He wills." And thus, therefore, the context and stitching of the life-giving thread of prayer, having been applied and unbroken, has been most wisely and learnedly constructed, and has reached down to us, keeping the same method.
The addition, therefore, of this voice, "Have mercy on me," the Fathers who followed them have made and ordered with these saving words, namely "Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God," and especially because of those who are still infants in virtue, namely the beginners and the imperfect. For those who have progressed and are perfect in Christ, through each one of those oracles, "Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God," or even sometimes through the sole invocation of "Jesus," are sufficient for themselves, and they embrace   and apply it as the universal work of prayer, and through it are filled with a joy ineffable and surpassing all sight and hearing. And thus, therefore, these most blessed men, dwelling outside the flesh and the world, imposing silence upon their senses, raised by the gift and grace into the most ardent and happiest love for the Divine which dwells within them, are cleansed and illuminated, and are made perfect, inasmuch as they look accurately at the supernatural and eternal and uncreated grace of the supersubstantial Godhead, in the part of a pledge, obscurely as in a mirror, contented by memory alone and meditation, as has been said, with one or another appellation of the Word of God and Man, through this they are lifted up into raptures and knowledge and revelation, which they experience in the Spirit without speech. In manifestation of which and most evident faith, our sweetest and most loving Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, whose words, acts, and deeds are, according to Him, Spirit and life to us, clearly revealed, saying: "Without me you can do nothing." And, "If you ask anything in my name, I will do it." And those things which follow and have been handed down to us.


[733] {#pg.147.733}
That it is permitted even for beginners to pray at times with the entire words of the prayer, and at times with a part of it, yet always within the heart, and that one should not continually change the words.
51. It is permitted even for beginners to pray at times with the entire words of the prayer, and at times with a part of it, yet within the heart and perpetually; for according to the holy Diadochus, "He who always dwells in his own heart departs from the things of this beautiful life." For one who walks in the Spirit cannot know the desires of the flesh, since he henceforth conducts his walk within the fortress of the virtues, having these virtues as it were the gatekeepers of the citadel of purity. Therefore, the schemes of the demons become henceforth ineffectual against him. And the holy Isaac also writes: "The heart of him who keeps watch over his soul every hour rejoices in revelations; and he who gathers his contemplation within himself beholds the radiance of the Spirit." Whoever has loathed all distraction beholds his Master within the depths of his heart, and one must not continually change the phrases of prayer, lest the mind, having become accustomed to constant change and shifting—to a kind of instability and wavering—remain unsteady and unfruitful, like trees that are constantly moved and transplanted.
That the fruit of praying within the heart also requires much time, and struggle, and violence, and that every good thing is accomplished through much toil and time.
52. And this praying always within the heart, and likewise the things that go beyond it, are not accomplished simply, or as it happens, or through brief and momentary toil. Even if this is indeed found rarely in some by an ineffable providence, it requires much time, and labor, and struggle of both body and soul, and much violence, and intensified effort for its accomplishment. For according to the portion of the gift of grace   that we hope to be granted in participation, it behooves us to exert our own struggles in proportion to our strength, and to measure out the hours; and this is, according to the holy Fathers, to cast out the enemy from the pastures of the heart and to establish Christ clearly within it. For the holy Isaac also says: "He who wishes to see the Lord makes an effort to cleanse his heart with the uninterrupted memory of God, and thus in the radiance of his intellect he shall behold the Lord at every hour." And the holy Barsanuphius says: "Unless the inward operation united with God helps a man, he toils in vain in outward things. For the inward operation brings purity along with the labor of the heart; and purity, in turn, [brings] true


[735] {#pg.147.735}
stillness of heart, and this stillness brings humility, and humility makes man a dwelling-place of God. And from this dwelling-place, the demons are cast out along with the passions, and thus man becomes a temple of God, full of sanctification, full of illumination, and of purity and grace. Blessed, then, is he who beholds his own Lord in the inner sanctum of the heart, pouring out his prayer with weeping before His goodness. And the pious John of Karpathos [says]: "Much struggle and time is needed in prayers, so that we may find in the undisturbed state of the mind another heavenly space within the heart, where Christ dwells, as the Apostle says: B 'Or do you not realize that Jesus Christ is in you? Unless indeed you fail to meet the test!' And the great Chrysostom [says]: "Incessantly cleave to the name of the Lord Jesus, that the heart may swallow the Lord, and the Lord the heart, and the two may become one." But this work is not of one day or two, but of long and much time; for much struggle and time is needed so that the enemy may be cast out and Christ may dwell within. And so much for these things; let the discourse return to what was proposed in order.
Concerning prayer of the heart that is not [yet] pure, and how one comes to pure and constant prayer.
53. From adhering to the aforementioned method of interior and pure and constant prayer—even if it is not perhaps otherwise pure and   constant—it is manifest that the one who struggles, despite the phantasies and thoughts that obstruct his prayer, comes to a habit of praying without violence and inconstancy, and [prays] purely and truly. That is, by keeping (the mind) in the heart, and not with force and contempt through the inspiration introducing and again extracting [the mind], but by always adhering to it and thus praying perpetually. For the holy Hesychios says: "He who does not have prayer free from thoughts has no weapon for battle; and by prayer I mean that which is ceaselessly active in the inner sanctum of the heart, so that by the invocation of Jesus Christ, the one who fights in secret may be scourged and the enemy may be burned."   And again: "Blessed is he who is thus joined to the prayer of Jesus in his understanding, and invokes Him unceasingly in his heart, just as air is united to our bodies, or as flame to wax." And again: "And as the sun, passing over the earth, makes the day, so the holy and venerable name of the Lord Jesus, shining continuously in the understanding, will generate unnumbered sun-like thoughts."
Concerning constant and pure prayer of the heart, and the ardor born from it.
54. This is and is called prayer of the heart—pure and constant, as has been said—from which a certain ardor is born in the heart, according to that: "My heart was warmed within me, and in my meditation, a fire shall be kindled." (Ps. XXXVIII, 4).


[737] {#pg.147.737}
This is the fire which the Lord Jesus Christ came to cast into the earth of our hearts, which previously bore thorns because of the passions, but now by grace brings forth the Spirit, as our Lord Jesus Christ says: "I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what will I, if it be already kindled?" (Luc. XII, 49). This fire, having once warmed and burned those about Cleopas, caused them to cry out to one another in ecstasy: "Was not our heart burning within us in the way?" (Luc. XXIV, 32). The great John of Damascus also says, in one of his hymns to the all-holy Theotokos: "The fire which lies hidden in the heart draws me to sing of the love of the Virgin."
St. Isaac also writes: "From intense labor is born the immeasurable warmth, which is kindled in the heart from the ardent desires that have newly come upon the intellect. This labor and watchfulness thin out the mind   with their warmth and provide it with vision; and as it progresses, the outpouring of tears is born from this warmth which arises from the grace of contemplation. After a little, the soul receives peace of thoughts from the unceasing tears. From the peace of thoughts, it is raised to the purity of the mind; through the purity of the mind, man comes to see the mysteries of God."
And after a few words: "After these things, the mind arrives at seeing revelations and signs, just as the prophet Ezekiel saw." And further: "Tears and the beating of the head in prayer, and rolling about with warmth, awaken the warmth of their sweetness within the heart; and with praised ecstasy, the heart flies toward God and cries: 'My soul hath thirsted after the strong, living God; when shall I come and appear before the face of God?' (Ps. XLI, 3), and so on."
And [the author] of the Ladder: "Fire having settled in the heart, it has awakened prayer; this having been aroused and caught up into heaven, a descent of fire in the upper room of the soul has come to pass."
Further: "Who then is the faithful and wise monk, who has kept his own warmth unquenchable, and until his departure, day by day,   adding fire to fire, and warmth to warmth, and desire to desire, and zeal to zeal, has not ceased?"
And St. Elias the Ecdicus: "When the soul, having desisted from external things, is joined to the Soul, then, like a flame surrounding it—just as fire [affects] iron—it renders it entirely ignited. It is indeed the same soul, but no longer touchable. For the ignited iron can no longer be grasped."
And further: "Blessed is he who in this life is deemed worthy to be seen as such; and having seen that his own sculpted form, by nature earthen, has by grace been made fiery!"
That warmth also has a different origin, and the one from pure prayer of the heart is more sovereign.
55. Know also that such warmth has the origin of its existence in us in various and manifold ways.


[739] {#pg.147.739}
And this is evident from the oracles of the saints set forth, but we hesitate to say [it comes] from the action itself; yet there is a way in which the warmth resulting from pure prayer of the heart is more sovereign than these. Progressing continuously with it, and increasing, it brings one to the subsistent light, that is, it renders the one in such a state enlightened in a subsistent manner, according to the Fathers.
What is the work of the warmth of the heart?
56. Such warmth immediately drives away the things that hinder the prior, pure prayer from being accomplished   perfectly. For our God is a fire, and a fire consuming the wickedness of the demons and of our passions. For the holy Diadochus also says: "When the heart receives the arrows of the demons with a certain sharp pain, such that it imagines it is the enemy himself bringing these weapons, then the soul, as if beginning to be cleansed, hates the passions with pain." Therefore, if one does not suffer greatly over the impudence of sin, one will not be able to rejoice richly in the goodness of righteousness. He, then, who wishes to purify his heart, let him inflame it perpetually with the memory of Jesus Christ, having this alone as his meditation and unceasing work. For it is not the case that those who wish to cast out their own corruption ought to pray   at one time and not at another; but rather, they must always be occupied with prayer in the custody of the mind, even if they should happen to be lodging somewhere outside the houses of prayer. For just as he who wishes to purify gold, if he allows the fire beneath the furnace to be extinguished even for a little while, causes the material to become hard again; so too he who remembers God at one time, but at another does not, loses through idleness what he seems to have acquired through prayer. It is, however, the characteristic of a man who is a lover of virtue to use the memory of God to consume the earthly element of the heart, so that in this way, with the evil being gradually consumed by the fire of the memory of the good, the soul may   return perfectly to its natural brightness with greater glory. And so, the mind remaining in the heart without hindrance, prays purely and without error, according to the holy one who says: "Then is prayer true and unerring, when the mind guards the heart while praying." And the holy Hesychius also writes: "This is a monk who is truly such, he who perfects watchfulness, and thus he is truly sober, who is a monk in the heart."
Concerning the longing and love that arises from fervent attention and prayer.
57. In such warmth, and with attention and prayer—that is, pure prayer—there is born in the heart a desire and divine love and charity toward the Lord Jesus Christ, who is always being remembered, as it is written: "Young maidens have loved me, they have drawn me," and that "I am wounded with love." And the holy Maximus also says: "All the virtues cooperate with the mind toward divine love, but most of all


[741] {#pg.147.741}
pure prayer. For by this the mind, taking wing toward God, is established outside of all things."
On tears of the heart; and further on divine desire and love.
58. From this heart, a tear for the most part flows forth, cleansing and fattening him who has acquired these things through charity, but not softening and drying them. For this is what they work: the one from divine fear, and the other from divine love, through an intense and unrestrained desire and love for the remembered Lord Jesus Christ. And the soul, inspired, cries out: "You have charmed me with desire, O Christ, and have changed me with your divine love." And: "You are the whole, O Savior, sweetness; you are all desire and yearning; you are wholly beyond   comprehension; you are wholly indescribable beauty." And with Paul, the herald of Christ, it cries out: "The charity of God compasses us," and: "Who shall separate us from the charity of Christ? Shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or hunger, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword?" And again: "I am sure that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature shall be able to separate us from the charity of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord."
Exhortation not to seek anything beyond measure; and also an incitement to the continuous memory of our Lord Jesus Christ in the heart.
59. If, therefore, one is to be deemed worthy of these things, and of all that follows—which it is not timely to speak of now—do not seek, it says, for what pertains to the season before the season. And good is not good when it is not done well. And according to the holy Mark, it is not profitable to know things that come later before the performance of things that come earlier; for knowledge puffs up on account of idleness, but charity edifies by enduring all things. One   must hasten and always strive, as has been said, to carry the memory of the Lord Jesus Christ continuously in the depth of the heart, and not outwardly or superficially, as the same blessed Mark also says concerning this: "Unless the inmost and hidden and sincere space of our heart be opened through universal and intellectual hope, it is not possible to know firmly Him who dwells within, nor to know whether our rational sacrifices have been accepted or not."
On ardent zeal, and the divine appearance within us, and the substantial illumination of grace.
60. For thus one will readily turn away, not only from evil works, but also from passionate thoughts and unseemly fantasies, as it is written: "Walk in the spirit, and you shall not fulfill the desires of the flesh." Nay rather, he will depart from every thought and every fantasy, as burning them up with an ardent zeal for virtue, so to speak, and   expelling every act of malice, whether through the senses or through the mind, which previously operated within him, together with the leaders of these things, the demons who rejoice in alien evil.


[743] {#pg.147.743}
A Terrible is he to the demons and beloved of God and His angels, who with burning zeal eradicates the thorns planted within him by the enemy. And he will reach a state of progress so as to have from this a certainty of the love for Him, and of the manifest appearance, and indwelling of the substantial and most divine light of grace. Or, if you wish to express it this way, he will quite brightly run back to that nobility and spiritual adoption given to us from above through the grace of baptism. And again, holy Isaac says: «This is Jerusalem, and the kingdom of God, which is hidden within us according to the word of the Lord. This place is the cloud of the glory of God, into which only the pure in heart shall enter to behold the face of their own Master.» Only let him not seek the appearance of God, lest he receive the one who is truly darkness, and pretends to be light.
On divine operation, and that which is contrary.
61. When, however, his mind sees light not seeking it, let him not accept it immediately, nor yet reject it, as the holy Mark says, for «There is an operation of grace unknown to the infant. And there is another [operation] of malice, very similar to the truth. It is good for those who are not erring not to contemplate such things, nor to curse them for the sake of truth; but in all things to take refuge in God through hope. For He Himself knows what is useful in both cases; but let him ask the one who has grace and power before God to teach him, and to discern.»
On the illuminated and unerring master.
62. And if he finds one who can teach, not only as he has known from the divine Scripture, but as he himself has also blessedily experienced the divine illumination, thanks be to God. If not, it is better not to accept [it], but to take refuge in God in humility, deeming himself unworthy of such high merit and contemplation with a sincere heart; just as it has been said, and from those things which will be said, and as we have been initiated, by the grace of Christ, from lips that do not lie, moved and speaking by the Holy Spirit; and from the God-inspired Scriptures and from personal experience.   On true and false light, that is, on divine and evil light.
63. For even if, in some of their writings, our glorious Fathers give us the signs of unerring light and of that which is of deception, as indeed the thrice-blessed Paul did when he spoke to a disciple of his who asked him about such a matter, that "the light of the opposing power is like fire, smoky, and conforms to material fire; and when a soul that is a friend of virtue and pure sees it, it is without joy and rejects it. But the light of the good is good, and most pleasing, and pure; and as it comes it sanctifies, and fills the soul with light and joy and serenity, and makes it gentle and merciful." And others say similar things. But nevertheless, you hear the aforesaid things also from one delivering them by living voice,


[745] {#pg.147.745}
and so you shall likewise hear about this in due time; for now is not the time.
On base and noble phantasia, and how one must approach them.
A 64. Since a little while ago we mentioned phantasia, and base phantasia, it is most useful, as it seems to us, to speak briefly about it, or rather about all phantasia, as far as is possible. For this cursed thing resists the pure and heart-felt prayer, and the singular and unerring activity of the mind, with great intensity. Whence the divine Fathers express themselves many times about it and against it. This multi-form phantasia, then—like the fabled Daedalus, and many-headed like the Hydra—has been called by the saints a kind of bridge for the demons. For through it, the murderous spirits   pass across and cross over, communicating and mingling with the soul, making it a hive of drones and a dwelling-place of fruitless and passionate thoughts. This phantasia, then, is to be rejected altogether; unless perhaps you wish, for the sake of repentance, and contrition, and mourning, and humility—and above all, for the meditation on the things that are—to set a noble phantasia against a base one, and to weigh them against each other; and by mixing that with this, and acting in opposition, and like a deserter having basely cast off his shield, having fallen defeated and cast down, you may be able to celebrate a triumph. And so, by acting in this way, you would be the author not only of causing no harm, but even of profit to yourself, as one who directs his own affairs with steady judgment,   destroying the base phantasia with a noble one, and striking and killing these enemies with the weapons of their opposites, just as divine David of old did to Goliath.
That not only base phantasia, but also noble phantasia, is to be rejected by the saints for pure prayer and for the simple and singular activity of the mind.
65. This, however, is a struggle for those who are still infants, that is, for beginners. For those who have advanced in time cast away the base phantasia altogether along with the noble one, and make them vanish—burning them up and dissolving them like wax before the face of fire—because of pure prayer, and the unformed stripping away and nakedness of the mind from all things, for the sake of the simple approach to God;   or if you will, for the sake of receiving [Him], and of that unconfigured and singular union. For the holy Hesychius also says: "Every thought is a phantasia in the mind of some sensible thing." For the Assyrian, that is the spirit, is not able to deceive in any other way unless he uses the things that are sensible and familiar to us. And the holy Diadochus: "Since every thought enters the heart through the phantasia of certain sensible things, then the blessed light of the Godhead shines upon it when it has completely found rest from all things, and has become unconfigured from them, if indeed the splendor of that Light appears to the pure mind through the privation of all thoughts." And the great Basil:


[747] {#pg.147.747}
A "Just as the Lord does not dwell in temples made by hands, so neither does He dwell in certain configurations and mental images." For these are cast forth as barriers to the soul that has been corrupted, which is not able to gaze purely toward the truth, but is still held by the mirror and the enigma. And the divine Evagrius: "God is said to sit there, where He is known; hence the pure mind is called the throne of God." The thought of God, therefore, will not be found in the thoughts that configure the mind, but in thoughts that do not configure it. Wherefore, he who prays must be separated entirely from the thoughts that configure the mind; for the mind will be configured in one way when it contemplates the mind, and will be disposed in another way when it contemplates the Word of God.   From this we learn how spiritual knowledge detaches the mind from the thoughts that configure it, and, rendering it unconfigured, presents it to God. And holy Maximus in the *Scholia* on the great Dionysius: "Phantasy is one thing, and thought—that is, the concept—is another. For they arise from different faculties, and they differ in the nature of their movement. For thought is a kind of efficacy and action; but phantasy is a passion and a figurative representation that brings news of something sensible, or as of something sensible. And sense perception perceives beings according to an obtuse formation. But the mind touches—that is, perceives—beings in another   way, and not as sense perception does. Concerning, then, the corporeal or the spiritual, in which we previously said the senses also exist, the movement is passive and figurative. But judgment and intellect are to be granted to the soul and to the mind. Imagination, therefore, must be removed from this intellect of the mind. Imagination is divided into three parts: the first is the capacity for imaging that provides the sensible form to the things that cause the perception; the second is that which fashions a type from the residues remaining from these things, which does not have images resting upon anything, which they properly call 'phantastic'; the third is that in which all pleasure and the imagination of what is thought to be good, or the sadness of that which seems evil,   is composed. No phantasy, therefore, as has been said, has a place in God; for He is, once and for all, simply beyond thought and transcends it. And again the great Basil: "The mind that is not dissipated upon external things, nor scattered toward the world through the senses, returns to itself; and through itself it ascends to the thought of God, and, being illuminated by that beauty, it receives a forgetting of its own nature." You, therefore, knowing these things, strive at all hours to pray to God without phantasy, without figure, and without form, as a whole with the whole, with a pure mind and with a pure soul; for holy Maximus also speaks thus.
Concerning the mind, soul, and heart that are pure and perfect.
§ 66. Concerning the pure mind.—A pure mind is that which has been separated from ignorance, and is illuminated by the divine light.


[749] {#pg.147.749}
A Concerning a pure soul.—A pure soul is that which has been liberated from the passions, and is incessantly gladdened by divine love.
Concerning a pure heart.—A pure heart is that which presents itself to God entirely without form and unconfigured; it is ready to be impressed only by His own types, through which He is naturally accustomed to manifest Himself. Following these, let the following also be added.
Concerning a perfect mind.—A perfect mind is that which, through true faith, has known the One who cannot be penetrated, and has contemplated His works [i.e., the universe]; and has received from God, as far as is possible for a human being, the comprehensive knowledge of the providence and judgment that are in them.
Concerning a perfect soul.—A soul is perfect whose   passive faculty has inclined entirely toward God.
Concerning a perfect heart.—A perfect heart is, perhaps, called that which has no natural movement of any kind toward anything whatsoever; in it, as if on a polished tablet, because of its extreme simplicity, God arrives and inscribes His own laws.
Concerning the pure [mind].—Furthermore, to cleanse the mind, according to the holy Diadochus, belongs to the Holy Spirit alone; furthermore, to make the mind stand still, according to the Climax, belongs to the Holy Spirit alone. The holy Nilus also says: "If anyone wishes to see the state of the mind, let him divest himself of all thoughts, and then he will see it appearing like a sapphire or a heavenly color." And again: "The state of the mind is an intellectual height similar to a heavenly color, to which the light of the most holy Trinity comes at the time of prayer." And the holy Isaac [says]: "When the mind has stripped off the old man and put on the new man of grace, then it will see its own purity to be similar to the heavenly hue, which was named the place of God by the council of the children of Israel when He appeared to them on the mountain." Thus, therefore, by acting as has been said—that is, by praying purely, without fantasy, and without forms—you will be following in the footsteps of the saints. But if not, you will become a visionary instead of a hesychast, and instead of grapes you will harvest thorns. May this not happen to you!
How the prophets had visions.
67. If any assume that the visions, configurations, and revelations of the prophets occurred through fantasy and natural sequence, let them know that they have wandered far from the right goal and the truth. For the prophets—and now our mystagogues—did not see and have visions of what they saw and envisioned through some natural operation, order, or fantasy, but divinely and beyond nature, being configured and having visions by the ineffable power and grace of the Holy Spirit, as the great Basil says:   "By an ineffable power they have visions, and having a mind that is undistracted and pure, they have as it were the Word of God resounding within them." And   again: "The prophets saw, in the Spirit who directed them, the types..."


[751] {#pg.147.751}
of the governing mind." And the Theologian Gregory says: "This (that is, the Holy Spirit) operated previously in the angelic and celestial powers." And a little later: "Then in the Fathers and the prophets: some of whom represented God to themselves and knew Him, while others foretold the future; they had the governing mind molded by the Spirit, and were present to future things as if they were actually there."
Still further concerning phantasies, and the many and various contemplations.
68. If there are some who still doubt, as they accept phantasies and many and various contemplations, and resist us—thinking that they are adhering to the footsteps of the saints, and contending that the Theologian means that God is only shadowed forth by the mind, not from those things that are in Him, but from those things that are around Him, by a phantasy gathered from one thing to another into one certain image of truth, and so on; and that the divine Maximus says that the mind cannot become without passion   from actions alone, unless it receives many and various images; and that similarly other saints say things equal to these—let such persons know that these words of those blessed ones do not refer to the operation which is according to reception and the grace of knowledge and vision, which through experience itself joins man to God, but rather to that which is through effort [conatum], namely, that which proceeds from wisdom and from that contemplation which gathers together the analogies and harmonies of things, and inclines in some   way, albeit obscurely, to the thought of God—which is easy of access and thought for the many, or rather for all. So that whoever examines such oracles of the saints with reflection will clearly perceive that it was written: "From the greatness and beauty of created things, the Creator is proportionately perceived" [Wisd. 13:5], that is, from that profane, verbose, vain, and laborious knowledge of the world. For that, as an obscure handmaid, and one puffed up with learned sophistical and demonstrative thought, not following evangelical faith and humility and true assent, is driven far from the sacred doors. Our discourse now, however, is about the perfect and substantial illumination, just as the chosen apostles who, ascending the mountain of Tabor with Jesus, underwent an ineffably   beautiful and truly blessed transformation, and were accounted worthy to behold the invisible kingdom and Divinity, their sense of sight having been prepared for something more divine—that is, having been made spiritual by the right hand of the all-holy Spirit. For as far as the east is from the west, and heaven from earth, and as the soul excels the body, by so much does the operation and grace through reception excel that which is through effort. The latter, to be sure—that which is through effort—is profane, as we have said, and has its progress through the well-ordered motions of things, and the order and collection of images following one from another, and is extended to God in faith. The former, however—that which is through reception—is accustomed to be produced immediately by God Himself, substantially within the heart; and sometimes it even makes the body a participant in its own illumination and most divine light, which is above thought, by a supernatural illumination of the heart.


[753] {#pg.147.753}
according to   the most wise Maximus, not generating the unbegotten deification. For this saint says: "I call unbegotten deification that illumination which comes to pass according to the essential form of the Divinity; which has no generation, but an inconceivable manifestation in those who are worthy." The great Dionysius also speaks in harmony with what has been said: "One must know that our mind possesses a power for thinking, by which it perceives intelligible things; but it also possesses a union which transcends the nature of the mind, by which it is joined to things that are beyond itself." And the holy Isaac says: "We possess two psychic eyes, as the Fathers say, and the usefulness of the contemplation through each is not the same. For with one eye we see the things hidden in natures, that is, the power of God, and His wisdom, and His providence towards us, which is perceived from the holiness of His governance towards us; and with the other eye we behold the glory of His holy nature, whenever God deigns to lead us into spiritual mysteries." And the divine Diadochus says: "Wisdom and knowledge are gifts of the one Holy Spirit, as are all divine gifts, but each has its own proper energy. Wherefore the Apostle testifies that to one is given wisdom, and to another knowledge, by the same Spirit. For knowledge unites man to God by experience, without moving the soul to   reasonings about things. Therefore, some of those who pursue the monastic life are indeed illuminated by it in sense, but they do not arrive at divine reasonings. But wisdom, if it be given to someone with fear (and this is rare), manifests the very energies of knowledge; since the one is accustomed to illuminate by energy, the other by reason. And prayer, along with much tranquility and complete freedom from care, brings knowledge. But the unvain study of the oracles of God brings wisdom, and first the grace of the God who gives." And furthermore, the holy Maximus says in the Scholia: "The well of Jacob is Scripture; the water is the knowledge which is in Scripture; the deep is the difficult contemplation of the Scriptural enigmas; the drawing is the instruction through the letters of the divine Word, which the Lord did not have, since He was the Word Himself, and He gave to those who believe not the knowledge from instruction and meditation, but the ever-flowing, spiritual wisdom from grace, which never ceases, bestowing it upon the worthy. For the drawing, that is to say the instruction, receiving the smallest part of knowledge, leaves the whole, being unable by any reason to grasp it. But knowledge according to grace has the whole, and without meditation, it brings   forth such wisdom as is appropriate for men, for various needs." And again the holy Diadochus: "Our mind, for the most part, is moved with difficulty toward prayer; because, indeed, the volitional virtue is too narrow and constricted; but theology freely offers itself, because divine contemplation is broad and unconstrained. But let us not give ourselves the will to say many things, and let us not think to fly beyond measure, for cheerfulness, prayer,   and psalmody...


[755] {#pg.147.755}
and the reading of the holy Scriptures, to which we devote our time, should not allow us to neglect the discipline of learned men, the faith of whom is known through their writings. And while doing this, let us not permit the mind to mix its own words with the words of grace, nor to be distracted by vainglory, dispersed by excessive joy and talkativeness; but let us guard it far from every fantasy at the time of contemplation, and let us cultivate in it, from this, all tearful thoughts. For the one who rests in times of quiet, and who delights especially in the sweetness of prayer, not only remains free from the aforementioned faults, but is more and more renewed, so that he may cast himself vividly and without labor into divine thoughts by degrees, and abound in the knowledge of discernment with much humility. It must be known, however, that prayer excels every latitude; but it belongs only to those who are filled in every sense and faith with the grace of God. Have you heard? There is, he says, a prayer surpassing all latitude, which belongs only to those who, within and in the heart, in every sense and faith, are substantially and supernaturally flooded with the divine light of grace. The holy Isaac calls this "unsealed memory," meaning formless and imageless and simple. And other holy Fathers speak of it in other ways.
On the Five Powers of the Soul; and likewise also concerning the fantasies peculiar to the soul and the mind, and that it is necessary to flee entirely from fantasy, and figures, and types, and forms, in pure prayer and in the simple and unified operation of the mind.
69. But, since it has been demonstrated   that the soul can imagine not only from demons but also naturally from itself through its five powers—namely the mind, the intellect, opinion, fantasy, and sense, just as the body has five senses: sight, smell, hearing, taste, and touch—and since fantasy is, as we have said, one of the soul's powers through which the soul is possessed of the faculty of imagining, it is necessary to govern and temper it well in those things which pertain to it, to incite those powers which most closely join it to God, both in the present age and in the future, and to direct them toward God; but as for the rest, it is necessary to care for them   as is fitting, and to use them, and to do them. It must be inquired, therefore, what the Fathers have said concerning all these things, and what seems probable. And the holy Maximus says: "Since the soul by itself, that is, through its own substance, is rational and intellectual, and altogether subsists by itself. And if it subsists by itself, it will act by itself and according to itself naturally, and with the body, naturally thinking and reasoning, and never naturally granting rest to the spiritual powers inherent within it; for those things which by nature belong to any substance [remain]..."


[756] {#pg.147.756}


[757] {#pg.147.757}
as long as it exists and subsists, cannot be taken away.   The soul, therefore, which from the moment it was created has always existed and subsisted through God who created it, always thinks, reasons, and knows—both by itself and with the body—through itself and its own nature. Thus, no argument will be found capable of separating the soul from those things that naturally belong to it, nor through the body, after its dissolution. Since, therefore, we know—and are instructed by the holy ones—that the mind and the intellect are moved and operate toward God both in the present age and in the one to come, while the other powers do so in the present age alone as being proper to this age, it is necessary, therefore, that the soul, as a skilled governor and naturally ruling over them, should not only in the present age, as we have said, direct and move its labor, mind, and thought completely and ardently toward God, and unite with Him during the time of pure, spiritual, single, and simple prayer; but it is necessary, I say, that it completely separate them from fantasy and from the other powers. For as Saint Nilus says:   "The order of prayer is a state without passion, which with most ardent love snatches the philosopher and spiritual mind to spiritual height." For by acting in this way, the soul will preserve the dignity that befits and adorns it.
Further concerning the mind.
70. Likewise, it is necessary that the mind itself, being an indivisible, simple, and self-sufficient substance, clean and luminous, should keep and guard itself   untainted and separated from that—namely, from fantasy; for the mind inherently possesses a natural power to return to itself, to attend to itself, and to be moved. For this is the rest of the mind, which is granted to it by divine grace, as the Climacicus says: "To make the mind rest is nothing but [the work] of the Holy Spirit." For even if, in that it is a power of the soul, the mind is moved and exists in some way from it, yet it is and is called its eye, and it possesses its own natural power   that is self-subsistent, as we have said. Therefore, when the mind remains disposed relative to the soul and its powers, it is then as a potential mind, and is called the natural man. But if it recovers its own natural, simple, and essential dignity—the splendor that is indivisible, self-sufficient, and self-governing—that is, if it is delivered from bodily and psychic natural relations and movements, and if it is deemed worthy to transition from being a potential mind to becoming a mind in act, that is, if it rises to the supernatural and spiritual man, then it always returns to itself without straying, and through itself ascends firmly and constantly to the thought of God. This thought has neither form nor figure, but is simple, as the Great Basil says: "The mind that is not scattered upon external things, nor diffused over the world by the senses, returns to itself, and through itself ascends to the thought of God; and, glowing and illumined by that beauty, it receives the knowledge of His nature." And thus, therefore, the image of God


[759] {#pg.147.759}
and His likeness, being a mind, and through itself immediately and intellectually being united and joined to the divine, that is to say, to God. This operation is the motion in a circle, that is, the return and turning of the mind to itself, and its union, and the union through itself to God, which alone is truly unerring and faultless, as it is a union that is disengaged, immediate, beyond thought, and a vision beyond sight. And the great Dionysius says: “The motion of the soul is indeed circular, that is, its entry into itself from external things; and the simple involution of its intellectual powers, as in a circle, which provides it with unerringness, and turns it from many things   from without, and gathers it first into itself, and then, having become uniform, unites it to the powers that are unified simply, and thus leads it to the Beautiful and Good, which is above all things that exist, and is one and the same, and unbegotten and immortal and eternal. But the soul is moved in a circle in as much as it is properly illuminated by divine knowledge; not mentally and unitively, but logically and periodically, and as though by mixed and transitive faculties. But the straight way is when it does not enter into itself, and is not moved by a single intellect (for that is posterior, as I said, to the motion in a circle), but proceeds to things around it, and is led from external things, as from various complex and manifold symbols, to simple and unified   contemplation.” And the holy Maximus says: “Having received an immediate union with God, the mind is able to be entirely empty and free from thinking and from being thought of. When, therefore, it lets go of this faculty, thinking of something of those things that are after God, it is convicted of breaking the union that is above thought, through which, so long as it is with God, as though supernatural and by participation itself become God, it transgresses the law of its nature as an immovable end.” And again: “A pure mind has received a relationship regarding the Cause in a union beyond thought, according to which, having brought to a rest its manifold natural motion and relationship toward things after the Cause, it clings only unknowably, having become, in the unspeakable outcome, partaker of the most blessed silence   that is above thought, which neither speech nor thought can fully manifest, but only experience through participation, of those who have been deemed worthy of the enjoyments beyond thought; of which a sign, easy to see and manifest to all, is the soul’s total insensibility and rest regarding its disposition toward this present age.” To this, therefore, the mind, neither being assisted by the soul—that is, to be always moved toward God—nor by itself attaining and performing what is its own—that is, returning to itself and thus ascending disengagedly to the thought of God—or rather not reaping this from either part, but being joined to fantasy, is now henceforth made manifold, and is far distant from God.


[761] {#pg.147.761}
Still concerning pure prayer. A 71. And saint Nilus says: "Strive to keep your mind quiet and silent at the time of prayer, and thus you will be able to pray; furthermore, I will say my own [thought], which I have also said to the younger ones: Blessed is the mind which at the time of prayer has acquired a perfect formlessness." And saint Philotheos: "It is rare to find those who act in peace regarding reason; and it belongs only to those who strive to have divine joy and consolation within themselves through this thing perpetually." And the great Basil: "A good prayer is that which forms an effective thought of God in the soul; and this is the indwelling of God, namely, to hold God in oneself through memory, when the continuity of memory is not interrupted by earthly cares, nor is the mind disturbed by unexpected passions, but the lover of God, escaping all these,   departs toward God."
That the apatheia of the mind is one thing, and true prayer another, which is even greater.
72. It must be known, therefore, this also, that, if even according to saint Maximus, "The mind cannot become free from passion through action alone without desire, unless many and varied contemplations receive it," yet again, according to the most divine Nilus, it is possible for one who has become free from passion not to pray truly, but to be made manifold, and to be far distant from God. For this Father says concerning such a matter thus: "Even if the mind is above bodily contemplation, it has not yet contemplated the perfect place of God; for it can be in the knowledge of thoughts, and be made manifold toward it." And further: "He who has attained apatheia does not yet pray truly; for he can be in mere thoughts, and be distracted by   their histories, and be far distant from God." And further: "Not because the mind lingers in the mere thoughts of things, has it already reached the place of prayer; for it can be in the contemplation of things and chatter in their arguments; which, even if they are mere words, but as theorems belonging to things, they mold the mind, and lead it far away from God." And the one of the Ladder also says: "If the mind has learned to pray truly, these speak to the Lord dominantly and face to face, as those who speak words toward the king's ear." From these and such things, you can accurately understand the difference of both types, and by comparison their dissimilarity, since the one is through reception, and the other through effort. For of the one, the work is cares, and many and varied contemplations.   Of the other, the work is true prayer. Moreover, that the apatheia of the mind is one thing, and true prayer another. Furthermore, that he who possesses true prayer, according to the saints, is by every necessity also naturally disposed to possess a mind free from passion, but he who possesses only a mind free from passion has not been able to possess also true prayer. And these things are thus; but let the discourse return to what is proposed to us. Since not only those things which we have said, but also the memory of good and evil things itself, frequently are accustomed to mold the mind and lead it to fantasy;


[763] {#pg.147.763}
of this—for this, too, we must speak a little—is the memory of both good and evil, which is wont, in a certain way, to present itself suddenly to the mind and provoke fantasy. It is therefore necessary to say a little about this as well.
Still concerning fantasies, and the images of the mind, and the signs of error and of truth; and what are the signs of error.
75. If you are living in stillness and wish to be alone with God alone, never receive any sensible or intelligible thing that you may see, whether inside or outside yourself, even if it be the supposed form of Christ, or an angel, or the appearance of a saint, or a manifestation of light that appears to the mind. But remain incredulous and heavy/wary toward it—even if it seems good—before you have asked those who are experienced, as we have said. For this is most useful, and most dear and acceptable to God. Always keep your mind without color, without form, without image, without quality, and without quantity. Cleave only to the words of prayer, and apply and contemplate them within the movements of the heart, as the Climacus says: “The beginning of prayer is to pursue the words throughout their preludes by means of soliloquy; the middle is to have the mind attentive to what is being said; and the end is a rapture toward the Lord.” And Saint Nilus likewise says: “The supreme prayer of the perfect is a certain rapture of the mind, a total withdrawal from all things that are according to the senses, with the spirit communing with God through ineffable groanings—He who looks upon the disposition of the heart as an inscribed book, opened up, showing its will in silent signs.” Just as Paul was rapt up to the third heaven, not knowing whether he was in the body or out of the body; similarly, Peter went up to the roof to pray and saw the vision of the sheet. The second prayer, after the first, is to pronounce the words while the mind follows with a subsequent compunction,   knowing to whom it addresses its petition. But prayer that is interrupted and dissipated by bodily thoughts has departed from the state of the one who is praying. Remain, therefore, in these things and do not accept others until you have attained peace and have asked those who are experienced, as has been said. These are the signs of error that we have announced, and others similar to them. But see also what are the signs of truth. The signs of truth, and of the good and life-giving Spirit, are love, joy, peace, long-suffering, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness,   temperance, and the rest, as the divine Apostle says, calling them all fruits of the Holy Spirit. He says also again: “Walk as children of light. For the fruit of the Spirit is in all goodness and justice and truth,” of which error possesses the direct opposite. And one of the wise men, being asked by someone, says: “Concerning the secure way of salvation, beloved, as you have said, there are many ways that lead to life, and many that lead to death.” And proceeding further: “You have one way that leads to life: the observance of the commandments of Christ. In these commandments you will find every form of virtue, but especially these three: humility, charity, and mercy, without which no one will see the Lord.” And a little later: “These three are the invincible weapons against the demons, which the Holy Trinity has bestowed upon us: I mean humility and charity and


[765] {#pg.147.765}
mercy, against which even the whole swarm of demons cannot look. For there is not among them the slightest trace of humility, since they were blinded by pride and eternal fire was prepared for them. Where is there among them, or even a shadow of, charity or mercy—they who have fostered unceasing hatred toward the human race and do not cease to wage war against it? Let us then be armored with these weapons, which whoever puts on becomes invincible to his enemies.” And a little later: “This triple-woven cord, which the Holy Trinity wove and joined together, we see to be both three and one; three, indeed, in names, or if you will, also in persons; but one in power and efficacy, and in that closeness, inclination, and familiarity which it has with God.” Concerning these the Master said: “My yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matt. xi, 30). And the disciple whom he loved: “And his commandments are not heavy” (I John v, 3). And after a few words: “For this reason, the soul that is mingled with God through purity of soul, and through the keeping of the commandments, and possesses these three weapons, which are God Himself, puts on God Himself and becomes god by participation, through humility, mercy, and charity, and having passed beyond the material dyad and having transcended the head of the law—I mean charity—is joined to the supersubstantial and life-creating Trinity, conversing with her immediately, adding light to light and being suffused with ceaseless and eternal joy.” But enough has been said regarding these things. It is worth while, however, just as we have mentioned from a part of the signs and fruits of error and truth (whence, from these very fruits, according to the divine Paul, we may know those who are at work, of what spirit they are), so also to discourse briefly from the Fathers concerning both kinds of excitation—that is, regarding the divine and true grace, and the false and contrary one. Thus, therefore, does the divine Diadochus speak concerning this.
Concerning divine and false excitation.
“When our mind begins to perceive the consolation of the Holy Spirit, then Satan also, in some pleasant sensory way, in the silence of the night, when one is coming into the inclination of a very light sleep, excites the soul. If, therefore, the mind is found to be holding the holy name of the Lord Jesus with very fervent memory, and uses that holy and glorious name as a weapon against the deception, the deceiver of guile withdraws, but henceforth he kindles a manifest war against the soul.
