Whence, recognizing the deception of the evil one accurately, the mind progresses further into the experience of discernment.” And again: “The good consolation occurs while the body is awake, or also when it is about to come into some semblance of sleep, when one is in fervent memory of God, and as it were glued to His charity; but that of the deception occurs when, as I said, the wrestler has come into some light sleep, with a middling memory


[767] {#pg.147.767}
of God. For the one, as being from God, clearly wishes to urge the souls of those who wrestle in piety, in a great outpouring of soul, toward His love. But the other, since it is accustomed to toss the soul in some wind of delusion, attempts to steal, through the sleep of the body, the experience of the sense of the healthy mind, especially when it is lukewarm regarding the memory of God. If, therefore, the mind is found, as I said, cautiously remembering the Lord Jesus Christ, it scatters that sweet-seeming breeze of the enemy, and rejoicing, moves to war against him, as having, beyond grace, a second successful weapon: the boasting derived from experience. And again: If by a certain motion, free from images and doubt, the soul is kindled toward the love of God, drawing its body   as well into the depths of that ineffable charity—whether the body be awake or, in the way I have mentioned, entering into sleep—being led by the holy grace, and thinking of nothing else at all save only that toward which it is moved, one must know that this is the activity of the Holy Spirit. For, being thoroughly suffused with this ineffable sweetness, it can think of nothing else, since it rejoices in a joy that is never remitted. If, however, the mind conceives any ambiguous or sordid thought while engaged in this, even if it uses the holy name for defense against the evil one, and not rather solely for the love of God, one must understand that such an excitation is from the deceiver, in the guise of joy. But that joy is qualitatively and structurally chaotic, for it is the enemy wishing to seduce the soul. For when he sees the mind precisely   boasting in the experience of his own sensation, then, as I said, he invites the soul with certain fair-seeming excitations, so that, as it is distracted by that shallow and liquid sweetness, the mixing of the deceiver may remain unknown to it. From this, therefore, we shall know the spirit of truth and the spirit of delusion. It is impossible, however, for anyone to taste the divine goodness sensibly, or to experience the wickedness of the demons sensibly, unless one first persuades himself that grace truly resides in the depths of the mind, whereas evil spirits dwell in the parts of the heart—a thing the demons never wish for men to believe, lest the mind, knowing this precisely, should arm the memory of God against them. You have now enough on this subject, and you should be content; for one should not cross beyond the Pillars of Gades, and if you find honey, eat but a little,   lest, having had your fill, you vomit it up.
On divine pleasure, which springs from the heart.
66. Or rather, it is more timely and appropriate to say: Who shall announce the sweetness of honey to those who have not yet tasted it, and much more, incomparably, the divine pleasure and supernatural joy, life-giving and ever-flowing, which springs from a pure and true heart, and leaps up with perpetual streams? As the God-man Jesus says: "Whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him, shall not thirst forever; but the


[769] {#pg.147.769}
water that I will give him shall become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life." And again: "If anyone thirsts, let him come to Me and drink." "He who believes in Me, as the Scripture has said, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water." But He said this concerning the Spirit, says the Theologian, which those believing in Him were about to receive; and the great Paul: "God has sent forth the Spirit of His Son into our hearts, crying: Abba, Father."
That this spiritual joy is manifold, and nameless.
76. This spiritual joy is supernatural, lifegiving, and substantial splendor; it is called, mystically, the darkness that is above light, and the inexplicable beauty, and the greatest of things desired, and inspection, and the vision of God, and deification; but it remains unnamed after it has been named, and unknown after it has been known, and inconceivable after it has been conceived. And the great Dionysius says: "According to this, we pray to reach the super-luminous darkness, and through blindness and ignorance to see and to know Him who is beyond vision and knowledge—that is, to see and to know this very thing, that He is not visible and not knowable; for this is indeed to see and to know, and to praise the Supersubstantial   supersubstantially through the removal of all beings." And further: "The divine darkness is the inaccessible light in which God is said to dwell; and it is invisible on account of its superabundant splendor, and inaccessible on account of the excess of its supersubstantial effusion. In this light is he who is deemed worthy to know and see God; by this very fact of not seeing and not knowing, he truly enters into that which is beyond vision and knowledge; knowing this very thing, that He is beyond all things sensible and intelligible." And the great Basil says: "The flashes of divine beauty are altogether ineffable and indescribable; speech cannot express them, nor hearing receive them. Even if you mention the splendors of the morning star,   or the brightness of the moon, or the light of the sun, all are vile in comparison to that glory, and fall further short in comparison to the true light than deep night and gloomy darkness fall short of the purest midday. This beauty is invisible to eyes of flesh, but graspable by the soul and mind alone. And if at any time it has shone upon any of the saints, it has left behind in them an unendurable sting of longing, so that, exulting with joy for the future life, they would say: 'Woe is me, that my sojourning is prolonged!' and 'My soul thirsted for God, the strong, the living; when shall I come and appear before the face of my God?' And, 'To depart and be with Christ is far better.' And, D 'Now dismiss your servant, Master, according to your word, in peace'; considering this present life a prison-house. For they, since they could not be sated with the contemplation of the divine beauty, wished that, through all eternal life, the contemplation of the splendor of the Lord might be extended along with it. And the Theologian says: 'Whose fear is the keeping of the commandments,


[771] {#pg.147.771}
is the cleansing of the flesh, which surrounds the soul like a cloud, and does not permit it to see the divine rays; whose inundation is illumination, and illumination is the fulfillment of desire for those who desire the greatest things, or the Greatest [God] Himself, or things beyond the great.' And the divine Gregory of Nyssa says: 'If you should empty out, through the care of a virtuous life, the grime that has formed on your heart, divine beauty will shine forth for you, as is wont to happen with iron. For when, through the whetstone, that which was just before black is stripped of its rust, it sends forth from itself certain rays and shines with brightness toward the sun; so also the inner man, whom the Lord calls heart, once it has scrubbed off the poisonous grime that has sprouted upon its form through evil corruption, will again retrieve its likeness to the archetype, and will be good; for good follows in every way upon that which is good.' And saint Nilus: 'Blessed is he who embraces the ignorance which is inseparable from prayer.' And the [author] of the Ladder: 'The abyss of mourning beheld consolation, the cleansing of the heart received illumination; illumination is an ineffable operation, glimpsed invisibly and understood unknowingly.'   For this reason, those who like the ancient Mary have chosen this good portion and way of life — the spiritual and unstealable one — are thrice-blessed and deemed worthy of such God-befitting good fortune, so that with great and ecstatic joy, it is permitted to them, along with the divine Paul, to be inspired openly and to cry out together: 'But when the kindness and the philanthropy of God our Savior appeared, not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to His mercy He saved us, through the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, which He poured out on us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Savior, that being justified by His grace, we should become heirs according to the hope of eternal life' (Tit. III, 4-7); and again: 'Who also has anointed us and sealed us, and given us the earnest of the Spirit in our hearts' (II Cor. I, 21-22); and: 'But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us' (II Cor. IV, 7). And   those men were such; but may it be for us also, by their prayers to the Lord that persuade God, to share partly, like them, in mercy and in grace.
That it is necessary by all means for him to be of a gentle heart who desires to live in peace absolutely.
77. But this, O child, you must know now in due time before all else, and along with all else, that just as he who wishes to learn to shoot an arrow well does not aim his bow without marks, so he who wishes to learn to live in peace must have, as his mark, to be always gentle of heart. And saint Isidore says: 'It is not sufficient for virtue to practice, but it is necessary to be moderate in the practice as well. For if, starting the contest of gentleness, we fight with a troubled mind, it is nothing other than wishing indeed to attain salvation, but not wishing to do the things that contribute to it.' And before him the divine David: 'He will guide the meek in judgment; He will teach—


[773] {#pg.147.773}
the meek His ways. And the son of Sirach: 'To the meek are mysteries revealed.' And the sweetest Jesus: 'Learn from me, for I am meek and lowly in heart, and you shall find rest for your souls.' And: 'To whom shall I look, but to him who is meek and quiet, and who trembles at My words?' And: 'Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth,' that is, the heart, bringing forth fruit by grace: thirty, sixty, and a hundred-fold, according to the order of the beginners, the intermediate, and the perfect. For that man will not be troubled, nor will he be troubled by others, if the discourse is not yet concerning piety.
How meekness is achieved in us, and concerning the tripartite soul: the irascible, the desiderative, and the rational.
You can easily achieve this, if you turn away from everything at once and move your soul toward love, remaining silent for the most part, eating moderately, and always praying, as it has been said to the Fathers: 'Bridle the irascible part of the soul with love; mortify its desiderative part with temperance; and give wings to its rational part with prayer: and the light of the mind will never be dimmed.' And: 'The bridle of anger is timely silence; of irrational desire,   measured food; of the stubborn mind, one-thought prayer.' And again: 'There are three virtues which provide light to the mind always: not knowing the malice of any man; bearing what happens without disturbance; and doing good to those who do evil. These three virtues beget three other virtues greater than themselves: not knowing the malice of man begets love; bearing what happens without disturbance begets meekness; and doing good to those who do evil grants peace.' And again: 'There are three moral states, more general among monks: the first is not to sin in action; the second, not to let passionate thoughts linger in the soul; and the third, to view the forms of women and of those who cause sorrow, without passion, in the mind.'
That one must repent quickly for accidental lapses, and thus wisely secure oneself for the future.
79. But if it should happen at some time that you are disturbed, or that you slip into some fault, and miss the mark of what is proper, you must immediately be reconciled with the person you have grieved or who has grieved you; and you must repent from the soul, mourn and weep, and reproach yourself. And thus, for the future, you must be heedful and secure yourself most wisely, as the Lord Jesus teaches: 'If you offer your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go, first be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.' And the apostle Paul: 'All bitterness and wrath...'


[775] {#pg.147.775}
and anger, and clamor, and blasphemy, be put away from you, with all malice. And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you.' And: 'Be ye angry, and sin not.' And: 'Let not the sun go down upon your wrath.' And: 'Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath.' And: 'Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good.' And this indeed is said concerning mutual reconciliation.
Of slipping and repentance.
Concerning slipping, St. Isaac says: "We should not grieve when we slip in something, but when we remain in it. For slipping happens often even to the perfect; but remaining in it is complete destruction. The sorrow, however, that we feel for our own slips is reckoned to us, by grace, as a place of pure work. He who slips a second time in the hope of repentance walks before God with craftiness; upon him death falls unexpectedly, and he does not reach the time of his hope to fulfill the works of virtue." And further: "It is necessary," he says, "for us to know at every hour that in these twenty-four hours of night and day we are in need of repentance. The understanding of the name 'repentance,' as we have known it from the true nature of things, is this: it is a stretch of supplication at every hour, in prayer filled with compunction, approaching God for the remission of past things; and sorrow for the guarding of those to come." And again: "Grace upon grace, repentance has been given to men. For repentance is a second regeneration from God, and the pledge which we received from faith, through repentance we receive as His grace. Repentance is the door of mercy, which is opened to those who seek it. Through this door we enter into the divine mercy, and outside this entrance, we shall not find mercy. Because all have sinned, according to the divine Scripture, justified freely by His grace. Repentance is the second grace, and it is born in the heart from faith and fear. And fear is the paternal rod which steers us until we reach the spiritual paradise; and when we have reached it, it leaves us and turns back. Paradise is the love of God, in which is the delight of all blessings." And again: "Just as it is impossible to cross the great sea without a ship and a boat, so no one can cross to love without fear. We can pass through the foul sea that is spread between us and the spiritual paradise by the boat of repentance, which holds the rowing-oars of fear. But if the rowing-oars of fear do not steer this boat of repentance, through which we pass the sea of this world toward God, we are submerged in that foul sea."


[777] {#pg.147.777}
81. Repentance is a ship; fear is its helmsman; charity is the divine harbor. Fear therefore establishes us in the ship of repentance and sends us across the foul sea of this life; and it leads us to the divine harbor, which is charity, into which all those who toil and are burdened through repentance arrive. And when we reach charity, we have reached God, and our journey is finished, and we have crossed over to the island which is beyond this world, where the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit are. Concerning sorrow according to God, the Savior speaks thus: "Blessed are they that mourn, for they shall be comforted."
Further concerning tears, the holy Isaac writes this: "Tears during prayer are a sign of the mercy of God, of which the soul has been deemed worthy in its repentance; they indicate that it has been accepted and has begun to enter into the plain of purity through tears. For unless thoughts of what is passing away are cast off, and they cast from themselves the hope of the world, and there is stirred up within them contempt for it, and they begin to prepare good provisions for their departure from the world, and thoughts of certain things that are there in heaven begin to be moved in the soul, the eyes cannot weep. For tears are multiplied and increase more and more from pure and constant converse, from many and continuous thoughts, and from those that come readily and from the memory of some slight thing formed in the mind, and the heart grieving from the memory of it, and from these [things] tears are increased and grow yet more."   And he of the Ladder says: "As fire consumes stubble, so the pure tear consumes every defilement, whether apparent or conceptual." Further: "Let us acquire pure and sincere tears for our own dissolution; for in them there is no theft or conceit; rather, there is purification, progress in charity toward God, the washing away of sin, and the deprivation of passions." Further: "Do not trust your springs before perfect purification; for wine that is enclosed in casks immediately from the winepress does not have stability." Further: "Tears which proceed from fear possess within themselves their own safeguard; but those of charity, before charity is perfect, are in some cases exposed to those who would plunder them, unless perhaps the fire which is to be ever-remembered, at the time of its operation, has entirely kindled the heart. And it is a wondrous thing how that which is more humble is more secure in the time of its fire." Further: "A tear of departure has brought forth fear; but when fear has brought forth security, joy has appeared; and as inexpressible joy has ceased, the flower of holy charity has sprouted."
Regarding self-reproach, the great Antony says: "This is the great work of a man, that he should cast his own fault upon himself before God, and expect temptation until his very last breath." And another holy Father, being asked, "What is the greater thing you have found, Father, in this way?" replied saying, "To reproach oneself in all things." This, the one who had asked approved, and said to him, "There is no other way than this." And Abbot   Poemen […]


[779] {#pg.147.779}
A said: "All the virtues entered this world with a sigh. Take away one virtue, and outside of it, a man stands with toil." And they asked him, "What is this one?" And he says: "That a man should reproach himself at all times." He said again: "He who reproaches himself, whatever may happen to him, whether loss, or disgrace, or any affliction whatsoever, has anticipated it by judging himself worthy of it, and he is never disturbed."
On attention and the need to be wisely confirmed.
82. In like manner, regarding attention and confirmation, the divine Paul writes: "See how carefully you walk; not as unwise, but as wise, redeeming the time, because the days are evil" (Eph. v, 15). And holy Isaac says: "O wisdom, how admirable you are, and how you foresee all things from afar! Blessed is he who finds you; for he has been delivered from the sloth of youth. If anyone trades through a small profit—that is, provision—the healing of great passions, he does well. For this is wisdom, that one should always be vigilant even in the smallest and least things being done by him. For he treasures up great rest for himself, and does not sleep, lest anything contrary happen to him; but he cuts off the causes of evil before the time, and through the briefest matters sustains a small sadness, through it dissipating the greater ones and advancing. Therefore also the Wise Man says: 'Be vigilant and attentive for your life; for sleep is a relative of thought, and an image of the true immortal.'   The Hierophant Basil also says: 'Whoever is slothful in small things, do not trust him to excel in matters of greatness.'"
That one ought to act seriously in all the things aforementioned; but above all, that we should be tranquil and gentle, and that it is necessary to invoke the Lord Jesus Christ purely within the heart, if we desire to act in peace.
83. Because of all these things, set yourself to work seriously on the things aforementioned; but above all,   that you may be tranquil and gentle, and with a clean conscience, invoke the Lord Jesus Christ in the depths of the heart, as we have said. For in this way, advancing by this path, you will possess divine grace resting in your soul. For the Climacus also says: "He who is encumbered by anger and conceit, and hypocrisy and the memory of injuries, will never dare to see the trace of tranquility, lest he should thereby gain an ecstasy; but if one is pure from these, he will eventually know what is advantageous; though I think not even he." And indeed, you will not only have grace resting in your soul, but also having your soul resting completely from those things that formerly troubled it, namely demons and passions. For even if they trouble it again, they do not succeed, because it does not cling to them, nor does it desire the pleasure that comes from them.
On good and ecstatic love, and on divine beauty.
84. For the whole longing of such a one, and the inward


[781] {#pg.147.781}
disposition of his soul, gazes toward the supreme beauty, which the Fathers have called the sum of all desirable things.   And the great Basil says: “When the love of piety takes hold of the soul, every form of warfare is for it a laughing-stock, and all those who tear it apart for the sake of the One whom it loves, benefit rather than strike it.” And again: “What is more wonderful than the divine beauty? What thought is more pleasant than divine magnificence? What yearning of the soul is as vehement and as unbearable as that which is produced by God in a soul purged of all malice, and which, from a true disposition, says: ‘I am wounded by love’?”
On warfare, and on instructive withdrawal,
and on abandonment by aversion.
85. Now, war is waged by way of instructive withdrawal, not by way of abandonment through aversion. Why? So that his mind may not be exalted on account of the good it has found; but, being warred upon and instructed, it always puts on humility, by which alone it not only conquers those who arrogantly wage war against it, but is also continuously deemed worthy of greater gifts, progressing as much as human nature allows, bound and weighed down by necessary cords and the burden of the flesh, and journeying toward the perfection and impassibility that is in Christ. And Saint Diadochus says: “The Lord Himself says that Satan has fallen like lightning from the heavens,   so that the deformed one might not look upon the habitations of the holy angels.” How, then, can the human mind, which is not deemed worthy of the communion of good servants, have a common dwelling-place with God? But they will say that this happens by way of withdrawal, and they will say nothing more. For instructive withdrawal in no way deprives the soul of the divine light; it only hides, as I have already said many times, the presence of grace from the mind, so that it may be urged forward—just as the soul, through the bitterness of the demons, is urged, because of all fear and great humility, to seek out the help that comes from God, recognizing bit by bit the malice of its enemy. Just as if a mother were to briefly push away from her arms a child who is unruly regarding the laws of breastfeeding,   so that, being terrified by some repulsive men standing around him, or by any wild beasts whatever, he might return to his mother’s bosom with great fear and tears. But the withdrawal that occurs by way of aversion delivers the soul that does not wish to have God to the demons, as if it were a prisoner. We, however, are not children of abandonment—may it never be!—but we believe ourselves to be true infants of the grace of God, nourished by it with small withdrawals and frequent consolations, so that, through the goodness of God, we may hasten to arrive at a perfect man, unto the measure of age. And again: “The instructive withdrawal indeed brings much sorrow and humility, and a diffidence proportionate to the soul, so that its ambitious and dauntless part may fittingly come to humility;   but straightway it brings the fear of God and tears of confession into the heart, and a vehement desire for the best silence. But the abandonment that comes by way of aversion to God is filled with desperation, and diffidence, and anger


[783] {#pg.147.783}
and permits the soul to be filled with pride. We must, therefore, know the experience of both kinds of abandonment, and according to the manner of each, we must approach God. In the former case, we owe Him thanksgiving along with our apology, inasmuch as He chastised the intemperance of our mind by the delay of consolation, so that, as a good Father, He might teach us the difference between virtue and vice. But in the latter case, we owe unending confession of sins, incessant tears, and more complete withdrawal, so that we might thereby be able, by the addition of labors, to appease God at last, so that He might look again, as before, into our hearts.
Nevertheless, it must be known that, when the battle between the soul and Satan takes place by way of a providential encounter—I mean by the instructional abandonment—grace withdraws itself, as I have already said; yet it cooperates secretly with the soul by its assistance, so that it may show the victory to be that of the soul alone against its enemies.   And Saint Isaac says: "It is impossible for a man, without those temptations that occur by divine permission, to become wise in spiritual wars, and to know his own Provider, and to sense his God, and to be strengthened in His faith secretly, unless he receives it by the power of the experience which he has undergone. And when grace sees that conceit has begun in his mind even a little, and he has begun to think great things about himself, it immediately permits temptations to be strengthened and to prevail against him, until he learns his own infirmity, and flees, and possesses God in humility. And in these things man comes to the measure of a perfect man, in the faith and hope of the Son of God, and is exalted toward love."
For the love of God toward man is known to be admirable when he happens to be in the midst of circumstances that cut off his hope; and therein God shows His power in the salvation that He brings upon him. For man never learns the divine power in rest and relief; and God never showed His own energy perceptibly   except in a place of stillness, and in the desert, and in places devoid of the encounters and the tumult of living alongside men.
On Apathy, and what human apathy is.
86. Further, it is necessary here to add a word from a part on apathy and perfection, and after a little, to put an end to the present treatise. Hear what the great Basil says:   "He who has become a lover of God, and desires to grasp even the smallest portion of His apathy, and of His spiritual holiness, and of that tranquility, and freedom from disturbance, and gentleness, and of the happiness and joy that is born from these, strives to withdraw his thoughts far from every material passion that defiles the soul. He looks upon divine things with a pure and unobscured eye; he is filled inexhaustibly with the light that rises from thence; and after he has exercised his soul into such a habit and state, he becomes, as far as is possible, similar to God, and loves and desires Him, inasmuch as he


[785] {#pg.147.785}
has sustained a great and difficult struggle and, being freed from the commixture of matter, is able, with a mind pure and separated from the intermingling of bodily passions, to commune with God.   And this is concerning *apatheia* (dispassion). But concerning what human *apatheia* is, the holy Isaac writes as follows: "Apatheia is not the failure to feel the passions, but the failure to accept them. For from the many and varied virtues, both manifest and hidden, which one has acquired, the passions have become weak within them, and they cannot easily rise up against the soul; and the intellect does not need to pay attention to them at all times. For at every moment it is filled with its own thoughts, through meditation and the conversation of the best ways of life, which move in the understanding within the mind. And when the passions begin to be moved and to be troubled, the intellect is suddenly snatched away from their proximity, by a certain understanding that looks down into the mind; and the passions are left idle in it, as the blessed Mark said: 'The mind, fulfilling the acts of the virtues by the grace of God, and abounding in knowledge, feels little of the evil and irrational part of the soul.' For its knowledge snatches it up to the heights and alienates it from all things that are in the world; and because of the purity, subtilty, lightness, and keenness of their mind, and because of their continued exercise, their mind is cleansed and shown to be clear,   because their flesh has been withered by the leisure of stillness (*hesychia*) and the long persistence therein. For this reason, contemplation is easily and quickly attached to each one, and the theory within them leads them, to their own astonishment; and in this they are multiplied a hundredfold in theories; and their intellect never lacks material for understanding; and they are never outside those things which the fruit of the Spirit produces in them. And through long-accustomed habit, those memories that move the passions in the soul are erased from their hearts, as is the strength of the power of the devil. For when the soul does not dally with the passions, nor associate with them in their meditation, by being held fast by another care without ceasing, the strength of the claws of the passions is unable to take hold of its spiritual senses." And the divine Diadochus says: "Apatheia is not the state of not being attacked by demons—for then we would have to depart from the world, according to the Apostle—but the state of remaining unvanquished while being attacked by them. For those steel-clad soldiers are indeed shot at by their adversaries, and they hear the sound of the archery, and they even see the very arrows being sent against them, but they are not struck because of the solidity of their martial   garments. But while those men, armored in iron, remain unvanquished while under attack, we, however,   armored with the light of the holy all-


[787] {#pg.147.787}
-armor, and with the helmet of the Savior, having armed ourselves with all that is good, let us break the dark phalanxes of the demons. For it is not the mere ceasing to do evil that brings purity, but also the total abolition of evil through diligence in good deeds.» And Saint Maximus also divides apathia in four ways, saying this: «I call the first apathia the motionlessness of the body regarding sin in its operation. I call the second apathia the complete casting away of passionate thoughts in the soul, through which the motion of the passions, which the first apathia extinguishes, is withered away, having no passionate thoughts to ignite it into action. I call the third apathia the total stillness of desire regarding the passions, through which the second also naturally comes to be, established by the purity of the thoughts. I call the fourth apathia the complete discarding of all sensible images in the intellect, through which the third takes its origin, as it no longer possesses the images of sensible things that give form in it to the icons of the passions.» Further: «Apathia is a peaceful state of the soul whereby it becomes difficult to move toward wickedness.»
Further concerning apathia and perfection
87.   And indeed, Saint Ephrem also, concerning apathia and perfection, declares thus: «Those who are passionless, reaching out insatiably toward the supreme desirable object, make their perfection unfinishable; for there is no end to eternal goods. And it is perfect, insofar as it relates to the measure of human capacity. Yet it is unfinishable, as it always surpasses itself with daily additions, and is elevated continuously in its ascents toward God.» Similarly, Saint Nilus also speaks thus concerning perfection: «Two perfections must be understood: one temporal, and the other eternal; concerning which the Apostle writes: 'When that which is perfect is come, then that which is in part shall be abolished' (1 Cor. xiii, 10). For when it says 'when that which is perfect is come,' it signifies that here we are unable to attain divine perfection.» Further: «The divine Paul recognizes two perfections; and he knows the same man to be both perfect and not perfect: insofar as he relates to the present life, the man is called perfect; but as he relates to Him who is truly perfect, he is not perfect. Therefore he says, 'Not that I have already attained, or am already perfected' (Philipp. iii, 12). And a little later   he says: 'Let us therefore, as many as are perfect, be thus minded' (Ibid. 15).»
Concerning the passionate, the sweetly-passionate, the strongly-passionate, and the lack of passion
88. Saint Elias the Ekdikos also says: «Evil matter: of the body—passion; of the soul—sweet-passion; of the mind—strong-passion. It is indicted, the first by touch; the second by the remaining senses; the last by a contrary disposition.» Further: «The sweetly-passionate one is near to the passionate one; the strongly-passionate one to the sweetly-passionate; but far from both is the passionless one.»
What it is to experience the passionate, the sweetly-passionate, the strongly-passionate, and the passionless; and concerning the cure of each
89. One is passionate who possesses the sinful [act]


[789] {#pg.147.789}
more violently than the thought, even if for the time being he does not sin outwardly. One is sweetly-passionate who possesses the operation of sin weaker than the thought, even if he suffers [it] outwardly. One is strongly-passionate who inclines more to the freedom than to the servitude of the intermediate things. One would be passionless, who is ignorant of the difference between all these things. Likewise, however, concerning the cure of both, he declares the following: corporeal passion is cast out from the soul through fasting and prayer; the sweetly-passionate, through vigils and silence; the strongly-passionate, through stillness and attention; and passionlessness consists in the memory of God.
On faith, hope, and love.
8. But since faith, hope, and love are the beginning, the middle, and the end of all good things—or, if you would prefer to say, the leader and the guide—that threefold cord, and God-woven, and above all, love, because God is and is called love, it is not right not to complete by these also what is lacking in the present treatise. Or rather, since even according to holy Isaac one receives the perfection of the many fruits of the Spirit when he is accounted worthy of perfect love.
Let us mention a little about it also. For indeed, the author of the *Ladder* writes:   “Now finally, after all that has been said, these three remain, binding fast and holding the bond of all: faith, hope, love; but the greatest of these is love, for God is named [by it].” I, however, see the one as a ray, the other as light, the third as a circle, but all as one radiance and brightness. For the one can do and create all things; the second, the mercy of God encircles, and makes it unashamed; and the third never falls, nor ceases to run, nor allows him whom it has wounded to rest from that blessed madness. And further: “The discourse about love is known to the angels, and to them, according to the operation of illumination, love is God.” He who wishes to state the limit of this is like a blind man measuring the sand in an abyss. Love, according to its quality, is a likeness of God, as far as is possible for mortals; according to its operation, it is an intoxication of the soul; according to its property, it is a fountain of faith, an abyss of long-suffering, a sea of humility. Love is truly the repulsion of every contrary thought, since love does not imagine evil. Love, and passionlessness, and adoption are distinguished by names only;   as light, and fire, and flame run together into one operation, so also think concerning these. And the holy Diadochus: “Let faith, hope, and love, my brothers, lead every spiritual contemplation, but love most of all. For the former teach one to despise visible goods, but love joins the soul itself to the virtues of God, investigating the invisible God with an intellectual sense.” And further: “There is one love of the soul, the natural one, and another which is brought about in it from the holy Spirit. For the former is stirred proportionally by our own will when we wish, and therefore it is easily snatched away by evil spirits when we do not violently master our own inclination.”


[791] {#pg.147.791}
And it so inflames the soul toward the love of God that all the parts of the soul are then gathered into an immense disposition of simplicity, for the mind, being then as it were pregnant from the spiritual energy, gushes forth a certain fountain of love and joy. And Saint Isaac says: “Charity which arises from certain things is like a small lamp, nourished by oil, and thus its light is maintained, or like a torrent flowing from rain, the flow of which ceases when the material that produces it fails. But that charity which has God as its author is like a springing fountain, and its waves are never interrupted; for He alone is the source of charity, and its unfailing substance.”   And again, when asked what the perfection of the manifold fruits of the Spirit is, he answered: “When someone is deemed worthy of the perfect charity of God.” And being asked again how one knows that one has reached this, he said: “When the memory of God is stirred in his consciousness, his heart is immediately moved in His love, and his eyes pour forth tears abundantly; for it is the custom of love to draw tears from the memory of those things which are loved, and such a one is never lacking in tears. For he never lacks the material which carries him into the memory of God, so that even in his sleep he converses with God; for such is the custom of love, to do these things, and this is the perfection of men in this life of theirs.”   And furthermore: “The charity of God is hot by nature, and when it falls upon someone beyond measure, it makes that soul ecstatic. For this reason the heart of the one who has felt it cannot contain it or endure it, but according to the measure of the quality and the charity that has come upon him, an unusual change is seen in him. And these are its sensible signs: the man’s face becomes fiery and joyful, and his body is warmed, fear and shame depart from him, and he becomes as it were ecstatic,   and the faculty that gathers the mind flees from him, and he becomes as one out of his mind, counting even terrible death as joy, and the contemplation of his mind never suffers any interruption from the thought of heavenly things. And though absent, he converses as if present, though unseen by anyone. His knowledge and natural vision pass away, and he is not sensibly aware of his own movement by which he moves among things. And if he does anything, he does not feel it at all, having his mind hovering in this contemplation, and his reflection always converses with another. Apostles and martyrs were once inebriated with this spiritual drunkenness; and some, traveling around the whole world, labored and were burdened with injuries; others, with mangled limbs, poured out their blood like water, and while suffering the most terrible things, did not flag, but endured them generously. And although wise, they were held as foolish, and others wandered in deserts and mountains, and in caves and in the holes of the earth; and in such turmoil, they were not perturbed. May God grant us to attain this foolishness.


[793] {#pg.147.793}
On Holy Communion; and on the good things that the continuous reception of this, with a pure conscience, provides for us.
A 91. Nothing contributes and helps us so much toward the purification of the soul, the illumination of the mind, the sanctification of the body, and the transformation and immortality of both toward that which is more divine—nay, more, toward the repulsion of passions and demons, or, to speak more appropriately, toward union and a supernatural conjunction and blending with God—as the continuous reception and communion, with a pure heart and   upright disposition, as far as is possible for man, of the holy, immaculate, immortal, and life-giving mysteries; we speak of that very venerable body and blood of our Lord and God and Savior, Jesus Christ. Therefore, it is most necessary that we also set forth some things concerning this, and devote time to this care, and thus bring our discourse to an end.
And this, therefore, is manifest, not only from what the saints say, but much more manifest from the very words of the Author of life and truth. For He says: «I am the bread of life» C; and, «This is the bread which comes down from heaven, that if anyone eats of it, he will not die. I am the living bread which came down from heaven; if anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever. And the bread that I shall give is My flesh for the life of the world.» And, «Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man, and drink His blood, you have no life in you; he who eats My flesh and drinks My blood has eternal life.» And further: «For My flesh is food indeed, and My blood   is drink indeed; he who eats My flesh and drinks My blood abides in Me, and I in him. As the living Father sent Me, and I live because of the Father, so he who eats Me, he also will live because of Me. This is the bread which came down from heaven; and he who eats this bread will live forever.» And Christ’s disciple Paul says these things: «Brethren, I received from the Lord that which also I delivered to you, that the Lord Jesus in the same night in which He was betrayed took bread, and when He had given thanks, He broke it and said, Take, eat; this is My body which is broken for you: do this in remembrance of Me. In the same manner also the cup, after supper, saying, This cup is the new Testament in My blood; do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of Me. For as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death till He comes. Therefore, whoever eats this bread or drinks this cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread and drink of that cup. For he who eats and drinks in an unworthy manner eats and drinks judgment to himself, not discerning the Lord’s body. Therefore, among you many are weak and infirm...


[795] {#pg.147.795}
and many are asleep. If we judged ourselves, we would not surely be judged. But when we are judged, we are chastened by the Lord, that we may not be condemned with this world.” A What it is necessary to learn regarding the miracle of the sacred mysteries; and what it is, and why it is given, and what its utility is.
92. Chrysostom writes: “It is necessary to learn what the miracle of the mysteries is, and why it is given, and what the utility of this matter is. We are one body and members, from the flesh of our Lord Jesus Christ, and from his bones. But let those who have been initiated give ear to what is said, so that we may not only become this according to charity, but may in very reality be blended into that same flesh;   this is effected by the food which He has bestowed upon us, wishing to show us the love which He has for us. Therefore He has mingled Himself with us and implanted His body in us, so that we might become one, as a body united to a head. For this belongs to those who love vehemently. Hinting at this, Job spoke of his servants, to whom he was passionately desirable, for in showing their love, they said: ‘Who would give us to be filled with his flesh?’ Therefore Christ also has done this, leading us to a greater friendship and manifesting His love for us, not only offering Himself to be seen by those who desire Him, but also to be touched and eaten; and He willed that we should be united and connected to His flesh, and that our entire desire should be fulfilled.” And further: “Those who partake of this most holy body and venerated blood stand with angels and archangels and the heavenly powers, clothed in the royal garment of Christ itself and holding heavenly weapons. But they have not yet said anything; for they have put on the King Himself. But just as it is great and   awesome and marvelous, so if you approach with purity, you have approached unto salvation; but if with an evil conscience, unto condemnation and punishment. For he who eats and drinks unworthily, eats and drinks judgment to himself. For if those who defile the royal purple are punished no less than those who have torn it, it is altogether consistent that those who receive the body with a defiled conscience should undergo the same punishment as those who pierced it with nails. See, therefore, how Paul revealed this punishment, saying: ‘He who has despised the law of Moses, without mercy, on the testimony of two or three witnesses, dies. Of how much worse punishment do you think he will be worthy, who has trampled underfoot the Son of God, and has considered the blood of the covenant common, in which he was sanctified?’   Whoever, therefore, we are who partake of this body, whoever we are who taste this blood, consider that we are tasting Him who sits on high, who is worshipped by the angels, who is near the omnipotent power. Oh! How many ways are opened unto us for salvation! He has made us His body, He has rendered us participants of His body, and none of these things draws us back from evil! O, the indolence!"


[797] {#pg.147.797}
O, the insensibility!   And again: “A certain wonderful old man told me that he had been accounted worthy to see and hear such a thing: that those who are about to depart from hence, if they have happened to be partakers of the mysteries with a pure conscience, when they are on the point of death, the angels, escorting them on account of that which was received, lead them away from hence.”
And the divine John Damascene says: “Since we are twofold and composite, it behooves us that our birth and likewise our nourishment should be twofold and composite. Our birth, therefore, is given to us through water and the Spirit, but our food is the bread of life itself, our Lord Jesus Christ, who descended from heaven. And just as in baptism, since it is the custom for men to be washed with water   and anointed with oil, He joined the grace of the Spirit to the water and oil and made them a laver of regeneration, so, since it is our custom to eat bread and to drink water and wine, He joined His own divinity to these and made them His body and blood, so that through things habitual and natural we might attain to things supernatural.”
The body is truly joined to the divinity, *the body born of the holy Virgin, not that that body which we receive descends from heaven, but that the bread itself and the wine are changed into the body and blood of God. But if you inquire into the manner of how   this comes to pass, it suffices for you to hear that it is through the Holy Spirit—just as from the holy Theotokos, through the Holy Spirit, the Lord took flesh unto Himself and in Himself—and we know nothing more. But because the Word of God is true and effectual and omnipotent, while the mode is inscrutable, it becomes, therefore, to those who receive it worthily with faith, for the remission of sins and for eternal life, and for the preservation of soul and body; but to those who partake in unbelief and unworthily, it becomes for punishment and torment, just as the death of the Lord. And the bread and the wine are not a figure of the body   and blood of Christ—God forbid!—but the body of Christ itself, deified, and the blood itself. “For my flesh,” He says, “is food indeed, and my blood is drink indeed.”
It is the body and blood of Christ, descending into the substance of our soul and body, not being consumed, not corrupting, not passing into the draught, but into our substance and preservation, a cleanser of all filth; and even if it finds gold alloyed with dross, it cleanses it through the refining fire that we may not be condemned in the future with the world. Cleansed through it, we are united to the body of Christ and to His Spirit, and we become the body of Christ. This bread is the beginning of the future bread, which is the supersubstantial bread; for “supersubstantial” signifies either that which is future, that is to say, of the future age, or that which is taken for the preservation of our substance. The flesh of the Lord is a life-giving spirit, because it was conceived from the life-giving Spirit; for that which is born of the Spirit is spirit. This


[799] {#pg.147.799}
A however, is spoken of as antitypes of things to come, not as though it were not truly the body and blood of Christ, but because now, through these, we partake of Christ’s divinity, whereas then, we shall do so mentally through vision alone. And the most divine Macarius says: "Just as wine is infused into all the limbs of the one drinking, and the wine becomes in him, and he in the wine, so too, he who drinks the blood of Christ is watered by the Spirit of Divinity, and it is infused into the perfected soul, and the soul into it; and thus, having been sanctified, it becomes worthy of the Lord." For all, he says, have been given that same Spirit to drink; and through the Eucharist of the bread, those who partake of the Holy Spirit in truth are counted worthy to become partakers, and thus the soul, being worthy, can live for ages. And just as for the body, life is not from itself, but from without, that is to say from the earth, so too did God   will for the soul to have—not from its own nature, but from His own Divinity, from His own Spirit and light—food, drink, and clothing, which is the true life of the soul. For the divine nature has also the bread of life, He who said, "I am the bread of life," and living water, and wine that gladdens, and the oil of gladness. And Saint Isidore says: "The reception of the divine mysteries is called communion, because it grants us union with Christ and makes us partakers of His kingdom." And the venerable Nilus says: "It is impossible for the faithful to be saved in any other way, and to receive the remission of sins, and to attain the kingdom of heaven, unless he receives with fear, faith, and desire the mystical and immaculate body and blood of Christ." Likewise, the great Basil writes in his letter to the patrician Caesaria:   "And to communicate and receive the holy body and blood of Christ every day is good and beneficial, the Lord Himself saying, 'He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him, and has eternal life.' For who doubts that to partake of life continuously is nothing other than to live in many ways? We, however, communicate four times every week: on the Lord's Day, on Wednesday, on Friday, and on Saturday, and on other days if the memorial of some saint occurs; on which days, I think, the saint also celebrated. For he could not do so daily, being burdened by so many cares." And Saint Apollo also said that "a monk ought, if possible, to communicate in the mysteries of Christ every day. For he who keeps himself away from these, keeps himself away from God; but he who does this continuously receives the flesh continuously. For the saving voice says: 'He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him.' It is incumbent, therefore, upon monks to make   a perpetual remembrance of the saving passion. They must, therefore, always be prepared and so dispose themselves that they may be worthy to receive the sacred mysteries, since in this way we are made worthy of the remission of sins." And Climax also says: "If another body, when touching a body, is changed in its efficacy, how shall he not be changed who touches the body of God with innocent hands?" And it is written in the Geronticon: "John of Bostra, a holy man and one having power over unclean spirits, demons


[801] {#pg.147.801}
who were dwelling in certain girls who were mad and being wickedly acted upon by them, asked, 'What things do you fear from the Christians?' They replied: 'You truly have three great things: one which you wear about your neck, and one which you wash in at the Church, and one which you eat in the communion.' And when questioned again, 'Of these three, which do you fear more?' they answered: 'If you guard well what you receive, none of us is able to harm a Christian. But there are things which our enemies fear more than the others: the Cross, Baptism, and Communion.'"   The end of all the matters explored in detail, and a specific exhortation to the one who asked.
93. See now, most beloved child, your request has been fulfilled, with God. Whether it is in accordance with your intent and purpose, we do not know precisely; but it is in accordance with our power, and what is according to one’s power is pleasing to God. See to it, therefore, that your eagerness to learn and your zeal do not stop at this, but that you may also appear eager and fervent in works. For the illustrious brother of the Lord says: "My beloved brethren, be doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves. For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he is like a man observing his natural face in a mirror; for he observed himself, went away, and immediately forgot what kind of man he was. But he who looked into the perfect law of liberty and continued in it, and is not a forgetful hearer but a doer of the work, this one will be blessed in what he does."   How one ought to hear and receive the spiritual sayings of the Fathers.
94. And before all these things, in order that you may faithfully and with the proper reverence receive and listen to the holy and spiritual sayings of the Fathers, remember what holy Macarius says: "Spiritual things are unreachable to the inexperienced; but the communion of the Holy Spirit and the heavenly treasures of the Spirit take hold of a holy and faithful soul, and they become manifest only to him who has experienced them; but to the uninitiated, it is not even possible to conceive of them at all." Listen, therefore, to the Fathers regarding these things religiously, until it befalls you, as you believe, to be deemed worthy of attaining them. For then you will know by the very experience of the eyes of the soul what good things and mysteries the souls of Christians are able to commune with even here. For if you are in this state, you will most quickly gather the fruit and benefit of the things written and heard, and from both learning and acting, you will progress so as to be able to exhort others and lead them by that same experience to things more divine and to those unknown to the many. May this come to pass for you, relying upon and guided by the most powerful hand of the Lord Jesus Christ! Amen. Since, however, satiety of speech is hostile to the ears, just as too much food is to the body, and since every measure is indeed best, we must be satisfied


[803] {#pg.147.803}
with having avoided that satiety, and embracing moderation as the best course, having lingered only a little while in the discourse, and having sketched out a sort of summary of the present treatise, thus to cast the anchor of our discourse there.
Recapitulation, and how one ought to pray, and concerning true illumination and divine power.
95. The Fathers say: He who desires to be vigilant in speech must constantly hasten to pray purely and undistractedly within his heart through the inhalation of his nostrils, attending only to the words of the prayer, and meditating and pondering the phrases—namely: "Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me"—until the time of the illumination of the mind in the heart, as the holy Diadochus says: "Whoever meditates ceaselessly in the depth of their heart upon the glorious and much-desired name of the Lord Jesus, these are able at some point to see the light of the mind." Once this has happened, by the impulse of God, from that time forward we shall walk the remainder of the course of our life according to God as if in the light, or rather, having become sons of light, we shall proceed without wandering and without stumbling, as Jesus, the Giver of Light, says: "While you have the light, believe in the light, that you may become sons of light; and: I am the light of the world; he who follows me will not walk in darkness,   but will have the light of life." And David cries out such things to the Lord: "In your light we shall see light." And the most divine Paul: "God, who said light shall shine out of darkness, he has shone in our hearts." For through Him, as through an inextinguishable and most brilliant lamp, those who are truly faithful are guided and proceed beyond the sensible realm; and for them, being pure in heart, the heavenly gate is opened, which is the gate of this life, a life similar to that of the angels and of this sublime state. And again, for these persons, as if from a solar disc, it rises, and they are enabled to investigate, to judge, to discern, to foresee, and things like these. And altogether through Him there shines before their eyes the revelation and manifestation of the hidden mysteries; they are filled in the Holy Spirit with   supernatural and divine power; and through this spiritual power their burden is lightened, or rather the heaviness of the flesh is diminished, lifted up, and they fly over it. By the grace of the power of this Holy Spirit who illuminates, although they were still clothed in flesh, certain holy Fathers, as if void of matter and body, crossed inaccessible lights and boat-traversed seas without sinking, and carried out long journeys of many days in an instant, and performed other extraordinary things in heaven, on earth, in the sun, in the sea, in the deserts, in cities, in every place and region, among beasts and among reptiles, and in a word in all creation and in all the elements; and they were glorified through all things, and while they stood in prayer, their holy and venerable bodies were raised from the earth as if they had wings; and by that divine and consuming and imma-


[805] {#pg.147.805}
immaterial fire of grace, they were incinerated of their bodily thickness and weight, and enabled to be lifted up lightly. O wonderful thing! Transformed and reshaped toward what is more divine, by the wonder-working hand of the power and grace dwelling within them. And after death, the bodies of some remain holy and incorruptible, manifestly testifying to the supernatural grace and power that dwelt in them and dwells in all sincere believers. After the common and universal resurrection, through the same power shining in the Spirit, as if they had acquired wings, they will be caught up in the clouds to meet the Lord, as the most divine Paul, teacher of secrets, says: “And so they will always be with the Lord.”   To these things also the Spirit-inspired David sings: “O Lord, in the light of thy countenance they shall walk, and in thy name they shall rejoice all the day”—that is, the eternal one—“and in thy righteousness they shall be exalted, for thou art the boast of their strength.” And, “In thy good pleasure our horn shall be exalted.” And again: “The strong ones of God were raised up highly from the earth.” And the most loud-voiced Isaiah thus declares: “They that wait upon the Lord shall put forth wings; they shall renew their strength.” And Saint Macarius says: “Every soul which through faith and the zeal of all the virtues has been rendered worthy of being perfectly clothed with Christ in power and faith thenceforth, and has been united with the celestial light of the incorruptible image, is found worthy to receive substantial knowledge of the heavenly mysteries. And on the day of the resurrection, by the same celestial image of glory, the body, being glorified together with the soul and snatched up into the heavens by the Spirit, according to that which is written, to meet the Lord in the air, having been found worthy to be conformed to the body of his glory, shall reign together with the soul for ages.”
Another recapitulation
26. The beginning and origin of these new and ineffable words is the previously mentioned state of total freedom from care, stillness, attention, and prayer; these possess as a foundation—as it were a firmament and an impregnable rampart—the fulfillment of all the divinizing commandments according to one’s power. From this freedom from care, stillness, attention, and prayer, we say, comes the movement and fervor in the heart   which burns up the passions and the demons, and purifies the heart as if in a furnace; and from this ardor follows the desire for the Lord Jesus Christ, and an unceasing love. From this, the sweet outflow of tears of the heart flows in streams, through which the soul and the body, as if by hyssop, are cleansed and nourished by repentance, charity, and thanksgiving and confession. From these things come the calm and peace of thoughts, which has no limit, as it surpasses every mind. From these things follows the snow-bright illumination; and finally, as far as it is possible for man, apathy; and the resurrection of the soul before the resurrection of the body, and the...


[807] {#pg.147.807}
image and likeness of the posterior; and through action and contemplation, through faith and hope and love, a reformation and conversion. A direction toward God and an immediate union with Him, an ecstasy, and   a cessation, a perfect rest, in the present time indeed as in a mirror and in an enigma and in a pledge; but in the future, a vision face to face, and the perfect and complete participation of God, and His eternal enjoyment.
That this is truly the unerring, and true, and tradition-bearing, and godly way of life, namely the stillness born of obedience; which is also called by the saints, and rightly so, the life hidden in Christ.
97. This is the way,   and the godly spiritual life, and the sacred operation of those who are truly Christians; it is the true, and unerring, and unadulterated, and clearly the life hidden in Christ. This the God-Man and most sweet Jesus opened up and initiated; the divine apostles traversed it; and after them followed those who were their successors, our illustrious leaders and teachers; who from the beginning, from the very first presence of Christ on earth, and down to our own day, have shone like luminaries in the world, with the brightness of their life-giving words and with   their wonder-working deeds; who have handed down to those even in our time this good seed, this sacred leaven, the holy first-fruits, the inviolable deposit, the grace, the power from on high, the precious pearl, the divine inheritance of the Father, the treasure hidden in the field, the pledge of the Holy Spirit, the royal seal, the living and leaping water, the divine fire, the venerable salt, the charisma, the seal, the light, and things similar to these; which shall also be given as an inheritance, and mystically transmitted through generations of generations, until the very   second presence of Christ on earth. For He who promised is truthful, saying, “And behold, I am with you all the days, even unto the end of the age.” Amen.
That even if there be other ways of salvation, yet this one is pre-eminent, and the queen, and leads to adoption.
98. Even if there are other ways and manner of life, and if you will, good works that serve to guide toward salvation and bring to rest the one who follows them, just as indeed there are, and lead to servitude or mercenary labor, and end there, just as it has been said that there are many mansions with the Father given by the Savior; yet this one is the queen and most excellent, and superior to all works, as the soul is superior to the body; inasmuch as it renews one into the adoption of God from earth and dust, and wonderfully makes the man who enters into it a god in the Spirit, as the great Basil says: “When the Holy Spirit has come upon the soul of man, He gave life, He gave immortality, He raised up the one lying fallen.” And that which is moved by the Holy Spirit with an eternal motion has become a holy living being, and man has received the dignity of the Holy Spirit in


[809] {#pg.147.809}
him, of prophet, apostle, angel, and of God; though he was previously mere earth and ashes.
That because of the excellence of its operation, this way of life bears many names.
99. Therefore, the divine Fathers have celebrated it with many and various glorious names. They have called it a learned way, an action worthy of praise, and ingenious contemplation; a prayer excelling all breadth; watchfulness of the mind; spiritual work; the work of the age to come; the angelic life; the heavenly way of acting; divine conversation; the region of the living; mystical intuition; the spiritual table; the divine paradise; heaven; the   heavenly palace; the kingdom of God; the light-transcending darkness; a life hidden in Christ; the supernatural vision of God; and names similar to these. Following these divine Fathers—while we live in clay and brick, with evil and impure thoughts, words, and works—we have ardently determined to fulfill your request, most beloved one; truly, just as you have asked, we have not hesitated to speak even beyond our measure, on account of our love for you and the command of the Fathers. The leader of this angelic life is the new and ineffable providence and incarnation of the Word and Son of God, the good pleasure of the unbegotten Father, and the cooperation of the Holy Spirit.
ETHICON
That with the help and grace of God, it behooves us to hasten and struggle as much as we can, so that we may be deemed worthy even now, as if by a pledge, of such supernatural and most great gifts; and that we may not, through a little sloth, lose these—alas!—which God forbid.
100. Since such and so great goods are set before us, beloved, not only in hopes and in promises to be fulfilled in the future, but in truth and in reality already, let us hasten, we implore you, while we have time; let us run, let us struggle, so that we too, through a small and temporary zeal and brief toil—and, for the most part, by the gift and grace of God—may be deemed worthy of them. “For the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the glory that shall be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII, 18), as that divine herald Paul says; let us listen to him. Nay, rather, by hastening from now on, even we shall find it   as if in the beginning and by way of a pledge. For if those who are chosen for royal kinship and for communion from a lowly station do everything—in work, word, and intent, and by reaching for even those things unreachable—and yet often despise their very lives for the sake of such glory and honor, which is fleeting and temporary, and which sometimes leads to total destruction rather than to any usefulness, how much more does it behoove us to strive and hasten, who are invited to the communion, and marriage, and union of God, the King of all kings and Creator, and the only One incorruptible and existing eternally, and [Who gives] His glory and bo-


[811] {#pg.147.811}
honor to His own, glorious and lasting; and furthermore, that we have received the power to become children of God. "For as many," He says, "as received Him, to them He gave the power to become children of God, to those who believe in His name." He gives power; He does not draw us tyrannically nor force us against our own will. For tyranny always arms the one who is oppressed against the oppressor, so that evil may be cured by evil. But in this way He honors the preeminent dignity of our free will, so that the good may be brought about entirely by the benevolence and grace of the working God, while yet the act is also one of our own will and care. And He, although He is God and Lord, did whatever was necessary for Him to do; for He created all alike, and died for all, so that He might save all equally. To us, however, was left the freedom to approach, to believe, to enter into friendship, and with fear and fervor and love to serve that merciful Lord who truly and solicitously loved us; so that for our sake He willingly consented to undergo death, and indeed a shameful death, that He might deliver us from the tyranny of the devil, that ancient enemy, and reconcile us to the Father and God, making us heirs of God and joint-heirs with Himself—a thing most paradoxical and most blessed.   Let us not, then, through small and brief despondency, and carelessness, and worldly pleasure, of whatever kind, cast ourselves away from such and so great goods, and honors, and enjoyments; but let us do everything, and let us work; and if need be, let us not spare even our life for His sake, just as He, though being God, did for our sake, so that we may thus be deemed worthy of all these gifts and crowns, both now and forever. May all of us be granted to attain these, by the benevolence and grace of Him, the all-good and merciful One, our Lord and God and Savior Jesus Christ, who humbled Himself so much for our sake, and who effectively and abundantly bestows His supernatural and deifying grace from then on even to those who are humble in such a way; for to Him is due all glory, and honor, and worship, together with His unbegotten and most pure Father, and His co-eternal, and all-holy, and good, and life-giving Spirit, now and ever, and to the ages of ages. Amen.
CHAPTERS ON PRAYER
